I N T R O D U C T I ON 
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, 
having   been authorized by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Twenty –Fourth      Report 
on the Demands for Grants (2003-04) pertaining to the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries  
2.         The Committee heard the oral evidence of the Secretary and other representatives of the Ministry
of Agro and Rural Industries on 31 st March, 03. The Committee also considered the pre- budget 
expectation and post budget reactions of   the Ministry of Agro and Ru ral Industries to have in-depth 
account of the impact of budget  proposals (2003-04) on the Agro an d Rural Industries a as whole , 
including  units in private sector.  
3. The Committee examined the relevant documents and  budget -papers furnished by the Ministry . The 
Committee is thankful to the repres entatives of Ministry of Agro and Rural Indus tries    who appeared
before the Committee.  The Committee also wishes to  thank the Ministry  for furnishing the replies to
the questionnaire and the points raised during the course of   oral evidence.   
4.         The Committee at its meeting held on   6th May 03 considered and adopted the Report. 
 
  
  
REPORT 
Agro and Rural Industries play an important role in national economy because of the vast
potential of this sector in terms of sustainable employment generation and dispersal of industries in rural
areas. With the onset of globalizat ion and liberalized econom ic scenario in the country, the Agro and
Rural Industries Sector has been envisaged and acknowledged as one  of the major avenues available for
creation of employment and to en sure balanced economic growth.  Added to the already existing
regional imbalances, opening up of the economy to ma rket   forces with mi nimum control mechanisms,
was a real and potent threat to at taining the avowed objective of balanced economic development. Since
this sector is the major non-farm sector with a vast potential to create and sustain employment across the 
country, specifically the backward and rural areas it is necessary to reinforce and strengthen the
functioning of the sector as a whole, by highlighting its presen t status and ensu ring timely policy
interventions needed. Further streamlining by way of  restructuring field agen cies and the sector’s 
competitive policy positioning has enhanced its inhe rent strength to forge ah ead and ensure balanced
growth.  
1.1       In view of the growing significance of Agro and Rural Industries, the Ministry of Agro & Rural
Industries was carved out of the erstwhile Ministry of  Small Scale Industri es and Agro & Rural
Industries   w.e.f. 1 st September 2001. The need was felt for carving out a Se parate Ministry because 
ofthe increasing criticality of the sector in the libe ralized economic set up needed  to be reinforced. As a
major sector with vast employmen t potential on a sustainable basis exploiting optimally the indigenous
wealth available especiall y by way of traditional craft and t echniques, a separate Ministr y of A gro &

Rural Industries was a necessity, which was formally recognized.  
  
1.2       The Committee understands that Agro and Rural Industries has tremendous scope and potential 
for gainful employment and boosting ba lanced economic growth and development thereby changing the
status of India’s developing econom y to a developed economy keeping in  view the fact that the large
chunk of India’s population resi de in rural areas.   The onus lies on the Ministry of ARI, carved out o f 
the erstwhile Ministry  of SSI and ARI on 1 st September 2001, to translate th is dream into a reality by
undertaking key issues concerning the Agro and Rural Industries synergistically and effectively. 
1.3       The main function of the Ministry is to  formulate policy measures for the growth of rural
industries for achieving rapid increase in gainful employment and balanced re gional growth, which are
among the main objectives underlying th e strategy of industrialization in the country. It also supervises
and coordinates the activities of different promotional agencies operating at the Central and State Level. 
The Ministry acts as a nodal agency for promotion and development of village and cottage industries as
well as tiny and micro enterprises in  both urban and rural areas.  The Charter for the Ministry describes
its objective as one to promote, ai d and foster growth of Agro a nd Rural Industries by providing them
institutional support in the areas  of marketing, export, technol ogy upgradation, training and common
facility services.  The constituents in the Ministry are:- 
(i)                  K&VI sector, 
(ii)                Coir sector,  
(iii)               Tiny and Micro Enterprises. 
1.4       Field agencies that implement policies and programmes relating to this sector are:- 
(i)                  Khadi & Village Industries Commission (KVIC) 
(ii)                Coir Board, 
(iii)               Office of DC (SSI) and 
(iv)              PMRY division.  
1.5       The Committee notes the structural   ar rangement of Ministry of ARI and at the same time
expects that all the field agencies, i.e. KVIC, Coir Board, office  of DC (SSI) and PMRY division would
perform their respective assigned task effectively a nd efficiently.   In this context, the Committee
recommends that all the wings of Ministry of ARI would discharge their functions and responsibilities in
such a manner that Agro and Rural Sector in ge neral may contribute to national economic growth and
development.  
1.6       The Ministry guides and coordinates with the implementing agencies to ensure development and
achievement as per the set mandate.T he Ministry has three-pronged role to play ,all of which aim at 
quality implementation of policies, programmes and sc hemes of the Ministry. In  the role of a policy
maker, the Ministry collects, collates and derives infe rences, which act as critic al input to further policy
formulation/amendments. In the role  of an advocate, the Ministry a dvocates and puts up ‘felt needs’ o f 
the stakeholders involved in the sector  as a whole. In the role of a fa cilitator, the Ministry facilitates,
coordinates and supports its fi eld agencies in implementing the programmes and schemes both
quantitatively and qualitatively. 
1.7       At present, the monitoring mechanism at the Ministry level includes both structured as well as
informal but regular monitori ng. Committee headed by Secretar y (ARI) periodically monitors
implementation of PMRY. A sim ilar Committee is being consti tuted for monitoring programmes
implemented by KVIC. At present, KVIC’s work is monitored based on their monthly progress report as
well as frequent interactions held  between the KVIC and Ministry at various levels.Work of Coir Board
is monitored on similar li nes as well as throu gh its board meetin gs. Measures, which would make the

Ministry’s role more effective and efficient, would be  frequent informal interactions with field agencies
and structured inputs from local public representatives. 
1.8              The Committee notes that the Ministry of ARI is entruste d with the functions/duties o f 
implementations of policies, prog rammes and schemes and in turn play the role of a policy maker,
advocate and a facilitator.  The Committee also finds that the Ministry monitors the activities undertaken
by its field’s agencies through formal  structure as well as informal meetings.  However, the Committee
is of the view that the Ministry  of ARI would act promptly as a policy maker, advocate and facilitato r
and promote Agro and Rural I ndustries by effective implementat ion of policies programmes and
schemes undertaken by its various field agencies without time a nd cost over run.  The existing
monitoring mechanism must ensure th at targets are achieved within th e stipulated time frame.  The
Committee further recommends that  the Ministry of ARI should have  review meetings  of its field
agencies to take stock of the progress made in the implementation of various schemes and programmes.

2.4       The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure over the non- acceptance of the request
made by KVIC for enhancement of fund for REGP by of Rs. 50 crore where as only a token amount o f
Rs. 2.67 crore has been provided by the Ministry of Finance.  The Committee is of the considered view
that REGP is a significant progr amme therefore, real istic calculation of th e fund required for REGP
must be undertaken and accordingly the fund should be earmarked so that the targets be achieved in time
and the programme should not suffer any longer for want of  insufficient funds.  
  
2.5       The Committee is of the opinion that  the Ministry of ARI s hould undertake an objective
assessment of the financial requi rement K&VI Sector, Coir Sector , Tiny and micro Enterprises, in
tandem with KVIC, Coir Board, PMRY  division and accordin gly take up the case with the Ministry o f
Finance and Planning Commission fo r providing the required fund as per the needs of the Industries, so
that no scheme should suffer due to lack of fund.  The Committee desires that efforts should be taken for
avoiding the gap between the projected demand and the actual fund earmarked for specific purpose in
one particular financial year.

7.0       Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana. 
7.1       The Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana was announced by the Prime Minister on 15th August 1993 
for creation of sustainable self -employment opportunities for th e educated unemployed youth. The 
objective of the Prime Minister’s Ro zgar Yojana (PMRY) is to miti gate the problem of unemployment 
amongst the educated  unemployed youth through se tting up of self-employe d tiny units. The scheme 
came into operation on 2 nd October, 1993. The scheme was designe d to provide employment to more 
than a million persons by setting up of 7 lakh mi cro-enterprises by the educated unemployed youth 
during the 8th five year Plan. These self-employment ventures  were to be set up through industry,
services & business routes. It was envisaged that on an av erage each enterprise .set up would generate
employment for 2 persons.  As reported by the RB I, 7.748 lakh persons have been sanctioned loans
under PMRY, since its inception during the 8th five year Plan. The scheme continued in the 9"' five yea r 
Plan and the scheme is continuing during 10th Five Year Plan.

it a realistic criteria.  The Co mmittee feels that the family in come of Rs. 40,000 per annum hardly
fulfills the bare needs of a family  consisting of 2-3 persons.  Moreove r, the devaluation /depreciation o f
rupee further over the years has also necessitated the need for raising the limit of family income.  One of
the reasons of low recovery of loans under PMRY may be construed from the fact that loan amount goes
to fulfilling the basic needs of beneficiaries or his family members.  Therefore, it seems reasonable that
suitable amendment in the family income criteria  under PMRY may be brought fourth by raising the
existing limit of Rs. 40,000 to Rs. 1.5 lakh. 
8.0       STRENGTHS, WEAKNESSES,  OPPORTUNITIES AN D THREADS (SWOT)
ANALYSIS OF PMRY. 
Strengths: 
                  1.            The spread of the Scheme is uni form in both urban as well as  rural areas of the country. As
per the findings of the second round of the evaluation on the PMRY disbursement of the
beneficiaries in rural and urban areas is 49.9% and 50.1% respectively. 
                  2.            Against the target of 18 lakh, loans have been  sanctioned to 20.40 lakh and disbursed to 
16.00 lakh educated unempl oyed youth between 1993-94 – 2001-02.  Employment 
opportunities have been  estimated to be created for about 24 lakh people during the same
period. 
                  3.            According to 2nd round of Evaluation study, assets that have been created is 89.7% of cases 
disbursed loan. 
Weaknesses: 
Declining recovery rate: 
                  1.            The recovery of loan overdue s under the PMRY Scheme has been declining.  It was 37.2
per cent for the half year ending March 2000 and has come down to 34.8 per cent for the half
year ending March 2002.   
                  2.            The overall amount of loan di sbursed under the Scheme has been stagnating around Rs.57,
000/- to Rs.58, 000/- per beneficiar y despite enhancement in th e maximum project cost from
Rs.1 lakh to Rs.2 lakh. 
                  3.            There is gap between number of cases sanctioned and disbursed by banks.

                  4.            During VIII plan, the disbursement was 6.52 lakh against sanction of 7.75 lakh.  Similarly,

Opportunities: 
                  1.            In a situation where employme nt opportunities in organized sectors and Govt. sectors have
been virtually stagnating or declining, PMRY Scheme has emerged a major scheme o f
employment generation in the country. 
                  2.            The successful self employed units set up under the PMRY can graduate into higher scale

The bank/financial institutions can help successful  PMRY units to graduate successfully into
higher scale of operation.   
8.1       The Committee recommends that the Mini stry of ARI should make in -depth SWOT analysis o f 
PMRY and thereafter undertakes massive action for combating its thr eats, and overcoming its
weaknesses.  More and more avenues should be explored for tracing oppor tunities for employment
generation.  The Committee is of the view that the best cr iteria to assess the opera tional efficiency of a
programme are to observe its spread and its capaci ty to serve the down- tr odden people and its welfare 
instinct and its inherent strength to  uplift the standard of living of pe ople in general.  Adequate measure
may be undertaken fo r popularization of PMRY a nd for changing the mind set of financial institutions
for making it pro customer and with further enhanced budgetary allocation, PMRY could make a dent in
the india’s year of problems of  unemployment and poverty.  PMRY division may also undertake cost 
benefit analysis of the pr ogramme and effort should be made for ensuring that actions are being taken
for achieving the basic objectives of the programme in a time bound frame.

 9.15    Evaluation and objective Assessment of PMRY 
Replying to the committee’s query  as to  the states where PMRY was a full all success; the 
states where PMRY did marginally good and the st ates where PMRY failed miserably, along with
reasons for such performance, the Ministry of Agro and Rural I ndustries stated the States where PMRY
was a full all success are Punjab and Himachal Pradesh (disburseme nt vis-à-vis targets is 80% an d 
above).  The States where PMRY is working satisfactorily are Haryana, Rajasthan, M.P. U.P.,
Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry, Lakshadweep etc. (i.e. disbursement vis-à-
vis targets is 60% & above).  The States where PMRY has failed ar e: Delhi, J&K, West Bengal and
North Eastern States e.g. Manipur , Meghalaya, Nagaland, Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh etc. (i.e.
disbursement vis-à-vis targets ar e 30 pr cent or less). The States where disbursement under the Scheme
is 80% and above those States wh ere recovery of loan overdues is  around 55%. (Punjab – 57.3 per cent 
for the half year ended March 2001) . The States where the Scheme has been implemented satisfactorily
are the States where th e recovery of loan overdues is between 40 per cent to 45 per cent.  (i.e. Haryana
43.1 per cent; U.P. 45.6 percent; Rajasthan 42.1 per cent; Gujarat 61.2 per cent; Karnataka 48.1 per cent
for the half year ended March 2001).  The States where disbursements are less than 30% of the target are
the States where recovery of loan overdues is very low.  The recovery of lo an overdues for the period
ending March, 2001 was 1.0 per cent in Manipur 1.7 per cent in Nagaland; 13.0 per cent in Assam; 16.7
per cent in West Ben gal for the half year ended March, 2001.  In  J&K, the recovery of loan overdues is

11.28   Marketing Strategy of KVIC 
The marketing strategy of KVIC is to focus on its eco friendly and natural product range. Khadi
& Village Industries sector produces  goods and services both. In villa ge industries service based units
basically cover local area needs and marketing is not much of a problem. With rega rd to non-consumer 
goods normally units established have good market as most of such products are intermediary products
used by other industries. Main di fficulty is in consumer goods a nd khadi. For both these products areas
of intervention involves a detail ed marketing strategy for publicit y, branding and brand promotion,
design input, better packaging etc.  Accessing private marketing cha nnel, modernization of existing
channels, organizing large scale e xhibitions are important aspects. Marketing federations have been
formed with various village industries federations to  act as facilitator outsi de the governmental set up.
Design / packaging development scheme and renovation of marketing outlets scheme has been launched.
11.29   For the open consumer market, KVIC has de veloped “Sarvodaya Brand”  consisting of FMCG 
products like Toilet Soap, Pickles, Honey, etc., “K hadi” for exclusive up-m arket and export products 
like Essential Oils, Herbal Products, Designer Garments etc.  and “Desi Aahaar” for  Organic foods like 
Cereals, Spices Powder, Pulses, Ja ggery, etc. and the same have been  launched at Mumbai and Delhi in
select Outlets.  Based on the experience it is felt that a professional Marketing Agency / Federation is
required, so that KVIC does not get involved in Departmental Trading Ac tivities, since institutions and
marketing professionals can play a better and effect ive role in marketing these products.  A Marketing
Confederation has recently been c onstituted out of existing Khadi & V. I. Federations and has also been
accorded provisional recognition by KVIC.  The Conf ederation is expected to take up aggressive
marketing for KVI products with active support of KVIC.

11.43   IMPACT OF VAT ON VILLAGE INDUSTRY PRODUCTS 
Reacting to the Committee’s que ry regarding impact of VAT on the village industry products 
Chief Executive Officer, Khadi and Village Commission commented as under:- 
“VAT has replaced the Sales Tax with effect from 01.04.2003; three St ates have already agreed to
implement it.  Most of the States had exempted us from paying Sales Tax.  Unfortunately, in the last two
to three years, Sales Tax has been imposed in cer tain States.  For exampl e, in respect of Khadi
industries, Tamil Nadu has declared rebate only fo r products produced in their States, not for those
which are coming from outside.  Si milarly, some other States have extended a rebate for only those
village industries, which are situated in their States.  In my opinion, zero- based budgeting must be done 
for the village industries sector.  We  have written to all the State Go vernments, to the chief Ministers
and the concerned ministers.  Th e Secretary has also written to the empowered committee on VAT, to
consider this viewpoint.  Also, th e minister has written a letter requesting for ‘across the board’ set-up 
for the khadi and village industries sector.  The ec onomic scale of the vill age and khadi industries is
low.  If this minor advantage of not having to pay Sales Tax is extended, it wi ll help these industries a
lot.” 
11.44   The Committee observes that 16 more states have agreed to  the VAT structure of taxation
system. However, the Committee re commends that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries should
examine the case of feasibi lity of applying the  Zero- based budgeting for the vill age industry sector and
accordingly advocate the exemptions of tax across  the board for institution or entrepreneur, which is
registered with the Khadi and Village Industries Board or Khadi and Village Industries Commission.

12.33   COOPERATIVISATION SCHEME 
12.33.1            The objectives of the co-operati visation scheme were forma tion of viable coir co-
operatives and revitalisation of the potentially viable dormant societies and bringing the coir workers in
to the co-operative fold so that the quality a nd quantity of production impr oves, workers get bette r
wages and they are freed from e xploitation of middlemen and the i ndustry is put on a sound footing.  It
was aimed to bring 80% of the work-force in the industry under co-operative  fold through of the 
scheme. Coir Board is the m onitoring agency of the Scheme.             The objectives of the scheme are
yet to be achieved due to a mult iplicity of reasons. The Institut e of Rural Management which had
conducted an evaluative study on th e scheme, opined that the “Schem e of Co-operativisation in Coi r 
Industry as it is envisaged and implemented need s to undergo drastic revision to meet the emerging
challenges. The Integrated Coir Development Project is one of the components of the Co-operativisation 
Scheme.  It envisages setting up of new primary co-operatives, modernisation and expansion of existing 
co-operatives, improved handlooms, curling units and automatic spinni ng units etc.   The Project is 
being implemented with the assistance of National Co-operative Development Corporation (NCDC) and 
the coir producing States concerned. Assistance under this component is still being released.   
12.33.2            The Committee is of view that  the objectives of the co- operativisation scheme i.e. 
formation of viable coir co-operatives and revitalizat ion of the potentially viab le dormant societies and 
bringing the coir workers in to the co-operati ve fold  for improving th e quality and quantity o f 
production and putting industry on a sound footing is a unique mission in Coir Industry.    Therefore, the
suggestion of the Institute of Rural Management  that the Scheme of Co-operativisation in Coir Industry 
as it is envisaged and implemen ted needs to undergo drastic revisi on to meet the emerging challenges,
needs attention of the government . The National Co-operative Deve lopment Corporation (NCDC) may 
be entrusted with greater role for implementation of co-operativisation scheme. 
12.34   Model Coir Village Scheme  
12.34.1            Coir Board has been implement ing the Model Coir Village Scheme from the year 1983
which provides assistance to coir workers to improve their working and living conditions.  The
assistance is provided to coir wo rkers in all coir producing States/U Ts of the country.  During the last
three years, no villages were a dopted under the Scheme as the Mini stry did not accord sanction fo r
continuation of the scheme afte r 1999-2000.  In 1999, the Mi nistry entrusted the Institute of Rural
Management, Anand, Gujarat to conduct an evalua tive study on the implemen tation of the scheme. 
After conducting the study, the IRMA recommended that  the programme merits continuance because it
is the only one of its kind.  But it needs to be rest ructured.  In line with the recommendations of the
IRMA, the Board drafted and submitted a scheme na med Production Oriented Welfare Scheme for Coi r
Workers to the Ministry for approval. 
12.34.2            The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of ARI should approve the Production
Oriented Welfare Schemes for Coir Workers as the follow up programme of Model Coir Village Yojana
which was a unique Yojana.  After all the fruits of development must reach to the lowest rung of society
and of course the workers as well who are the actual warriors of industrialization process.  So long, India
remains a Welfare State,  the provisions for Welfa re measures must continue for carrying out the
constitutional obligations.   The Co mmittee agrees with the views of  Institute of Rural Management,
Anand, Gujarat for continuance of Model Coir Village Yojana.

12.37   Merger of Coconut Developm ent Board and Coir Board for bette r co-ordination and Integrated 
planning. 
12.37.1            Responding to the proposal of the merger of Coconut Development Board and Coi r
Board for better co-ordination a nd integrated planning, the Minist ry of ARI has communicated the
committee that the Coconut Development Board is concentrated on production of coconut while the
Coir Board is concentrated on coir fibre and allied products.  The raw- material for coir  industry is the 
coconut husk, a byproduct of coconut industry.  The focu s of the above Boards ar e different.  The coi r
industry by and large provides employment to 5,86,000 peopl e and it is an export oriented industry and
earn foreign exchange to the tune  of Rs.320 crores annually. The base of raw-material availability is 
expanded.  Technical know-how for coir industry is  lacking in the non-traditional coconut growing 
areas.  It is necessary to pr ovide the requisite technical guida nce through a professional body like Coi r
Board.

employment generation in rural areas, development of new pr oducts, skill development in non-

achieved. There are different types of natural fibres like bana na fibre, pineapple fibr e, sisal, bimal, etc.

15.1     The Finance Minister  in his budget speech of the year 1999-2000 announced a scheme called the

industrial clusters in the country  every year so that it can boost up the rural economy by creating more
employment  avenues for the rural youth in the non -farm sector, and slow dow n the migration of the 
rural artisans to towns/cities. Th e 0ffice of the Developm ent Commissioner(Small Scale Industries) was
made the coordinating agency and the KVIC was envisage d to play an important role in setting up these
clusters as well as making good use of its extensive marketing outlets.  No fund was provided separately
for the programme and it was fe lt that various Ministries/ De partments are having their own
programmes in this area which could be coordi nated and their synergie s exploited for greate r
impact.Consequent upon the bifurcatio n of business between the Ministry  of SSI and Ministry of ARI,
the scheme is being coordinated by the Ministry  of ARI recently, sinc e Sep 2002. The programme is
being implemented by NABARD and SIDBI in 31 and 14 clusters respectively. So far KVIC has already
launched the programme in 22 clusters  The state wi se position of implementation  of the programme is
placed at annexure.

population, whose fate has been shuttered with ifs and buts under the scourge of poverty and
unemployment due to negative imp act of colonialism and neo-coloni alism , is a password to the worl d 
of economic freedom. Only thing re quired  is the translation of positi ve intention of a programme into
the  reality of the day. 
  
15.4     The Committee desires that NPRI’s scope should not be limited to just as gap filling arrangement
and it’s thrust should be widened as  a full fledged programme.  The Committee feels that government’s 
intention is gradually moving in this direction, that’s why, the Planning Commission has also constituted
Task Force on rural industrialization.  Need is to have a holistic and co-ordinated approach.  
  
15.5     The Committee, however, desires to point out the lacuna  in NPRI by highlighting  the fact that
no fund has been specifically made for th e programme on the a ssumption that various
Ministries/Departments havi ng their own programmes would co-ordinate and synergies fo
r 
implementing the Programme.  The Committee notes that all the programme s/schemes, presently
scattered into various ministries. All these progr ammes are to be integrated and co-ordinated fo r 
injecting synergy into the program me for its sure success and timel y implementation. The Ministry o f
Argo and Rural Industries should be bracketed as the nodal Ministry as  the vanguard of NPRI.  The
most important aspects for successful  implementation of a programme is  the credit flow .  NPRI is a
programme without specific and separate fund.  This is the setb ack at the very inception stage. 
Therefore, the Committee recomme nds that a Common corpus Fund  should be made, and the money
which presently goes to various sc hemes under different De partments/Ministries, should be put in this
Corpus Fund  intended for Comprehensive and co-o rdinated efforts for ru ral industrialization and 
development.   
15.6     The Committee is extremely pained to note  that the provision of Rs. 90 lakhs under the Scheme
was reduced to Rs. 63 lakhs at RE stage for 2002- 03 as the proposals were  not received from the 
States/UTs and the quarterly e xpenditure was not made.  Adequa te Awareness Programme has to be
organized by the implementing agencies of the pr ogramme i.e. KVIC, SIDIBI and NABARD.  The
Service of Regional Rural Banks may also be presse d into in the implementation of NPRI.le in the
scheme.  
 15.7    SWOT analysis (strength Weakness, Opportunities and Threats) of NPRI 
15.7.1  The Committee was apprised of the SWOT analysis of NPRI which is mentioned under:- 
Strength: Providing Common Facilit ies in a Cluster, Financial Assistance for infrastructure,
Training Facilities & Providing Marketing Facilities, to create jobs under Non-farm sector. 
Weakness:  Non availability of good NGOs and implementing agen cies at the field level fo r
implementation at various stages/centers.. 
Opportunities:  Cluster Developm ent Programme, Thrust Areas for rural enterprises, Marketing
network & Brand Creation, Science & Technol ogy inputs for higher qua lity & productivity &
HRD input for rural entrepreneurship & skill upgradation. 
Threats: Threat from organized sector and globalisation of world market.  
15.7.2  The scheme is in the initial stage of implementation. The problems arising out of implementation
of the programme shall be taken care of from time to time.

15.8     Rural entrepreneurs and skill up-gradation  
15.8.1  The rural entrepreneurs in  the clusters are being trai ned to the desired technological
advancements and skill upgradation for effective development of th e clusters. Scope of the scheme
covers extending financial assistan ce  for the purpose of diagnostic st udy of the cluster, demonstration
and development of modern tools and kits and vari ous other technical inputs, training and strengthening
of NGO/cluster agent, establishm ent of Common Facility Centres et c. Also the major implementing
agencies are providing training to the entrepreneurs and creating awar eness by way of  exhibitions/fai r
wherever required.  
  
15.8.2  The Committee is of the opinion that technol ogical advancement and skill up-gradation fo r 
effective development of the cluster is a must. 
             
15.9     Role of KVIC under NPRI 
15.9.1  The KVIC is envisaged to play an important role  in setting up these clus ters as well as making
good use of its extensive marketing out lets. KVIC had decided to take up 50 clusters every year. So fa r
KVIC has already launched the programme in 22 clusters. KVIC has introduced a common brand name,
viz. ‘ Sarvodaya’ for six products for intensifying ma rketing efforts in their schemes. Initially, the
Sarvodaya brand name is covering th e selected village industries products namely, toilet soap, agarbatti,
and honey, pickles spices. These products are being sold through sales outlets of KVIC. 
15.9.2  The Committee, while appreciating the role of KVIC in general in setting up of cluster an d
providing marketing network and br and endowment, desires that KVIC should intensify its Mission fo r
rural industrialization. 
15.10   Participation of private entrepreneurs in NPRI and popularization of NPRI 
15.10.1  NPRI is being implemented through States/UTs with the help of   State Level Implementation 
Committee and District Level Implementation Committee. These committees are having members of 
KVIC, SIDBI, and NABARD, lead bank representatives. At central level, the concerned ministries have 
been included in the constitution of Inter-ministerial Task Force. The programme is implemented 
through an implementing agency/nodal agency, which may be a local NGO with good past track record 
ensuring participation of private enterprise. The scheme is being publicised by involving participation of 
the State agencies and local NGOs. All the states have been notified for taking up the cluster 
development under the scheme. They are required to constitute and notify DLIC and SLIC and submit 
the proposals.  
  
15.10.2            The Committee hopes that part icipation of private entr epreneur and NGO’s would 
promote the cluster under NPRI.  Th e Committee further desires that  the State level implementation
Committee and district level Implementation Committee should play pro -active Role in implementation 
of NPRI.

19.0     Tiny and Micro Enterprises 
19.1     Tiny Enterprises are such units which ha ve investment in plan t and machinery upto Rs.25.00
Lakhs.   As such all such industria l activities which are el igible for registration as  SSI are also eligible
for registration in the tiny sector as  long as its investment in plant and machinery is upto the prescribed
limit of Rs.25.00 lakhs   The majori ty activities in Khadi & Coir I ndustry which are predominantly in
rural areas and have investment below Rs. 25 lakhs are covered under Tiny/Micro enterprises in Agro &

            After examining the eligibility criteria for PMRY the Committee ha s arrived at a conclusion that 
while the basis of age, educational qualification, residence and defaulter clause of eligibility criteria are
logical and rational, however, eligibility clause as regards the family income needs modification to make
it a realistic criteria.  The Com mittee feels that the family income  of Rs. 40,000  per annum hardly
fulfills the bare needs of a family  consisting of 2-3 persons.  Moreove r, the devaluation /depreciation o f
rupee further over the years has also necessitated the need for raising the limit of family income.  One of
the reasons of low recovery of loans under PMRY may be construed from the fact that loan amount goes

suitable amendment in the family income criteria  under PMRY may be brought fourth by raising the
existing limit of Rs. 40,000 to Rs. 1.5 lakh.

REPORT
 
Steel Authority of India (SAIL), the leading steel making company in India and the World’s thirteenth largest steel
producer in terms of crude steel production, is a Company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1956 and is an
enterprise of the Government of India. SAIL was incorporated in January, 1973 as a holding company for steel and associated
input industries.  From 1973  to 1978, several steel and alloy  manufacturing companies  and iron ore mines were merged into
and  combined with SAIL’s  operation, while the Government of India (GOI) transferred the ownership  of certain consulting,
construction, mining and fire bricks operation from SAIL to other entities. 
 
  The authorized capital of SAIL is Rs. 5000 crore and the paid-up capital of the Company as on 31
st December 2002
was Rs. 4,130.40 crore of which 85.82% was held by the Government of India and the balance 14.18% by the financial
institutions/GDR-holders banks/employees/individuals etc.  The Company recorded a sales turnover of Rs. 15502 crore in
2001-02, however, due to fall in international prices of steel products,  coupled with continued sluggishness in the economy,
the price realization in the domestic market during 2001-02 declined, resulting into the post-tax net loss to the tune of Rs.
1706.89 crore during the year 2001-02.  As a result of loss, the Company has not declared a dividend for the year ended 31
st
march, 2002.  The gross margin (profit before depreciation and interest) and net loss for the nine-months ended 31 st
December, 2002 was Rs. 1334.40 crore and Rs. 545.96 crore respectively.  The company recorded a sales turnover of Rs.
13097.43 crore during this period. 
 
            Global Steel Industry for the measure part of 2001 remained a victim of slow down in demand, sliding price levels,
low realizations, losses and/or falling profits.  However, from the beginning of 2002, the industry entered a recovery phase,
with the gradual firming up of international prices and demand.  During the  financial year 2002-03, the market is signaling an
upward trend.   The year 2003 may well see a price rise in the domestic and the  international steel market.  There have been
price increases in steel products, which have been absorbed by the market.  There has been improvement in production also as
compared to last year and efforts are being made towards achieving maximum capacity utilization matching with the
increased market demand.  The company is vigorously giving greater thrust on the cost control measures during the current
year as well.  With the improvement in market demand, increase in net sales realization and cost control efforts, the company
expects much better results during the financial year 2002-03.
The turnaround in the market trends is reflected most prominently in the performance of the public sector steel giant,
Steel Authority of India Ltd. The unaudited financial results of SAIL for April-December (Q3) 2002 reveals a sharp
improvement in the performance with losses being slashed to Rs. 79 crore in Q3 ’02 - an improvement of Rs. 507 crore over
the corresponding period of the previous year. SAIL’s loss for April-December ’02 was brought to a level of Rs. 558 crore,
showing a recovery of 57 per cent over the results of the same period in 2001. This helped the company to post a cash profit
of Rs 215 crore in Q3 ’02 as against a loss of Rs 297 crore in Q3 ’01 and a cash profit of Rs. 305 crore in the first nine months
of the current financial year.  SAIL had suffered a cash loss of Rs. 434 crore during the corresponding period in the last fiscal.

SAIL markets and sells most of its products through in house Central Marketing Organisation (CMO) which has a
wide network  of 38 Branch Offices and 47 outlets located in major cities and towns throughout India.  International Trade
Division of SAIL looks after export of steel products to countries worldwide.  Raw materials Division manages operations of
key captive mines and quarries  of SAIL.  The captive mines of iron ore and flux meet most of the iron ore requirement and
half of the flux  requirement   of SAIL.
 
SAIL has undertaken major modernization programmes at Durgapur, Rourkela and Bokaro Steel Plants. Under the
modernization programmes, energy efficient Basic, Oxygen Furnace (BOF) technology for steel-making has been adopted in
place of obsolete Open Hearth Furnaces at Durgapur and Rourkela.  Instead of Ingot Casting, Continuous Casting facilities
have been provided in all the three Plants. The modernization projects are being funded from the internal resource of SAIL
without any budgetary support from the Government.  The total investment in modernization of the three plants is likely to be
about Rs. 12,650 crore.
 
 The main objectives of modernization are:
 
(i)

(ii)                Improvement in productivity and yields
(iii)               Reduction in energy consumption
(iv)              Improvement in quality of products
(v)                Reduction in cost of production
(vi)              Reduced environmental pollution
 
 
                  Modernisation of Durgapur Steel Plant
                        The Modernisation of Durgapur Steel Plant was approved in Feb'89 by the Government at an estimated cost of
Rs.2668 crore with foreign exchange (FE) component of Rs.685 crore (Base date: 3
rd Qtr. 88). The revised cost
estimate of DSP Modernisation works out to Rs.5074.71 crore (FE: Rs.1375.42 crore) on base date of 2 nd Qtr.
1999.

The DSP management stated that   modernisation of Durgapur Steel Plant was undertaken due to deterioration
in the quality of raw material, ageing of the plant, obsolete technology, inadequate air pollution control measures and
technological imbalance.  The basic objectives underlying the modernization scheme of DSP were Enabling  the Plant to
attain properly matched steady integrated operation; Improvement in quality and consistency of raw material; Upgradation of
technology; Reduction in cost of production; Pollution Control;  and Improvement in quality of steel produced

were controlled from Moscow and the manufacturing units and transporting authorities had to adhere to the delivery schedules
and commitments.  Subsequent to the break-up of USSR into different Nations, these manufacturing units were being
controlled by different authorities and a number of new regulations were introduced.  This resulted in delay in  manufacturing
activities.  Tyazhpromexport (TPE)’s job has suffered seriously, resulting in delays in supply of imported equipment,
structures and refractories from Russia for four global packages viz, Blast Furnace, Sinter Plant, Basic Oxygen Furnaces and
Raw Material Handling Complex.

Rourkela Steel Plant was initially set up with a capacity of 1 million tonne per annum (Mtpa) of ingot steel in 1960-61
with German technical assistance. The capacity of the Plant was expanded to 1.8 Mtpa in 1969.       The main units of RSP
upto 1.8 Mtpa stage were Coke Ovens, Blast Furnaces, Steel Melting Shop, Rolling Mills consisting of Hot Rolling Mills &
Cold Rolling Mills, Electric Sheet Mill and ERW Pipe Plant. The Special Plate Mill and SW Pip~ Plant were installed later in
1976. Further, a Silicon Steel Mill, consisting of Cold Rolled Non Oriented (CRNO) and Cold Rolled Grain Oriented
(CRGO), was added in Oct'84 and Apr'89 respectively. The main saleable products of RSP are Plates, HR Coils & Sheets, CR
Coils & Sheets, Galvanised Sheets, Tin !Plates, ERW Pipes, SW Pipes and Silicon Steel Sheets.  While the 1 Mtpa stage Plant
operated, more or less, satisfactorily by reaching its rated capacity in 1964-65, the expanded capacity could never be
achieved. The best production level of 1.5 Mtpa of ingot steel was achieved in 1976-77 after which the production capacity
deteriorated. The unsatisfactory performance level was attributable to various factors like deteriorating and inconsistent
quality of raw materials and technological obsolescence. Various studies were carried out to determine the manner in  which
the optimum performance level of the Plant could be achieved. Based on these studies, a scheme for "Renovation &
Technological Upgradation"
(Modernization) of the Plant was considered.
 
The Modernisation of Rourkela Steel Plant was approved by the Government in Oct'89 at a cost of Rs.2461 crores
with FE Component of Rs.396 crores (Base date: 4th Qtr. 88). Government further 'approved in May'92 the revised cost
estimate (RCE-I) of Rs.3954 crores with FE Component of Rs.714 crores (Base date: 1 st Qtr. 92). The revised cost estimate
(RCE-II) of RSP. Modernization works out to Rs.5105.29 crore (FE: Rs.706 crore) on base date of 2nd Qtr'99.

  Modernisation Of Bokaro  Steel Plant
 
            Bokaro Steel Plant, conceived in 1959, is the fourth steel plant among the integrated steel plants in the public sector.
The Plant was conceived in 1959 as a 4 MT plant right from the conceptual stage, 1.7 MT being an intermediate stage for the
project. The construction work for the project was started in late Sixties and the Plant went into commercial production in
1972 with the commissioning of its first Blast Furnace. Steel making adopting the BOF route began a year later. The
downstream facilities -Slabbing Mill, Hot Strip Mill and Cold Rolling Mill were put into operation in stages. The. 1.7 MT
stage was completed in 1978 with the commissioning of third Blast Furnace. The work of 4 MT Expansion was. taken ~p
simultaneously and was progressively completed by Nov'90.     The entire steel making process of Bokaro Steel Plant was
based on the Ingot Casting route which was a technology prevalent in late Sixties. Considering the  various advantages of
Continuous Casting as regards to yield improvement,  conservation of energy and improved quality, Govt. of India sanctioned
Stage I  Modernisation of Bokaro Steel Plant in Jul'93 with a commissioning schedule of Jul'97. All major contracts were
awarded in 12 months. Trials for the Steel Refining Unit were started in Sep'97 and the first Continuous Casting Machine
started its trial runs in Nov'97. Subsequently, all units of Stage I Modernisation have been completed by Jan'00. With the
upgradation of the Hot Strip Mill, the quality of the finished products is of international standard and is being well accepted in
both global and domestic market. As a flat product plant, Bokaro's products include a wide range of Hot Rolled and Cold
Rolled Coils, Plates and Sheets, Galvanised Sheets and Black Plates, serving the needs of railways, tube makers and
automobile industry , L.PG cylinder manufacturers, defence and Petro-based  Industry etc. Quality conscious Bokaro is also
concerned with customers' satisfaction.
 
Approval & Implementation
 
The Modernisation (Phase-l) of Bokaro Steel Plant   was approved by the Government in Jul'93 at a cost of Rs.1625.79
crores (Base date: 1st Qtr.'93) with FE Component of Rs.283.50 crores. The revised cost (RCE-I) of Rs.1792.90 crores (Base
date: 1st Qtr.'94) with FE Component of Rs.301 crores was approved by the Government in Aug'94. The revised cost estimate
(RCE-II) of BSL Modernisation works out to Rs.2468.18 crore (FE: Rs.420.77 crore) on base date: 3rd Qtr.'98.

                  Financial & Business Restructuring in SAIL
 
A number of steps were initiated to combat the declining profitability. The Govt. of India also approved a financial and
business restructuring package  to improve the cost competitiveness of steel industry. While, the financial  restructuring
measures are aimed at mitigating the financial risk by improving the Company’s debt servicing capability, the business
restructuring measures will provide a long term competitiveness in its core business of carbon steel.
 
The financial restructuring of SAIL comprises of:
 
(i)
                  Waiver of loans advanced to it from Steel Development Fund (SDF) to a value of Rs.5073 crores and Rs.381
crores from the Govt. of India.
(ii)                Provision of Govt. Guarantee with 50% interest subsidy for loan and interest thereon of Rs.1500 crores to be
raised by SAIL from the market to finance reduction in manpower through Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS).
(iii)               Government guarantee for loan and interest thereon of Rs.1500 crores to be raised by SAIL from the market
primarily for meeting repayment obligation on past loans during 1999-2000.
 
Business Restructuring Envisages:
 
Divestment of  non-core assets while protecting jobs of existing employees.
(A) Captive Power Plants at BSL, DSP, RSP and BSP.
(i)
                  2x60 MW Captive Power Plant-II at RSP and the Central Power Training Institute at Rourkela. 
(ii)                2x60 MW Captive Power Plant-II at DSP.
(iii)               122 MW (2x55 MW + 12 MW back pressure turbine) Captive Power Plant-I, 3x60 MW Captive Power Plant-II
and steam generating capacity of 660 MT/hour at BSL.
(iv)              74 MW captive power plant  (CPP II) at BSP Bhilai.

TASKS COMPLETED
1.Divestment Of Power Plants:
The captive power plants at Rourkela, Durgapur, Bokaro and Bhilai have already been divested, with NTPC as the partner for
the power plants at RSP, DSP&BSP,  and DVC at BSL.
The sale value of these Power Plants was Rs. 1061 Crores and the capital gain achieved was Rs.777 Crores.
2. Redesigning of incentive systems
A new incentive scheme with higher weightage to Cost, Quality and Profitability has been implemented w.e.f June 1, 2001.

Business Performance Review, strategic planning and budgeting process, promotion policy has been redesigned  and
implemented.

Re-organisation of Product management Group into Flats, Longs, Rural Marketing, Special Steel and Distribution Channel
Groups completed.

executives were trained in Product Profile Application, Negotiation Skills and Business Finance to enhance sales force
effectiveness.
Around 90 executives have been inducted in CMO sales force, from both Plants/Units.

NKA and BKA together account for sales volume for Rs.8000 crores per year. Cross  functional teams, Key Account
Managers and PIC/PAC have been identified for each key account.

R&D Inputs in SAIL Plants
 
The focus of R&D activities has been to improve steel technologies in SAIL with the aim to reduce cost and improve
product quality and address the market requirements of new value added products.
 
The R&D Centre of SAIL (RDCIS) has contributed significantly in the development of a number of Process
Technologies.  Some of these are:
 
(i)
                  Continuous casting of CRNO steel at RSP.  This has helped RSP to close down ingot casting shop and high
energy consuming slabbing mill.  As a result, RSP became the first plant in SAIL to route 100% of production through
continuous casting.
 
(ii)
                Introduction of innovative technologies, use of higher percentage of imported coal and optimization of process
parameters have significantly improved blast furnace productivity in SAIL plants.

Help required from the Government
(A)       Coal
i)
                    Steep price increase by CIL over the years has been putting lot of pressure on our competitiveness in the market.
Long-term pricing mechanism is being discussed between SAIL and coal companies, however, it is proposed that
there should be an independent arbitrator to look into the pricing mechanism of domestic coking coal.
ii)                   The availability of indigenous coal is depleting at a very fast rate, thus forcing higher usage of imported coking
coal in the coal blend and consequent pressure on ports. Haldia port is most economical for transportation of
imported coal as three integrated steel plants of SAIL are located in the Eastern Region. Capacity at Haldia  port is
inadequate for handling coal for supply to these steel plants. Moreover, due to low draft at Haldia Port, SAIL is
constrained to part unload the ships at Vizag or Paradip port before bringing it to Haldia port. Help is required for
upgradation of Haldia port.
 
(B)   Power
 
Production in steel plants has been affected in H-1 by inconsistencies in power supply.  This was especially so
in eastern region where four of SAIL’s plants are located.  There were a large number of total power failures,
voltage dips and frequency of power supply remained abnormally high for long durations.
 
High frequency of power supply resulted in loss of captive power generation, equipment damage and erosion
in life of rotating equipment, apart from increased power bill due to higher drawal of power.
 
It is expected that incidence of high frequency will come down after the proposed interconnections of Eastern
grid with North/South in October/ November 2002. However, it is felt that appreciable improvement can be
obtained only by implementation of ‘Availability Based Tariff’.
 
 
(C)             To meet the full compliance of Pollution Control norms in Coke Ovens as per the directives of MOEF, large
scale financial investment is called for.  A provision of Rs. 1000 crores has been made in 10
th Five Year Plan
which will allow us to take up rebuilding of not more than 6 batteries over the next 5 years.  If SAIL has to stick to
the stringent regulatory requirement to make all 21 batteries fully compliant within a tightened time frame, SAIL
will have to seek financial assistance from Government to ensure full compliance in batteries.  Towards this end,
SAIL has proposed Rs. 80 crore assistance from Govt. in 2003-04 BE.

        CHAPTER I
Introduction
1.         When ceasefire was declared with the Naga insurgents in 1964, the Government of India made a commitment to ensure rapid
industrial development to wean people of Nagaland away from violence. The Paper Mill Project was conceived in Nagaland in the late
60s. Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company Limited was incorporated in 1971. This was first and only large & medium unit in the State of
Nagaland and the first paper mill in the central public sector in the North Eastern region. It generated great hope and enthusiasm among
the people of Nagaland. This project was conceived with the following technical specifications:
(i)
                  Capacity : 100 Tons per day i.e. 33000 tons per annum
(ii)                Product : Writing and printing paper
(iii)               Basic Raw Material : 60% Bamboo, 40% Reed
(iv)              Power Requirement : 13 MW
(v)                8 MW to be generated internally from waste head of boilers, 5 MW to be supplied from State Grid
(vi)              Hindustan Paper Corporation, A Central PSU executed the project.
(vii)             Entire responsibility of management rested with HPC.
1.1       The local people donated 700 acres of land for the mill and housing colonies in Tuli area of Nagaland. 126 sq. kilometers of
bamboo forest land was purchased for captive plantation and was leased to NPCC. Water from river Melak was harnessed for water
supply to the Mill. In anticipation of demand from the mill, large scale bamboo plantation took place in private lands.
 
1.2       The project took 10 years to complete. Paper machines for both lines of production were imported from Sweden. Boilers were
supplied by Walchand Nagar Industries. The mill started making commercial production in 1982 with defective boilers. One of the
boilers failed in the trial test and insufficient heat from the remaining boilers kept the Turbine Generator (TG) set idle. The Mill
primarily depended on power supply from the State which accessed power from Assam grid. Thus, the power supply was unstable
besides being costlier.
 
1.3       The defective boilers crippled performance of the mill. The envisaged 60% captive power from Turbine Generator set was not
available and hence the capacity utilization was poor, ranging between 3% to 19%. One of the two production lines i.e. Reed Line was
never utilized. Peak capacity utilization reached 60% on some days whenever power supply was stable. The mill continued to make
losses due to under capacity utilization. The production was abruptly suspended in 1992 as the net worth of the company was eroded and
it was declared sick. Subsequently, it was referred to BIFR in 1992.
 
1.4       The operating agency i.e. IDBI framed a revival proposal and recommended – (1) Capital restructuring; (2) Operation at 60 TPD;
and (3) Fresh investment of Rs. 16.5 crore. Government of India accepted the proposal as approved by the BIFR and it was taken out of
purview of BIFR in 1996. Government of India carried out capital restructuring but did not infuse fresh funds except for VRS, hence

126th Report on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/126threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:42:01]
production could not be resumed and it was again referred to BIFR in 1998 for the second time. IDBI was again appointed operating
agency and a Draft Rehabilitation Scheme (DRS) was submitted by them which recommended revival at 60 TPD, fresh investment of 55
cores, other reliefs and concessions applicable to new industrial units in the North Eastern region  and a marginal viability was
envisaged. Nagaland Government agreed to support DRS for its share of reliefs and concessions and fresh investment. However,
Government of India declined to support this Scheme. The decision of Government of India was conveyed to BIFR who in turn asked
the IDBI to advertise for change of management. Although IDBI advertised for change of management, no expression of interest was
received. This position was conveyed to BIFR and thereafter the matter was taken up by Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) who decided
to take a fresh view.
1.5       An Expert team consisting of Hindustan Paper Corporation, Central Pulp and Paper Research Institute and State Government
officers was sent to determine the technical viability of the Scheme. The team recommended revival at 120 TPD of value added paper for
technical and economic viability and an approximate investment to the tune of 150 crores. The MHA directed to carry out the Scheme by
outside consultants. Outside consultants were identified. The cost of detailed project report was to the tune of 30-35 lakhs. The
Department for Development of North Eastern Region agreed to meet the cost of project. However, BIFR refused to grant any further
time and issued orders of winding up.
 
1.6       However, it is worth mentioning that infrastructure development over the years in Nagaland was favourable for revival of the
company. The details of the development are as under:
·
                    Railway line extended to Tuli
·                    Upgraded to broad gauge
·                    Kohima-Mokokchung-Tuli-Amguri road upgraded to National Highway
·                    66/33 HT transmission lines extended to TULI
·                    TULI transformer upgraded from 1.6 to 7.5 MVA
·                    Power availability improved by commissioning 75 MW Doyang and 24 MW Likhimro hydel projects
·                    Substantial investment for road connectivity of Tuli with rest of the State.
 
·                    Coal and Limestone available within a radius of 250 kilometers
·                    Communication and transport facilities many times better than 30 years back.
 
1.7       In the circumstances stated above, the following options are there:
·
                    Wind up and spend Rs.107 crore for closure.
·                    Revive and let HPC manage with the existing arrangement
·                    Revive and privatize as a going concern
 
            Revival is the most feasible and desirable option also compatible with Central Government policy on sick PSUs.
1.8       The matter relating to NPPC was raised by the Members almost in every meeting of the Department related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry when Demands for Grants came up for discussion.  The management of HPC constantly informed the
committee that the company has become non-operational due to insurgency problem in Nagaland.  The Ministry of Heavy Industry also
in their annual reports routinely stated that the company, which came out of the purview of BIFR due to financial restructuring again
became sick as the revival scheme could not be put into operation due to law and order problem, lack of infrastructure and absence of
banking facilities.
1.9       The Committee has been noting over the past years the stereotype statement of the HPC as well as the Ministry of Heavy
Industry.  Law and Order situation has been cited as a major cause for the non-revival of the company.  In this context, the committee
noted that the President of India in his address to Parliament on 25
th February 2002 had said “ The peace process in Nagaland has been
strengthened with satisfactory progress of talks with various militant groups.  What is specially heartening n the last one year is that
people of Nagaland have come out strongly in favour of peace, dialogue  and development, often by staging spontaneous mass

126th Report on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/126threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:42:01]
activities”.  Since law and order situation appears to have improved in Nagaland, the committee felt that a beginning may be made
towards reviving NPPCL for the benefit of the people of Nagaland.
CHAPTER II
Discussion with various Central Ministries, State Government and PSUs
2.         The sub-Committee-II for Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises had meetings with the Department of Heavy Industry,
Department for Development of North Eastern Region, Railway Board, Department of Industrial Policy and Promotion, Chief Secretary,
State of Nagaland, representatives of Hindustan Paper Corporation, Nagaland Pulp and Paper Corporation, Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd.
and Gas Authority of India Ltd. to explore the possibility of reviving the Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company.  Members of Parliament of
the State of Nagaland also attended the meetings as special invitees.  The date-wise details of the meeting are given below.
 
Meeting held on 15th April 2002
2.1       At the outset, the Sub-Committee-III heard the Secretaries, Department of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, Department
for Development of North Eastern Region, Chief Secretary, Nagaland, and CMD, Hindustan Paper Corporation, regarding revival of
Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company Ltd.
 
2.2       After hearing the Secretaries of the concerned departments and the Chief Secretary Government of Nagaland, the Committee
recommended that the State Government and employees of the Nagaland Pulp and Paper co. Ltd. should make an appeal to AAIFR
before whom the case was pending for grant of stay.  The committee further recommended that simultaneously, the HPC would call for
bids from the reputed consultants and place an order for preparation of a Detailed Project Report.  The Secretary, Department for
Development of North Eastern Region, assured the committee that his Department would bear 50% of the cost of preparing the Detailed
Project Report.  Secretary, Department of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises, also agreed to meet the balance 50% of the cost.  The
sub-committee observed that after preparation of the Report, the sub-committee would examine the viability of reviving the said
company and thereafter it would request the Government of India and Government of Nagaland to help the company.  The sub-
committee also decided that there was still need for participation of MPs representing the State of Nagaland and Chief Secretary and
other concerned officers of the Government of Nagaland in the ensuing meetings of the sub-committee in regard to revival of NPPC
Ltd. 
 
Meeting held on 24
th June 2002
2.3       At the outset, the Convenor wanted to know the status of the revival scheme of the Nagaland Pulp and Paper Company Ltd.
(NPPC).  Secretary, Department of Heavy Industries, informed the Committee that in pursuance of the directions given by the
Committee at its meeting held on 15 th April 2002, an appeal against BIFR’s decision on closure of NPCC was filed by the Government
of Nagaland and NPPC with AAIFR and also M/s Development Consultants Pvt. LTd., Kolkata, a consultant in the pulp and paper
industry were appointed on April 22, 2002 for preparation of a Detailed Project Report.  The consultant was to give a Preliminary
Viability Report (PVR) on August 22, 2002 and a final draft report on November 22, 2002.  AAIFR, after hearing the parties concerned,
had agreed to an extension and fixed the next date of hearing for 10 th September 2002 and had directed that copies of the PVR may be
given to them as soon as it is available.  The Covenor thereupon asked the consultant about the status of the PVR.  The consultant
informed that the PVR would be submitted by 22 th August 2002.  The Convenor directed that efforts may be made to expedite the
finalisation of the report before 22th August 2002.  Convenor also directed the Department of Heavy Industry to extend all possible help
to the consultants so as to enable them to prepare their report quickly. 
Meeting held on 12th December 2002
2.4       At the outset, the Convenor recalled that revival of Nagaland Pulp and paper Corporation was important because Government of
India was very particular that the area should be developed, there should be employment potentiality and insurgency reduced.  The

126th Report on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/126threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:42:01]
projection as given was likely to be production of 45000 tonnes of paper.  It would get the original benefits of concession and the
consultants had taken that into consideration and prepared a detailed report on that basis.  Estimates came to Rs.250 crores.  The
feasibility report had two factors where the company may raise 250 crores or raise 50% and borrow 50%.  Borrowing 50% would not be
very difficult.  The company was presently under reference to BIFR.  They had given some more time to revive this plant.  The matter
now rested with the Ministry of Heavy Industry and Nagaland Government.  The Convenor wanted to know from the Ministry of Heavy
Industry about the present position.
 
2.5       Secretary, Heavy Industry informed that they had received the comments of the holding company.  Although nothing had been
said about the avenues from where the finance had to be raised while the liabilities had not been taken into account which were to the
tune of 130-140 crores.  However, the Ministry would look into it.
 
2.6       CMD, Hindustan Paper Corporation, informed that on certain technical issues the company agreed with the consultants. They
were taking availability projection as if it was a green field project.  At the same time, the company would be using existing assets
without considering the liabilities.  It did not indicate what treatment would be given to equity, loan and accumulated losses of Rs.197
crores as on 31.3.02. Even with the projections based on the premise that the company would get the excise exemption and 100%
capacity utilisation, their estimated earnings would be only Rs.138 crores.  So even after 10 years accumulated losses would not get
wiped out.  This issue needed to be considered.  He further informed that the company had only touched about 20% utilisation. 
Estimating 100% utilisation in three years was being over-optimistic.  Next point was that the project completion period was taken as 24
months.  Unless and until the critical equipment supplied and erection took place in at least 15-18 months, 24 months would not be a
realistic schedule.  There were logistic inadequacies.  Next factor was that working capital was slightly on the lower side.  The
company’s requirements would be higher.  Then there was the issue of requirement of gas.  Gas availability assurance was not there. 
Besides, HPC was in 1987 pay structure.  To attract good personnel this needed revision. 
 
2.7       HPC further agreed with certain technical analysis except for one issue.  This was related to the capacity utilisation issue.  When
the plant was installed, it undertook production of 100 tonnes per day for 330 operating days.  The normative level for Indian processing
industry was 333.33 days.  Consultants had taken 345 operating days and had assumed production level of 140 tonnes per day.  Then it
was assumed that within three years of operation it would go to 100 percent.  These were optimistic estimates but it was better to have a
realistic view.
 
2.8       The Convenor observed that boilers, turbines and erection plant had to be changed.  Infrastructure also needed improvement. The
land was available.  He enquired whether it could be done with Rs.240-250 crores.  HPC informed that the new green field plan would
cost 530 crores.  Due technical justifications had been given and some contingencies had been kept and so they had arrived at a figure of
Rs.250-260 crores.
 
2.9       Shri K. Sangatham, Member Lok Sabha, informed that the boilers bought earlier were second hand.  It was the mismanagement
of the company, which was responsible for this kind of sorry state of affairs.  The resources were mismanaged.  When the company was
started, the State of Nagaland was not properly equipped.  Civil Servants did not know what was happening.  But now there were people
who were ready to work there.  The state had officers who were experienced and willing to work.  Raw materials could also be supplied
in required quantity.  The industry could be revived with the help of various departments of Government of India.
 
2.10     Thereafter, the Convenor raised two points regarding gas and railways.  Representative of GAIL informed that the job of original
allocation of gas was made in 1986 and ONGC was to supply the gas.  The route was to be provided by HP, which failed to do so and so
ONGC could not lay the pipeline.  In 1991-92 this allocation was transferred to GAIL and the ministry told them that agreement should
be signed between ONGC and GAIL.  It could not take place.  From 1986 the gas was coming from Assam to the paper plant.  Since
then the availability of gas had gone down.  If gas was available, GAIL would lay the pipeline and supply it.  Representative of Railways
informed that broad gauge line was ready between Anomi and Tuli and they could carry any traffic on this route.

2.11     Representative of Nagaland Government informed that the viability of the company had been established.  So the first task would
be to review the decision of Government of India.  Then funding had to be found.  As far as the State Government was concerned, it was
going to get this mill revived because this mill was the only source which could lead to economic regeneration of the state.  So from the
state government it would get whatever assistance was required.  The State Government would be very happy if the decision on the
revival of the mill was taken as early as possible.
 
2.12     As far as communication was concerned, he informed that the road passing through Tuli had been upgraded to national highway. 
The work on the road was on.  The railway line had also come.  The communication had improved ten times to what it was 30 years
ago.  Telephone communication had also improved.  As far as law and order situation was concerned, there was a ceasefire going on
between the factions and negotiations were at a very advanced stage.  So, insurgency related law and order situation had improved quite
a lot in the last five years.
 
2.13     The representative of Nagaland further informed that Nagaland had recently commissioned two projects.  The entire state had
been covered under 66 KV grid which had been extended to Tuli also.  Electrical sub-stations had also been upgraded.  Transmission line

2.14     The representative of Department of Development of North East Region informed that there were certain things which should be
looked into like gas availability and other things.  As far as money part was concerned, their department had no budget proposals for

2.15     After hearing all the Ministries/Departments/State Government of Nagaland/HPC/GAIL/HUDCO, the Committee directed that
Ministry of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises should look into the matter and come back with a suitable proposal for reviving the
NPPCL.

crores.  However, it came to the notice of the Committee that the cost of the revival scheme had gone up.  He wanted to know the details

2.18     He further informed that there was capital expenditure of 301 crores for payment to pressing creditors, which was to the tune of
Rs.13.92 crores, cash loans was 10.38 crores, margin money was 10.22 crores, and 3.50 crores for fresh VRS.  Total came to 339.43
crores.
 
2.19     The Convenor observed that it should be taken as a fresh project.  Only when government gave a clear indication that it would be
a fresh project, it would be possible to work on its viability.
 
2.20     Chief Secretary, Government of Nagaland informed that the State Government were prepared to make contribution in terms of

126th Report on Industry

their equity share.  Their equity holding was 1:18 and to that extent they were prepared to invest funds.  They were also prepared to write
off whatever was payable to them by the NPPC on account of electricity and other payments. This came to about Rs.6 crores. 
 
2.21     Joint Secretary, Department of Heavy Industry, informed that as the situation stood, the cost of revival cost of the project was

end of 10 years and this would be insufficient to wipe out the present accumulated losses of Rs.197.38 crores.  Central Pulp and Paper
Research Institute agreed that the project was viable technically but economic feasibility would have to be separately examined. 
According to the Economic Advisor, price sensitivity was an issue that needed to be addressed.  Even if there was a variation of 5-10%

2.23     He further stated that excise duty exemption should be made available for 25 years.  Transport subsidy must also be available.

2.24     The Convenor observed that that difficulties were there but if the concerned departments also put all the initiative, then it should

The Convenor further observed that the whole attitude of the committee was that the unit should be revived, whatever the cost.  Today

2.25     When Members wanted to know what happened to the 10% of budget money from each ministry which would be put in the
central pool for North East development, Secretary, Department for Development of North Eastern Region, informed that the idea was
not that each department would give its gross budgetary support.  10% of the GBS is to be used in the NE and whatever amount was not

CHAPTER III
Observations/Recommendations
3.         After hearing the Department of heavy Industry, Department for Development of North Eastern Region (DONER) and Hindustan
Paper Corporation, the committee understands that the main question relates to funding the project and this aspect is to be made clear
before the AAIFR in its next hearing to be held on 1 st July 2003.  It is clear that the NPPC is to be wound up if funding of the project
does not take place.  The committee, however, understands that the Government did not take the revival of NPPC seriously.  This is
corroborated by the fact that on NPPC’s first reference to BIFR, Government of India carried out capital restructuring without infusing
fresh funds except for VRS.  Moreover, the Ministry of Home Affairs appointed a team of experts for the revival of the company.  That
team recommended revival at 12 TPD of value added paper for technical and economic viability with an investment of Rs.150 crores. 
The Ministry of Home Affairs decided to carry our detailed project report and DONER agreed to meet the cost of DPR, which was to the
tune of Rs.30-35 lakhs.  In spite of this, BIFR refused to grant any further time and issued orders for winding up.
3.1       This shows that the case was not properly presented before the BIFR.  When the Ministry of Home Affairs decided to appoint a
consultant to explore the viability of the project, what prompted BIFR to issue orders to wind up the company without going into the
merit of the case, is not understood.
3.2       The DONER has been created for the development of North Eastern Region but it cannot contribute funds for NPPC from non-
lapsable pool as their mandate is to aid only new projects.  In fact, DONER should be made a model agency for the development of the
North Eastern Region, which should encompass not only new projects but also the existing units if any meaningful role is to be played
by the newly created department. DONER should play a leading role for the development of the North East in coordination with
concerned central ministries to usher in real development of the North East.  The Committee notes that out of Rs.1600 crores non-
lapsable pool for North East, Rs.550 crores goes to the budget of DONER for creation/completion of last mile projects in social
infrastructure.  The committee feels that the balance fund may be tapped for funding revival of the company.
 
3.3       The Committee notes that the cost of closure is Rs.107 crores.  In addition Rs.112 crores worth of investment is sunk.
3.4       It has been the committee’s stand that the greenfield fresh project emphasis is from the point of view of Government’s writing off
the loans.
 
3.5       In the light of the views expressed by the HPC, Central Pulp and Paper Research Institute and Economic Advisor to DHI on how
to make the company viable, excise duty exemption for 25 years coupled with transport subsidy should be made available to the
company.  NPPC should also have assured supply of bamboo for a period of 15 years.
3.6       The committee took up the case of NPCC as the peace process in Nagaland is going on and industrial development of Nagaland
should go hand in hand with the peace process.
In case NPPC is wound up the immediate impact would be –
-
                     Colossal waste of all investment made in infrastructure
-                     Serious erosion of credibility of Central Government in sensitive border area.
-                     Wrong signals to ongoing peace process
-                     accentuate already alarming unemployment situation
-                     Nagaland would be wiped of the map of large industries of India.

I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having   been  authorized  by the Commi ttee, hereby present this  One hund

CHAPTER - I 
MOU SYSTEM 
1.         The Memorandum of Undertaking (MOU)  is a negotia ted document between the Government, acting as the owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific
PSE. It contain the intentions, obligations and mutual responsib ilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MOU makes an at tempt to move the management of PSEs
from management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.  
OBJECTIVES OF THE MOU SYSTEM  
1.1       The objectives of the MOU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy and accountability of the management; to remove the
fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise  to pursue through clearly laid down performance targets   in the  MOU and to enable the evaluation of managerial
performance through objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to stimulate improved performance.  
1.2       Under the agreement the enterprises undertake to achieve the targets set in the agreement at the beginning of the yea r. Thus the MOU covers both financial
performance as well as non-financial performance. Under this syst em performance of the company is categorized into five categori es namely: excellent,very good, good, fair,
and poor. 
THE GENESIS OF MOU SYSTEM 
1.3       The genesis of the policy of Memorandum of Understa nding can be traced to the report of the Arjun Sengupta Commitee. One of the recommendations of this
Committee was for the introduction of the system of MOU for measurement of performance of public enterprises. The MOU system wa s introduced on an experimental basis
in 1987-88. It was based on the French system. From 1989-90 the signaling system was adopted and it remains in vogue till now. 
One of the most important difference between the French system and the signaling system is the possibility of making an overall  judgment on the enterprises performance in
the latter system. In the performance contracts belonging to the Fr ench system, one could only point out whether a particular t arget was met or not. This created grea t
difficulty for making an overall judgement regarding enterprises performance. The signalling system overcomes this problem by a dopting the system of "five point scale" and
"criteria weight" which ultimately result in calculation of "composite score" or an index of the performance of the enterprise  
PREPARATION OF MOU 
1.4       Based on the guidelines issued by the DPE in October/November, the draft MOUs are prepared by PSEs and forwarded to t he Administrative Ministry and DPE by
