CHAPTER - I 
  
  
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT  
  
RECOMMENDATION 
  
1.1        FUNCTIONAL STRUCTURE OF SAIL – AN INTRODUCTION 
  
The Committee while noting the func tional structure of SAIL is of  the view that each and every
organ of SAIL would perform their respective task so as to achieve the over all objectives and mission
of the company. The Committee hopes that each pa rt/division of the SAIL functions in complete
equilibrium to achieve its corporate goal. 
                                                                                                                        (Para 1.6) 
Action Taken 
  
1.1.1    The Board of Directors of  the Steel Authority of India Li mited (SAIL) has approved a vision
statement for SAIL.  Further, th e Board approves every year an Op eration Budget for SAIL at the
beginning of the financial year detailing therein the physical parameters and financial performance to be
achieved during the year.  Beside s, Capital Expenditure budget is also approved by the Board, which
inter alia, includes the schemes aiming at improvement  in quality and productivi ty.  A detailed micro-
level planning is done at various/units  level to achieve these.  As suc h, all the organs of SAIL including
the management and the Board of  Directors work towards achiev ing the objectives and mission o f
SAIL.  In order to improve the f unctioning of the Board a nd also to comply with the Securities and
Exchange Board of India (SEBI) requirements, the Board has been re-constituted, which now comprise 
more than 50% of independent Directors. 
  
RECOMMENDATION 
  
1.2        FUNCTIONAL STRUCTURE OF SAIL – AN INTRODUCTION 
  
The Committee is of the considered view that in a liberalised and globalised economy decision 
making process should be quick and without unnecessary control and regulations.  Therefore, the 
Committee feels that the steel plants in public sector should be given maximum autonomy in their 
functioning so as to cope with the pulls and pressures of market economy. 
                                                                                                                        (Para 1.12) 
  
ACTION TAKEN 
  
1.2.1    Govt. of India has identi fied SAIL as one of the Navrat na companies and granted enhanced
autonomy for its operations.  As such SAIL has suff icient autonomy in functioning and decision making
process to take quick decision and cope with the pulls and pressures of market economy. 
  
RECOMMENDATION 
  
1.3     INTRODUCTION OF NEW TECHNOLOGY 
  
The Committee, while taking note of the new technologies as intr oduced in the primary areas during the
modernisation process at DSP, is pleased to observe that the hot me tal and the crude steel production in
DSP has stabilized qualitatively a nd as well as quantitatively.  The Committee hopes that the new
technology introduced in DSP would enable DSP to improve upon financial performance.

1.4     Results OF Modernisation 
  
The committee, while noting the results of m odernisation, recommends that DSP management
should leave no stone untur ned to make optimum utilisation of facilities.  The Committee strongly
believes that DSP would be  able to make net profit in the ye ar 2003-04 by making optimum utilisation 
of facilities available at DSP as a result of implementation of modernisation package. 
(Para 2.8.2)
ACTION TAKEN  
  
1.4.1    DSP is making all out efforts to make optimum utilisation of modernised facilities.  DSP 
operated at almost 100% saleable steel capacity utilization in 2002-03 with its continuous casting 
operating at 126% of capacity.  The business plan for 2003-04 envisages saleable steel production at 
104% of capacity and further improvement in efficiency parameters. A net profit of Rs. 7 crore has been 
achieved during the first quarter of 2003-04.
 
  
RECOMMENDATIONS 
 
1.5       Time over-run 
  
The Committee is constrained to express its concern that almost all modernization packages for DSP 
suffered from time over-run. The delay caused in implementation of modernisation package led to cost 
over run. 
                                                (Para 2.9.2)
1.6       Steps Were Taken For Timely Completion 
  
The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure at the fact that although steps were taken for 
timely completion of modernisation package it was all in vain because they package proved inefficient 
and ineffective as the modernisation projects suffered both the time and the cost over-run. 
(Para 2.10.2)
                         
1.7     Reasons For Cost Over-Run 
  
The Committee notes that reasons for cost over-run ar e mainly increase in volume of work, inclusion of 
new items, price escalation, exchange rate variation, increase in duties and taxes and increase in interest
payments due to change in mode of  financing. The Committee is constrained to express its anguish over
the fact that the modernisation of Durgapur Steel Plant was approved in Feb., 1989 by Govt. at an
estimated cost of Rs. 2668 crore with FE component of Rs. 685 crore ( Base date: 3rd quarter 1988). The 
revised cost estimate of DSP modernisation worked out to Rs. 5074.71 crore (FE: 1375.42 crore) on
base date of 2nd quarter 1999. As per Govt’s approval, the project was to be completed by March, 1993.
The modernisation was completed in March 1998 with an overall delay of 60 months.  
(Para 2.11.4)

3.11     Delay Aspects In The Modernization Process – An Enquiry Committee 
  
The Committee notes that the Revised Cost Es timates for Modernisation of DSP, RSP & BSL
after restructuring have been Rs.4372 Crore, Rs.4186 Crore and Rs.1943 Crore respectively.  The cost
over-runs in the case of DSP is 64 %, RSP 6% and BSL 8%.  The cost over-run had occurred for DSP, 
RSP and BSL Modernisation basically due to two factors i.e. i) payments made for escalation, FE parity,
interest during construction, etc. within the completion schedule and ii) payments made for the above,
beyond the completion schedule.  In the case of escalation, the payments have been made as pe r
contractual provision, by and large wi thin the contractual completion period only.  To contain the time
over-run, SAIL had taken many correcti ve steps such as rigorous m onitoring/follow-up and frequent 
project reviews at all levels including Chairman SA IL and Secretary (Steel), rigorous follow-up of sub-
vendors/vendors’ manufacturing work, fi nancial assistance to the contr actors, direct payment to sub-
vendors for early supply of  equipment, rendering back-up support to the contractor s by way of giving 
construction equipments such  as cranes, dozers, etc. and, in some  cases, taking over the jobs from the
defaulting contracting ag encies and executing the same through alternative agenci es for curtailing
delays.  Despite the corrective st eps taken by SAIL, the time over-r un had occurred for these three 
Modernisation projects, wh ich was beyond the control of SAIL, ma inly due to delay in engineering
works by the contractors, delay in ordering & supply of indigenous equipments, inadequate mobilisation
of resources by the contractors and funds constraint of contractors lik e EPI, HEC, HSCL etc.  Besides
the above, in case of DSP Modern isation, disintegration of the erst while USSR and also resulted in
delays in supply of imported equipments, structures & refractories.

FOURTEENTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman, Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry , 
having been authorised by the Committee, present this Fourteenth Report of the Committee 
on the Demands for Grants for 1995-96 of the Ministry of Steel. 
2. The Committee started examination of Ministry's demands by seeking views of the 
representatives of Chambers of Commerce such as FICCI and the CII on the performance of 
the steel sector and the impact of the recent budget proposals relating to Ministry of Steel. 
The Committee also heard the views of representatives of Central trade unions in the same 
context. 
3. At its subsequent meeting held on the 7th April, 1995, the Committee heard oral 
evidence tendered by the Secretary. Ministry of Steel on the Performance Budget for 1995-
96 in connection with the Dema!lds for Grants of the Ministry. 
4. The Committee eonsidered the Ministry's budgetary proposals in three sittings and 
adopted the report at its sittin~ held on the 28th April, 1995. 
S. The Committee was given to understand that the total demand of ~inistry as per 
Demand No. 75 for 1995-96 is to the tune of Rs. 294.46 crore out of which Rs. 284.50 crore 
is for the Plan sector and remaining Rs. 9.96 crore have been allocated to non-plan 
activities. 
6. Taking into account the documents and other material made available to it and the oral 
evidence tendered before it by the representatives of industry. trade unions and the Ministry 
of Steel, the Committee would like to make the following recommendations and suggestions: 
6.01 The Committee is constrained to make one preliminary observation. A perusal of the 
budgetary allocations for the Ministry · of Steel for the years 1993-94, 1994-95 and 1995-96 
would suggest that the allocations are declining steadily over the years. Were the factor of 
inflation to be taken into account, the real content of the outlay proposed for the Ministry 
would appear to be declining at an. even sharper gradient. True, in the ambience of 
liberalisation, the authorities could be influenced by the judgement that the role of the 
government in propelling -industrial growth is going to be progressively less and less from 
now on, justifying cutbacks in the outlays for hithertocrucially important ministries, such as 
the Ministry of Steel.. But certain other aspects of the emerging reality, the Committee feels, 
should also be taken into account. If industrial growth is to grow at the rate of around 10 to 
12 per cent for the next decade or thereabouts, as is being assumed i~ official circles, the 
significance of steel, one of the mQst basic intermediate products, would loom large in the 
industrial landscape. For instance, aceording to projections incorporated in the rerformance 
Budget, 1995-96 of the Ministry of Steel, the domestic demand of steel would more than 
·double by the year 2001-02 from the present level of 15 .million tons. Such an increase in the 
demand for steel would call for a corresponding expansion of steel output. It could be that 
official prognosis is that the bulk of this increase in production would take place in the 
private sector. The assumption may initially sound plausible, ' but, given the capital 
intensiveness of the industry, is not altogether realistic. The fading away of the government 
from the steel sector reflected in the declining share of steel produGtion in public sector 

2 
plants in total output, would also need a reappraisal from another point of view. The experience 
garnered over the past few years has imparted one important lesson: public expenditure of a 
substantial order, which would have its impact on the demand for industrial goods, is still called 
for for sustaining industrial growth in the country. A more active role for the government might, 
judged from both these· points of view, be necessary to maintain an improved tempo of 
industrial activity. And irrespective of the relative roles of the public and private sectors, it has 
to be ensured that the development of the domestic steel industry is not hampered because of, 
for instance, the laqk of raw iron ore. This would necessitate large-scale investments, including 
for opening new mines. Extensive dependence on private mining activity for the purpose could 
entail several uncertainties. To pick another example, to ensure the supply Of ooking coal of the 
right specifications and quantum, it would be necessary to set up a network of new washeries. 
At the same time, it might be crucially important to open up, after careful exploratory activity, 
such mines as would offer prospects' '?f quality coal with a lower content of ash and sulphur. All 
this would, in addition to private initiative require public investment of a considerable order. 
While the Steel Authority of India can ey and large be expected henceforth to be self-sustaining, 
the range of activities just referred to might call for resources for which budgetary provision 
would appear to be desirable. Consideri~g all aspects together, the Committee would strongly 
recommend that the phase of progressive contraction of budgetary allocations for the Ministry of 
Steel be swiftly brought to an end. 
6.0Z The Committee has taken note of the reductions in the rates of import duty on steel items 
in the budget for 1995-96. The import duty on sponge iron, scrap and non-alloy steel has been 
reduced from the level of 30 per cent to 20 per cent; on ingots, from 50 per cent to 20 per cent; 
on stainless steel coils from 50 per cent to' 30 per cent; on C.R. coils from 40 per cent to 30 per 
cent; and on all other items from 50 per cent to 40 per cent. Whether it is desirable to proceed 
with the opening up of the domestic steel industry to external competition at a somewhat more 
gradual pace is a moot question. It would, in the view of the Committee, in any case have been 
desirable to have the rate of import duty imposed on a finished steel item kept at a higher level 
than the rates of duty on the corre·sponding non-finished items. Even this precaution does not 
appear to have been followed jn the current year's proposals. Given the huge excess capacity in 
steel-producing units in Western Europe, the United States of America and Japan, the 
downward adjustments in the import duty levels incorporated in this year's budget proposals 
could, in the opinion of the Committee, affect the viability of domestic producers, more so since 
they would also have to take into account the impact of inflation on the structure of cost. It is a 
matter of some disquiet that one of the main producers has already announced an across-the: 
board increase in the prices of several items because of cost escalation. In the circumstances, the 
Ministry of Steel, the Committee feels, would be justified to make a representation to the 
Ministries of Finance and Commerce that the roll-back of import duty rates on steel categories 
should proceed at a more circumspect tempo. What is also worth watching is the prospect of 
selective dumping by foreign exporters of steel items taking advantage of the liberalised import 
duty structure in India. That this aspect of the matter deserves to be kept is mind in confirmed 
by the comparison of the landed cost of selected steel categories with the ex-stockyard price of 
corresponding categories supplied by Indian producers on the eve of the budget proposals. The 
lowering of the rates of duty would seem to stack the decks further against the domestic units.

6.03 The Committee would now refer to another aspect of liberalisation as far as the steel 
industry is concerned, namely, the limited withdrawal of steel freight equalisation. Under the 
scheme of freight equalisation which was in operation between 1956 and 1992, the main steel 
producers used to collect from the buyers the equalised freight element built into the prices 
of iron and steel items and credit them with the Joint Plant Committee. The equalised 
freight element was calculated on the basis of the average distance of the steel plants from 
the different destinations. Whenever the actual freight was less than the equalised freight 
that was collected, the producers were liable to pay the difference to the JPC. Similarly 
when the actual freight incurred was higher than the equalised freight element, the 
difference was payable by the JPC to the producers. The scheme was abolished with effect 
from January, 1992. The producers were however advised by the authorities to fix ex­
stockyard prices on the basis of either the actual freight or the freight element as existed 
prior to deregulation whichever was lower. As a result, while the freight disadvantage to the 
States or areas proximately located to the steel plants has been partially removed, the 
situation as it has emerged can hardly be described as complete deregulation. Be that as it 
may, now that three years of the partial abolition of freight equalisation has been completed, 
a study of the impact of the new system on the consumption and use of the various steel 
items in the different parts of the country, would in view of the Committee, be well worth 
undertaking. Consumers in the relatively proximat~ areas could claim that since the freight 
subsidy being offered to areas remote from the steel · plants is still borne by the producers 
and added to the prices that are charged, they are not getting the full benefit of deregulation. 
The position is admittedly anomolou~ and d~serves examination in some depth. 
Even if such an appraisal is not immediately feasible, it is in any event necessary to 
consider separately the consequences of high freight on mini-steel plants located in regions 
and areas away from the location of the main steel producers. The socially felt need which 
led to the encouragement of mini-steel plants was to disperse industrial production in nooks 
and corners of the country. While several of these plants are currently either sick or closed 
for a wide variety of reasons, the non-availability of steel items at reasonable prices has been 
one contributory factor for the lack of viability. The recommendations made by the 
Committee in its Fourth Report for restoring the mini-steel plants to health could be 
reiterated here. It might be considered whether, in addition to the existing array of relief and 
concessions, a special transport subsidy could not be declared for mini-steel plants located in 
backward regions, particularly the north-east sector, on a case-by-case basis. 
6.04 In the introductory paragraphs above, the Committee has referred to the challenge of 
ensuring adequate supply of iron ore to meet the demands of a fast ~xpanding steel industry. 
It is important that a careful appraisal is undertaken of the domestic availability of iron ore 
of different specifications over the next decade. The domestic production of iron ore is 

currently at around 58 million tons per annum, of which about 30 million tons are 
earmarked for export. But since domestic demand for the ore is projected to increase to 
roughly 66 million tons by 2001-02, even assuming exports to be pegged at present levels, 
overall output would have to go up close to 100 million tons per annum in the course of the 
next five years. The Committee has taken note of the official projections regarding 
additional raising of iron ore from existing non-captive mines in the Bihar-Orissa sector, 
from the mines under the charge of the National Mineral Development Corporation in 
Madhya Pradesh and from the captive mines maintained by the Steel Authority of India in 
Orissa. It has also taken into account the new explorations that are on the anvil by the 
NMDC and the SAIL. None of these projections however give ground for confidence that 
an increase in overall production of iron ore by something like 40 million tons is achievable 
in the course of the next few years. 
In order to reach the level of ore production called for, three alternative possibilities are 
worth examination: (a) a vastly expanded scale of investment in mining operations by the 
public sector units, including the SAIL and the NMDC, which would conceivably however 
require substantial additional budgetary allocations; (b) a drastic cut-back in exports from 
the present level of 30 million tons, thereby incurring loss in foreign exchange earnings; and 
(c) large-scale deployment of external capital into the iron ore mining sector. Alternative (c) 
is unlikely to materialise given the short time-frame. The choice therefore has to be between 
(a) and (b), or a combination of the two. If domestic production of iron ore · cannot be 
augmented to an adequate extent because of a constraint of resources, exports would need 
to be curtailed. It is in any case in the nation's interest that the emphasis remains on the 
export of fmished steel items rather than that of iron ore. The Committee 'would hope that 
whatever the decision or decisions, action is taken ahead of time so that the process of 
industrial growth is not held back because of non-availability of steel on account of non· 
availability of requisite quantities of iron ore. 
6.05 The Committee would urge a similar approach in appraising the availability of coking 
coal to feed the steel plants. It is somewhat unlikely that private investment will be 
forthcoming to the necessary extent to either augment the capacity of coal washeries ·or set 
up new washeries. The major burden of the task will devolve on the government, since most 
of the coal with high ash content is raised in the public sector mines. The choice therefore 
lies between either setting up more washeries or allocating funds for the exploration and 
development of mines with proven deposits of coal of high quality and low ash content. 
Given the fact that this country has the largest reserves of coal, it should not be difficult to 
shift ilie concentration of coal-raising from high ash content to low ash content terrains. 
If the NMDC and the SAIL cannot spare funds for the purpose, the Ministry of Steel, the 
Committee feels, should either on its own or in. conjunction with the Ministry of Coal, 
concentrate on such exploration and development activities. The outlay required for the 
purpose should come from additional appropriations in the budget of the Ministry or 
Miaistries. 
6.06 The availability of resources, there is no question, is a major stumbling block. The 
Committee is therefore compelled to revert in the present Report to the issue of 
disinvestment of public undertakings, in particular of the shares of the Steel Authority of 
India Limited, pursuant to the policy of liberalisation. According to data made available to 
the Committee, roughly 11 per cent of the paid-up equity of the SAIL have been disposed of 
in the course of the five phases of disinvestment undertaken since 1991-92. The total 
realisation from th~se ·rounds of disinvestment has worked to Rs. 1,023 crore. A large array 
of questions have been raised with respect to the mode of disposal of these shares and the 

lack of transparency in the modalities that were adopted. The Mid-term Review of the 
Economy, undertaken by the Indira Gandhi Institute of Development Research, has, 
through meticulous research , reached some tentative conclusions about the overall loss to 
the national exchequer because of the procedures followed in the disinvestments undertaken 
between 1991-92 and 1993-94. Admittedly, the conclusions arrived at in the IGIDR study are 
dependent on certain assumptions which may not be fully acceptable . Even so, it is worth 
taking note of the tentative findings in this paper, which suggest that, given the extent of 
under-valuation of the shares disposed of, the aggregate loss of revenue suffered by the 
SAIL from the disinvestments during the rounds of 1991-92, 1992-93 and 1993-94 would 
amount to nearly Rs. 1,030 crore. On the basis of this judgement, the shares would appear 
to have been sold at less than 50 per cent of their true worth . The Committee has reason to 
feel perturbed over such findings because there is little ground for assuming that the 
government intends to draw a curtain on similar disinvestment activities in the future. The 
budget for 1995-96 has announced a further disinvestment of public sector equity to the 
extent of Rs. 7,000 crore during the year, and the SAIL would conceivably be called upon to 
again part with a sizeable slice of its equities. Mistakes are a part of life's activities and if the 
government has incurred severe losses from certain past transactions, all that can be urged 
upon it is that these mistakes be rectified and not repeated in future operations. In order to 
draw the appropriate l~ssons from the experience of. the disinvestments since 1991-92, it is 
therefore necessary, the Committee feels, that the Comptroller and Auditor General of India 
be invited to embark on an appraisal of the disinvestment of the SAIL shares so that the right 
lessons could be drawn therefrom. In this connection, the Committee would also like to be 
assured that the proposed floatation of Euro-issues by the SAIL, reportedly amounting to 350 
million dollars, should be done in such a manner that the shares are not under-valued 
compared to prevailing market quotations in the country. Given the comfortable foreign 
exchange position, the Committee is not altogether convinced of the necessity for such a 
floatation. But, whatever the underlying reasons for the decision, it is important to ensure 
that the shares are not under-priced. 
6.07 A number of other related matters deserve mention. The history of the recent 
rounds of modernisation of the Durgapur, Bokaro and Rourkela plants bears witness that 
delays encountered in the course of the implementation of renewal and restructuring lead to 
considerable escalation in cost. "The modernisation of the Indian Iron and Steel Company 
should not be afflicted by similar ptocastination . ..:Pte· overall cost of the rehabilitation 
package proposal placed by the Steel Authority of India before the Board of Industrial and 
Financial Reconstruction does not seem excessive when compared to the cost of the 
rehabilitation packages implemented in the case of the three Hindustan Steel units. The 
Board of Industrial and Financial Reconstruction, the Committee understands, has 
commissioned the Industrial Development Bank of India·· to make a further appraisal of the 
SAIL proposal and the IDBI in its turn has sought the advice of a ·well-known Consultancy 
finn. Should the appraisal at these various levels of the SAIL package prove to be 
satisfactory and promise a reasonably good rate of return, there would seem to be little 
point in delaying further action on the proposal to modernise the liSCO on the ground that 
the BIFR has still to offer its final view. One significant issue could centre on the reported 
requirement of budgetary ·funds, estimated by SAIL to amount to around Rs. 1,100 crore. 
As this amount would need to be provided over a period of five years, the annual budgetary 
burden would appear to be moderate when account is taken of the aggregate value of the 
additional steel to be produced from the renovated and modernised plant. The Committee 
would stress its view that a major proportion of the amount raised through the sale of Steel 

v 
Authority of India Llmlted shares in the open market should be channelled for purposes of 
rehabilitation of SAn. units In difficulty, such as the liSCO. The Committee would also hope 
that care would be taken to maintain the tempo of progress in the functioning of the 
Visakhapatnam Steel Plant and its continual renewal and modernisation. 
6.08 The Committee would like to append a few supplementary remarks with respect to 
the Vijayanagar Steel Limited in Karnataka and Neelachal Ispat Nigam Limited in Orissa. 
These were initially placed under the umbrella of the SAIL, but the respective State 
governments were persuaded to take them over before the plants c,ould be commissioned. It 
is however unlikely that the State governments would have the necessary resources to 
complete the on-going works and make the units viable for production ·of saleable steel 
items. The Steel Authority of India may currently consider these two projects as no longer 
its burden. From tlie point of view of the nation, however, the investment funds already 
sunk in the two projects would be wasted if these are not completed. The Committee would 
expect the Ministry of Steel, along with SAIL authorities, to extend a helping hand to the 
respective State governments and offer technical advice as well as financial accommodation so 
that the units could be nurtured to a state where they are able to attain commercial viability. 
It would also recommend that a similar exercise be under taken In respect of the Visvesveraya 
Iron and Steel Limited (VISL) in Karnataka. In this connection, the feasibility of using the 
left-over resources lying with the Steel Development Fund for rehabilitati.qg the just· 
mentioned units may be examined. A part of the SDF could also be deployed for reactivating 
some of the mini-steel and rerolling mills i.l the country. 
6.09 Finally, the Committee would like to reiterate the views expressed In its Twelfth 
Report on the functioning of the National Renewal Fund. From a perusal of the Ministry's 
Annual Report as well as of the Performance Budget for 1994-95, it is abundantly clear th~t 
the old malaise continues and the National Renewal Fund has hardly been utilised for 
purposes beyond that of meeting the requirements of the Voluntary Retirement Scheme. It 
is for consideration whether, since concrete schemes for re-training and re-deployment of 
workers, which were supposed to be an integral part of the NRF as originally envisaged, has 
failed to take ofT, its funds allocated to the Ministry of Steel could not be directly utilised for 
rmancing the renewal of a number of steel units, big and small. By proceeding in this manner, 
society would at least be able to safeguard the employment of thousands of workers, a task 
which the NRF, as at present deployed, has failed to accomplish. 
6.10 The Committee hopes that, in the light of the recommendations included in this 
Report, the Ministry of Steel would feel encouraged to re-cast its demands for grants as well 
as obtain the sanction of the Ministry of Finance for seeking additional appropriations.

NEW DELHI;                
December 18, 2003     
                                    
                            
 DR.P.C. ALEXANDER

 Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
REPORT
1.1       The present  Action Taken Report (of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry) is
Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in the  Committee’s 126 th Report  on  Nagaland
Pulp and Paper Company Limited which  was presented and laid to the Parliament on 8 th May, 2003. The  Nagaland
Pulp and Paper Company Limited, incorporated in 1971,  was the First and only large & medium unit in the State of
Nagaland and the first paper mill in the central public sector in the North Eastern region. This project was conceived
with the technical specifications of Capacity of 100 Tons per day i.e. 33000 tons per annum producing writing and
printing paper which required 60% of bamboo and 40% of reed as basic raw material and 13MW (8MW to be generated
internally form waste head of boilers and 5MW to be supplied from State Grid).  Hindustan Paper Co-operation
undertook the managerial responsibility to execute the project.  However, the project to 10 years to complete and the
mill started making commercial production in 1982 with scores of problems from the very beginning.  As a result the
mill continued to make losses due to under capacity utilization  which ranged between 3% to 19% and at times  the peak
capacity utilization remained merely 60%. The production was abruptly suspended in 1992 as the net worth of the
company was eroded and it was declared sick. Subsequently, it was referred to BIFR in 1992.
1.2       The operating agency i.e. IDBI framed a revival proposal and recommended – (1) Capital restructuring; (2)
Operation at 60 TPD; and (3) Fresh investment of Rs. 16.5 crore. Government of India accepted the proposal as
approved by the BIFR and it was taken out of purview of BIFR in 1996. Government of India carried out capital
restructuring but did not infuse fresh funds except for VRS, hence production could not be resumed and it was again

140th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/140threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:43:11]
referred to BIFR in 1998 for the second time. IDBI was again appointed operating agency and a Draft Rehabilitation
Scheme (DRS) was submitted by them which recommended revival at 60 TPD, fresh investment of 55 cores, other
reliefs and concessions applicable to new industrial units in the North Eastern region  and a marginal viability was
envisaged. Nagaland Government agreed to support DRS for its share of reliefs and concessions and fresh investment.
However, Government of India declined to support this Scheme. The decision of Government of India was conveyed to
BIFR who in turn asked the IDBI to advertise for change of management. Although IDBI advertised for change of
management, no expression of interest was received. This position was conveyed to BIFR and thereafter the matter was
taken up by Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) who decided to take a fresh view.
1.3       An Expert team consisting of Hindustan Paper Corporation, Central Pulp and Paper Research Institute and State
Government officers was sent to determine the technical viability of the Scheme. The team recommended revival at 120
TPD of value added paper for technical and economic viability and an approximate investment to the tune of 150 crores.
The MHA directed to carry out the Scheme by outside consultants. Outside consultants were identified. The cost of
detailed project report was to the tune of 30-35 lakhs. The Department for Development of North Eastern Region agreed
to meet the cost of project. However, BIFR refused to grant any further time and issued orders of winding up.
1.4       The matter relating to NPPC was raised by the Members almost in every meeting of the Department related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry when Demands for Grants came up for discussion.  The management of
HPC constantly informed the committee that the company has become non-operational due to insurgency problem in
Nagaland.  The Ministry of Heavy Industry also in their annual reports routinely stated that the company, which came
out of the purview of BIFR due to financial restructuring again became sick as the revival scheme could not be put into
operation due to law and order problem, lack of infrastructure and absence of banking facilities.The Committee has been
noting over the past years the stereotype statement of the HPC as well as the Ministry of Heavy Industry.  Law and
Order situation has been cited as a major cause for the non-revival of the company.  Since law and order situation
appears to have improved in Nagaland, the committee felt that a beginning may be made towards reviving NPPCL for
the benefit of the people of Nagaland.
1.5       The Committee’s 126
th Report was the outcome of  series of meetings held by the Sub-Committee-III on 15 th
April, 24th June, 12th December, 2002 and 23rd April, 2003 with the Central Ministries, State Governments and PSUs. 
After hearing the  Department of heavy Industry, Department for Development of North Eastern Region (DONER) and
Hindustan Paper Corporation, the Committee understood that the main question related to funding the project was to be
made clear before the AAIFR in its  hearing scheduled  on 1st July 2003. 
1.6       The Committee, however, observed that the Government did not take the revival of NPPC seriously.  The
DONER was created for the development of North Eastern Region but it could not contribute funds for NPPC from non-
lapsable pool as their mandate is to aid only new projects.  In fact, DONER could be made a model agency for the
development of the North Eastern Region, which should encompass not only new projects but also the existing units if
any meaningful role is to be played by the newly created department. The Committee viewed that DONER could play a
leading role for the development of the North East in coordination with concerned central ministries to usher in real

140th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/140threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:43:11]
development of the North East.  The Committee noted that out of Rs.1600 crores non-lapsable pool for North East,
Rs.550 crores goes to the budget of DONER for creation/completion of last mile projects in social infrastructure.  The
Committee felt that the balance fund may be tapped for funding revival of the company.
1.7       The Committee noted that the cost of closure is Rs.107 crores.  In addition Rs.112 crores worth of investment is
sunk.    In the light of the views expressed by the HPC, Central Pulp and Paper Research Institute and Economic
Advisor to DHI on how to make the company viable, excise duty exemption for 25 years coupled with transport subsidy
should be made available to the company.  NPPC should also have assured supply of bamboo for a period of 15 years.
The Committee took up the case of NPCC as the peace process in Nagaland is going on and industrial development of
Nagaland should go hand in hand with the peace process.
1.8       The Committee was of the opinion that in case NPPC is wound up the immediate impact would be –
(i)
                  Colossal waste of all investment made in infrastructure
(ii)                Serious erosion of credibility of Central Government in sensitive border area.
(iii)               Wrong signals to ongoing peace process
(iv)              accentuate already alarming unemployment situation
(v)                Nagaland would be wiped of the map of large industries of India.
1.9       The committee noted that a number of sick PSUs have been given more than one revival schemes and feels that
no discrimination should be made in the case of NPPC in view of its location.  The Committee hoped that Government
of India, in view of the sensitivity of the matter, would not belie the hopes of Nagaland  people.
 
1.10     Committee’s recommendation in 126
th Report
(i)                  DHI and Government of Nagaland should properly place the matter before the AAIFR, specially with
reference to the funding position.  Since Rs.250 crores is not required at one go, this can be arranged in a
phased manner.
(ii)                Excise exemption for 25 years coupled with transport subsidy be provided to NPPC as a special
dispensation.
(iii)               Assured supply of bamboo be made available for a period of 15 years.
(iv)              Since the proposal involves financial implications, the clearance of Union Cabinet be obtained at the
earliest.

nd September, 2003 under the Chairmanship of

REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE
CHAPTER-I
 
STATUS OF COIR INDUSTRIES IN WEST BENGAL
 
            West Bengal holds fifth position in the country in respect of production of coconuts.  There is a potential
for development of coir industries in the state.  The annual production of coconut in West Bengal is of the order
of 324.3 million nuts with an area of 24,200 hectors for coconut cultivation.  Annual coconut production of five
prominent states of the country is given in the table below:
 
Production of Coconut
 
State Annual Production (in million nuts)
Kerala 5167.0
Tamil Nadu 3222.0
Karnataka 1670.3
Andhra Pradesh 1051.8
West Bengal 389.20
 
           
The area under coconut cultivation in West Bengal during 2002-2003 was placed at 28300 hectares and the
production of coconut is estimated at 389.20 million nuts.  The production of coir fibre in the State is estimated at 186
M.T. per annum.  Coconut is cultivated in 17 districts of West Bengal in which Murshidabad District was the largest
producer of coconut followed by South 24 Pargana, Midnapur (West and East), North 24 Parganas and Howrah.  These
five districts together constitute 79% of total production in the State.  About 15% of total production of coconut is
consumed for domestic uses.  60 to 65% of coconut produced in the State are plucked at the tender stage only due to
increasing demand for tender coconut in the State.  There are about 327 coir units registered with District Industries
Centres.  These units are engaged in the manufacture of bristle/mechanized fibre, coir rope, coir products including
rubberized coir.  Besides, there are 264 Janatha mattress making units.  The turnover of registered and unregistered units
amounted to Rs. 710 lakhs.  The coir industry in West Bengal provides employment to 3140 people, out of which 88%
of workers is in cottage  units.  About 1200 women are engaged in coir activities.  There are two coir cooperative
societies,  of which one is running well.  The State Government is running two coir training centers, one at Uluberia in
Howrah district and the other at Dhanchiberia in South 24 Parganas District. 
 
 
The breakup of registered coir units working in West Bengal is given below:-

Fibre Unit 9 Nos.
Coir yarn making units 22 Nos.
Rope making units 23 Nos.
Rubberized coir units 9 Nos.
Janatha mattress making unit 264 Nos.
 
Assistance  extended by Coir Board
 
            The Sub-Committee was apprised that the Coir board had assisted the growth and development of Coir
Industries in West Bengal in the following manner:-
 
(i)
                  Under the Integrated Coir Development Project, the Government of West Bengal started a coir yarn
spinning unit with 50 motorised rats at an outlay of Rs. 12.57 lakhs at Bagnan CADC, Narimangal Cooperative
Coir Industrial Society, Howrah.  The Government of India released an amount of Rs. 2.52 lakhs towards
Government of India share to the Government of West Bengal during 2000-01.
 
(ii)
                The Coir Board conducted two Entrepreneurship Development Programmes and two Quality Development
Programmes in West Bengal during 1999-2000.
 
(iii)               Under the Model Coir Village Scheme, the Coir Board has sanctioned Rs. 6 lakhs for implementing welfare
programmes like Common work sheds, Common Facility Centre, drinking water facilities, sanitary latrine in the
coir activities concentrated villages in the Hirapur Grama Panchayat and Bagnan in Howrah District.
 
(iv)
              The Board has released Rs. 4,99,458/- to set up 7 coir units in West Bengal.
 
(v)                29 candidates from West Bengal have been trained at Board’s Training Centre at Alleppey and 131
candidates have been trained at Regional Coir Training & Development Centre, Bhubaneswar, Orissa, as
detailed below:-
 
Advanced Training Course (1 year duration) 17 candidates
Coir Technology Course (6 months duration) 7 candidates
Coir Craft Training Course 5 women candidates
Training in spinning coir yarn at RCTDC 131 candidates
 
Scope for development of coir industry in West Bengal
 
            The Sub-Committee observed that the major constraint in West Bengal for the growth and development of Coir
Industries was about 60 to 65% of coconuts produced in the State are plucked in tender stage.  Only 20% of the total
production has been considered as available for extraction of fibre  which works out to 77.84 million coconuts’ husk. 
All the above available husk of 77.84 million nuts cannot be used for fibre extraction because of the following reasons:
 
(i)
                  There is no system for collection of coconut husks from consumers of coconuts in the State.  Only coconut
traders and goladars (stockists) are the sources of husks as they collect coconuts from primary agricultural
markets of different districts, remove coconut for onward disposal to their clients and keep the husks for
selling to the processors.
(ii)

Problems for development of Coir Industries in the State

            During the course of interaction with the representatives of the State Government the Sub-Committee came
across that the following major problems are being faced by the Coir Industries in West Bengal:-
 
(i)
                 In West Bengal most of the available coconut husk are used for non-remunerative purpose such as
fuel.  About 352 families residing in the district of Howrah and south 24-Parganas are engaged in
crushing of husk by conventional method of wet and hammering.  Thus, they are manufacturing low
cost mattress fibre which could be used for manufacture of value-added coir products.  Only very
nominal portion of the available husk are defibered mechanically for use in the coir industries.
(ii)                Non-existence of any traditional artisans having traditional skill in making coir yarn and other downstream
coir products.
(iii)               Lack of infrastructure for providing training for creating of large number of artisans making yarn and
downstream products.  Existing Training-cum-Servicing Centers of the state Government can provide
training only to a very small numbers of trainees.  Besides, the existing centers are not equipped with modern
machines and technical men like those of Coir Board.
(iv)
              Husk available in West Bengal are unsuitable for extraction by easy process of hand crushing.  Fibre can be
extracted only by mechanical process which involve capital investment.  As a result there are very few
mechanized defibering units and the production of fibre in this State is negligible.  The individual units are to
depend on the supply of fibre from the other states at higher price.
(v)                Lack of product diversification and absence of improved dying process are other factors.  We are still
producing only coir yarn and door mattress of limited variety.
(vi)              Absences of natural soaking places like that of Kerala, non-existence of any collection system of husk,
increasing rate of plucking of tender coconuts etc. also responsible for unsatisfactory development of coir
industries in the state.
(vii)
             Lack of awareness among the people about the use of coconut husk and its value in respect of employment
and income generation, lack of knowledgeable persons, technical institution on coir etc. are also responsible.
 
The Sub-Committee understands that although the state of West Bengal has the potential  growth of the Coir
Industies but at the same time scores of problems are confronting the policy maker for generating proliferation of
coir Industries in the state.  It is fact that there is higher consumption of tender coconut (60 to 65%) and only 20% of
the coconut husk can be made available for coir industry. There is absence of an organized system for collection of
coconut husk from consumers of coconut.  Only coconut traders and Goladars (Stockists) are the sources of husk. 
Traders are available only  in 3 districts viz. Howrah, South 24-Parganas and Midnapur.  Moreover, The coir
processing equipments and machineries available in the State are very old, outdated and obsolete. Poor quality of
raw-material, lack of awareness on the latest development and absence modernized product diversification, further
aggravate the problem. Besides scarcity of skilled manpower and low skill of the existing coir workers, Low
productivity, low management; low investment; lack of entrepreneurs and  no separate wing/officer to look after the
coir development under the State Government are the hurdles in the growth and development of coir industry.
 
Programmes for development of Coir Industries in the State The Government of West Bengal informed as
under:-
 
(i)                 It has been planned to encourage private entrepreneurs to set up defibring units in the state to
increase the production and supply of coir fibre.  A few new defibring units have already been set-up.
(ii)                The existing Training-cum-Service Centre of Uluberia in the district of Howrah and at Dhanchiberia in the
district of South 24-Parganas  will be revived and reopened for production and supply of coir fibre and for
providing training on manufacture of coir products within the current financial year.
(iii)
               The Coir Board may consider for setting up of a Branch/Training Centre in West Bengal so that the
interested entrepreneurs may get technical support.

As per the instruction given by the Committee, the Chairman, Coir Board held discussions on 6.6.2003 with the

CHAPTER-V
Observations/Conclusions and Recommendation of the Committee
            Steps to explore the potential of coir industries in non-traditional States like West Bengal, Orissa, Bihar
and Jharkhand.
            The Committee in its 91st report on Performance of Coir Board stated  that adequate steps must be
undertaken to explore the potential of coir industries in non-traditional States like West Bengal, Orissa, Bihar
and Jharkhand as by giving impetus to the Coir Industry to a non traditional states would enhance the
productions of Coir Industry as well as open new avenues for sustainable employment generation and poverty
alleviation.  The Committee appreciates the Government of West Bengal and the Coir Board for implementing
the suggestion of the Committee so suitably in the State of West Bengal and Union Territory of Andaman and
Nicobar.
ROLE OF COIR BOARD
            The Committee in its 91
st report on ‘Coir Board—A Performance Review’ has made a detailed study of
performance of Coir Board.  However, the Committee appreciates the role of coir board and the West Bengal
Government in chalking out action plan for the promotion and proliferation of coir industries in West Bengal and
Andaman & Nicobar on the suggestion and guidelines of the sub-Committee of Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry for the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries during its study visits to Kolkata and Port
Blair.  The Committee desires that the Coir Board should emphasize on the participation of the Private Sector and
NGOs in the development of the Coir industry for optimum utilization of resources, exploitation of untapped export
market, national level project for creation of awareness about Coir Products, up-gradation of technology, brand
endowment, institutionalization and co-operatization of Coir Sector, development of  Coir Industry, adequate stress on
R&D activities, sketching of appropriate marketing strategy for development of  Coir Industry as a whole. 
Resilient Monitoring-mechanism
The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries and the must guide the Coir Board  in the
execution of action plan meant for West Bengal and Andman & Nicobar.  A resilient monitoring mechanism is required
for timely implementation of developmental programmes and for achieving the cherished objectives and mission
underlining each and every scheme.  The Committee recommends that the Coir Board should be guided by the principle
of management by objectives (MBO) and not merely management by activities.  The Committee is of the view that

West Bengal.  Therefore, the State Department of industries has to play the pivotal role in guiding the developmental
pattern within a determined economic policy.  By having statistical information at the grass root level, that is at the
block and the district level, the District magistrate or the Development commissioner of the region should come out with

root level is desirable.
Potential of Employment generation by coir manufacturing units
            The Committee knows that since Coir Industry is an employment intensive  industry efforts should be
made for searching avenues for generating sustainable and regular employment in the Coir Sector.  
Employment of large number of women in the Coir Sector would fulfill the dreams of empowerment of women
and due share to the economically and socially  backward classes (SCs/STs/OBCs) would enhance the standard of
living of people of weaker section of society.  
Enhancement of the performance and operational efficiency of coir sector
The Committee recommends that the following measures may be undertaken for the enhancement of the
performance and operational efficiency of coir sector in West Bengal and Andaman and Nicobar :-
(i)

Catalogue Shows;

             External Market Development Assistance; Assistance for Sales Promotion Tour and for

(vii)             Awards to be instituted by the State/UT Government/ Coir Board for outstand ­ing
performance in different fields would have positive impact on the performance and operational
efficiency of Coir Sector. 
 EXPORT PROMOTION
            The Committee recommends that the Coir Board should explore the potential of growth in export of coir
and coir products both in terms of quantity and value as produced in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar. The
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries should take promotional steps to
enhance the export potential of Coir Products. The Committee recommends that necessary infrastructure in the
form of offices of the Coir Board may be set up in Kolkata for arranging awareness programmes and training
programmes for the benefit of private entrepreneurs and labourers.
The Committee recommends that a thrust may be given to boost export of coir products and assistance of

The Committee recommends that both the State and UT Governments may be advised to set up a separate
cell for the coir industry in their respective departments of industry, preferably under the SSI sector.  The

the nodal agency for the development of coir where there is coconut cultivation, and entrusted with the

provided by the Coir Board in extending training, especially in the production of value-added goods and in

 Steps  to promote fair competition among producers and exporters of coir and coir products
            The Committee desires that the Coir Board should promote fair competition from among the exporters

R&D Activities being conducted by Coir Board

Collection of Coconut Husk
 
The Committee observes that the Coir Industry gravely suffers from shortage of fiber both white and brown
which sometime has to be imported.  The shortage is mainly because of absence of adequate machinery for collection of
coconut husk from consumers of coconuts in the States in general andWest Bengal and Andaman and Nicobar in
particular.  In the State of West Bengal only the coconut traders or Goldars who collect the husk from the primary
coconut agriculturist market.  The Committee feels that existing arrangements are able to collect only 180 tonnes brown
fiber annually.  With the available husks there is scope of at least 10 modern markets brown fiber manufacturing units to
enhance the production to the level 200 mt per annum.  The Committee, therefore, impress upon the Coir Board and the
Government of West Bengal to make serious efforts for the intensive collection of husk and the system needs to be
institutionalized.
 
            The Committee further impress upon the Government to take a holistic view of the problems being faced
in the Car Nicobar area.  A serious planning is the need of the hour to provide logistic support to the Car
Nicobar Islands.  In order to solve the problem the husk collection, the Committee suggest if it is not possible at
the local level the outside agencies may be brought in to do the job even on commercial line. 
 
            The Committee further recommends that the Government also facilitate the Governments of West Bengal
and  Andaman and Nicobar the logistic support for import of brown fibre from the neighbouring country like Sri
Lanka and Philipines in order to meet the shortage of brown fibre. 
 
Coir Industrial Infrastructure
 
            The Committee recommends that in all major coconut growing areas in the state of West Bengal and the
Union Territory of Andaman & Nicobar, more  clusters may be identified where coir industrial activities may be
established.  In these clusters coir industrial infrastructure should be set up preferably in the private sector. 
Basic techno-economic feasibility/consultancy can be given by the Coir Board for setting up such production
infrastructure.   The Committee further recommends that suitable state level project may be evolved for creation
of awareness about coir products, development of market, production of new and diversified goods of mass
consumption and quality assurance.  A Regional Coir Trade Information Centre may be opened for collection
analyisis its dissemination of information in the state of West Bengal, Andaman & Nicobar, Orissa, Jharkhand
and Bihar.  It should become one of the principal activities of the Coir Board in the region.  Coir sector can be
developed in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar through flow of information especially marketing and
technology, which is possible through IT assisted programmes.
 
Technology Up-gradation
 
            The Committee reiterates its observation as made in its 91
st Report that Technological upgradation is a
sina qua non  for the development of the coir industry.  Eco-friendly process and production technologies,
development of cost-effective and efficient machinery with higher productivity, which reduces drudgery will have
to be developed.  Progress in the development of coir machinery has been very tardy.  The Committee
understands that once the potential of the coir industries in West Bengal  and Andaman & Nicobar are being
assessed the next step should be to strengthen  the  R & D projects.  In this regard, the Committee recommends
that special efforts have to be made to identify the potential coir machinery manufacturers who can be supported
with appropriate technology transfer from any available areas.  This activity may be taken up as joint venture
programmes with greater emphasis on private sector participation ensuring faster commercialization. 
 
            The Committee feels that the  State Government of West Bengal and UT  Government of Andaman &
Nicobar in consultation with the Coir Board  should aim at rapid modernization for the overall sustainable
development of the coir industry, focusing on research and development, quality improvement, human resource
development, better marketing of products and welfare support to the needy, particularly the less-privileged
group like women coir workers who constitute more than 80 per cent  of the work-force.  The Committee stresses
the need for greater emphasis on the involvement of the private sector as well as the concerned state

government.  The Committee recommends that the Coir Board, in coordination with State Governments should
make an endeavour to undertake more sponsored R & D projects in association with reputed agencies in both the
public and private sectors.
 
HRD- Related Activities
           
The Committee feels that appropriate manpower development programme for skill up-gradation in
various fields, especially in non-traditional areas, is to be devised.  Efforts for upgradation of the skill of artisans
and technical/managerial personnel required for the industry are to be organized in coordination with NGOs,
cooperative societies and other state government institutions.  State level training institutions should also be
revitalized to enable them to undertake HRD-related activities.
 
Credit Flow to Coir Industries in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar
           
The Committee feels that the financial assistance for technology upgradation, revitalization and
augmentation of training centers in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar is required .  Such assistance should
also be given for cluster development programmes and marketing both for internal consumption and export. 
Since there is total absence of credit plan for the coir industries in most of the states including Kerala and West
Bengal as coir industries is not being identified as the Key Industry, the Committee recommends that all the
bankers and the district collectors in the state of West Bengal and UT of Andaman & Nicobar  should ensure
that credit plan for coir industries is shown in the district level credit plan.  In this regard the Committee
recommends that Reserve Bank of India should ensure that all the banks at the apex level must be given
direction to the state level unions to provide credit to coir industries.  Once the outlay is provided then it is  to be
decided for each district, as to how adequate credit flow has to earmarked for priority sector and non-priority
sector.   The Government has to ensure in co-ordination of banks and financial instructions that the credit flow
to coir industry should be given  made available without procedural hassles it is only then there would be
maximum utilization of the potential of the coir industries in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar because coir
industry in the said region are in the dire need of smooth credit flow for getting more fibre  manufacturing
activities and markets the products which is essential for the survival of the industry.
 
Transport Subsidy to the coir industries in Andaman and Nicobar
 
            The Committee is of the considered view that for the promotion and proliferation of coir industries in
Andaman and Nicobar transport subsidy and freight subsidy should be given to the areas which are at some
locational disadvantages.  The Ministry of ARI may take up this issue with the Ministry of Finance.
 There is a
need to formulate graded level of transport subsidy i. e. somebody who is at the Car Nicobar should be given
higher level of subsidy then the one at Port Blair.   That is because there are some inherited challenges in the
Island with the population of 3,57,000 out of that the so called urban population at Port Blair is 2,56,00 having a
different population composition than the population composition of the main land.  The island has a very small
market.  Any industry which needs to be sustained has to look at the main land for the market.  There is very
high freight cost handling cost and labour cost.   The price index is very high when the products come to main
land market, they become un competitive.   Therefore, the Island needs to be treated at a separated footing as
comparing to the other man land state because of connectivity problem, labour cost etc.
 
  Assistance of coir board to the coir industries in Andaman and Nicobar
 
            The Committee recommends that the coir board should start the training activities and then promote
establishment of coir industries in the Andaman and Nicobar.  The coir board has to chalk out a net work of
marketing tie-ups and organize co-operative sort of show-room.  Andaman and Nicobar needs holistic schemes
for the promotion and proliferation of coir industries.

RECOMMENDATION
1.1       Structural And Functional Pattern of the Department of   Mines
The Committee notes the structural and functional pattern of the Department of   Mines,   the  Secretariat  for the 
Department of  Mines and  is of the  view  that structural aspect must  match the functional requirement and working  
of  the  organisation with adequate degree  of co-ordination and collaboration   among  various units  thus contributing
on  their  part    in the overall functioning of the organisation in the interest of national  economy .
                                                                                                                        ( Para 1.8 )
                                                                                                                                               
ACTION TAKEN      
 
1.1.1    The structure of the Ministry  of Mines, together with the subordinate offices and other organisations under its
control is adequately geared to its functional requirements and responsibilities. The functions can be broadly categorised
into Survey  and related activities aimed at identifying  mineral resources on the  mainland and offshore, natural hazard
mitigation and environmental preservation; regulation of mining activity; policy for  promotion and development of
mineral resources and mobilising private sector  and foreign investment for the purpose;  Research and Development
with the aim of developing state of the art technology and processes in mineral development and mining activities.
These activities are being performed through the Geological Survey of India (GSI), Mineral Exploration Corporation
Ltd(MECL), the Indian Bureau of Mines(IBM),  Public Sector Undertakings,  3 R&D Organisations viz National
Institute of Rock Mechanics (NIRM), Jawaharlal Nehru Aluminium Research and Development  Design Centre
(JNARDDC) and National Institute of Miners Health (NIMH),  and institutional arrangements for regular interaction
with the State Government  and the Industry viz the Mineral Advisory Council(MAC), Quarterly Performance Review
meetings/Governing Body meetings of the various organisations under the Ministry and meetings of the MAC are being
held regularly  to monitor the operational aspects and review issues relating to Policy requirements.
 
RECOMMENDATION

            The Committee appreciates the achievement of target of NALCO during the year 2002-03.  The Committee has 
reason to accept the non-achievement of the target by Hindustan Copper Limited due to its operational in-efficiency 
during 2002-03 but the Committee is constrained to express its displeasure over the non-achievement of target by

RECOMMENDATION
 
1.3       Philosophy behind the budget proposals
 
            The Committee is pleased to note that  the economic philosophy behind the budget proposals of the Ministry of
Mines is broadly based on the principle that extensive survey and investigation should be carried out in the field of
minerals in which the country is deficient or which are of strategic importance for the country. The Committee strongly
feels that the budget proposals for the year 2003-04 pertaining to the Ministry of Mines are expected to prove as an
instrument to march forward towards the national goal of overall development in the era of liberalized and globalised
economy.   The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of Mines , discharging its core activities as well as its
responsibility and role as a facilitator in the liberalized and globalised economy must guide the organizations and its
PSUs to determine the national goals for growth and development of Mining Industry (i.e. identification of goals,
mineral specific industry wise), Chalking out set of programmes, course of Action required and overall monitoring  for
execution of the plans without time and cost over run.  Any effort for shrugging of its responsibility would raise a
question mark on  the raison-de-itre for   the Ministry of Mines.

            The Committee reiterates its recommendations that in the case of winding up/liquidation of the company the
interest of the workers/employees be protected in all respects.  The committee further made its recommends that the
large tracts of land/other assets should be properly utilized and the assets of the company should not be allowed to
deteriorate owing to inadequate/lack of maintenance.  Regular maintenance of the asset may be kept.  Proper utilization
of asset of the company in the case of winding up means  its proper disposal/strategic sale and mitigation of the
company’s liability of optimum appropriation of proceeds of such strategic sale and not the utilization of the plants and

sate of BGML.

Action Taken   
1.12.1  The efforts made by Government to revive the company go back to the period when BGML was referred to
BIFR in 1992. BIFR had appointed  the Industrial Credit and Investment Corporation of India(ICICI) as the Operating
Agency (OA). ICICI had prepared a rehabilitation scheme and submitted the same to the Government. The
rehabilitation scheme prepared by ICICI involved a very substantial  fresh infusion of funds by the Government of
India. The matter was considered in detail and the Government decided in June, 1997 that the scheme was not feasible
and acceptable.
1.12.2  The Government also  explored  the possibility of rehabilitating BGML through joint venture route.  A
Committee under the chairmanship of the then Additional Secretary (Mines) was constituted for this purpose  The
Committee had appointed M/s S.B. Billimoria and Company as consultants and advertised in national and international
press calling for expressions of interest from potential  co-promoters for participation in the revival of BGML. In
response to the advertisement 20 parties had sent their pre-bid expression of interest, only 11 bought the bid documents
and only 3 submitted their proposal. The Committee finally concluded that none of the bidders were technically,
financially or otherwise capable of undertaking the revival process  through the joint venture route.
1.12.3  The Cabinet in its meeting held on 22
nd December, 1999 directed that BIFR be informed that BGML may now
be allowed to be wound up under the provisions of Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions), Act, 1985 after all
the employees on the rolls of the Company as on 31.3.1999 are offered the benefit of the separation scheme. In the wake
of this the BIFR recommended winding up of the company and, separately the Ministry of Labour issued  closure
orders. These orders were challenged in the High Court of Karnataka.
1.12.4  As regards gold reserves in area technical and geological assessment was carried out by different agencies and
experts including independent international agencies like UNDP who based their report on exploration work done in and
around KGF. However, it did not result in the discovery of  any economically  mineable gold deposits.
1.12.5  The Hon’ble high Court of Karnataka had been apprised of the position during the hearings. In its final order
dated 16.9.03, the High Court has upheld these orders, and has also made certain recommendations regarding the
Voluntary Separation Scheme etc. Further action is being taken in the light of the judgement.
1.12.6  Rs. 15 crores had been released during 2002-03 to BGML to release the employees of BGML in connection with

RECOMMENDATION
 
3.8       Mineral Advisory Council
 
            The Committee is of the view that the Mineral Advisory Council should meet  at least four times in a year to sort
out the problems being faced by Mining Industry and suggest possible solutions and if required modification in the
existing legal framework.  The Committee feels that interaction of the representatives of Central Government, State
Governments and investors in Mining Sector would solve the mutual problems and thus the consensus-ad-idem and
common efforts so evolved would lead to rapid growth and development of Mining Industry in general.
                                                                                                                        ( Para 8.4)
Action Taken   
 
3.8.1    Mineral Advisory Council  is a  High Powered Committee having the Minister in-charge of Mines  as chairman
and  it has  representation from  all concerned Central Ministries/Deptts. and  major minerals  producing States as
permanent member  and other states  as  members  on rotational  basis, besides  leading  mining companies  and
Federation of  Indian  Minerals  Industries(FIMI).  Normally,  Mineral Advisory Council  is  constituted  for  a period
of  four years  and its meetings  are held  annually.  Since  it is  a forum for  interaction among Central Government,
State Govts. and the Industry to sort out  problems being faced by States and the  Industry, views  of all  the Stake
holders are  solicited  and these are consolidated, processed and analysed before   convening  the meeting of  MAC. 
Interactions on various issues are being held in various other fora such as the  Conference of  the State Ministers of 
Mining & Geology,   tripartite meetings among the  Central Govt., State Govts. and investors and  issue specific
meetings and disucssions.    Based  on the discussions and decisions taken in these meetings  necessary amendments  in
the Act if required  and subordinate legislation  are also  carried out  in  consultation with  Legislative Deptt.  Keeping
all this in view,   it may not be possible, feasible or necessary  to hold  meetings of  MAC on a quarterly basis.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.8.2    The Committee is of the view that Mineral Advisory Council may play the proactive role in solving the mutual
problems being faced by Mining Industry and thus encourage common efforts of the policy maker and the Centre and
the State level only when it meets frequently or at least twice a year i.e. once for chalking out the necessary course of
action for accelerating the mining activities and second meeting to review the progress made.  Alternatively a
Committee consisting of representatives of Central Government, State Governments and investors in Mining Sector may
be constituted for brining the modification in the existing legal framework and striking the consensus-ad-idem to resolve
the mutual disputes and undertaking massive action for the rapid growth and development of mining industry in
general.  The said Committee may meet at least quarterly a year.
 
RECOMMENDATIONS
 
Percolation of the National Policy to the State Level
 
            The Committee feels it imperative that policies that emanate from the Central Government should percolate to
the State Government as well as the implementing agencies in the spirit in which these policies are pronounced.  It is
expected that the Mineral Advisory Council in its meeting should persuade the representative of the State Government
as well as the implementing agencies to bring out the necessary amendments in the existing laws, rules and regulations
to harmonize  the policy and practice.
( Para 8.6)

Action Taken   
 
3.10.1  The Ministry agrees with the recommendation and action accordingly is    already being taken. Entry 54 of  the
List –I of the Constitution  gives powers  to the Central  Government  for  regulation of mines  and mineral 
development to the extent  to which such  regulation and development  under the control of  Union  is declared  by 
Parliament  by law  to be expedient  in the public interest. Parliament  has enacted  the   Mines and
Minerals(Development & Regulation)Act,1957 under entry 54  of List-I  to provide for regulation of  mines  and
development of minerals  under the control of  the  Union. Mineral  concession for  major minerals which are
economically and strategically important are governed by  the provision of  the  MMDR,Act,1957 and the two basic
rules viz. MCR,1960 and MCDR,1988 framed  under the Act. Any  amendments   in the Act and the rules decided  in
any forum,   including meeting of MAC, are   carried out  by the Central Government and are equally applicable to 
State Govts.  operating under these rules for grant of  mineral concession for  major minerals.  As regards   grant  of 
mineral concession for minor mineral defined  under  section 3(e) of the Act,  State Governments  are empowered to
frame  their own rules  under Sec.15 of the Act for grant  of  minerals concession  for minor mineral.
 
3.10.2  The Mineral Advisory Council inter-alia reviews the implementation of the mining law, rules and regulations by 
the State Governments and other implementing agencies. In addition to this, the Ministry has also set up a Committee
with representation from the States and concerned central organisations, to identify areas for further action, including
amendments in the law, to ensure that the intent of the policy can be translated  into matching action at the
implementation levels.
 
3.10.3  In view of the above, the Ministry of Mines would humbly submit to the Committee that the objective of the
Committee behind recommending setting up of a review panel for examining various issues regarding National Policy,
desired legislative changes, etc. is being met through alternate  structured arrangements in the Ministry of Mines.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.10.4  The Committee understands the constitutional division and demarcation of the legislative and the administrative
powers of the Centre and the State and is aware of the relevant  laws and rules pertaining to the mining operation and
activities.  However, what the Committee wishes to communicate is the responsibility of the policy makers and
executive mechanism to percolate the message of the national policy at the grass root level.  It is in this respect, that the
Committee recommended that  the Mineral Advisory Council in its meeting should persuade the representative of the
State Government as well as the implementing agencies to bring out the necessary amendments in the existing laws,
rules and regulations to harmonize  the policy and practice.
 
3.10.5  The Committee wishes to point out that the minerals are the hidden treasure beneath the earth and its mining and
commercial utilization is the only way for making use of it for the economic growth and development of the region and
bringing forth general prosperity in the lives of the people inhabiting in the region.  However, it is a naked fact that
mineral enriched zone of India i.e. Bihar, Jharkhand, Orissa, Chhatisgarh, Rajasthan, Madhya Pradesh etc., have been
among the poorest states of India. Mineral based Industrialization is yet to make headway in this part of India.

3.15     Impact of globalisation and liberalization
 
            The Committee is pleased to note that the Government has liberalized the legal framework for the mining
regime, as well as progressively opened up the mining and mineral sector for foreign investment. Statutory amendments
have been carried out by which greater powers have been delegated to the States for streamlining the mining regime,
along with security of tenure for the investors, for globalising the  Indian mineral sector, the policy regime concerning
foreign direct investment has been made more liberal.  The Committee notes that  all proposals for foreign direct
investment up to 100%  in the mining sector, except for precious stones and diamonds, are eligible for automatic
approval.   However, the committee is of the view that the Ministry of Mines should undertake comparative study of the
legal frame work of countries leading in Mining activities and mull out the relevant provisions for incorporating the
same in the Indian Mining legal frame work.  The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of Mines should
also study the negative impact of globalization and liberalization and must  undertake suitable and resilient measure for
over coming the negative impact of globalization and liberalization on the Mining Sector.
                                                                                                                        ( Para 21.3)
Action Taken   
 
3.15.1  Efforts are being continously made to adopt best practices in mining law and procedures and incorporate them in
the Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and the  two basic rules namely Mineral Concession
Rules, 1960 and Mineral Conservation & Development Rules, 1988. Amendments in the Act and the Rules are widely
discussed with the Industry, State Govts. and other stake holders and their views  suitably incorporated to provide equal
level playing field for both public and private investors,  including foreign investors.
 
3.15.2  It may be mentioned that under the mining law, only companies registered in India can be granted mineral
concessions. Therefore, while globalisation and liberalization have paved the way for greater capital inflow for the
mining sector, the law ensures that there is no negative fall-out through operation of   foreign companies  which is not
subject to the laws of the land.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
