3.17     Minimum time gap during the process of  grant of mineral concession,
 
             So far as the involvement of a number of agencies  in the grant of mineral concessions before the
commencement of  actual operation acting as a deterrent factor is concerned, it is suggested that the Ministry of Mines
should  come forward with the proposal /suggestions for the absolutely  required structures, stages and process for the
grant of Mineral concession vis-à-vis the existing system.   The Committee is of the view that there should be minimum
time gap during the process of  grant of mineral concession, clearance from the Ministry  of Environment and Forest 
and the final commencement of actual operation.
( Para 22.5)
 
Action Taken
 
3.17.1  From time to time suggestions are made to the Government for formulating a single window  clearance
mechanism. The mineral concessions are granted by the State Governments under the Mines and Minerals
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1957(MMDR Act) and rules framed thereunder. The investors are required to take
other clearances for working the mineral concessions granted, for example: permission for aerial surveys from the
Director General of Civil Aviation, clearances under various statutes administered by the Ministry of Environment and
Forest. etc. Since the clearance are granted under different statutes, the Government has laid emphasis on the State
Governments/various Departments to work in coordination, so that investors could be benefited. The Ministry  of Mines
has sensitized the State Governments and various Central Ministries/Departments on the need to work in coordination

4.13     Fiscal Issues Pertaining to Mining Industry
The Committee after having giving a proper thought to the fiscal related proposals as suggested by FIMI and the
Ministry of Mines has arrived at the conclusion  that the Ministry of Finance should give due consideration to the
following items for the rapid growth and development of mining sector:-
In regard to the Section 35E of the Income Tax Act, 1961, the costs incurred during the pre production period should be
amortizable from the year of commencement of commercial production over the balance period of mining lease, or a
lesser period at the option of the lessee.  Accordingly, therefore, all expenditure incurred prior to commercial production
including the expenditure incurred on site and development acquisition should be eligible for amortization over the
minmum lease period of 20 years or a leser period at the option of the lessee.  The section 35E of the Income Tax Act,

DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman,

LEVEL  PLAYING  FIELD  FOR
THE  INDIAN  CAPITAL  GOODS  INDUSTRY
 
CHAPTER - I
IMPACT  OF  FISCAL  POLICY  AND  EXIM POLICY  ON  CAPITAL  GOODS  INDUSTRIES
        In early eighties, when India's economy was on an uptrend, there was need for investment in the infrastructure sector.
Investment from within India was not forthcoming mainly because of higher rate of interest and private sector risk aversions.
Investment during those years was mainly from multilateral/bilateral funding agencies. For judicious usage of these funds, the
projects were established under International Competitive Bidding procedures. Indian companies were also eligible to participate
in the bidding procedure. Overseas suppliers could enjoy soft export financing from their exim banking and other export benefits
prevailing in those countries. The Indian companies were also extended the duty free raw material imports and refund of excise
duty on their finished goods to have a level playing field. Supplies to such projects were termed as Deemed Exports.
        As a part of the commitment given to WTO, the peak rate of customs duty was to be brought down to a level agreed with
WTO in a time bound matter and accordingly the rate of customs duty for the project was also reduced gradually. Project import

143rdreport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/143rdreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:45:13]
duty for the power projects was settled at 20% + Nil CVD since 1992-93.
        Since the import tariffs were coming down, the domestic industry was facing tough competition from the foreign suppliers.
Till the time the customs duty was 20% with nil CVD, the domestic industry was getting the refund of Terminal Excise Duty as
most of the projects were multilateral/bilateral funded projects. Later, as the economic conditions improved, the investment started
coming from within the country as well. Recognizing the importance of infrastructure projects in area of power and refinery
sector, DGFT announced that the supplies to such projects will be treated as deemed exports, even if these were not funded by
multilateral/bilateral agencies. Therefore all the supplies to power projects were treated as deemed exports w.e.f. 31.3.97. in the
absence of CVD on the direct import under Project Imports, there was no level playing field for the domestic industry, as there
supplies were subjected to Excise Duty. Therefore, domestic industry represented to the Government for refund of TED, which
was permitted by DGFT from 18.10.96.
1.3   After 18.10.1996, there were equal opportunities for the foreign suppliers and the domestic suppliers as the imports were
subjected to customs duty @ 22% with Nil CVD and domestic supplier was getting the refund of TED. This position remained
unchanged till 28.02.99.
1.4   During the period 1996-99, power projects attracted basic customs duty of 20% with Nil CVD. The terminal excise duty paid
by Indian manufacturers was refunded by the office of DGFT. This provided protection of 20% to indigenous industry against the
disadvantages suffered on account of sales tax and other local levies on inputs/final product, higher cost of finance, infrastructure
inadequacies etc.
1.5   During the budget of 1999-2000, the customs duty was reduced to 5.5% from 22% but CVD was imposed @16%. The
overall impact on the imported goods was 22.38%. Therefore this change in the duty structure had not impacted much on the
imports. Domestic suppliers continued to get the refund of TED in spite of imposition of CVD @ 16%. But DGFT while
announcing the Exim Policy effective from the year 2000, discontinued the refund of TED to the domestic suppliers. Although the
domestic suppliers were permitted duty free imports, the earlier gap between the foreign supplier and domestic supplier, which
was 2.38% reduced to 8.03% [22.38% - 16% + 1.65% (5.5% of the import content of 30%)]. This gap has been further reduced to
7.45%, since the surcharge of customs duty is withdrawn [21.8% - 16% + 1.65% (5% of import content of 30%)]. This has put the
domestic suppliers in a disadvantageous position.
1.6   It is pertinent to note that prior to 31.3.2000 i.e. date when refund of terminal excise duty was withdrawn, domestic
manufacturers have secured orders under international competitive bidding by passing on to the customer the benefit of refund of
TED as applicable in the extant Exim Policy. In case of power and fertilizer projects, where the cycle time for competition is
normally 3-4 years, the schedule for supply of capital goods is invariably 3 years.
1.7   In all such contracts, excise duty is charged extra over and above the basic price of the equipment. Since excise duty was
refundable to the manufacturer, it was not included in the price settled with customers. With the withdrawal of this refund, the
16% excise duty being quite substantial has to be borne by the manufacturer. In all such contracts where customers are neither
agreeable to renegotiate the prices to compensate the manufacturers nor are they ready to pay the applicable excise duty, the
domestic suppliers are adversely affected resulting in heavy financial loss.
1.8   In this regard the Committee notes that the objective of the Exim Policy has been outlined in the Exim Policy at para 1.4,
which is reproduced below :
(a)  To facilitate sustained growth in exports to attain a share of at least 1% of global merchandise trade.
(b)  To stimulate sustained economic growth by providing access to essential raw materials, intermediates, components,
consumables and capital goods required for augmenting production and providing services.
(c)  To enhance the technological strength and efficiency of Indian agriculture, industry and services, thereby improving their
competitive strength while generating new employment opportunities, and to encourage the attainment of internationally
accepted standards of equality.
(d)  To provide consumers with good quality goods and services at internationally competitive prices while at the same time
creating a level playing field for the domestic producers.
         As state at (d) above, the Central Government provides a level playing field for the domestic producers and therefore,
wherever, the domestic producer secure orders even from within India, such supplies are treated as Deemed Exports. Provided,
that such orders are obtained by the domestic producers against International Competitive Bidding Procedures. Deemed Exports
are eligible for any/all benefits in respects of manufacture and supply of goods.
1.9   Following different types of Power Projects are installed in India : 
(a)  power projects financed by multilateral or bilateral agencies/funds
(b)  power projects with domestic funding
(c)  mega power projects
(d)  nuclear power projects
(e)  captive power plants
1.10So far as the power projects covered under (a), (c) and (d) above, all the benefits viz.
(i)   Advance license and Deemed Exports
(ii)  Deemed Exports drawback; and

143rdreport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/143rdreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:45:13]
(iii)  Refund of TED
are available to the domestic suppliers, but regarding power projects under (b) above, only two benefits namely Advance License
for deemed exports and deemed exports drawback are available.
        In this category of projects, the domestic industry has been requesting the Central Government for refund of TED, which was
withdrawn on the supplies made from 1.4.2000. It was mentioned that the domestic industry is suffering from cost disadvantages
like inadequate and high cost of infrastructure, higher cost of financing, sales tax, octroi and other taxes etc., which are of the tune
of 14% to 23% depending upon the location of the project and the supplier. The customs duty should be pegged at 20%. In the
light of budget speech given by Finance Minister who stated in his budget speech that by the year 2004-05, there would be two
basic rates of customs duties namely, 10% covering generally raw materials, intermediates and components and 20% covering
generally final products.
 
CHAPTER - II
IMPLEMENTATION  OF  36
TH, 45TH AND  59TH  REPORTS
2.0   India is still a developing country and the domestic industry continues to suffer cost disadvantages such as sales tax, octroi,
higher cost of finances and infrastructure, bottlenecks to the extent of 14% to 23% while competing with foreign companies. The
domestic industry therefore should be compensated in one way or the other.
2.1   The Industrial Policy of 1991 started the process of de-licensing. The process of de-regulation was aimed at enlarging
competition and allowing new firms to enter the markets. The market was opened up to domestic entrepreneurs/industrialists,
which was reserved for public sector undertakings, and foreign capital was provided free entry up to 51% equity in high
technology areas. With the advent of globalisation, when World Bank-aided projects started to come to country, the lifting of
import control and drastic reduction of import duties, competition from overseas posed a problem to the domestic capital goods
industry. It has become difficult to stay in the race for this industry in the face of stiff competition from the multinational giants.
2.2   Despite the tremendous odds even on date, there are examples of various domestic Indian companies in sectors like
automobiles, steel, engineering, etc. in both public and private sectors that have successfully withstood the changes brought about
by the liberalization of Indian economy, for example Maruti and Tata cars are being exported. TISCO has been recognized as one
of the least cost steel producers in the world and companies like IRCON, BHEL and L&T have been successfully executing
contracts abroad. These companies have managed to meet the stiff competition from foreign giants but the absence of a level
playing field put increasing pressures on their competitiveness and profitability.
2.3   The committee deliberated upon the matter and in its 36th Report observed as under :
"One such company (BHEL) which has successfully withstood the changes brought about by the liberalization of Indian
economy. The impressive track record of it calls for a special mention of its achievements. As a matter of fact, BHEL is a
role model for other PSUs of Ministry of Heavy Industry. For it has managed to stay in the race despite the odds faced by
it as a result of stiff competition unleashed by the multinational giants operating in its field of specialization namely,
manufacture of power plants. Though BHEL has managed to sustain its viability yet it is facing some unfair challenges.
The absence of a level playing field vis-a-vis its multinational competitors has been posing stiff challenges to the
company. This is leading to an ever-increasing pressure on its profitability. Despite this, the company has been constantly
upgrading its technology and has also been successful in acquiring state of the art technology used in HVDC power
projects. This reflects the commitments of the company as a whole to serve the nation even when the odds are stacked
against it. Therefore, what this company requires is a little help from the Government in the form of suitable policy
measures. In this regard, the sub-committee draws the attention of the Government to the issues of price and purchase
preference to BHEL, and import duty concessions to the foreign companies. Though in some cases price and purchase
preference is granted to the PSUs, the positive results of this measure are negated by the import duty concessions
extended to the foreign companies by the Government. These concessions and exemptions are precisely the reasons for
the playing field not being level for domestic companies or for that matter PSUs as the bids offered by foreign players are
much lower in comparison to the ones offered by PSUs. In other words, the competition is killed well before it begins.
The committee believes that the need of the hour is not to go back to the days of protectionism rather to provide a level
playing field to all the players for the sake of healthy competition.
Committee's Recommedations
2.4   In view of the above, the committee has come to the conclusion that the Government should take necessary policy measures
to extend 15% price and purchase preference to BHEL vis-a-vis its bids for domestic power projects. It also recommends that the
Government should review its policy of giving duty concessions to the foreign companies in as much as it leads to disadvantages
to the domestic companies especially the PSUs. It is the considered view of the committee that foreign companies should not be
shown favour at the expense of domestic companies.
2.5   Comments from Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises are as under :
"The Ministry has taken up the following issues with the Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Commerce, the issue
relating to restoration of refund of terminal excise duty as available to domestic bidders in the Exim Policy 1999-2000.
2.6   Ministry of Commerce declined the proposal of this ministry to restore refund of Terminal Excise Duty (TED) in EXIM
Policy 1999-2000, as these benefits are directly related to the incidence of Customs Duty (CD) and Counter Veiling Duty (CVD)
on the imports for the project, i.e. whenever the imports are exempted from the incidence of CVD, the domestic supplier is given
the benefit of refund of TED. In the budget 2000-2001, in respect of power projects other than mega-power projects, fertilizer
projects and refineries, CVD has been increased to 16% and therefore the benefits of refund of TED is withdrawn from such
projects.

entitled for the benefit of refund of TED. This issue was discussed specifically with DOR at the time of the formulation of
EXIM Policy, (Revised Edition: 2000) and it was decided that all the supplies effected from 1.4.2000 will not be entitled for
refund of TED. This is also because of the fact that any import which would have taken place after 1.4.2000, would have
been subjected to the imposition of CVD.

import that is permitted freely under this Policy is subsequently subjected to any restriction or regulation then the shipment of the
export or import which is made within the original validity of the irrevocable letter of credit established before the date of
imposition of such restriction shall be ordinarily permitted. Accordingly, this transitional arrangement provides protection only
where a free item is subjected to import or export restrictions subsequently. Exim Policy does not envisage any transitional
arrangement consequent to change in duty structure. Since refund of TED has been withdrawn consequent to imposition of 16%
CVD, no transitional arrangement is possible.

OBSERVATIONS/ RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
6.0   With the announcement of New Industrial Policy 1991 and concomitant policy initiatives that followed, resulted in huge
impetus to industrial activity in the country. This warranted huge capital investments in infrastructure and to meet this
investments, finances were at times obtained from multilateral funding agencies like World Bank, Asia Development Bank, etc.
6.1   In the hitherto  scenario, even the supplies made to these projects also qualified for Deemed Export benefits and the present
procurement of these funding agencies also stipulated that price preference to the extent that are consciously quantified by the host
country for such projects in the form of tariff only barriers or customs/excise/countervailing duties.
6.2   At the same time, it is important to note that in spite of the spirit of new industrial policy being carried out through
liberalization of linkages like monetary policy, liberalization of licensing including introduction of automatic routes, progressive
reduction of interest rates, the Indian capital goods industry had not attained a state of level playing ground with the international
capital goods manufacturers due to comparative higher cost of capital, sales taxes and other levies at State Government levels,
higher infrastructure bottlenecks, etc. hence, it is imperative that the level playing field had to be accorded to the Indian capital
goods industry to the extent that is recognizable by the multilateral funding agencies through fiscal instruments.
6.3   One of the objectives of Exim Policy is to provide consumers with good quality good and services at internationally
competitive prices while at the same time a level playing field for the domestic players. Central Government provides a level
playing field for the domestic producers and therefore, wherever, the domestic producers secure orders even from within India,
such suppliers are treated as Deemed Exports, provided such orders are secured through International Competitive Bidding
procedure. Deemed Exports are eligible for all benefits in respect of manufacture and supply of goods.
6.4   All power projects are entitled to get (i) advance license and Deemed Exports, (ii) Deemed Exports drawback and (iii)
Refund of TED. But domestic suppliers in power projects with domestic funding are getting only first two benefits. Prior to
1.4.2000, such suppliers were getting many more benefits. With the announcement of Exim Policy on 1.4.2000 the refund of RED
was discontinued with the reduction of BCD and imposition of CVD. Such mid term policy changes resulted in either the
manufacturer/supplier absorbing substantial loss or project cost substantially going up. When the matter was taken up with DGFT,
they maintained that changes effected in the Exim Policy came into affect immediately and all supplies effected from 1.4.2000 are
not entitled for TED.
6.5   Initially, Ministry of Power supported the contention of Department of Heavy Industries for restoration of refund of TED.
However, when the Committee directed that Committee of Secretaries be constituted and a report be given in the matter, the
Ministry of Power submitted a separate note (Annexure VI).
6.6   The Committee understands from the oral evidence tendered by the Department of Heavy Industries and Ministry of Power
that although a conclusion was reached at the meeting of Committee of Secretaries and Joint Secretaries of Department of
Revenue and Department of Heavy Industries and Ministry of Power, did work out the number and it was felt that the number,
which were being worked out, came to a stage where there was no increase in the cost of the project. Ministry of Power, however,
thought that apart from an increase or decrease in the project cost, the input of competition is necessary.
6.7    In the present scenario the domestic industries get an advantage of 4.4%. if BCD is 21% and CVD is 0% and TED is
restored, the domestic industries would get a substantial advantage over foreign bidder. The new arrangement will constrain the
competition and foreign bidders would shy away from bidding. Moreover, this kind of margin does not exist in today’s
competition. If there were limited bids, the cost would be higher than the estimates. Whenever, there are large numbers of parties
participating in the bid, there would be competitive rate leading to reduction of cost of package. In case of limited bids, the cost of
power would be higher and ultimately people have to bear the brunt of such a limited bidding. India’s cost of power is three times
higher than China who is India’s close competitor.
6.8    Moreover, foreign exchange fluctuation on a long term basis and interest regime should be taken into account before
finalizing any scheme for the domestic industry. Foreign exchange fluctuation is very good today and Indian companies are able
to get foreign exchange on a long-term basis. Today, rate of interest has also come down which is a motivating factor for reducing
the cost of product. Large industries are able to get finance form lead banks at 7% which was 12% or 13% 3 year ago.
6.9    Indian industries are facing higher tariff which is a major constrain for the Indian industries. A Committee headed by Deputy
Chairman, Planning Commission, is looking after all these issues. In view of this, present status quo may be maintained till all
issues are addressed.
6.10  There is one task force also, which is looking after investment and reforms in power sector and other aspects for giving
incentives to power sector. When it finalises its study, all those things will be taken into account during budget exercise.
6.11  The Committee observes that the basic concept of Exim Policy was to provide a level playing field between domestic
supplier and foreign suppler. If started form those projects which were funded by multilateral agencies where items were allowed
under zero duty to give the domestic suppliers a level playing field so that can they can compete with the foreign companies. But
in the light of Chaturvedi Repot, BCD was brought down from 20% to 5% and CVD was intorduced 16% and TED was
withdrawn. CVD was the protection given to domestic industry over and above 5% BCD. The industries are supposed to have a
built in cushion of 5% and they are getting the  deemed export benefit. But there are certain inefficiencies and bottlenecks in our
systems. The domestic industries have to pay various taxes to the State Governments and they have some legacies of the past in
the form of townships, which are social obligations, and the cost of this in our country is very high. These disadvantages are not
neutralized. The Committee feels that some sort of balance is to be stuck to neutralize the disadvantage faced by the domestic
industries.
6.12  The Committee observes that Government should see how domestic industry would survive in the present globalised world.
Government has to see the interest of domestic industries compared to the foreign comparies. Government should also look into

143rdreport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/143rdreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:45:13]
the matter relating to the local taxes domestic industry has to pay.
6.13  The Committee is not against globalisation process, but at the same time it would also want to see to it that reasonable
protection is given to the domestic industries. Similarly, power cost should not go up in the larger interest of the consumers but it
should be seen that capital industry is also protected.
6.14  The Committee is booking at it in a larger perspective, that is, the interest of the country. Every ministry has its own
problem, but they have to find a way to protect the domestic industry. There should be a give and take attitude.
6.15  If a contract has been awarded earlier and if Government make any changes in policy, the whole contract remains in
dispute. This makes projects very difficult. The Committee, therefore, recommends that whenever change is made in the
Exim Policy, it should be for the prospective contracts.
6.16  Since disadvantage forced by the domestic industries due to mid term policy change, the Committee recommends
that where orders/letters of intent has been placed before 31.3.2000 for power and fertilizer projects, the provision of Exim
Policy of 1999-2000 may be made applicable to allow refund of Terminal Excise Duty.
6.17  In the present scenario, there are three stake holders with redard to the establishment of power projects, namely, the Project,
Revenue Department, and lastly the Domestic suppliers.
6.18  The project cost can be reduced if the import duties are reduced but in that case, there will be adverse impact on the revenue
and the domestic suppliers will also be adversely affected. To balance the interests of all parties, if the overall duties which are
presently 21.8% (5% CD + 16% CVD) are reduced to a single customs duty of 20%, the project cost shall come down by 1.8%
and the effect of revenue will not be substantial.
6.19  In view of the proposal of reduction of CVD to NIL from present rate of 16%, the domestic industry shall become eligible
for refund of TED. The refund of TED to the domestic supplier is also essential as they supper from other cost disadvantages like
Sales Tax, infrastructure bottleneck, higher cost of finances etc. which together account for 14% to 23%.
6.20  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the duty structure should be rationlised as under:
  l            Customs Duty 20%
  l            CVD - nill
  l   With corresponding refund of TED to the domestic suppliers
6.21  The Committee finally recommends that Government should take into account the recommendations made by this
Committee while doing the budget exercise (2004-05) and provide a level playing field for the Indian capital goods
industry.

CHAPTER - I
Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
1.1       Jurisdiction of Ministry of ARI
 
The Committee notes that the Ministry of ARI is entrusted with the functions/duties of implementations of
policies, programmes and schemes and in turn play the role of a policy maker, advocate and a facilitator.  The
Committee also finds that the Ministry monitors the activities undertaken by its fields agencies through formal
structure as well as informal meetings.  However, the Committee is of the view that the Ministry of ARI would
act promptly as a policy maker, advocate and facilitator and promote Agro and Rural Industries by effective
implementation of policies, programmes and schemes undertaken by its various field agencies without time and
cost over run.  The existing monitoring mechanism must ensure that targets are achieved within the stipulated
time frames.  The Committee further recommends that the Ministry of ARI should have review meetings of its
field agencies to take stock of the progress made in the implementation of various schemes and programmes.
(Para- 1.8)
 
Action Taken
 
1.1.1    The monitoring mechanism has been strengthened in the Ministry and Priority Agenda for Action has been
evolved for Coir, KVIC and PMRY at the level of implementing agencies and regular interaction is held by the Ministry
officials besides the monitoring mechanism during their official visits to the respective organizations and when the
Chief Executives/Chairman of KVIC/Coir Board visit this Ministry.   A Confederation of Promotion of Khadi and
Village Industries has been set up to give a boost to the marketing effort of KVIC.  This is being done to ensure that the
targets set forth for the year 2003-04 are achieved.    During 2002-03, the implementation of Rural Employment
Generation Programme (REGP) was decentralized. As a result of re-organisation of the scheme, KVIC could give
employment to 3.61 lakh as against the target of 4.00 Lakh i.e. 90%.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
1.2       Objective assessment of the financial requirement of K&VI Sector
 
The Committee is of the opinion that the Ministry of ARI should undertake an objective assessment of the
financial requirement of K&VI Sector, Coir Sector, Tiny and micro Enterprises, in tandem with KVIC, Coir
Board, PMRY division and accordingly take up the case with the Ministry of Finance and Planning Commission
for providing the required fund as per the needs of the Industries, so that no scheme should suffer due to lack of
fund.  The Committee desires that efforts should be taken for avoiding the gap between the projected demand
and the actual fund earmarked for specific purpose in one particular financial year.
(Para-2.5)

Action Taken
 
1.2.1    The Ministry of ARI while projecting its demand in the plan for 2004-05 has made an objective assessment of
the requirement of funds for the KVI Sector, Coir Sector and Tiny and micro enterprises based on the needs of the
industries and on the target of job creation as decided in the 10
th Plan document. Accordingly, the Ministry has already
projected a BE demand of Rs.801.56 crores for 2004-05. However, the final plan size will be based on resource
availability and competing claims of various Ministries.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
1.3       Non achievement of Targets
 
The Committee further expresses its concern that the targets have not been achieved by KVIC and Coir
Board during 2002-03, which shows that monitoring mechanism has to be strengthened to make it vigilant and
effective. The Committee hopes that target would be achieved during 2003-04.
(Para 2.10)
Action Taken
 
1.3.1    During the year 2003-04, the monitoring mechanism at the level of Ministry of ARI has been strengthened and
monthly and quarterly reviews of targets are made at the level of Secretary. KVIC and Coir Board have also taken
several steps for streamlining the implementation mechanism to ensure that their prime objectives of employment
generation and export promotion are met. In the case of KVIC, the REGP Programme has been decentralized and
release of funds at the Ministry level is done on a regular basis during 2003-04. As a result, achievement under REGP
for 2003-04 (1
st half year) has been 0.88 lakh jobs as against 0.46 lakh jobs achieved during the same period in 2002-03.
Similarly, in case of Coir Board, exports have shown an increase of 3.5% in value and 8% in quantity during the first
half of the year compared to the same period last year.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
1.4       Appropriations of funds for Xth Five Year Plan
 
The committee notes the financial projections/ appropriations of funds for Xth Five Year Plan for KVIC
(Non-NE states as well as NE Region) and in respect of Coir Board and expresses the hope that the funds so
earmarked would be fully utilized and physical targets would be achieved accordingly.
(Para 3.6)
 
Action Taken
 
1.4.1    The Ministry of ARI has released 60% of the budgetary allocation by October, 2003 so that the implementing
agencies i.e. KVIC , Coir Board and PMRY division are able to fully utilize their budgetary allocation for 2003-04
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
1.5       Problem of unemployment and poverty
 
The Committee is of the view that Government should chalk out long term and short-term policy to deal
with the twin problem of unemployment and poverty.  Since the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industry has greater
role to play (with unemployment and poverty being widespread in rural areas) in opening the avenues for gainful
employment.  It is a well known fact that employment generation would enhance the purchasing power in the
economy which in turn would boost the consumption pattern in rural economy and their demand in the market. 
Demand-driven economy would automatically lift the standard of living of people residing in the rural areas
thereby the system so developed would arrest the urban migration as well.

(Para 3.7)     
Action Taken
 
1.5.1    The Ministry of ARI has based its targets for employment generation on the S.P. Gupta report for creating
10million job opportunities per annum. The S.P. Gupta report has been prepared keeping in view the twin objectives of
employment generation and poverty alleviation for all sectors of the economy. As per the said report, a target of creating
3.75 million jobs has been fixed for the Ministry of ARI for the 10
th Plan Period. Accordingly, actual targets of
employment generation are fixed based on the overall target and the achievement during the previous year. During
2003-04, the target for REGP has been revised from 4 lakh jobs to 5 lakh jobs, while the target for PMRY has been
maintained at 3.3. lakh jobs.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
1.6
              Appropriation of fund under Revenue Section
 
The Committee takes note of the appropriation of fund under Revenue Section earmarked for KVIC,
Coir Board, PMRY and NPRI for meeting the plan and non-plan expenditure during the year 2002-03. The plan
outlay for revenue expenditure in BE during the year 2002-03 was to the tune of Rs.578.00 crore while the same
has been projected at the level of Rs.579.40 crore for the year 2003-04. A minute observation of appropriation of
plan outlay under Revenue Section for KVIC during 2002-03 reveals that while the actual expenditure as on 24
th
March, 2003 in terms of Interest Subsidy (Khadi), interest subsidy (VI) has been as per budget estimation and
revised estimation whereas the expenditure exceeded the projected figure for Khadi grant (Rs.6986 lakh against
budget estimation and revised estimation of Rs.6930 Lakh while the expenditure remained short of estimated and
revised estimate in terms of Khadi loan, VI Grant, VI loan S&T (Khadi) and S&T (VI). The Committee desires
that the Ministry of ARI should explain the reasons for these variations in the Action Taken Note of present
report.
(Para 4.11)
ACTION TAKEN
 
1.6.1    The Interest Subsidy under Khadi & Village Industries has been the same as per the BE & RE because this is
only for book adjustment and for which no fund is released by the Ministry.
 
Khadi Grant  
 
1.6.2    There was expenditure of Rs. 69.86 lakhs on Khadi grant during the year 2002-03 against RE of Rs. 69.3 lakhs. 
It was due to the reason that the RE amount of Rs. 69.30 lakhs was exclusive of provision for NER regions whereas
expenditure of Rs. 69.86 lakhs included expenditure for NER regions.
 
Khadi Loan
 
1.6.3    KVIC is not perceived to be a financing institution as per the recommendations of the High Powered Committee
and financial institutions are not encouraged to provide loan for Khadi.  Due to these reasons, there were less
applications from khadi institutions and only an amount of Rs. 21 lakhs was disbursed against the budgetary provision
of Rs. 134 lakhs. (RE) during 2002-03.
 
V.I. Loan
 
1.6.4    As per recommendations of the High Powered Committee set up by the Govt, KVIC is no longer perceived to be
a financial institution.  Therefore institutions are not encouraged to obtain loan from KVIC for setting up of village
industries.  Village industries are now being set up under REGP for which bank loans are obtained by
institutions/entrepreneurs directly.  However, subsidy of 25% to 30% is being given by KVIC.  Due to these reasons,
release of loan is for setting up of VI industries has been discontinued and only a token provision of Rs. 1 lakh has been
kept in the budget to meet commitments of the previous years.  However, no amount was released during the year 2002-

RECOMMENDATION
 
 1.7     Non-Plan Expenditure Under Revenue Section
 
The committee while examining the actual appropriation of non-plan expenditure for KVIC and coir board
during the year 2002-03, notes that the expenditure decreased by Rs. 10 lakhs for KVIC (projected at Rs. 8477 lakhs
against the BE 2002-03 of Rs. 8487) due to Government’s strict economy instructions while the same increased by Rs.
10 lakhs for coir board due to payment of increment benefit etc to the staff of the Cori-Board.  The Committee is of the
view that a good budget keeps the non-plan expenditure under control while impetus is given on plan expenditure.
(Para-4.13)
ACTION TAKEN
 
1.7.1    The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for compliance.
 
RECOMMENDATION
 
1.8     Rationalization Of Expenditure Under Revenue Section
   
The response to the Committee’s question pertaining to the measures/steps undertaken by the Ministry of ARI
for rationalizing the expenditure under Revenue section accounts are got audited from the Comptroller and Auditor
General of India or his nominee and a utilization certificate in respect of funds are obtained, is not a logical succinct
explanation.  The manager at the helm of financial management in the Ministry of ARI should appreciate that auditing,
by C & AG or his nominee and obtaining of utilizing certificate is a post expenditure of the fund earmarked, while steps
for rationalization of non-plan expenditure, if any, is a pre-expenditure exercise, where scope and strategy for
rationalizing the expenditure is searched and chalked out and the cannons of such strategy is being observed during the
process of expense of fund and ultimately at the end of the financial year success or failure of the rationalization
strategy could be examined.  The committee hopes that the Ministry of ARI would appreciate the process and system for
rationalization of non-plan expenditure and translate the same into action during the financial year 2003-04 and
accordingly inform the committee the out come of rationalization strategy as adopted by the Ministry.
(Para-4.14)
 
Action Taken
 
1.8.1    For 2003-04, the Ministry of ARI has examined all the items of non-plan expenditure in consultation with the
Department of Expenditure in an effort to see that there is rationalization in non-plan expenditure. Accordingly,
Department of Expenditure has recommended a reduction of Rs.25 crores under Interest Subsidy (Khadi) and Interest
Subsidy (VI) on the non-plan side as the same is only a book adjustment and does not involve any cash outgo from the
exchequer. Accordingly, Ministry of Finance has recommended that Interest Subsidy (Khadi) and Interest Subsidy (VI)
should be reduced from the present level of Rs.28.36 crores to Rs.3.36 crores for RE 2003-04.

RECOMMENDATION
 
1.9       Secretarial services for the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries
 
Presently, the Secretarial services for the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries are shared with the Ministry of
SSI which as per the opinion adequately addresses the requirements of the Ministry of ARI, the Committee is of the
view that the Government may think for providing a separate secretariat economic services especially for the Ministry
of Agro and Rural Industries because the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries has a tremendous role to play in the
building of rural economy of India which in turn would transform the economic structure of the nation and in case the
separate secretariat economic structure of the nation and in case the separate secretariat economic services for Ministry
of ARI is not feasible the Government should chalk out a scheme for shifting of surplus officer and staff from the
Department/ Ministry where business has decreased and also in light of the fact that Expenditure Reforms Commission
decreased and also in light of the fact that Expenditure Reforms Commission (ERC) has recommended either for closure
or rightsizing of Department/ Ministry.
(Para-6.1)
Action Taken
 
1.9.1    The Ministry of ARI was created in September, 2001. A proposal was sent to the Department of Expenditure for
allocation of additional staff for the Ministry of SSI and the Ministry of ARI to enable them to function as full-fledged
Ministries with separate Secretariat Economic Services. Department of Expenditure has agreed with the proposal in
principle for allocation of additional staff. The Ministry of SSI and Ministry of ARI have now taken up the matter with
Department of IPP, Ministry of Commerce and Industry to post the additional requirement of staff. Once adequate
complement of staff is made available to the Ministry of SSI and Ministry of ARI, it will be possible for creating
separate Secretariat Economic Services for the Ministry of ARI.
 
RECOMMENDATION
           
1.10     Shortage of fund for Entrepreneurial Development Programme
 
The Committee is quite concerned to observe that for the year 2002-03 against the projected requirement of
Rs.180.00 crore, only Rs.152.10 crore have been provided under the budget allocation.  The result was shortage of fund
for Entrepreneurial Development Programme.  Again the projected requirement of funds for the PMRY was Rs.180.00
crore for the plan target of 2.20 lakh beneficiaries for the PMRY for the year 2003-04 against which only Rs.152.10
crore have been earmarked at B.E. Stage.  The Committee does not appreciate the regular use of the system of
adjustment of surplus/deficit of the preceding years to the following year just because PMRY is an on going scheme. 
The system should not be used as a matter of routine practice.  It may be used rarely only under compelling
circumstances and preference should be given/efforts must be made for the provision of sufficient fund for PMRY. 
(Para 7.6.2)
Action Taken
 
1.10.1  During the year 2002-03, the allocated budget for the PMRY Scheme was Rs.152.10 crores.  In addition
Rs.16.90 crores were earmarked for the non lapsable common pool for the NE States including Sikkim.  Hence, the total
funds available for the year 2002-03 was 169.00 crores.  The shortage of funds for entrepreneurial development

RECOMMENDATION
           
1.11     Target under PMRY
 
The Committee is of the opinion that government should fix the target under PMRY keeping in mind the stark
reality of population growth rate, quantum of poverty and absolute number of unemployment (disguised unemployment
as well as seasonal employment).  Need of the hour is formulation of Integrated and Total Planning after having
objective assessment of empirical fact and figures.  The rate of employment generations must be twice/thrice than the
population growth rate so that the problem of unemployment gets out rooted in a time bound manner.  The Committee
would be pleased to observe that the planning is done for exploring employment generation at the geometrical rate and
population growth be limited at the arithmetical rate.  Though at the first instance the suggestion may seem illusive but
to change the fate of India it has to be done and government must strive in this direction.  This is possible only through
coordinated and total Planning and when the problems of Population, Poverty and unemployment are studied and
visualized in a holistic manner and policy maker has to go beyond the cocoon of department/ministries of the
government.
(Para-7.6.3)
RECOMMENDATION
           
1.12     Responsibility of Government to combat the problem of poverty population and unemployment
 
The Committee feels that while the management of assets and prosperity may be left to the private parties and its
management may well be done by private company/individual or government through investment or disinvestments but
the management of poverty, population and unemployment has to be borne by government apparatus.  As no private
company or parties would willingly come forward to address these monstrous problem of Indian economy.  It is the
obligation of state and government to genuinely come forward to address the problems of Indian economy.  It adds to
the duties and responsibility of the government the welfare nature of Indian State and its Constitutional obligation.  The
policy maker of the nation has to keep these fact in mind while fixing the target for employment generation be it PMRY,
on REGP, or Jai Prakash Narayan Rozgar Yojana or any other employment generation Programme.  The rate of
employment must be higher than the population growth rate and the objective of total employment must be a time bound
programme.  The Committee hopes that government in general and the Ministry of ARI in particular would come
forward to take the initiative in this direction and the Planning Commission would lend its helping hand for realistic
allocation of fund for the employment generation programme.
(Para 7.6.4)
Action Taken

1.21.1  Coir industry is a labour intensive industry engaging more than half a million people in the coconut producing

exclusively for women is being implemented successfully in all coir producing states. The introduction of motorised

pronounced aspect of empowering rural women folk and enlisting their participation in the development of the nation.
The industry uses a renewable resource, coconut husk for generating employment through various stages of processing
such as fibre extraction, spinning of coir yarn, manufacture of coir products, pith processing etc. The production of coir
fibre in India has increased manifold during the last decade due to various efforts undertaken in this regard for the
promotion of coir industry in the traditional areas such as Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh, Orissa etc. A large
number of new units for fibre extraction, manufacture of curled coir and rubberized coir have come up in these States.

1,07,160 number of additional employment has been generated during the last 3 years.

of age, educational qualification, residence and defaulter clause of eligibility criteria are logical and rational, however,
eligibility clause as regards the family income needs modification to make it a realistic criteria.  The Committee feels
that the family income of Rs.40,000 per annum hardly fulfills the bare needs of a family consisting of 2-3 persons. 
Moreover, the devaluation/depreciation of rupee further over the years has also necessitated the need for raising the
limit of family income.  One of the reasons of low recovery of loans under PMRY may be construed from the fact that
loan amount goes to fulfilling the basic needs of beneficiaries or his family members.  Therefore, it seems reasonable

Board , the Ministry of ARI may chalk out the mandate of its functioning. The Committee also suggests that Coir Board

opinion that Coir Board should act promptly and should not hesitate in undertaking new roles.

Action Taken
 
2.12.1   Coir Board is an autonomous organization established by the Central Government under the provision of the
Coir Industries Act 1953 for promoting the overall development of coir industry and upliftment of the living conditions
of workers engaged in this traditional cottage industry. The Coir Board is functioning under the Ministry of Agro and
Rural Industries, and the Coconut Development Board is functioning under the Agricultural Ministry. The Coconut
Development Board concentrates on the overall development of coconut cultivation in India. The areas of thrust are
different for the two organizations. The merger of Coir Board with Coconut Development Board will ultimately result in
loading additional activities on the Coconut Development Board. The focus of attention will vary and the very purpose
of establishment of a Coir Board will remain unfulfilled. In order to make a significant and impressive impact on the
development of coir industry, it is necessary to focus attention to a limited agenda rather than concentrating on
multifarious activities.
 
2.12.2  The coir industry generates additional employment in rural areas through coir processing activities with
minimum investment per job for which focused attention by professional agency like Coir Board is necessary to lead the
industry. The merger of Coir Board with Coconut Development Board is not likely to attract any tangible achievement
in the development of coir industry.  There is already proper co-ordination with the Coconut Development Board. The
Chairman, Coir Board is a member of the Board of Directors of Coconut Development Board.
           
2.12.3  The Government of India reviewed the performance of Coir Board in the wake of recommendations of the
Expenditure Reform Commission by engaging Administrative Staff College of India (ASCI) Hyderabad. Among other
things, they were asked to examine whether similar activities are also being undertaken by any other organizations and
if so, whether there is scope for merging or winding up any of these organizations to avoid unnecessary duplication. The
ASCI have meticulously examined the issue and recommended that as such there is no overlap with the roles of Coir
Board in such activities. The ASCI in their second report on Challenges for the Coir Industry in the New Millennium
have recommended several measures for developing coir industry in India through Coir Board.
 
2.12.4  As suggested by the Standing Committee, the Board has chalked out a scheme for enhancing the utilization of
coconut husk for coir industry. The 10
th Five Year Plan of the Coir Board envisages enhancement of the utilization of
coconut husk from 37% to 50% . The Coir Board has approved a project for manufacturing platform mounted mobile
defibering unit with private participation.

3.5       Potential And Scope For Development Of Village Industries
 
The committee is of the view that village area has vast potential and scope for development of village industries,
which require the support of government.  A comprehensive Planning is required.  The Ministry of ARI is supposed to

development of the village industries. It is for this reason that the target for employment generation through village
industries has been enhanced for the 10
th Plan Period from 20 lakhs to 25 lakhs. As a result, the target under REGP for
2003-04 has been enhanced from 4 lakh to 5 lakh jobs. The strategy adopted by the KVIC is to allow free hand in the

and if it is found technically feasible and economically viable, besides satisfying the other parameters of REGP, the

demand based and the projects are taken up based on their feasibility and viability. The KVIC is in close touch with the

The Committee is of the view that the objectives of the Cooperativisation scheme i.e. Formation of viable
coir cooperatives and revitalization of the potentially dormant viable societies and bringing the coir workers in to
the cooperative fold for improving the quality and quantity of production and putting industry on a sound
footing is a unique mission in Coir Industry. Therefore, the suggestion of the Institute of Rural Management that
the Scheme of Cooperativisation in Coir Industry as it is envisaged and implemented needs to undergo drastic
revision to meet the emerging challenges needs attention of the Government. The National Cooperative
Development Corporation (NCDC) may be entrusted with greater role for implementation of Cooperativisation
Scheme.
(Para-12.33.2)
 
 
Action Taken
 
3.13.1  Proposals for Cooperativisation have to come from State Governments through NCDC. Copies of the report of
the Institute of Rural Management on Cooperativisation in coir industry have been sent to all coir producing States/UTs
for information. Since the coir industry is at different stages of development in different States/UTs their requirements
are also different. Hence, before formulating proposals for restructuring the scheme, the States/UTs have been requested
to submit suggestions in the light of the recommendations of IRMA. On receipt of their suggestions, proposals for
restructuring the scheme can be formulated and submitted to the Govt. for approval. In the new scheme, the National
Cooperative Development Corporation will be entrusted with a greater role.
 
 
 
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.13.2  The Committee desires that  in order to implement the suggestion of Institute of Rural Management for
formation of viable  coir co-operatives  and revitalization  of the  potential of the dormant  viable societies, the
Coir Board/the Ministry of ARI should take up  effective follow up action with the State Government.  It is
expected that National Cooperative Development Corporation   would play its pro-active role  in this regard. 
Moreover, the coir board should undertake steps for synchronization of developmental  pattern of coir industries
in various States where the Coir Industries are in various stages of the Development so that Programme for Co-
operative movement can be formulated with greater emphasis.

(Para-12.34.2)

3.20     Lacuna in NPRI
 
The Committee, however, desires to point out the lacuna in NPRI by highlighting the fact that no fund has been
specifically made for programme on the assumption that various Ministries/Departments having their own programmes
would co-ordinate and synergies for implementing the Programme.  The Committee notes that all the
programme/schemes presently scattered into various ministries.  These programmes are to be integrated and co-
ordinated for injecting synergy into the programme for its sure success and timely implementation. The Ministry of
Agro and rural Industries should be bracketed as the nodal ministry as the vanguard of NPRI.  The most important
aspects for successful implementation of a programme is the credit flow.  NPRI is a programme without specific and  
separate fund. This is the setback at the very inception stage. Therefore, the Committee recommends that a common
corpus Fund should be made and the money which presently goes to various Schemes under different
Departments/ministries, should be put in this Corpus Fund intended for Comprehensive and coordinated effort for rural
industrialization and development.
(Para-15.5)
Action Taken
 
3.20.1  It is true that no funds were allocated during 1999-2000 and 2000-01 for NRPI separately.  The implementing
agencies are to fund  from their own sources.  However, a scheme on NPRI has been formulated to facilitate the
implementation of the programme and funds amounting to Rs. 40 lakh and Rs. 90 lakhs were allocated for
implementation of the scheme during 2001-02 and 2002-03.  During 2003-04 also funds amounting to Rs. 90 lakhs are
available under the scheme.  The Ministry feels that there is no need for a Common Corpus Fund as the Ministry has
been assigned the role of a co-ordinator.  Therefore, the Ministry aims to synergise efforts of all agencies involved in the
rural cluster development for achieving rural industrialization & to promote efforts of such agencies by way of
providing financial assistance as well as ensuring co-ordination with other agencies.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.20.2  The Committee  expect that the Ministry of ARI must go beyond  its assigned the role of a co-ordinator and
facilitator so far as the implementation of the  programmes under rural industrialization is concerned.  In this regard the
Ministry of ARI must assess the actual financial requirement  for the formulation and implementation of  sustainable
programmes for rural industrialization  as only the true rural industrialization would lead to the rapid development of 
rural economy  in India.

3.25     Implementing the employment programmes
 

144th Report On Industry

The facts pointed out by the Ministry of ARI that the activities undertaken by the various agencies implementing
the employment programmes have led to decentralization of programme and lack of uniformity in approach, are of
concern of the committee.  That is why the committee stresses that in order to bring uniformity in approach and
implementation of employment generation programmes, all schemes should be integrated and co-ordinated under one
Ministry and uniformity should be brought in the mode of implementation of schemes.
(Para-18.9)
Action Taken
 
3.25.1  The Ministry is implementing two Employment Generation Programmes namely the PMRY and REGP. Both
these programmes have different clienteles. The PMRY is meant for the educated unemployed in urban and rural areas
between the age group of 18-35 years below a certain income limit. It basically deals with small size projects up to Rs.2
lakhs only. In case of REGP, there is no income or age limit for the entrepreneurs and projects up to Rs.25 lakhs can be
taken up under the Scheme. The only criteria is that it should be set up in rural areas and should generate at least one job
for Rs.50,000 fixed capital investment. It can be seen that the target group for REGP is quite different from that for
PMRY. Thus, the focus is on the entrepreneur in both these schemes. On the other hand, employment generation
schemes by the other Ministries like Ministry of RD are targeted at the people below the poverty line and the main focus
is more on poverty alleviation through self-help groups and less on enterprise building.  Thus, it will be difficult to bring
uniformity in the mode of implementation of all schemes and it is submitted that the effort should be to fine-tune the
existing schemes so as to make them more viable and responsive to the needs of the people.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.25.2  It is on the basis of information furnished by the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries the Committee
recommended that  in order to bring uniformity in approach and implementation of employment generation
programmes, all schemes should be integrated and co-ordinated under one Ministry and uniformity should be brought in
the mode of implementation of schemes.  The Committee while recommending for bringing all the schemes under one
Ministry does not intend to dilute the modalities and target groups of the employment generation programme.  Rather
the  Committee intends that with the administration of all the employment generation programmes under one Ministry
will give the “focused–attention” of the Government to combat the twin problem of unemployment and poverty.  The
Committee, therefore, reiterates its view point and recommendation.

RECOMMENDATION
 
3.26     Synergistic approach towards implementation of rural infrastructural development
 
The Committee is of the view that integrated planning and Coordinated efforts is essential to give greater
thrust and result oriented efforts and for adopting synergistic approach towards implementation of rural
infrastructural development projects, employment generation programmes and ultimately the rural
industrialization and development would ultimately lead to poverty allocation .  Therefore, the Committee
recommends that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries may be either integrated and merged with Ministry
of Rural Development, Ministry of Poverty Alleviation, Food Processing or a Committee of Secretaries headed by
Senior most Secretary of these Ministries be constituted for better coordination and result oriented approach.
The intention of the proposal is to adopt the Unified and Integrated Planning System and holistic approach to
strike out the very roots of poverty and   undertake the implementation of well knitted policies/programmes to
develop the rural economy with co-ordinated and concerted efforts.    
(Para-20.1.2)  
Action Taken
 
3.26.1  The roles of the Ministries of Agro & Rural Industries, Rural Development and Food Processing are quite
different and do not overlap except in a few areas. While the role of Ministry of Rural Development is poverty
alleviation and that of Ministry of ARI is employment generation. In case of Ministry of rural Development, the projects
taken up are meant for the people below poverty line and per unit investment is Rs.50,000. Most of the work is done

144th Report On Industry

through self-help groups in rural areas. In case of Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries, the emphasis is on employment
generation through individual entrepreneurs. The Project cost can go up to Rs.25 lakhs and individual enterprise is
encouraged for setting up projects that will generate employment. In case of Ministry of Food Processing Industries, the
focus is on the specialized area of food processing and covers all types of projects including large scale projects. The
Allocation of Business for the three Ministries is well defined and there is perhaps no need for further integration at the
Committee of Secretaries level.
 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
 
3.26.2  The Committee understands that the soul of India dwells in village area and in order to transform the
status of Indian economy from developing to a developed one, a very serious effort is required to overhaul the
rural economy by undertaking  programmes for rural industrialization and development.  It is here at the
“Unified and Integrated Planning System and holistic approach” to strike out the very roots of poverty and  to 
undertake the implementation of well knitted policies/programmes is required for the purpose.   The Committee
knows that the Allocation of Business well defines the jurisdiction of the Ministries/Departments of
Government.   However, strict  adherence to the principle of water tight compartmentalization would not help in
the smooth transaction of the business of the Government.  An integrated and co-ordinated planning and
approach is required.  It is under this vision the Committee recommended that the Ministry of Agro and Rural
Industries may be either integrated and merged with Ministry of Rural Development, Ministry of Poverty
Alleviation, Food Processing or a Committee of Secretaries headed by Senior most Secretary of these Ministries
be constituted for better coordination and result oriented approach.

The Committee recommends for either the merger of all Government’s schemes for employment

REPORT
CHAPTER-I
 
THE STEEL SECTOR
1.1       Steel is crucial to the development of any modern economy. It has  technologically strong forward and backward
linkages in terms of material flow and income generation.   The growth of  many of  advanced economies have been
largely shaped by the strength of their steel industry during their early stages of development.    Some of the newly
industrializing  countries like South Korea, China and Brazil among others have built up substantial capacities not only
to support their rapidly growing domestic economies, but also to export significantly. 
 
1.1.2    The liberalization of the economy since 1991-1992  in India has witnessed a spate of new capacity additions in
the private steel sector.  Steel Plants in private sector are now  producing  two-third of the total finished products.  Long-
term growth prospect of steel industry is encouraging a large number of people to set up greenfield capacities with
modern technology in the private sector.  These units  with state  of-the art technology are more viable than the units in
the public sector.  Under an era of liberalization and with the lowering of international trade barriers competitiveness of
the industry has become crucial not only for increasing exports but also in competing with imports in the domestic
market as  Steel industry in India had been adversely affected in the past by the rationalization and reduction of duties
resulting in lower tariff protection against imports, to South East Asian currency crisis, Russian Rouble devaluation,
lower international prices and the consequent meltdown and dumping.  Global Steel Industry for the major part of 2001
remained a victim of slow down in demand, sliding price levels, low realizations, losses and falling profits.  However,
from the beginning of 2002, the industry entered a recovery phase, with the gradual firming up of international prices
and demand.  These trends largely persist to date.   The year 2003 has  seen a price rise in the domestic and the 
international steel market. 
 
1.1.3    In  India the production, prices and consumption of steel have witnessed a steady rise over the last few months.
Domestic prices have firmed up in the face of strong demand – both domestic and foreign. There has been a robust
growth in exports following a quantum jump in GP/GC exports. The salient trends for April-January 2003 and April ’01
- January ‘02 period are given below. The items pertain to finished (carbon) steel.

1.1.4    Better price realizations have led to an improvement in financial performance for most of the domestic steel
plants. Coupled with this has come the revival of economic growth and the recovery of the key end-user sectors of
steel.  With the continued focus on infrastructure development and construction activities (including housing) – the
industry mood is upbeat.
 
1.2.0    Industrial output – as measured by the Index of Industrial Production (IIP) –
 
1.2.1    It grew 6.4% in December 2002 as against 2.8% during the correpsonding month last year and for the April ’02 -
January ‘03 period, it reported a 5.5% growth against a mere 2.6% growth in same period last year. For this period,
Manufacturing (5.8%), Electricity (3.8%) and Mining (5.4%) – all recorded impressive growths, as compared with the
same period last year, for which respective sectoral growth rates are 2.8%, 2.9% and 1%. (Source: CSO)
 
1.2.2    Impressive performance of the core sector continued in January 2003 with finished steel and cement continuing
to boost growth in the six infrastructure industries whose index rose to 5.2% in April-January ’03 as compared to a low
3.1 % in same period last year.  (Source: CSO)
 
1.3.0    Budget (2003-04) and the Indian Steel Industry
 
1.3.1    With the measures proposed in both the Railway Budget 2003-04 and the Union budget 2003-04, the outlook in
the steel industry is positive. The policy measures proposed in the Railway Budget 2003-04 promise to benefit industry
in general and the iron and steel industry in particular. The proposed rationalization of freight structure, reduction in the
number of classifications, the market orientation introduced through peak and off-peak rates, the incentives to big
shippers in the form of lower rates, if they move more materials, the reduction in freight rates for short distance ranging
up to 100 km as well as the general reductions in the freight rates for finished steel and pig iron – help in lowering the
overall costs and increasing competitiveness. The stress on laying of new tracks, broadening of existing ones, addition
of new trains and a series of developmental projects are all expected to boost demand for steel.
 
1.3.2    Union Budget 2003-04 has proposed measures that are meant  for improving the environment in which the iron
and steel industry operates. Most prominent is the significant thrust provided to infrastructure development in the
country – roads, ports,  airports and housing - and this in turn is expected to lead to a substantial increase in the domestic
steel demand. Reduction of excise on passenger cars and appliances like air conditioners is also expected to indirectly
impact steel industry favourably. 
 
1.3.3    There may be no direct correlation between the International steel production growth rate and the domestic
growth rate.  Although a  global rise in demand may have similar impact on the industry in India as well as globally, a 
domestic rise in demand may, in fact, lead to strong growth in production in the country leaving the global production
rate practically unaffected.  Therefore, it may be difficult to estimate whether domestic growth rate will catch up with
the global trends.  In fact, while the global annual production growth rate in the last ten years or so has been at less than
2 per cent, the figure for India has been at about 6 per cent.  There are greater chances that the steel industry growth rate
in India will be higher than the global rate in the medium and the long term.
 
1.3.4    Major Indian steel companies have already hiked prices of steel items – though, mostly flat products from the
beginning of the fiscal 2002-03. This is seen in line with international trends where prices have been rising since
beginning of 2002 and is an inevitable fallout of the globalization process. Domestic price rises have persisted in 2003
in the face of a steel demand that has shown signs of stabilizing.
 
1.4.0    Price Volatality
           
1.4.1    The year 2003 opened with rounds of price hikes – of both long and flat which have given the current market

145th report of Committee on Industry

trends further buoyancy. In January 2003, SAIL, Tata Steel and other flat steel producers increased prices of flat
products by an average Rs 600-1000 per tonne while SAIL and RINL have hiked long steel prices by Rs. 200-300
per tonne. This has pushed up hot rolled coil prices in the domestic market, with basic grade price of the commodity
being around Rs 17,500-18,000 per tonne (average). Similarly, the growth in the construction segment in particular
and the infrastructure segment in general has prompted fresh hikes in long steel prices. Internationally too, trends (W.
European fob levels) remain strong: galvanized coil prices are in the range of $445-485/tonne; cold rolled coils,
$390-430/tonne and hot rolled coils at around $300-325/tonne. (Source: Metal Bulletin).
 
1.4.2    The turnaround in the market trends is reflected most prominently in the performance of the public sector steel
giant, Steel Authority of India Ltd. The unaudited financial results of SAIL for April-December (Q3) 2002 reveals a
sharp improvement in the performance with losses being slashed to Rs. 79 crore in Q3 ’02 - an improvement of Rs. 507
crore over the corresponding period of the previous year. SAIL’s loss for April-December ’02 was brought to a level of
Rs. 558 crore, showing a recovery of 57 per cent over the results of the same period in 2001. This helped the company
to post a cash profit of Rs 215 crore in Q3 ’02 as against a loss of Rs 297 crore in Q3 ’01 and a cash profit of Rs. 305
crore in the first nine months of the current financial year.  SAIL had suffered a cash loss of Rs. 434 crore during the
corresponding period in the last fiscal.
 
1.4.3    For the other PSU, namely RINL (VSP) for the period, Q2 (July-September) ’02, net profit has gone up by 119%
and turnover 16% as compared to quarter ending June ’02 (Q1).          The Indian steel companies are free to raise prices
at any time, depending on their commercial judgement.  The conditions for price increases are local in the first place. 
Some such conditions may be created by external developments in the context of the free external trade regime.
Fluctuations in international prices can always have corresponding impact on the pricing decisions of the Indian
companies.       The world prices of almost all steel products have risen significantly since January 2002. The extent of
price rise has been significant for flat products like HR coils, CR sheets and galvanised sheets.  In view of this, the
Indian steel companies have also raised prices to the extent that may be supported by domestic market conditions.
 
1.4.4    In a deregulated and liberalized environment, prices are determined by the free interplay of market forces. 
Government does not intervene in the market to influence prices.  The main reason for the recent upswing in steel price
has been the global increase in the demand for steel.  The domestic prices have followed the general pattern of
international prices.  The increase in demand from the domestic steel consuming industries has further reinforced the
upward movement of prices.  Sharp rise in the cost of metallic and certain other critical inputs like iron ore, coal, coke,
nickel and ferro alloys has also contributed to the rise in prices.
 
1.5.0    Recommendation for change in the existing duty structure for Union Budget 2004-05    
 
1.5.1    Ministry of Steel had sent its recommendation for change in the existing duty structure for Union Budget 2004-
05 to Department of Revenue, keeping in view the interest of both the steel manufacturers and the steel consumers.  The
changes in the duty structure announced recently by Ministry of Finance have addressed concerns in some areas
especially of the steel consuming sector viz.
 
(a)
                The peak rate of import duty has been reduced to 20%.
(b)               4% SAD on all imports has been abolished.
(c)                Import duty on Nickel has been lowered from 10% to 5%.
 
1.5.2    Import Duty on most of the steel items used by the downstream industries like Semis, HR Sheets/Plates and HR
Coils is imposed at the peak rate, which has been lowered by 5%.  This and the abolition of 4% SAD would reduce the
cost of import of steel by more than 10%.  Reduction in duty on Nickel from 10% to 5% would give a boost to the
growth of the domestic Stainless Steel Industry.
 
1.5.3    Earlier, as a measure of import facilitation, Government has also withdrawn steel items from the purview of
DGFT Notification No. 44 and provided the option to downstream steel consumers to meet their requirements through
imports.  The steel consumers have also been able to get a favourable judgement from the Calcutta High Court as the
Honuorable Court has ordered removal of the mechanism of floor price on import of prime grade HR Coil.

1.5.4    As for export incentives to the exporters it is stated that steel exporters are not being given any specific
incentives other than those generally available to commodity exporters.  However, it is understood that DGFT under

1.5.5    Therefore, despite the fact that the Government does not intervene directly in the market, the steps taken during

1.5.6    As for the specific problem faced by the Foundry units the pig iron price rise is a response to the general rise in
the prices of steel in the world market and the resulting large demand for metallics to produce steel.  The price rise is

CHAPTER-II
 
THE SMALL SCALE SECTOR
 
2.1       There is a very big segment of Small Scale Industries engaged in manufacturing various domestic and industrial
products consuming Iron and Steel in prime and semi-finished form as raw materials for their manufacturing activities. 
This segment includes the forging and casting industries, steel furniture manufacturing, Bicycle parts industries,
Agricultural implements industries etc.  Most of these industries are located in Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Gujarat,
Maharashtra and Andhra Pradesh.  Various other SSI and Tiny units spread throughout the length and breadth of the
country also use iron and steel as basic raw material to a great extent.
 
2.1.1    Iron and Steel industry is the main supplier of basic raw material for the light engineering industry such as
Bicycles, Auto Parts, Hard Ware and Hand Tools.  Since last year, the small scale industries are facing problems due to
non-availability of iron and steel, in adequate quantities along with a steep hike in prices.  It is stated that the decontrol
policy has set the cartel of steel manufacturers free in fixing steel price.  The cartel of steel manufacturers has increased
the steel price arbitrarily and the small scale industries are finding it difficult to absorb the rise in prices.
