INTRODUCTION
 
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Forty-seventh Report of Sub-Committee-II for Ministry of Small
Scale Industries on Credit Flow to SSI Sector in the Region of Bulandshahar, Uttar Pradesh pertaining to the Ministry of
Small Scale Industry.
2.      The Sub-Committee for Ministry of Small Scale Industries (of Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry) heard views of the representatives of SSI Associations in the Region of Bulandshahar,
Government of Uttar Pradesh and the Ministry of SSI at New Delhi on 23rd August, 2003. This report is based upon the
views emerged out of the deliberations held on that day.
3.      The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted the Draft report at
its meeting held on the 25
th August, 2004.
 
NEW DELHI
25th August, 2004
SANTOSH BAGRODIA
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
 
REPORT
         Small Scale Industry (SSI) Sector is playing a most important and self-motivated role to generate the employment,
remove the poorness, modernization, reformation of technology and globalisation of the Indian Economy in terms of
low investment, high potential for employment generation and wider dispersal of industries in rural and semi­-urban
areas preventing migration to big cities. This sector offers and ensures a more equitable distribution of national income
and facilitates effective mobilization of resources of capital and skill, which might otherwise remain unutilised.
2.      This sector offers and ensures a more equitable distribution of national income and facilitates effective
mobilization of resources of capital and skill, which might otherwise remain unutilised. It further stimulates the growth
of industrial entrepreneurship and promotes and diffuses the pattern of ownership and location. Over 40% of the gross
turnover in manufacturing activities as also around one-third of our exports are contributed by SSI sector. In the area of
employment generation, significant contribution is made by SSI sector both modern and traditional units which account
for employment of over 192.23 lakhs workers and production in rupee terms is projected to reach Rs.7,42,021 crore
during financial year 2002-03.
3.      During the course of examination of Demand for Grants 2003-04 pertaining to the Ministry of Small Scale
Industries, the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry took up the issue of credit flow to SSI
sector in detail. The Committee was informed that the SSI sector, producing a wide range of products, accounts for
around 95 per cent of the industrial units in the country, contributing to 40 per cent of the manufacturing sector output
and approximately one third of the Nation’s exports. As on March, 2002, there were 34.42 lakhs SSI units providing
direct employment to around 192.23 lakhs persons. As per the estimates of the Office of the Development
Commissioner (SSI), the output of SSI sector at current prices aggregated Rs.6,90,316 crore during the year 2001-02
and exports at the level of Rs.69.797 crore during the 2000-01. During the financial year 2002-03, the production of SSI
sector is projected to reach at Rs.7,42,021 crore. The sector also acts as a nursery for promoting entrepreneurial talents
and as a catalyst in the industrial growth.
4.      The Ministry of SSI has apprised the Committee that the total advance to SSI from the Public Sector Banks went
up in absolute terms from Rs.48,445 crores in March, 2001 to Rs.49,743 crores in March, 2002. The percentage of SSI
advances to Net Bank Credit (NBC) however, declined from 14.2 % as at the end of March, 2001 to 12.5 % at the end
of March, 2002. The RBI’s study of the specialized SSI/general branches has revealed that adequate credit is being
made available to all viable projects.
5.      The potential of SSI sector as a core area for growth and development of economy has been well recognized by the
Government. The Government has taken steps to remove the bottlenecks and thereby pave the way for accelerating the

147th Report of The Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/147threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:45:17]
growth of this sector. Amongst the bottlenecks to be removed for the growth of SSI the major factor has been the
problem of bank credit to this sector. The streamlining of flow of bank credit has been a constant challenge not only
before the Government but also to the banking and financial institutions.
6.      The Committee on Industry has deliberated on the aspect of Credit Flow to SSI Sector at length in its 45 th Report
which was presented to the Parliament on 8th August, 2001. Having gone through the Action Taken Notes submitted by
the Ministry of SSI on that report the Committee through its Sub-Committee on SSI took up the scrutiny of practical
problems being faced by SSI at the ground level as far as the credit flow to these units are concerned.
7.      The Committee identified certain regions/states like Maharashtra, Himachal Pradesh, Delhi and adjoining NOIDA
and Ghaziabad area to understand the problems of the units and also suggested the remedial measures. In the process the
Committee and its Sub-Committee had opportunities to interact not only with the representatives of the Ministry of
SSIs, Government of India but also with the State Governments, Banking and Financial Institutions and the
representatives of National/Regional/Local SSI Federations. As a sequel to this process of study the Committee came to
know about the problems being faced by the SSI units in the District Bulandshahar in western Uttar Pradesh region. The
Committee interacted with the representatives of SSI Federation of that area, representatives of Government of Uttar
Pradesh and Ministry of SSI, Government of India in this connection on 23rd August, 2003 at New Delhi.
INDUSTRIAL  SCENARIO  OF  THE  BULANDSHAHAR
8.      Bulandshahar is an agriculture dominated district of Western Uttar Pradesh. The industrial scenario of
Bulandshahar (except Sikandarabad area) does not reflect very high industrial growth. There are mainly small, tiny,
cottage and handicraft units spread over the district. The District has branches of 17 banks for fulfilling the credit
requirements. The main products manufactured in the District include sugar, paint, dairy products, flour, animal feed,
edible oils, pottery and ceramics and various types of chemicals etc. The handicraft works include zari , pottery and
handlooms.
9.      The gross output of the SSI units in Bulandshahar District during 2001-02 was to the tune of Rs.260.35 crore. The
industry-wise break-up of these units engaged in manufacturing mainly comprise of following goods:
(i)   wooden industrial goods;
(ii)   articles of Porcelain or China, earthenware, imitation Porcelain or common pottery, including earthen statues;
(iii)  bricks;
(iv)  basic iron and steel items; and
(v)  pumps, compressors, taps and valves including hand-pumps, vacuum pumps, air and other gas-compressors
etc.
10.    Khurja Tehsil of this district is famous for its pottery, where a significant number of exporting units are set up. The
Office of Development Commissioner for SSI has taken up modernisation  programme of Pottery Industry cluster in
Khurja under UPTECH Scheme (now called Small Industry Cluster Development Programme). The Implementing
Agency is Khurja Pottery Manufacturers Association (KPMA), Khurja and monitoring agency is Central Glass &
Ceramic Research Institute (CGCRI). Three interventions, namely, replacement of Saggar by Decker Plate, reduction in
Dead weight of Trolley and installation of Auto Off-On Burner have been taken up for implementation with an
objective to obtain quick results from the above interventions.
11.    Milk and milk products, especially milk powder apart from catering to the domestic market have export potential
also. If the milk processing industry is modernized its export potential will increase further. Similarly, agro and food
based industries also have a great export potential in the district. It may be noted that Bulandshahar is amongst the
leading districts of the country in terms of milk production. It produces 45 lakhs litres  of milk every day, 60% of which
is used by the industrial units.
IMPACT  OF  WTO  NORMS
12.    According to the Third All India Census of SSI units conducted by the Government of India, out of 8745 units in
the district, 5653 are closed or not traceable. Presently, nearly 3117 units are working. The detailed analysis, showed
that these units were very tiny units, and a very few of them had taken any credit facility from any financial institution
or availed any facility extended by the Government. The units in the districts cater to the domestic market and there is
hardly any competition from large producers or multinational corporations. Thus, there is no direct impact of WTO
visible on the SSI units in the district but the rate of setting up of SSI units has slowed down during the last five years.
13.    Although liberalization has exposed SSI units to stiff competition, it has led to new opportunities also. Small Scale

Industries in India have enough competitive strength to withstand the impact of the phasing out of Quantitative
Restrictions (QRs) and implementation of WTO agreements. Government is fully aware of the WTO environment and
has taken appropriate measures for preparing the small scale sector to meet the challenges of liberalization and
globalization. Government is also constantly monitoring the impact of the removal of QRs and WTO Agreements on the
economy including the SSIs in the country.
14.    With a view to create awareness among the SSI units Associations on WTO Agreements and their implication for
them, Ministry of SSI organised 28 Sensitization Workshops all over the country. Workshops on Intellectual Property
Rights (IPRs) are also being organized. The Ministry is also organizing seminars on Anti-Dumping investigations. The
Ministry of SSI is financially supporting Industry Associations to develop monitoring mechanisms on the performance
of four selected product clusters in terms of growth, removal of QRs, surge in imports, etc.
REHABILITATION  OF  SICK  UNITS
15.    According to the Third All India Census of working of SSI units the number of working units in Bulandshahar
district, as on 31
st March, 2001, was 3117. Out of these 78 units have outstanding loans. According to the census, the
number of sick units in the district was 17 and the number of incipient sick units was 59. The sick units and incipient
sick units taken together form 2.44 % of the total working units. Though the incidence of sickness is not very serious in
Bulandshahar, however, it is a matter of concern that financial institutions have not come forward for providing
rehabilitation package for the revival of sick units.
SSI  ASSOCIATIONS
Bulandshahar Industries Association
16.    The President, Bulandshahar Industries Association informed that they were not getting the benefits out of the
Credit Guarantee Fund Trust (CGFT) and added that none has been sanctioned any loan in the area. He suggested that a
committee of the leading banks in the district should be formed and it should meet once in a quarter. This Committee
should also have representatives from Industrial Associations, Banks and other related Departments. They should have
first hand knowledge regarding the loans sanctioned and if not the reasons thereof. It was further added that people were
interested in setting up small industries but they were ignorant of collateral security, which was not required to be
furnished while seeking bank loans it should have been accorded wide publicity and the information must have been on
the notice board, containing the details of the schemes being implemented. It was further suggested that the website of
the CGFT and banks should have updated information regarding loan applications received and the action taken thereon.
17.    The Committee was apprised that the association was starting an awareness programme  and a seminar was to be
conducted shortly. This seminar is for promoting the small industries and all banks and officials of the industries
department are required to cooperate. He also suggested that 2.5 % of guarantee money should be reduced to 1% so that
the Small Industries will feel comfortable.

20.    He also stated that the Bulandshahar  area should be attached with Delhi as lot of facilities are available there

OBSERVATIONS/RECOMMENDATIONS/CONCLUSIONS

147th Report of The Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/147threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:45:17]
42.    The Committee is constrained to note that benefit of the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries (CGFT )
are not reaching to the SSI entrepreneurs. The Committee recommends that the Government and the SIDBI to ensure
that all the requisite steps be taken for its success and an action taken report be furnished to Committee within three
months.
43.    The Committee understands that there is a lack of awareness amongst the SSI entrepreneurs about the various
schemes/facilities being offered by the Government and financial institutions. It has resulted in largely under financing
of various schemes. The Committee therefore recommends that the Government and financial institutions should give
wide publicity and conduct awareness campaigns on the loans schemes amongst the SSI entrepreneurs so that the
benefits of various schemes percolate down to the grass-root level. The Committee also directs that all the Banks in the
area should invariably display in every branch the facilities being offered by them as well the websites of Banks and
Government Organisations should be updated, especially in respect of the information regarding the Credit Guarantee
Fund Scheme.
44.    The Committee was informed that the SSI sector is under constant threat due to globalisation and their products
required to be marketed efficiently. The Committee appreciates the efforts and assistance extended by the NSIC.
However, the SSI associations demand that in addition to their existing activities, the NSIC should organize exhibitions
for promoting the marketing of the goods produced in the area is justified. The Committee also feels that NSIC should
certainly help the SSIs in this respect. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the NSIC should come forward to
organize exhibitions for displaying products of the SSI units in various metros so as to enable to get more orders to
make viable the existing units which suffer from the under utilization of capacities for want of orders.
45.    The Committee took note of the complaints of the apathetic attitude of the officers and staff of the State
Government and Banks. The entrepreneurs are harassed in the guise of rules and procedures and thus setting up of an
unit becomes a Herculean task. The Committee strongly feels that it has to be done away with if industry has to grow. It
is therefore required that a Committee be set up by the lead Bank i.e., Punjab National Bank consisting of Banks’
representatives, Director of Industries, local MP’s and MLA’s and members of the SSI associations to resolve the
problems of SSI entrepreneurs and monitor the lending of loans. This Committee should meet quarterly to review the
position. The Committee therefore recommends for constitution of the said Committee at the earliest.
46.    The Committee is very much concerned about the declining trend in credit flow to SSIs. The steps taken by the
Ministry of SSI to enhance credit flow to SSI sector are not adequate. The Committee is of the view that non-
compliance of the RBI guidelines is the major reason which has resulted in the decline of credit flow. The Committee,
therefore, impress upon the Government to take serious measures to arrest this trend. Further, the Committee
recommends that the Standard Advisory Committee on Credit Flow should be given more powers to monitor the
situation and advise the Government in this regard.
47.    The Committee was informed that the industrial units are scattered and there is no developed industrial area in the
district. The Committee therefore recommends that the State Government of Uttar Pradesh should be approached to
develop industrial estates to shelter the SSI units with necessary infrastructure.
48.    The Committee was also informed that the roads and transport facilities are grossly inadequate and the district has
no direct railway link. Moreover, by­pass roads are required to resolve the problem of traffic jam in Dadri and
Sikandrabad towns in the district. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government of India should extend
necessary support to the State Government of Uttar Pradesh to develop the necessary road and rail links for proper
growth of SSIs in the area.
49.    The Committee notes that taking into account the quantum of milk produced in the district which is next to Gujarat
and is in the non-cooperative sector, there is a strong demand for an organisational  support for procurement, processing
and transportation of the milk and also to provide the best price to the producers. The Committee therefore, recommends
that considering the quantum of milk produced the Government should provide necessary support either through
cooperative sector or by setting up a public sector unit to tap the potential available in the area in an organized manner.
50.    The Committee also observes that the SSI sector comprises of lot of units engaged in the food processing and there
is no exclusive zone for food processing in the area. It was also informed that adequate cold storage facility is not
available for these units. The Committee, therefore, recommends that necessary steps should be taken to set up food
processing zone in the area to assist the SSI units engaged in food processing and also to enhance cold storage facilities.

CHAPTER - I
MOU SYSTEM
         The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is a negotiated document between the Government, acting as the owner
of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific PSE. It contains the intentions, obligations and mutual responsibilities of
the Government and the PSE. Further, MoU makes an attempt to move the management of PSEs from management by
controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.
1.2    The genesis of the policy of Memorandum of Understanding can be traced to the report of the Arjun Sengupta
Committee. One of the recommendations of this Committee was for the introduction of the system of MoU for
measurement of performance of public enterprises. The MoU System was introduced on an experimental basis in 1987.
OBJECTIVES OF THE MOU SYSTEM
1.3    The objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy and
accountability of the management; to remove the fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise to pursue through
clearly laid down performance targets in the MoU and to enable the evaluation of managerial performance through
objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to stimulate
improved performance.
1.4    Under the agreement the enterprises undertake to achieve the targets set in the agreement at the beginning of the
year. Thus the MoU covers both financial performance as well as non-financial performance. Under this system
performance of the Company is ­categorized into five categories namely: excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor.
PREPARATION OF MOU
1.5    Based on the guidelines issued by the DPE in the month of October/November every year, the draft MoUs are
prepared by PSEs and forwarded to the concerned Administrative Ministry and DPE by December. The draft MoUs
indicate the performance targets on a five point scale as proposed by the PSE for the ensuing financial year for all crucial
parameters like production, sales, profits, etc. The PSEs are also expected to include dynamic parameters of significance
for strengthening the future potential of the enterprise, such as project implementation, R&D, Human Resource
Development, etc. Appropriate weights are assigned to each of these parameters. The draft MoU are discussed with the
PSE Administrative Ministries at the Adhoc Task Force (ATF) negotiation meetings arranged in DPE in the month of
March/soon after the April presentation of the Union Budget. Since the Budget has implications on performance targets,
the timing of the negotiation meetings is deliberately scheduled after the budget presentation. The appropriateness of the
parameters and weights and the soundness of the targets as also the commitments of the Government are examined in
detail at the negotiation meetings. The draft MoUs as finalised thereafter are placed before the High Power Committee

148th Report of The Committee on Industry

(HPC) comprising of the Cabinet Secretary as Chairman, Secretary, Finance, Expenditure, Planning Commission,
Programme Implementation, Chairman Public Enterprises Selection Board, Chief Economic Adviser and Secretary
Public Enterprises as Members, for approval. After approval, the respective Chief Executives and Secretaries.
EVALUATION
1.6    The evaluation of the MoU signing enterprises is done at the end of the year by the Ad-hoc ,Task Force (ATF) on
the basis of actual achievement vis-a-vis the MoU targets. Where the performance exceeds the target by the
predetermined stipulated level the enterprise is ranked as ‘excellent’ and when the target is just met, the enterprise is
ranked as ‘very good’ . In other cases, where the targets are not met the enterprise is ranked either ‘ good’ or ‘ fair’ or ‘
poor’ . Ranking depends on how the performance has been as compared to MOU targets.
1.7    The performance criteria should be assigned appropriate weights corresponding with their stated priorities in the
objectives. It should be ensured that they also reflect the perceived relative importance of the various criteria in the
judgement of the PSE/Ministry. The weight for physical criteria should be kept as low as possible. Instead, Efficiency and
Dynamic criteria should get higher weights. The weight for profit-related financial parameters would be 60 % in case of
PSEs operating under free market mechanism. The weight of 60 % would be distributed to; Gross Margin, Gross
Profit/Capital Employed and Net Profit/Net Worth, each having a weight of 20 % each. For PSEs operating under
administered prices, PSEs where Government is sole/almost sole customer & Trading, Consultancy, Engineering and
Financial PSEs, the weight would be 40%. The weight of 40 % would be distributed to, Gross Margin and Net Profit/Net
Worth, each having a weight of 20 % each. The PSEs which have been specially set up for implementing certain
Government policy directives will have no pre-determined financial parameters.
1.8    The targets set should be realistic and growth oriented. It should be ensured that the MoU targets flow from the
Corporate Vision/Plans formulated by the PSEs and there is linkage between them. In case there is any variation, reasons
thereof should be clearly specified. For qualitative indicators, the targets for each of the points on the 5-point scale should
be indicated in the performance matrix itself. If these targets are on a time scale, only such target, which falls within the
MoU year, is included.
1.9    The MoU should contain the past five years performance data on criteria included in the MoU in an appendix. It
should also indicate the projections for the next five years, as far as possible consistent with the corporate plan.
1.10  The report on MoU performance in respect of various PSUs is an exercise in the study of Memorandum of
Understanding of public sector undertakings undertaken by the Sub-Committee for Ministry of Heavy Industries and
Public Enterprises of the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry. This study includes, Rashtriya Ispat Nigam
Limited, Dredging Corporation of India both at Visakhapatnam and National Mineral Development Corporation Limited,
Bharat Dynamics Limited both at Hyderabad. The Committee undertook a study visit to Visakhapatnam and Hyderabad
on 22-23rd September, 2003 and met with the CMDs and other officials of these PSUs. The deliberations of the
Committee is explained in the following chapters".
CHAPTER II
RASHTRIYA ISPAT NIGAM LIMITED
Visakhapatnam Steel Plant
2.1    Rashtriya Ispat Nigam Limited ( RINL) is the corporate entity of Visakhapatnam Steel Plant (VSP) The steel plant
is located 26 km south of Visakhapatnam  city. The Company has a blast furnace grade limestone captive mine at
Jaggayapeta, a captive mine for Dolomite at Madharam, a Manganese ore captive mine at Cheepurupalli All the captive
mines are located in the State of Andhra Pradesh.
2:2    The Sub-Committee for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises visited the plant on 22nd September,
2003 as a part of its study visit to Visakhapatnam on the MOU performance in the Public Sector Enterprises The
Committee was apprised by the Chairman and Managing Director that the foundation stone of the steel plant was laid on
January 20, 1971 and the plant was dedicated to the nation on August 1, 1992. The plant has a capacity to produce 2.656
Mt of saleable steel, of which, 2.410 Mt is finished steel Besides receiving raw materials from the captive sources, the
steel plant meets its iron ore requirements from Bailadilla mines of National Mineral Development Corporation, coking
coal requirements through through and coal washeries of Coal India Limited, SMS grade limestone through imports
quartzite requirements through purchase and boiler coal from the coal mines of Mahanadi Coal Limited.
2.3    The product profile of the plant comprises wire rods, rounds, reinforcement bars (rebars), angles, channels beam

plant also exports power to AP Transco from its captive power plant The Company markets its products through
headquarter marketing office and a network oft regional offices, branch offices and stockyards spread through the
country. It also takes the help of consignment agents and consignment sales agents for the marketing of its products.
Export is carried out through the export wing of marketing division with the help of different agencies. The export wing
is situated at the headquarter. The Company is recognised as Star Trading House’ by the Director General of Foreign
Trade.
2.4    The end users of the steel products manufactured at the plant include, among others, construction industry,
automobile industry, engineering industry, re-rolling industry, forging, industry, cable industry, wire drawing industry;
fastener industry, electrode manufacturers and railways. The Company is ideally located to serve the southern market of
India.
2.5    The steel plant, having unique technological features, is a pioneer in introducing many new technologies in the
country. The production of TMT rebars by tempcore process is a shining example in this respect. Because of high level of
technology in the plant, the Company has a very good manufacturing capability to meet the needs of various customers.
The Company has been registering a steady and consistent growth in performance, proving that “success begets success”.
Achievement of updated capacities which once seemed to be impossible, has turned into a reality today. Records are
being created only to be broken again.

Steps taken to improve MOU performance
2.10  Consistent efforts are made for improving the performance of the Company. These efforts have resulted in
improved physical and fiscal performance, which have contributed to improved MOU performance.
2.11  Technological upgradation in various areas like cold and hot repairs of coke oven batteries; Bed height in sinter
machines; Oxygen enrichment in blast furnaces; Installation of amanoscope in Blast Furnaces; Introduction PLCs in BFs
; Modification of lance tip design in LD conveners; Slag splashing in LD converters; Installation of ladle furnace in steel
melt shop; Installation of gega cutting machine in continuous casting; Improvement of cooling system in continuous
casting; Implementation of higher levels of automation in BF, TPP, rolling mills, etc. Installation of fibre optic cable
network in the plant; Installation of server based RS-6000 computer; Implementation of cost reduction and waste
minimization initiatives; Increasing production of value added steels; Product-mix optimization; Thrust on training and
HRD ; Focus on research and development Completion of projects within time; Efficient financial management i.e.
swapping of high cost debts with lower cost debts, working capital management, etc.; and Customer relations
management.
2.12  RINL has a committed work force of 16,894 as on 31-3-2003. Out of these, 4,308 are executives and 12,586 are
non-executives. RINL has rationalized the designations of non-executive employees. The highly skilled category has been
designated as ‘charge man’, the skilled category as ‘ technician’ and the unskilled employees as ‘ khalasi’ RINL has
introduced multi-skilling concept since inception and the employees are trained as per this concept.
2.13  RINL follows a system of overlapping shifts, the first of its kind in the industry. This system ensures smooth change
over of the shifts and uninterrupted pace of operation of the plant during the shift change over. Another unique feature
followed at RINL is the uniform working hours for the ministerial and non-ministerial employees.
2.14  Training and human resource development is given a lot of importance at RINL. Each year, at least one-third of the
employees undergo various training sessions either at training and development centre or at centre for human resource
development (HRD) for sharpening their skills, with respect to both technical matters as well as human related issues.
Further, training is also imparted to the employees in safety, fire prevention, occupational health besides giving on- the
job training at shop floor.
2.15  Caring for stakeholders is one of the main thrust areas at RINL. Progress through systematization and through
empowering of employees is the main approach followed. Fearless environment with encouragement towards risk-taking
is helping the innovativeness at RINL. Motivation of employees towards production and productivity is achieved through
a well-designed-incentive scheme. Team approach is encouraged for all, the activities to achieve results. Process control
functions in the plant and control of product quality are carried out by the line operators. Quality assurance and
technology development (QA&TD) department facilitates these activities. Technology upgradation and product
diversification activity is carried out through R&D activities, which is not only the function of the research and
development (R&D) wing, but of each and every employee of the Company. Communication and knowledge sharing is
the route followed by the employees so that they can give their best to the Company.
2.16  The Company follows customer-centric approach in its activities since it is sincerely believed that the existence of
the Company is only due to its customers. It is also aware that in today’s competitive environment, unless and until it
gives its best, it cannot survive.

PERFORMANCE
2:19  The Committee takes note of the overall performance of the VSP particularly the financial crisis overcome by the
organization and reaching the ‘ Zero Debt’ level. The Committee was informed that the PSU was referred to BIFR in the
year 1998-99. It started recovering since then and its cash profit was likely to reach Rs.975 crores (approx.) in the year
2002-03. In terms of MOU performance also the PSU performed well and has been rated continuously ‘ Excellent’ since
2000-01. The production of value added steel products has also risen from a level of around 3 lakh tones in 2000-01 to
over 4.8 lakh tones in 2002­-03 and the efforts being taken by the PSU for new products, grades continued to be
developed every year to meet the market demand. The Committee appreciates the various steps taken to improve the
performance of the plant like, capacity utilization, optimum maintenance of equipments available and the ongoing
technological upgradations in various areas. The Committee also appreciates the thrust given by training and HRD
activities as well as the focus on the R&D taking place.
2.20  The Committee observes that the major raw material for production of steel is iron ore, which is supplied by NMDC
. The supply of Iron ore to VSP has been inconsistent for the past one year, especially in the rainy season. The ore is
currently supplied from Bailadilla and Dominalai Mines and the railway routes are severely affected during the rainy
seasons. The Committee is of the view that VSP should look out for expansion of its iron ores captive mines for smoother
operations of the plant, which will also help the VSP to achieve the set targets. The Committee further recommends that
the Mines identified by VSP like Chidi Mines and Ramaghat in Chattisgarh may be acquired by VSP to strengthen its
operations. The Government should render all necessary help in accomplishing this task.
2.21  The Committee further observes that as a part of its expansion plan, the focus in the first phase was on capacity
enhancement of 5 million tonnes with minimal investment, by exploiting the inherent potential of the existing facilities.
In this phase , the capacity of the Blast Furnaces was planned to be increased by using natural gas, which is likely to be
available in the Krishna-Godavari basin. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should ensure the
availability of natural gas from KG Basin at the earliest which is crucial for the Phase-I expansion programme of VSP.
EXPANSION ACTIVITIES
2.22  The Committee was informed that during the year 2003-04 the hot metal production was likely to cross 4.1 million
tonnes. The requirement of Coke for the additional hot metal production has to be sourced from the external agencies.
There is acute shortage of coke both in domestic and international market due to closure of some coke oven units and coal
mines in China. Whereas, VSP is having its own three coke oven batteries, which requires expansion. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the request of VSP for the fourth coke oven Battery should be cleared immediately to meet
the additional production target as well as the timely taking up of rebuilding of the present coke oven batteries.
2.23  The Committee observes that as a long-term measure and considering the inherent strengths of VSP a corporate
plan for expanding the capacity of VSP to 10 million tonnes by the year 2020 should be seriously taken up by the
Government so as to meet the increasing demand of steel in the country as well as the potential for export.
RAILWAY FREIGHT
2.24  The Committee was informed that the Railways have been charging 30% extra as surcharge for movement of iron
ore from Bailadilla to Visakhapatnam  for the past thirty years. Now, it has been reduced to 20% . As many years have
passed, the Railways have recovered the construction cost on this route, the surcharge must be completely waived off.
This will benefit the VSP which is moving the largest quantity of Iron ore on this line. The Committee, therefore, is of the
view that the Government should consider the request of VSP to waive the surcharge imposed on freight movements on
the line.
2.25  The Committee was also informed that the Railways, for the movement of materials for a distance less than 100
kms charge freight equivalent to 100 kms. The distance between VSP and Visakhapatnam  Port is around 23 kms,
However, the freight is charged equivalent to 100 kms, which is a great loss to VSP. The Committee is also of the view
that the Government should consider the request of VSP that the freight charges should be as per the actual distance basis.

CHAPTER-III
MoU PERFORMANCE IN RESPECT OF DREDGING CORPORATION OF INDIA (DCI)
3.1    In the 1960s, dredging requirements in the various ports were being catered to by the then Ministry of Shipping and
Transport which maintained a central dredging pool consisting of dredgers, hopper barges, tugs, survey launches and
other operational equipment. Subsequently, in 1968, considering the increased dredging requirements in the country,
various crafts and equipment were handed over to Shipping Corporation of India Ltd. (SCI) for managing on agency
basis. Over the years, the development of ports continued and taking into account the increasing dredging requirement in
the country , the Government decided to form a separate Company. Accordingly, in March, 1976, Dredging Corporation
of India Limited (DCI) was incorporated as a wholly owned Government of India Undertaking with the primary objective
of catering to the dredging requirements of various ports. However, the agency arrangement with SCI continued during
1976-77, and DCI commenced its full-fledged commercial operations from 1.4.1977.
3.2    The Sub-Committee for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises visited Visakhapatnam on 22
nd
September, 2003 as a part of its study visit to PSUs on MOU performance. The Committee was apprised by the CMD,
DCI that DCI has its Registered Office at New Delhi, Head Office at Visakhapatnam  and Offices at almost all the major
ports. DCI possesses 10 Trailer Suction Dredging and 2 Cutter Suction Dredgers. The Company was formed with an
authorized capital of Rs.3000 lakhs, of which Rs.2800 lakhs was fully paid up taken entirely by the Government of India.
In 1992, the Government disinvested 1.44 % of its share-holding and presently shares of the Company are listed in Delhi,
Mumbai and Kolkata Stock Exchanges. The DCI has again listed 20% of its stock for disinvestment in March, 2004
alongwith other PSUs which received overwhelming response in the market. The Company has been earning profit
consistently since its inception, and its turnover from a modest Rs.1986 lakhs in 1977-78 has risen to Rs.51952 lakhs; at a
capacity utilization of Rs.102% in 2002-03.
         The dredging capacity of the Company has increased from 155 lakh CuM. in 1977-78 to 798 lakh CuM. in 2002-03:
DCI’s main customers are Major Ports; Non­ Major Ports; Indian Navy; Shipyards and Private Ports.
3.3    DCI has always strived to meet the requirement of its customers and, on some occasions; DCI’s efforts were
appreciated by the customers. DCI has been awarded Mini-Ratna (Category-I) status by the Government during 1999.
DCI was upgraded to Schedule-“B” category with effect from lst April, 2002. To augment the dredging capacity, the
Company has acquired three Trailer Suction Hopper Dredgers each of 7400 Cu. M. hopper capacity, which were added to
the fleet during 1999, 2001 and 2002, respectively. DCI’s 10th plan outlay of Rs. 365 crores, inter alia, envisages
addition of one more Trailer Suction Dredger of 5000 Cu. M. hopper capacity, and a cutter Suction Dredger of 2000 Cu.
M. pumping capacity/hr.

3.7    The Committee takes note of the importance of dredging in improving our ports and thereby contributing to the
economic development. The horizon of dredging is fast expanding and its services are increasingly put to use in the
protection of environment. The DCI has been fully equipped to offer the complete range of such services in India as well
as abroad.

Suction Dredgers, upgradation of its existing fleet as well as to expand the services in India and abroad should be fully
taken care of by the Government considering the strategic service provided by the Corporation. The Committee further
observes that all the dredgers and equipments are bought from abroad. The Committee feels that the time has now come
for the Government to explore the possibility of manufacturing dredgers and related equipments and the machinery in the
country itself. It will not only give boost to the ship building industry but also help to meet the growing needs of DCI.

4.23  The Committee also appreciates the excellent R&D facilities available with NMDC which is comparable to any

“Centre of Excellence” by UNIDO. The Committee is of the view that development of such facilities should be

DEVELOPMENTAL ACTIVITIES
4.24  The Committee observes that a vast reserve of high grade iron ore is available at the disposal of NMDC in Bailadila
region. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should explore all possibilities to exploit it in view
of the growing need for steel and related products in the local and global market.
4.25  The Committee further observes that the NMDC is facing great difficulty in transportation of ores to various places,
availability of rakes, especially from Bailadila. It has been experienced that during the rainy season in Bailadila sector the
railway tracks get disturbed due to land slides etc. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should
ensure that the traffic system in the sector be well maintained for speedy and timely delivery of iron ores at the required
places.
4.26  The Committee was apprised that the NMDC was engaged in exploration of diamond and gold in the country. The
Committee is of the view that efforts of NMDC should be fully supported in their mining activities for diamond and gold
in the country.
EXPORT OPPORTUNITIES
4.27  The Committee was informed that NMDC had entered into 30 years agreement with Japan for export of iron ore
which had been successfully executed. Keeping in view the potential available with NMDC, the Committee recommends
that the NMDC may be made the sole agency in the export of minerals especially iron ore.
4.28  The Committee was also apprised that there was problem in the availability of ports for export purpose. It has been
stated that due to environmental reasons many major ports have restricted the movement of iron ore in their ports. The
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take necessary steps to ensure that the ports should
provide necessary facilities for the export of iron ore including construction of separate satellite-ports or separate berths,
if necessary.
4.29  The Committee observes that there is ever growing domestic and international market. There is a possibility of
additional production with marginal investment in the existing projects of NMDC which has great potential for export.
The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Government to take necessary steps to support NMDC in the export of iron
ore.
4.30  The Committee also observes that keeping in view the knowledge available with NMDC in the field of exploration
and mining there is great potential for consultancy services in this area. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should fully utilize this facility available with NMDC.
4.31  The Committee was informed that the NMDC has taken up several projects abroad. In view of the experience
gained in these projects, the Committee, recommends that the Government should extend necessary support in exploring
the opportunities for Joint-ventures in India as well as abroad for mineral exploration and mining.
PROTECTION OF NMDC
4.32  The Committee observes that due to liberalization, private competitors have also entered in the field of mineral
exploration and mining. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take necessary steps to
strengthen NMDC in every sphere so as to face the potential threat from private competitors.
4.33  The Committee further observes that the Government’s policy to allow captive mines for steel plants in private
sector is a great threat to the NMDC, which has vast reserves and potential to cater to the needs in the domestic and
international market. The Committee, therefore, recommends to review the policy of Government in this regard.
 
CHAPTER -V
MOU PERFORMANCE OF BHARAT DYNAMICS LIMITED (BDL)
5.1    Bharat Dynamics Limited (BDL), Hyderabad was established in 1970 to manufacture guided missiles. In 1989, it

was nominated as the Prime Production Agency for Missile Weapon Systems. The Company diversified to produce
Torpedo and Naval System from 2000 onwards. Government of India has invested Rs.115 crores in this wholly owned
Government Company. It is now one amongst a few strategic industries of the world having the capability to produce the
most advanced guided missile systems for the Armed Forces. The Company has been categorized as Mini Ratna due to its
consistent good performance.
Product Range of BDL
5.2    BDL has two manufacturing units. These are at Kanchanbagh (Hyderabad) and at Bhanur (Medak District). It
produces the following equipments: Milan Anti-tank Guided Missile (ATGM) (under Licence Agreement with Euro
missile of France) with a range of 2 KMs; Konkurs Anti-tank Guided Missile (ATGM) and Konkurs-M (Tandem
Warhead) under Licence Agreement from Russia, with a range of 4 Kms; Prithvi, Surface-to Surface Missile (SSM);
3UBK-20 (Gun launched Projectile) with a range of 5 Kms, under licence from Russia; Advanced Experimental Torpedo
(AET); Submarine Fired Decoy (SFD); and 9 MM Pistols. Training simulators for Anti Tank Guided Missiles (ATGM)
viz. ATGM Indoor and Outdoor Simulators, Konkurs simulators; Interactive Fire Arms Training Simulator for training in
Small Arms; Test Equipment viz., KLTE, KMTE, FLTE. BDL is also nominated as the Prime Production Agency for
Akash, Nag, Trishul (New version) Missiles under development by Defence Research and Development Organisation
(DRDO). These projects are in different stages of development. Further the Ministry of Defence has nominated BDL as
the production Agency for Refurbishment/Life Extension of various types of Missiles held in the inventory of the three
services. In addition, BDL has supplied Tow body to Aeronautical Development Establishment (ADE) and flow formed
tubes to Bhaba Atomic Research Centre (BARC).

Quality
5.8    Most of the products of the Company are single shot devices which call for utmost reliability. The quality policies
have been laid out to achieve this objective with emphasis on ensuring quality right from basic input levels till the
realization of the final product.
5.9    This quest for quality has resulted in three production divisions obtaining ISO­-9002 accreditation and the
Information Technology Division-ISO-9001 accreditation. The Company is now planning to upgrade this certification to
ISO-2000 version. The Electronics Testing Lab of BDL has been accredited by National Board for Accreditation for
Laboratories (NABL).
Diversification
5.10 Towards optimum utilization of established capacities, BDL would soon take-up production of Counter Measure

OBSERVATION/RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
ACHIEVEMENTS
5.20  The Committee appreciates the role of BDL in the national security. BDL is one amongst the strategic industries in
the world . The Committee also appreciates the substantial progress achieved by BDL in absorbing DRDO Technology
for manufacture of missiles in the country as well as various in-house developed products.
5.21  The Committee further appreciates BDL for being nominated as the Prime Production Agency for Akash, Nag,
Trishul, Agni for the Ministry of Defence. At the same time the Committee appreciates the attempts made by BDL in
refurbishing/ life expansion of various types of missiles in the inventory of three services. The Committee is of the view
that the BDL should be properly assisted in its efforts in refurbishing / life expansion of missiles which normally have a
life span of 10-15 years. By refurbishing their life can be extended to another 10 years which will be helpful in saving the
expenditure being incurred in manufacturing of new missiles. The Committee therefore recommends that the Government
should look into this aspect and extend all its support to BDL in the refurbishing of missiles.
5.22  The Committee was informed that apart from the contribution to the defence sector, BDL has been indirectly
helping 650 units in the Small Scale Industries (SSI) Sector which are engaged in manufacturing of various components
necessary for the production of Missiles. The Committee notes with satisfaction- the contribution by BDL in development
of economy as well as providing employment to thousands of people and fulfilling the social need of employment in the
society.
CONSTRAINTS
5.23  The Committee during the course of its interaction with the representatives of BDL understood the restrictions for
joint venture with various companies. Most of the products of BDL like Milan Anti-tank Guided Missile (ATGM)
Konkurs Anti-tank guided missiles (ATGM) and Konkurs -M (Tandem Warhead) are manufactured under Licence
Agreements with Euro missile of France and Russia respectively, which are a hindrance in transfer of technology
resulting in prolonging indigenisation of the products. The Committee therefore recommends that Government should
extend necessary support in promotion of joint ventures and indigenisation of various range of products of BDL as well
as modernisation of its products which are becoming obsolete in the race of time.
5.24  The Committee was also informed of the very limited market segment available for its licensed products, which is
an impediment in marketing Indian products in the international market. As compared to the price of products available in
the international markets the Indian products are cheaper and have great potential in the field of export. The Committee
is, therefore, of the view that the Government should explore all possibilities to establish a place for Indian products in
the international market.
5.25  The Committee also feels that the Government should review the restrictions on the export of Integrated Guided
Missile Development Programmes (IGMDP) products as there is large scope for earning foreign exchange.
5.26  The Committee was informed that the price of various range of products of BDL is fixed by the Government. As the
Government is the sole purchaser of its products, thereby earning of the organization is controlled by the Government and
there is mandatory 20% dividend to be paid to the Government. The Committee is of the view that in the era of opening

SAFETY
5.27  The Committee was informed about the fire accident that took place in the year 2001 due to which it was rated ‘
Fair’ in terms of MOU performance during the years 2000-0l and 2001-02. The Committee is of the view that in an
organisation of strategic importance, safety is an integral component of its performance. The Committee, therefore, urges
upon the Government to ensure safety measures to avoid such accidents in all strategic organisations.
FUTURE PLAN
5.28  The Committee is of the view that the growth of a country rests upon its defence capability also. Therefore, any
developing nation should not compromise in defence sector because of pressure from any quarter. The Committee was
informed that the BDL envisages induction of various products in the medium term and long term periods. The
Committee therefore, recommends to the Government to ensure that the future plan of BDL be fulfilled to produce a
range of products to put the country in the list of developed countries.

COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
PERFORMANCE
         The Committee takes note of the overall performance of the VSP particularly the financial crisis overcome by the
organization and reaching the ‘Zero Debt’ level. The Committee was informed that the PSU was referred to BIFR in the
year 1998-99. It started recovering since then and its cash profit was likely to reach Rs.975 crores (approx ) in the year
2002-03. In terms of MOU performance also the PSU performed well and has been rated continuously ‘ Excellent’ since
2000-01. The production of value added steel products has also risen from a level of around 3 lakh tones in 2000-01 to
over 4.8 lakh tones in 2002­-03 and the efforts being taken by the PSU for new products, grades continued to be
developed every year to meet the market demand. The Committee appreciates the various steps taken to improve the
performance of the plant like, capacity utilization, optimum maintenance of equipments available and the ongoing
technological upgradations in various areas. The Committee also appreciates the thrust given by training and HRD
activities a well as the focus on the R&D taking place.                                                                                                        
(Para 2.19)
         The Committee observes that the major raw material for production of steel is iron ore, which is supplied by NMDC
. The supply of Iron ore to VSP has been inconsistent for the past one year, especially in the rainy season. The ore is
currently supplied from Bailadilla and Dominalai Mines and the railway routes are severely affected during the rainy
seasons. The Committee is of the view that VSP should look out for expansion of its iron ores captive mines for smoother
operations of the plant, which will also help the VSP to achieve the set targets. The Committee further recommends that
the Mines identified by VSP like Chidi Mines and Ramaghat in Chhattisgarh may be acquired by VSP to strengthen its
operations. The Government should render all necessary help in accomplishing this task.                          (Para 2.20)
         The Committee further observes that as a part of its expansion plan, the focus in the first phase was on capacity
enhancement of 5 million tonnes with minimal investment, by exploiting the inherent potential of the existing facilities.
In this phase , the capacity of the Blast Furnaces was planned to be increased by using natural gas, which is likely to be
available in the Krishna-Godavari basin. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should ensure the
availability of natural gas from KG Basin at the earliest which is crucial for the Phase-I expansion programme of VSP.
(Para 2.21)

mines in China. Whereas, VSP is having its own three coke oven batteries, which requires expansion. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the request of VSP for the fourth coke oven Battery  should be cleared immediately to meet
the additional production target as well as the timely taking up of rebuilding of the present coke oven batteries.(Para 2.22)

RAILWAY FREIGHT
         The Committee was informed that the Railways have been charging 30% extra as surcharge for movement of iron

passed, the Railways have recovered the construction cost on this route, the surcharge must be completely waived off.

kms charge freight equivalent to 100 kms. The distance between VSP and Visakhapatnam  Port is around 23 kms.
However, the freight is charged equivalent to 100 kms, which is a great loss to VSP. The Committee is also of the view
that the Government should consider the request of VSP that the freight charges should be as per the actual distance
basis.         (Para 2.25)
POWER OF CEO ON FOREIGN TRAINING/VISITS
         It is necessary for any organization to be in the forefront to update its knowledge and learn the new technology for
process and productivity improvements. However, to achieve this objective, it is a must for the executives and non-
executives of the organization to be exposed to the environment where better production practices are followed both in
domestic and international arena. The Committee was informed that the recent guidelines issued by the Ministry of
Finance Office Memorandum No.7(4).E-Coord/2000, dt. 24.9.2000, do not allow the VSP to approve the tours of the
employees in connection with business study training and conferences, etc. The Committee is of the view that for better
performance of the organization it is necessary that the CEOs should be vested with this power to depute personnel for
seminars, training/study and exposure to advances technology. The Committee therefore, recommends that Government
should review the position in this regard.                                                                                               (Para 2.26)

dredging. It has the state of the art fleet of dredgers and related equipments of the world class. The Committee is of the
view that in order to keep pace with the demands of the future, the DCI’s ambitious plans to procure more Trailers,
Suction Dredgers, upgradation of its existing fleet as well as to expand the services in India and abroad should be fully
taken care of by the Government considering the strategic service provided by the Corporation. The Committee further
observes that all the dredgers and equipments are bought from abroad. The Committee feels that the time has now come

on Red Sea in Saudi Arabia and other Middle- East and South - East Asian countries. It has been looking forward for
projects in Taiwan  in the recent past. The Committee observes that the Government should extend necessary help in

Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take necessary steps to ensure that the ports should
provide necessary facilities for the export of iron ore including construction of separate satellite-ports or separate berths,
if necessary.         (Para 4.28)

148th Report of The Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/148threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:46:18]
         The Committee observes that there is ever growing domestic and international market. There is a possibility of
additional production with marginal investment in the existing projects of NMDC which has great potential for export.
The Committee, therefore, recommends to the Government to take necessary steps to support NMDC in the export of iron
ore.         (Para 4.29)
         The Committee also observes that keeping in view the knowledge available with NMDC in the field of exploration
and mining there is great potential for consultancy services in this area. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the
Government should fully utilize this facility available with NMDC.                                    (Para 4.30)
         The Committee was informed that the NMDC has taken up several projects abroad. In view of the experience
gained in these projects, the Committee, recommends that the Government should extend necessary support in exploring
the opportunities for Joint-ventures in India as well as abroad for mineral exploration and mining.(Para 4.31)
PROTECTION OF NMDC
         The Committee observes that due to liberalization, private competitors have also entered in the field of mineral
exploration and mining. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should take necessary steps to
strengthen NMDC in every sphere so as to face the potential threat from private competitors.(Para 4.32)
         The Committee further observes that the Government’s policy to allow captive mines for steel plants in private
sector is a great threat to the NMDC, which has vast reserves and potential to cater to the needs in the domestic and
international market. The Committee, therefore, recommends to review the policy of Government in this regard.(Para
4.33)
ACHIEVEMENTS
         The Committee appreciates the role of BDL in the national security. BDL is one amongst the strategic industries in
the world . The Committee also appreciates the substantial progress achieved by BDL in absorbing DRDO Technology
for manufacture of missiles in the country as well as various in house developed products.     (Para 5.20)
         The Committee further appreciates BDL for being nominated as the Prime Production Agency for Akash, Nag,
Trishul, Agni for the Ministry of Defence. At the same time the Committee appreciates the attempts made by BDL in
refurbishing/ life expansion of various types of missiles in the inventory of three services. The Committee is of the view
that the BDL should be properly assisted in its efforts in refurbishing / life expansion of missiles which normally have a
life span of 10-15 years. By refurbishing their life can be extended to another 10 years which will be helpful in saving the
expenditure being incurred in manufacturing of new missiles. The Committee therefore recommends that the Government
should look into this aspect and extend all its support to BDL in the refurbishing of missiles.                                            
(Para 5.21)
         The Committee was informed that apart from the contribution to the defence sector, BDL has been indirectly
helping 650 units in the Small Scale Industries (SSI) Sector which are engaged in manufacturing of various components
necessary for the production of Missiles. The Committee notes with satisfaction the contribution by BDL in development
of economy as well as providing employment to thousands of people and fulfilling the social need of employment in the
society.         (Para 5.22)
CONSTRAINTS
         The Committee during the course of its interaction with the representatives of BDL understood the restrictions for
joint venture with various companies. Most of the products of BDL like Milan Anti-tank Guided Missile (ATGM)
Konkurs Anti-tank Guided Missiles (ATGM) and Konkurs -M (Tandem Warhead) are manufactured under Licence
Agreements with Euro missile of France and Russia respectively, which are a hindrance in transfer of technology
resulting in prolonging indigenisation of the products. The Committee therefore recommends that Government should
extend necessary support in promotion of joint ventures and indigenisation of various range of products of BDL as well
as modernisation of its products which are becoming obsolete in the race of
time.                                                                                    (Para 5.23)
         The Committee was also informed of the very limited market segment available for its licensed products, which is
an impediment in marketing Indian products in the international market. As compared to the price of products available in
the international markets the Indian products are cheaper and have great potential in the field of export. The Committee
is, therefore, of the view that the Government should explore all possibilities to establish a place for Indian products in
the international market.                                                                                                       (Para 5.24)
         The Committee also feels that the Government should review the restrictions on the export of Integrated Guided
Missile Development Programmes (IGMDP) products as there is large scope for earning foreign exchange.        (Para
5.25)

         The Committee was informed that the price of various range of products of BDL is fixed by the Government. As the
Government is the sole purchaser of its products, thereby earning of the organization is controlled by the Government and
there is mandatory 20% dividend to be paid to the Government. The Committee is of the view that in the era of opening
up of economy, the Government should allow the BDL to fix the price of its products and make profit to promote its
developmental activities so as to compete in the international markets.                             (Para 5.26)
SAFETY
         The Committee was informed about the fire accident that took place in the year 2001 due to which it was rated
‘Fair’ in terms of MOU performance during the years 2000-01 and 2001-02. The Committee is of the view that in an
organisation of strategic importance, safety is an integral component of its performance. The Committee, therefore, urges
upon the Government to ensure safety measures to avoid such accidents in all strategic organisations.(Para 5.27)
FUTURE PLAN
         The Committee is of the view that the growth of a country rests upon its defence capability also. Therefore, any
developing nation should not compromise in defence sector because of pressure from any quarter. The Committee was
informed that the BDL envisages induction of various products in the medium term and long term periods. The
Committee therefore, recommends to the Government to ensure that the future plan of BDL be fulfilled to produce a
range of products to put the country in the list of developed countries.                                                        (Para 5.28)
