INTRODUCTION
 
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Forty-ninth Report on MoU Performance in respect of Public
Sector Undertakings pertaining to the Department of Public Enterprises.
2.      The Sub- Committee-III for Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises (of Department -related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry) heard the CMDs of Air India, Indian Airlines, Airports Authority of
India and other officials and representatives of the respective administrative Ministries on their MoU performance on
13th October, 2003. The present report is based on the deliberations of the meeting held that day.
3.      The Committee in its meeting held on 25th August, 2004 considered and adopted the Report.
 
NEW DELHI
25th August, 2004
SANTOSH BAGRODIA
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
 
 
REPORT
CHAPTER - I
MoU System
         The Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) is a negotiated document between the Government, acting as the
owner of Public Sector Enterprise (PSE) and a specific PSE. It contains the intentions, obligations and mutual
responsibilities of the Government and the PSE. Further, MoU makes an attempt to move the management of PSEs from
management by controls and procedures to management by results and objectives.
1.2    The genesis of the policy of Memorandum of Understanding can be traced to the report of the Arjun Sengupta
Committee. One of the recommendations of this Committee was for the introduction of the system of MoU for
measurement of performance of public enterprises.
Objectives of the MoU System
1.3    The objectives of the MoU system are to improve the performance of public enterprises by increasing autonomy
and accountability of the management; to remove the fuzziness in the goals and objectives of the enterprise to pursue
through clearly laid down performance targets in the MoU and to enable the evaluation of managerial performance
through objective criteria and provide a mechanism to reward good performance through performance incentives to
stimulate improved performance.
1.4    Under the agreement the enterprises undertake to achieve the targets set in the agreement at the beginning of the
year. Thus the MoU covers both financial performance as well as non-financial performance. Under this system
performance of the Company is ­categorized into five categories namely: excellent, very good, good, fair, and poor.
Preparation of MoU
1.5    Based on the guidelines issued by the Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) in the month of October/November,
the draft MoUs are prepared by PSEs and forwarded to the Administrative Ministry and DPE by December. The draft
MoUs indicate the performance targets on a five point scale as proposed by the PSE for the ensuing financial year for all
crucial parameters like production, sales, profits, etc. The PSEs are also expected to include dynamic parameters of
significance for strengthening the future potential of the enterprise, such as project implementation, R&D, Human
Resource Development, etc. Appropriate weights are assigned to each of these parameters. The draft MoU are discussed
with the PSE Administrative Ministries at the Adhoc Task Force (ATF) negotiation meetings arranged in DPE in the
month of March/April, soon after the presentation of the Union Budget. Since the Budget has implications on the
performance targets, the timing of the negotiation meetings is deliberately scheduled after the budget presentation. The
appropriateness of the parameters and weights and the soundness of the targets as also the commitments of the
Government are examined in detail at the negotiation meetings. The draft MoUs as finalised thereafter are placed before
the High Power Committee (HPC) comprising the Cabinet Secretary as Chairman, Secretary, Finance, Planning
Commission, Programme Implementation, Chairman Public Enterprises Selection Board, Chief Economic Adviser and

149th Report of The Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/149threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:47:19]
Secretary Public Enterprises as Members, for approval. After approval, the respective Chief Executives and Secretaries
sign them.
Evaluation of MoU
1.6    The evaluation of the MoU signing enterprises is done at the end of the year by the Adhoc Task Force (ATF) on
the basis of actual achievement vis-a-vis the MoU targets. Where the performance exceeds the target by the
predetermined stipulated level the enterprise is ranked as ‘excellent’ and when the target is just met, the enterprise is
ranked as ‘very good’ . In other cases, where the targets are not met the enterprise is ranked either ‘ good’ or ‘ fair’ or ‘
poor’ . Ranking depends on how the performance has been as compared to MoU targets.
1.7    The performance criteria should be assigned appropriate weights corresponding with their stated priorities in the
objectives. It should be ensured that they also reflect the perceived relative importance of the various criteria in the
judgement of the PSE/Ministry. The weight for physical criteria should be kept as low as possible. Instead, Efficiency
and Dynamic criteria should get higher weights. The weight for profit-related financial parameters would be 60 % in
case of PSEs operating under free market mechanism. The weight of 60 % would be distributed to, Gross Margin, Gross
Profit/Capital Employed and Net Profit/Net Worth, each having a weight of 20 % each. For PSEs operating under
administered prices, PSEs where Government is sole; almost sole customer & Trading, Consultancy, Engineering and
Financial PSEs, the weight would be
40 % . The weight of 40 % would be distributed to, Gross Margin and Net Profit/Net Worth, each having a weight of 20
% each. The PSEs which have been specially set up for implementing certain Government policy directives will have no
pre-determined financial parameters.
1.8    The targets set should be realistic and growth oriented. It should be ensured that the MoU targets flow from the
Corporate Vision/Plans formulated by the PSEs and there is linkage between them. In case there is any variation,
reasons thereof should be clearly specified. For qualitative indicators, the targets for each of the points on the 5-point
scale should be indicated in the performance matrix itself. If these targets are on a time scale, only such target, which
falls within the MoU year, is included.
1.9    The MoU should contain the past five years performance data on criteria included in the MoU in an appendix. It
should also indicate the projections for the next five years, as far as possible consistent with the corporate plan.
Civil Aviation Sector
1.10  The Committee had a derailed study on the MoU system in respect of various PSUs . The Civil Aviation Sector in
India is a striking example of the progress made in the ongoing liberalization process of the Indian Economy, which
began a decade ago. The last few years have seen a tremendous change in this sector with major policy initiatives
having been taken and implemented vigourously. Considering the importance of the Civil Aviation Sector in the
development of the country, the Committee decided to examine the MoU Performance in respect of the Civil Aviation
Sector of the country.
1.11  Before the induction of the private airlines in this sector, Air India (AI), Indian Airlines (IAL) and Airports
Authority of India (AAI) played a major role in the industry. Indian Airlines normally operates domestic flights in the
country including few neighbouring  countries, Air India mainly operates internationally and the Airports Authority of
India is concerned with the upkeep of the domestic as well as international airports and terminals of the country.
1.12  The Committee, in order to examine the performance of MoU system of the various airlines and conditions of the
airports in the country as also to suggest improvements therein, held a meeting on
15th October 2003 and had detailed discussions with Air India (AI), Indian Airlines (IAL), Airports Authority of India
(AAI) apart from the private airlines which included the Sahara and the Jet Airlines to draw a line of comparison as their
performance with the PSUs  in the sector. The Committee deliberated upon the subject, which is enumerated in the
following chapters.
 
CHAPTER - II
AIR INDIA LIMITED
2.      Air-India is India’s national flag carrier. Although air transport was born in India on February 18, 1911 when
Henri Piquet, flying a Humber bi-plane, carried mail from Allahabad to Naini Junction, some six miles away, the

149th Report of The Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/149threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:47:19]
scheduled services in India, in the real sense, began on October 15, 1932. It was on this day that J.R.D. Tata , the father
of Civil Aviation in India and founder of Air-India, took off from Drigh Road Airport, Karachi, in a tiny, light
single-engined de Havilland Puss Moth on his flight to Mumbai (then known as Bombay) via Ahmedabad. He landed
with his precious load of mail on a grass strip at Juhu, Mumbai.
Mr. Neville Vincent, a former Royal Air Force (RAF) pilot who had come to India from Britain  in 1929 on a brain-
storming tour, during which he had surveyed a number of possible, air routes. He saw the immense potential for aviation
in India. He along with J.R.D Tata  worked out a scheme for air service from Karachi to Mumbai, which heralded birth
of Tata Airlines.
Tata Airlines
2.1    Tata  Airlines, as Air-India was then known, consisted of one Puss Moth, one Leopard Moth, one palm- thatched
shed, one whole time pilot assisted by Tata  and Vincent, one part-time engineer, two apprentice- mechanics and
unlimited optimism. In 1933, the first full year of its operations Tata  Airlines flew 160,000 miles , carried 155
passengers and 10.71 tonnes of mail. Tata Airlines was converted into a Public Company under the name of Air-India in
August 1946. Going Global by the beginning of 1947, Air-India turned its attention to the international scene. Towards
the end of the 9th year, an agreement was reached with the Government of India for the formation of Air-India
International Limited to operate international services.
2.2    At Air-India’s request, the Government agreed to limit their capital participation to 49 per cent, subject to an
option to acquire, at any time, a further two per cent from Air-India. Air-India International, which was registered on
March 8, 1948, inaugurated its international services on June 8, 1948, with a weekly flight from Mumbai to London via
Cairo and Geneva with a Lockheed Constellation aircraft.
Nationalisation
2.3    The early’50s saw the financial condition of various airlines operating in India deteriorate to such an extent that
the Government decided to step in and nationalise the air transport industry and accordingly two autonomous
Corporations were created on August l, 1953. Indian Airlines was formed with the merger of eight domestic airlines to
operate domestic services, while Air-India International was established to operate the overseas services. The word
‘International’ was dropped in 1962. Effective March l, 1994, the airline has been functioning as Air-India Limited.
From a total of three stations served at the time of nationalisation , Air-India’s worldwide network today covers 44
destinations by operating services with its own aircraft and through code-shared flights.
New Thrust
2.4    At present there are 43 aircrafts in its fleet Air-India has expanded its fleet by inducting 14 aircrafts during the
years 2000-04 out of which three Boeing 747-400s and eleven Airbus 310s are on dry lease during the years 2000-04.
Induction of these dry leased aircraft has enabled Air-India to enhance frequencies to many existing destinations and
introduce several new flights. This includes introduction of a daily service on the India-Paris-New York sector; three
terminator flights to Frankfurt; three ­ flights to Chicago  via Frankfurt. Flights to Shanghai from Mumbai via Delhi-
Bangkok Twice weekly direct services between Ahmedabad and London. Air-India is further proposing to take two
more Boeing 747-400s on dry lease - one in June 2004 and the other in October 2004. These aircraft are being dry
leased for commencing flights to Los Angeles on the West Coast of United States. While initially, effective June 2004,
flights will be started on a thrice-weekly basis, the frequency would be increased to five per week in October 2004. Air-
India has incidentally, since December 2002, already doubled its capacity on the India-US sector - from ten to twenty
flights per week. Introduction of flights to Los Angeles would help increase services to US to 23 per week in June 2004
and to 25 per week in October 2004. Expansion of fleet through the dry-leasing route, pending acquisition of aircraft,
has also enabled Air-India to improve its ranking amongst world airlines on the basis of revenue earned and number of
passengers carried. According to a review published in September 2003 in Airline Business, an international magazine,
while Air-India’s ranking on the basis of revenue in 2002 has gone up to 51 from 54 in the preceding year, Air-India
stands at 54 (up from 61 in 2001) on the basis of passengers carried.
Network
2.5    In its ever-growing quest for providing direct services from various points in India, Air-India currently operates
flights from Mumbai, and 11 other Indian cities, viz. Ahmedabad, Bangalore, Chennai, Delhi, Goa, Hyderabad, Kochi,
Kolkata, Kozhikode, Lucknow and Thiruvananthapuram. Commencement of international operations from these cities

149th Report of The Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/149threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:47:19]
has obviated, to a very large extent, the need for passengers from these regions to necessarily travel to Mumbai and
Delhi, the traditional main gateways, for taking international flights . Passengers boarding or deplaning in these cities
can now complete their immigration and custom formalities at their city airport, both at the time of departure and
arrival. Air-India has simultaneously introduced fixed time departures for flights to the Gulf from Mumbai, Delhi and
Kochi. In the past two years, the number of flights operated to the Gulf has increased from 75 to 104.
Air India’s objectives
2.6    Air India’s objectives are stated to take effective steps to provide a high level of customer satisfaction; enhance its
competitive market standing and image as an international carrier; optimize its share of the air market to/from the
objectives of long­term  financial viability and sustainable growth; optimise the utilisation  of its resources ­aircraft
fleet and employees; achieve the highest level of safety of operations; increase the productivity and optimise the number
of employees through the expansion of capacity and the implementation of an attractive Voluntary Retirement Scheme
and assist in the Disinvestment in Hotel Corporation of India; develop global standards of efficiency through
benchmarking. Based on these above objectives, Air India is evaluated on three categories of parameters - Physical,
Financial and Other parameters.
MoU Performance
2.7    Air India has been signing the MoU with the Ministry of Civil Aviation since 1988 - 1989. Air India’s MoU
ratings based on audited results since 1998 - 1999 are as follows:
Year Score based on audited results Remarks
1998-1999 1.89 VERY GOOD
1999-2000 1.53 VERY GOOD
2000-01 MoU not signed —

INDIAN AIRLINES LIMITED
3.1    Indian Airlines Limited was incorporated under the Companies Act w.e.f. lst May 1992 with the main objective to
provide safe, efficient, adequate, economical and properly coordinated air transport services. As per the Air
Corporations (Transfer of Undertaking and Repeal) Ordinance 1994, the entire undertaking of Indian Airlines was
transferred and vested in the said company i.e. Indian Airlines Ltd w.e.f. 1st March 1994. The Company for the
purposes of functional convenience has been divided into four regions having their regional headquarters at the four
metros. The aircraft fleet of IA consists of a mix of aircraft including A300, A320, B737 and DO228, which operate on
domestic, as well as short/medium haul international sectors. At present the strength fleet of Indian Airlines is 62
including 11 dry leased Aircrafts inducted during the years
2001-04.
3.2    A wholly owned subsidiary of IAL styled as Airlines Allied Services Limited was formed on 13th September 1983
under the Companies Act. The total investment in this company stands at Rs.2.25 crores as on 3lst March 2003
comprising of 2,25,000 equity shares of Rs.100 each fully paid up. During the year 1996-97 IAL made available to this
subsidiary the entire fleet of 12 Boeing 737 aircraft for its operations under the banner of Alliance Air.
3.3    IAL, over the past many decades of its operations, has developed a modernized aircraft maintenance infrastructure,
which includes the Jet Engine Overhaul Shop at Delhi where overhauling as well as repairs of V-2500 and JT8O
engines as per international norms are carried out. Further, comprehensive inhouse repair facilities are also available for
repairs of airframe and components of various types of aircraft in maintenance workshops at Delhi, Mumbai, Hyderabad
and Kolkata. Besides, there is a full-fledged APU Overhaul Center at Kolkata for APUs of all types of aircraft.
3.4    Indian Airlines also has an in-house training establishment at Hyderabad, which has the latest equipment including
aircraft simulators for training of pilots/engineers. The Company also has a Real Time Reservation System to cater to its
wide network of operations.
3.5    The Company basically operates in a highly sensitive industry, which is extremely susceptible to the socio-
economic environment prevalent in the country as well as internationally. As the state carrier of India it is also entrusted
with the responsibility of operating on financially unviable routes much in excess of its requirements as per the
Government’s route dispersal guidelines.
3.6    The network of IAL spans over 61 stations in India and 16 stations abroad. IAL is operating 112 flights
constituting of over 300 departures per day (including Alliance Air). Over the past few years the market share of the
company has been on a steady decline. This is due to the fact that there has been a growth in the domestic capacity
which has been largely due to the additional aircraft inducted by the private airlines whereas the capacity offered by
Indian Airlines has remained almost constant. This, coupled with the increased cost of maintenance of an ageing fleet
has made a dent in the company’s profitability. Moreover, the financials of the company are very much dependent upon
various uncontrollable factors such as the price of Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF), Insurance costs, and landing & parking
charges etc.

CHAPTER V
OBSERVATIONS / RECOMMENDATIONS AND CONCLUSIONS OF THE COMMITTEE
         At the outset the Committee appreciates the services of the PSUs in the Civil Aviation Sector and observes that the
infrastructure, passenger service and the duty structure are the areas of great concern.
5.1    As regards the MoU performance of the three PSUs in the Civil Aviation Sector the Committee expresses its
concern on the problems being faced by them particularly the Air India and Indian Airlines, leading to fall in their
physical and financial performance  which have direct bearing on their MoU performance as these parameters have been
given more weightage. The Committee, therefore, urges upon the Government to look into the problems being faced by
the Civil Aviation Sector to improve their performance.
5.2    The Committee takes note of the suggestions made by the PSUs with regard to changes in the MoU format. The
Air India submitted that the MoU format only provides for an evaluation of the performance of the PSE vis-a-vis the
MoU targets and there is a need for adjusting the ratings obtained by the PSE to be reckoned with the level of actual
assistance provided by the Government vis-à-vis the agreed items in the MoU. The Committee, therefore, is of the view
that the Government should take into account the suggestion of Air India while signing MoU.
5.3    The Indian Airlines Limited have submitted that the MoU format for the service sector PSE should include more
physical parameters as compared to financial parameters and it should be given more weightage as the performance of
the companies in the service sector can be more minutely monitored in terms of physical achievements. The Committee
also appreciate it and recommends that appropriate weightage should be assigned to the physical parameters so as to
make it more effective in terms of the performance.
5.4    Committee is also of the view that the MoU system is to give more freedom to the PSE in their core functions in
order to enhance their performance thereby resulting in better service and contribution to the national economy. The
Committee therefore, recommends that the MoU system should be followed in true spirit.
5.5    The Committee is of the view that there has been under utilization and poor project implementation on the part of
the Air ports Authority of India which has added to the poor infrastructure. The Committee therefore, recommends that
the more weightage should be given to the parameters on project implementation in the MoU rating.
5.6    The Committee observes that the projects may be split into a number of works and awarded to several contractors
which could be completed well in time thereby avoiding the delay in implementation of the project which is a major
parameter.
5.7    During the course of interaction with the representatives of the PSEs the Committee was informed that the
Airports are not developed in a way as they have been in many developed countries, especially passenger amenities at
the Airports which have resulted in poor Aeronautical Revenue. The Committee takes serious note of the situation
prevailing in the airports and recommends that the Government should take necessary steps and report the same to the
Committee in their Action Taken Note on this Report.
5.8    The Committee has been informed about the state-of-the-art Instrument Landing System lying idle in the Delhi
Airport. It has also been informed that the pilots have been demanding extra pay to undergo training in the system
resulting in delay in utilization of the facility available with the AAI. The Committee takes serious note of the situation
and would like to be apprised of the latest position in this regard and the steps taken by the Government to resolve the
deadlock. The Committee further recommends that the Government should initiate inter- PSUs cooperation in a service
sector like Civil Aviation Sector so as to meet the quality in service as well as customer satisfaction.
5.9    The Committee has also taken note of the safety and security measures taken in the Civil Aviation Sector and
appreciates the efforts made by the Government in this regard.
5.10  The Committee has also taken note of the HRD activities under taken by PSUs and would like to impress upon the
Government that the constraints like age of the crew and deployment of the crew should be addressed properly which is
an important factor in the improvement of the performance of the PSEs in the Sector. The Committee therefore, would
like to be apprised of the position regarding these issues.
5.11  The Committee was apprised that the duty structure has direct bearing on the cost of Aviation Turbine Fuel (ATF)
thereby resulting in service implication on the performance of the sector. It was informed that if the cost is not brought

FIFTEENTH REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE

I, the Chairman, Department-Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry,
having been authorised by the Committee, present this Fifteenth Report of the Committee
on the Demands for Grants for 1995-96 of the Ministry of Mines.

2. The Committee, while examining the Ministry's demands for 1995-96, considered it
important to seek views of the representatives of Chambers of Commerce such as the FICCI
and the CCI on the performance of the mines sector and the impact of recent budget
proposals relating to the Ministry of Mines. At its subsequent meetings, the Committee
heard the views of representatives of Central Trade Unions in the same context.

3. The Committee had also an opportunity to hear oral evidence of the Secretary, Ministry
of Mines on the Performance Budget in the context of Demands for Grants of the Ministry.

4. The Committee considered and adopted the present report at its sitting held on the 28th
April, 1995.

5. Unlike in the case of a number of other Ministries, the budgetary allocation for the
Ministry of Mines has been showing a decline in recent years. Keeping to this trend, the
overall provision of Rs. 195.15 crore proposed for the Ministry for 1995-96 is lower than the
revised estimate of Rs. 197.55 crore for 1994-95. The Committee would like to have the
underlying issues related to such progressively shrinking allocations discussed afresh.
According to assumptions in official circles, the country is poised for an industrial
breakthough and an annual rate of industrial growth of 10 to 12 per cent is being confidently
predicted. An industrial expansion of this order, expected to sustain itself over a decade or
thereabouts, is bound to be variegated in nature. In such circumstances, there would be a
steadily rising demand for minerals of all descriptions, including those which are under the
administrative charge of the Ministry of Mines. This demand would need to be met. There
can be a point of view that the required additional supply of basic minerals which could
support an industrial explosion of this magnitude is to be ensured either through imports or
through the initiative of the private sector. In the current stage of economic development in
the country, and despite the strides the policy of liberalisation have made, it will be
hazardous to fall back on these two alternative sources of supply in entirety. Should the
private sector not be forthcoming or should open-ended imports not be possible, bottlenecks
might develop in crucial areas, frustrating expectations of high industrial growth, It is true
that the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 and the Mineral
Concession Rules, 1960 have been amended two years ago with the overt purpose of
attracting private investment, including foreign private investment, in the exploration of
minerals, especially those that are of high value. The experience of the past four years
should however convey a warning: while sizable foreign capital has flown into the country,
the bulk of it has been portfolio investments in the share markets. Actual investment in
industry and manufacturing proper, or in the core sectors such as mineral development, has
been only to a modest extent. Private domestic capital has been equally shy. To assume that
a reversal of. this trend will take place in the near future is not really warranted, Certainly
the global environment is such as not to encourage ४ hypothesis of this nature. It is therefore
imperative, in the committee’s view, that the authorities do not slacken their efforts to
intensify the exploration and exploitation of basic minerals necessary for sustaining the
country’s rapid industrial advance. The budgetary allocation for the Department of Mines
should move upwards rather than be allowed to taper away year after year.

5.1 The Committee would in this connection stress particularly the role the Geological

1


Survey of India could play in the emerging phase of industrialisation in the country. Within
the limited resources made available to it, the GSI has some major achievements to its credit
in the recent period, such as the exploration of new gold provinces in Rajasthan and Kerala
and striking rich new reserves of coal, lignite, zinc, lead and maganese. The nagging paucity
of funds has however affected the GSI’s programme of modernisation and has also
compelled it to narrow down its arena of activities to within a narrow groove and abstain
from initiatives which would be of immense long-term consequence for the nation’s industrial
growth. Such activities could cover the exploration of new vistas for enlarging the output of
minerals such as coal, bauxite, lignite, copper, zinc, manganese etc., with emphasis on
continuous improvement in the quality of the raisings. It is in fact possible to conceive a
certain division of responsibility between the GSI and the Mineral Exploration Corporation
Limited, also under the administrative jurisdiction” of the Ministry of Mines. Once the
reserves,are found by the GSI, it should be the task of the MECL to take charge of the
actual development of the mines. Unfortunately, perhaps because of the static nature of
budgetary allocations in recent years, the Corporation, there is ground for suspicion, is
marking time. In the opinion of the Committee, the authorities should make up their mind
to enlarge the scope of activities of the Corporation, intensifying its organic link with the
GSI. In case however the Government has no such intention, it would be preferable to fold
up the Corporation and save the annual allocations routinely made for it; the minor chores it
performs can be transferred to another public sector organisation such as the Indian Bureau
of Mines or the National Mineral Development Corporation. The Committee would take a
similar view with respect to the allocations for the Indian Bureau of Mines and
developmental grants to scientific institutions specialising in exploring the latest frontiers of
science and technology in the relevant fields. These allocations cannot but be described as
token and would hardly succeed iin equipping the nation with state-of-the-art knowledge and
information in regard to mining technology. The Committee strongly feels the need for 8
review, at the highest level, of the issue of relative allocations of budgetary funds for
scientific, industrial and technological research and investigations keeping in view the
country’s overall requirements in the short as well as the long run.

5.02 The attention of the Committee has been drawn to the likely impact of the downward
adjustment in the rates of import duty on copper and zinc in the budget for 1995-96. The
management of the Hindustan Copper Limited, for instance, apprehend a major decline in
their sales because of external competition, and the gross revenue of the unit, it is claimed,
would be reduced by Rs 42 crore on an annual basis. The price disadvantage vis-a-vis.
imported copper is also likely to widen because ‘of the increase in railway freight. The
overall affect would be to turn the estimated net profit of Rs. 5.35 crore registered in 1994
95 to a net loss of around Rs, 40 crore in 1995-96.

5.03 A similar predicament confronts the Hindustan Zinc Limited. The reduction in the
rate of import duty on zinc and its wastes and scraps from the level of 50 per cent to that of
35 per cent and on zinc-based finished products from 50 per cent to 40 per cent is likely to
affect the competitiveness of the Hindustan Zine extractions; the increase in rail freight has
to be considered in this case too. The Hindustan Zinc Limited was expected to make a profit
of around Rs. 4.23 crore in 1994-95. The lowering of import duty is now estimated to reduce
the earnings of the unit by close to Rs. 70 crore. The reduction in the rates of import duty
of lead too would, it has been suggested, lead to a decline in the profitablity of the unit to
the tune of Rs. 10 crore.

The Committee has reasons to believe that this alarmist picture painted by the public
sector units by way of the impact of intrusion of more liberal imports following the


3

downward adjustments in rates of import duty on minerals such as copper and zinc should
not be dismissed out of hand. The issues involved are of crucial relevance for the nation’s
long-range goals. Whether globalisation must proceed at such a breakneck speed that
indigenous units, installed over the years and involving enormous capital expenditure, must
go to the wall is a moot question. A great deal can be said in favour of stretching the
process of phasing out the burden of coping, with a situation arising out of the reduction in
rates of import duty even where such reduction of duty was generally expected. The
Committee would therefore suggest that the Ministry of Mines makes due representation so
that some of the adjustments in the rates of import duty announced through this year’s
budget are reconsidered. .

5.04 There are two other matters the Committee would specifically like to mention. It had
occasion in the past to refer to uncertainties shrouding the operations of Bharat Gold Mines.
An impression, howsoever unjustified, appears to be gaining ground that having referred the
case of the unit to the Board of Industrial and Financial Reconstruction, the authorities are
assuming their duty to have been accomplished. The BIFR as an institution has a very wide
ambit of responsibility. Its procedure for decision-making is, in the circumstances, somewhat
time-consuming. In the interim, the workers of the unit have been kept on the payroll and
their wage bill has been met by the Government by periodic release of funds; the production
of gold is however on the lower side in the mines. This arrangement is hardly satisfactory,
Receiving wages while not called upon to contribute any labour to the extent they are
capable of can be demoralising in the extreme to the working class and erode their sense of
dignity. The Committee still hope that its recommendations made in its Seventh report
would receive the Government’s acceptance and necessary funds would be made available so
that the rehabilitation of the unit could be undertaken expeditiously. In this connection, the
Committee has a suggestion to offer. Despite the commitment to use the resources made
available from the National Renewal Fund for retraining and redeployment of workers
engaged in units that are shut down as a consequence of liberalisation, the outlay
undertaken till now from the NRF has been almost exclusively for the purpose of meeting
the requirements of the Voluntary Retirement Scheme. This has been the general pattern in
all the Ministries availing of NRF resources, including the Ministry of Mines. It is for
consideration whether a part of the allocation under the NRF to the Ministry could not be
utilised for the rehabilitation and modernisation of Bharat Gold Mines.

5.05 A part of the NFR allocations, the Committee would suggest, be used to put into
shipshape the activities of the Sikkim Mining Corporation. One reason for the difficulties
faced by the Corporation is the reluctance of the Hindustan Zinc Limited to accept the lead
concentrates supplied by the former on the ground of presence of high impurities. Since both
units are under the administrative charge of the Ministry of Mines, it should not be beyond
the realm of possibility for it to hammer out a compromise which would serve both well. For
example, a washery could be set up to eliminate the impurities. within a definite time
interval. It is also for consideration whether the activities of the Sikkim Mining Corporation
could not be diversified, and the unit made the epicentre for processing @ number of basic
metals with a view to meeting the requirements of the north-eastern region. The Committee
hopes the necessary budgetary allocations for the purpose would be met.

5.06 The Committee considers it important to append a few comments on the state of the
aluminium industry which is under the operational jurisdiction of the Ministry of Mines.
India has rich bauxite resources and the installed capacity for the production of aluminum is
close to 650,000 tons per annum. Unfortunately, the actual production has languished at

॥२52050


4

around 450,000 tons in recent years. The main hurdle standing in the way of the realisation
of larger output, the Committee understands, is the lack of availability of power for
Processing bauxite. This issue needs to be sorted out as expeditiously as possible; it makes
little sense to import aluminium while domestic capacity remains unutilised because of
uncertainties of power supply. In case necessary discussions may be arranged by the Ministry

5.07 The Committee has taken note of the recent initiatives to encourage the. entry of
foreign capital in the area of mining. While it is yet too early to gauge the response of
foreign investors to the changes introduced in the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and
Development) Act, it is desirable that terms and conditions set for foreign participation in
mining activities are formulated in dequate detail and tabled in the two Houses of
Parliament. Since the administrative responsibility for mining operations taking place in the
country is shared by at least three Ministries—the Ministry of Mines, the Ministry of Coal
and the Ministry of Steel—it is exceedingly impotant that, on all vital policy issues, the
Ministries maintain the closest coperation with one another. In any event, the Committee
would stress the importance of the deployment of domestically evolved technology and skills
for mining development receiving due priority in official Programmes and projections.

REPORT
         The Department of Public Enterprises acts as a nodal agency for all central PSEs and assists in policy formulation
pertaining to the role of PSEs in the economy as also in laying down the policy guidelines on the performance improvement
and evaluation, financial accounting, personnel management and in related areas. It also collects, evaluates and maintains
information on several areas in respect of PSEs. DPE also provides an interface between the administrative Ministries and the
PSEs.
2.      The important role and tasks of the Department are listed below:
(i)     General policy relating to Public Sector.
(ii)     Matters relating to issue of Presidential Directives and guidelines to Public Sector Enterprises.
(iii)    Formulation of policy guidelines pertaining to Public Sector Enterprises in areas like performance improvement
and evaluation, financial management, personnel management, board structures, wage settlement, training,
industrial relation, vigilance, performance appraisal, etc.
(iv)    Matters relating to reservation of posts in the public sector enterprises for certain classes of citizens.

(vi)    Matters relating to delegation of powers to Board of Directors.

Departments except disputes relating to tax matters.

ORGANISATION OF DPE
3.      The Department is headed by a Secretary who is assisted by an establishment with an overall sanctioned strength of 121
personnel. The Department has following Five constituent Divisions:
(i)    The Financial Policy Division: It comprises the Public Enterprises Survey unit, the policy planning unit, the wage
policy unit and the work relating to disinvestment of shares of public sector enterprises.
(ii)    The Management Policy Division: It comprises the personnel policy unit, training unit, performance indicator and
work norms unit (PIWN Unit) and SC & ST Cell.
(iii)   The MOU Division; It comprises MOU Unit, Data Bank and Computer Cell.
(iv)   The Administration & Coordination Division: It comprises the Administration Library, Parliament and
Coordination Wings and Hindi Cell.
(v)   The Permanent Machinery of Arbitration (PMA): It provides a forum for settlement of commercial disputes
between two or more PSEs as well as between Government Departments and PSEs.
4.      The Committee was further informed of the brief resume of activities of the Department included an Annual Survey of
all CPSEs. The Survey is a repository of the information on performance of all CPSEs. The highlights of the performance may
be stated as under:
(i)    The Department issued new MOU guidelines based on interim report of Consultant (NCAER) and MOU were
signed with 100 CPSEs.
(ii)    To enhance the managerial capabilities of the Executives in the CPSEs, 47 Executive Development Programme
(EDPs) were organized.
(iii)   An appraisal of the performance of all the Mini-ratna CPSEs was made.
(iv)   Non-official part-time Directors have been appointed on the board of the Navratna PSEs and 24 of 44 Mini-ratna
PSEs. .
(v)   As a support system to CPSEs, Government have given purchase preference to CPSEs. During 2003-04, 35 CPSEs
and 2 privatised companies and 1 joint venture were benefited by getting orders of around Rs. 1500 Crores under
this scheme.
(vi)   12,200 rationalised employees of CPSEs were imparted retraining for rehabilitation under CRR scheme.
5.      The Committee was further informed that the extension of the purchase preference policy beyond 31.3.2004 and
enhancement of autonomy and financial power to CPSEs particularly Navratnas and Miniratnas  were under active
consideration of the Department for the year 2004-05.
6.      The Committee acknowledges DPE’s role as the nodal department for all the CPSEs and as such its importance in the
economic development of the country. While specific action is to be taken by the concerned administrative Ministry, DPE
provides policy framework and facilitates atmosphere for better productivity, smooth functioning and higher contribution to
national economy.

19.    In order to give greater functional autonomy to the management of CPSEs, the guidelines issued by the Department of
Public Enterprises have been reviewed and rationalized from time to time. Under Articles of Association, the Board of
Directors of PSEs enjoy autonomy in respect of recruitment, promotion and other service conditions of below Board level
employees. MOU signing companies have been delegated higher powers in respect of wage revision, for evolving incentive
scheme, voluntary retirement scheme and transfer of functional directors within PSU, etc.
NAVRATNA CPSEs
20.    In July, 1997 the Government identified 9 Public Sector Enterprises that had comparative advantages and potential to
emerge as global giants as Navratnas. These PSEs are given enhanced autonomy and delegation of powers to incur capital
expenditure, to enter into technology Joint Ventures/Strategic Alliances, to effect  organisational restructuring, to create and
wind up below Board level posts and to raise capital from domestic and international market. Restructuring of Board by
inducting at least 4 non-official Directors is a pre-condition for exercise of the enhanced powers. The 9 Navratna PSEs are
BHEL, BPCL, GAIL, HPCL, IOC, MTNL, NTPC, ONGC and SAIL.
MINIRATNA CPSEs
21.    In October 1997 the Government decided to grant enhanced autonomy and delegation of financial powers to other profit
making companies subject to certain eligibility conditions and guidelines to make them efficient and competitive. These
companies are called Miniratnas and these are in two categories, namely, Category I & II.
22.    The Committee was informed about the criteria for conferring the status of Miniratna  are (i) the PSE should be profit
making for the: last 3. years continuously and should have positive net worth, (ii) should not have defaulted in repayment of
loans/interest payment on loans due to government, (iii) should not depend upon budgetary support or government guarantee
and (iv) its Board is restructured by inducting at least 3 non official Directors PSEs which have made pre-tax profit of Rs.30
Crore or more in at least one of, the 3 years will be given Category I while others are given Category II status. The
administrative Ministries are empowered to declare a PSE as a Miniratna if it fulfils the eligibility conditions.
23.    The enhanced powers given to Miniratna PSEs include the power to incur capital expenditure, enter into joint ventures,
set up technological and strategic alliances and formulate schemes of human resources management. Presently there are 42
Miniratna PSEs (29 Category I and 13 Category II).
24.    The Committee desires DPE to furnish an appraisal of the effect of such status and directs the Department to ensure a
mechanism of making any assessment of the benefits of such schemes.
PROFESSIONALISATION
25.    The Committee was informed about the several measures that have been initiated to professionalise the management of
Public Enterprises. Induction of professionals on the Boards of PSEs as non-official part-time Directors is being done. As per
the guidelines issued by DPE, the number of such non-official part-time Directors should be at least 1/3rd of the actual
strength of the Board whereas the number of Government Directors on the Boards should not exceed two. As per SEBI’s
guidelines on corporate governance, in the cases of the listed companies headed by non-executive Chairman at least 1/3rd of
the Board should comprise Independent Directors and in the cases of companies headed by executive Chairman at least half of
the Board should comprise Independent Directors; According to the Navratna  and Miniratna  schemes, the Boards of these
companies should be professionalised by inducting a minimum of 4 non-official Directors in the case of Navratnas and 3 non-
official Directors in the case of Miniratnas before the Board exercise the enhanced powers.
26.    The Committee takes note of the fact that non-official Directors have been appointed in 24 of 44 Mini-Ratna  PSEs. The
remaining vacancies are yet to be filled up. The Committee therefore recommends that the non-official part time directors of
remaining Mini-ratna ‘PSEs must be appointed at the earliest to facilitate efficient functioning of the concerned PSEs.
27.    The Committee recommends that lower and medium level executives and technical staff too should be given opportunity
to enhance and upgrade their skills through regular short duration courses at reputed professional and technical institutions.
The Committee is of the view that views management techniques and office process must be adopted to make respective PSEs
competitive. For this there should be regular interface between PSE management and management experts and institutions.

29.    The Committee was apprised of the institutional mechanism for the MOU process. A High Power Committee of
Secretaries headed by the Cabinet Secretaries is the apex institution to finalise  the draft MOU before signed and to make year
end evaluation to assess the achievement of objectives and commitments. At the preliminary level, a Task Force provides
technical expertise for MOU negotiations .and evaluation. To maintain objectivity and credibility, the Task Force consists of
retired civil servants, executives of public sector, management professionals and independent members with considerable
experience.
30.    The guidelines for MOU are prepared by MOU Division and circulated among the respective PSEs and their
administrative Ministries. These guidelines indicate broad structure and aspects to be covered in the draft MOU including the
graded weights to be assigned to various parameters. The guidelines reflect main objectives of the Government and the
guidelines to the PSEs. The MOU Division in the Department of Public Enterprises acts as the permanent secretariat to this
High Power Committee and Task Force. The Division develops information and database on MOU signing PSEs. It monitors
the progress of MOUs. The Division also coordinates research and training on various aspects of MOU policy.
31.    Performance of MOU signing PSEs is evaluated twice in a year with reference to their MOU targets. First the
performance is evaluated on the basis of provisional results and secondly on the basis of audited data. ‘The PSEs are graded as
“Excellent”; “Very Good”, “Good”, “Fair” & “Poor” on’ the basis of the evaluation of MOUs.The summary performance of
MOUs signing PSEs as reflected in their MOU rating till 2002 is as follows.

32.    On the basis of interim report submitted by NCAER, new guidelines for the year 2004-05 were prepared and circulated
to MOU signing PSEs and Administrative Ministries. According to these guidelines, total weight in the MOU assessment
format has been divided into common parameters (80%), sector specific parameters (10%) and enterprise-specific parameters
(10%). Common parameters include financial and dynamic parameters and are applicable to all PSEs. Sector-specific
parameters reflect sectoral thrusts and priorities and enterprise-specific parameters reflect performance improvement measures
at the enterprise/unit level.
33.    The Committee observes that MoU system has been relevant in the past and still holds relevance in the current’ scenario
though it needs a review. It is desirable if the weightage  given to the financial parameters is significant and the targets should
be sufficiently high with a view to improve performance and productivity, year after year.
34.    The Committee also feels that the MoU Division in DPE, which implements the MoUs, needs to be strengthened by
induction of additional manpower. More funds needs to be allocated to MoU Division/DPE, so that it is able to get MoU
related studies done by professional bodies. It should also be ensured that senior officials of the administrative Ministries
actively associated in all MoU related matters.

PURCHASE  PREFERENCE  POLICY
37.    The Purchase Preference Policy provides purchase preference in supply of goods and services to the Government
Departments, Autonomous bodies and other PSEs if the price quoted by the supplying CPSE is within 10% of the lowest valid
bid price, other things being equal. Besides CPSEs, the policy is applicable to the joint venture companies where holding of
Government and / or CPSEs is 51% or more. The policy will also be available to those privatized CPSEs where specific
approval has been accorded for the specific periods from the date of disinvestment.
38.    The Committee acknowledges that the purchase preference policy, which was in force till 31.3.2002, has been extended
for two more years i.e. up to 31.3.2004 on its recommendation. The Committee recommends a study to be done on the
efficacy of this policy. In consonance with its pronounced policy, Government may consider to extend this policy for next 3 to
5 years.
PERMANENT  MACHINERY  OF  ARBITRATION
39.    The Committee was apprised of the mandate of the DPE in this regard. Permanent Machinery of Arbitrators has been set
up in Department of Public Enterprises for resolving commercial disputes except relating to taxation and Railways between
PSEs as well as between a PSE and a Central Government Department/Ministry.
40.    An appeal against the award of the Arbitrator can be made to the Secretary, Ministry of Law, in case either party is not
satisfied with the award. The decision of Secretary, Ministry of Law is final and binding on the parties. No appeal can be made
in the Court of Law/Tribunal against the decision of Secretary (Law).
41.    The Committee considers it to be a positive initiative. It desires to be apprised of the impact of this mechanism in speedy
settlement of disputes.
SCHEME  FOR  COUNSELLING,  RETRAINING  AND  REDEPLOYMENT
42.    The Committee takes note of the allocation of Rs. 30 crores made in the B.E. of 2004-05 out of which an amount of Rs.
26.40 crores is earmarked for Re-training, Re­deployment of rationalized workers of CPU’s. There is an increase of Rs. 17.40
crores from Rs. 9 crores in the R.E. of 2003-04 to Rs. 25.40 crores for the year 2004-05 under Plan allocation.
43.    About the allocation of Rs. 26.40 crores as budgetary support to Iron and Steel industries, it was explained to the
Committee that the CRR scheme falls under Iron and Steel Head of Development under Sectoral  Central Plan Outlay as
categorized by the Planning Commission for the purpose of budget allocation. However the expenditure to be incurred under
the CRR scheme is not limited only to Iron and Steel Industries but it covers other sectors also.
44.    The Committee was informed that with objective to rationalize the labour force in CPSEs VR Scheme was introduced in
CPSEs in 1988. The scheme was reformulated and notified in May, 2000. The objective and scope of the scheme is to provide
opportunities of counselling, retraining and redeployment to the rationalized employees of Central. Public Sector Enterprises
through short duration training programmes to enable them to adopt new vocations and take advantage of available
opportunities of self employment. The Department of Public Enterprises is the coordinating agency to arrange for government
funds on annual basis, monitor the implementation of the scheme with the nodal agencies and the CPSUs , and provide
necessary direction and guidance. Accordingly the DPE also draws the Plan of Action.
45.    The Committee expresses its concern that the displaced employee needs psychological counselling to absorb the trauma
of loss of job and to face the new circumstances. They need advise for the prudent management of compensation amount and
other financial benefits from the CPSU. They also need to be made aware of the new environment of market opportunities so
that they may, depending upon his aptitude and expertise, take up economic activities.
46.    The Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) selects suitable nodal agencies for implementing the scheme of counselling,
retraining and redeployment These agencies may be government/semi government and non government organization having
experience in the field. Financial assistance for such progragmme is provided to the nodal agencies by the DPE. In all 34 nodal
agencies have been selected so far all over the country. They are required to develop suitable curriculum and teaching material
for training. They maintain the data with regard to counselling , training, redeployment and self- employment of such
employees. Planning Commission also undertakes a midterm review of the CRR Scheme. The Director, Personnel of the
respective CPSUs are the key resource persons in respect of counselling , retraining and redeployment of rationalized
employees and maintains regular touch with the trainees and maintain records about their deployment either in new
organizations or self employment.

adopt new avocation through skill upgradation and entrepreneurship development to enable them to engage themselves in
income generating activities by taking advantage of market opportunities.
51.    The Committee is of the view that the financial assistance particularly under the Rural Employment Generation
Programme of the KVIC (Margin money scheme), Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY); various schemes formulated by
the SIDBI and other similar schemes of self employment, must be availed for the benefiit of VRS optees-of the PSUs.
Preference may be given to such employees in the schemes launched by Departments/Ministries of Agro and Rural Industries,
Small Scale Industries, Rural and Urban Development. Training and credit facilities should be extended also to the family
members of rationalized employees so that the family income can be enhanced. The respective PSEs and nodal agencies
should impart training according to region-specific requirements or in the traditional industries of the region.
52.    The Committee recommends that the facilities of medical, educational and other social securities should remain available
to the former employees in respective PSEs.
53.    The Committee is of the view that the social audit of such rationalization in respective PSEs should be conducted.
Rationalisation if remains unattended may become a factor of social disruption and delinquency in the region. The conclusions
of such social Auditing may help in upgrading the CRR Schemes.
BOARD  FOR  RECONSTRUCTION  OF  PUBLIC  SECTOR  ENTERPRISES  (BRPSES)
54.    The Committee takes note of the Finance Minister’s Budget speech, wherein it was proposed to establish a Board for
Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE) to advise the Government on the measures to be taken to restructure
PSEs, including cases where disinvestment or closure or sale is justified. The BRPSE is to examine each case objectively and
make recommendations on disinvestment, consistent with the NCMP.
55.    The Committee appreciates that the proposed Board as it is likely to expedite the process of advice to the questions of
revival, restructuring, disinvestment or closure, as the case may be. However, the exact details of its constitution, terms of
reference, modalities including the Ministry in which it is to be set up (locus) are under consideration of the Government. The
Committee urges upon the Government to finalise it at the earliest.
56.    The Committee observes that the recommendations of Expenditure Reforms Commission regarding the existence of
Department of Public Enterprises may be viewed considering the activities, achievements and proposed plans of the
Department. The Committee is of the view that the effective implementation of these plans is of critical importance for

         The Department of Heavy Industry (DHI) administers 48 Central Public Sector Enterprises (PSEs), a majority of
which are involved in the manufacture of capital goods for power, steel, petro-chemical and fertilizer, transport industry
etc. Apart from the PSEs, the Department of Heavy Industry focuses on promoting the development of automotive
sector, heavy electrical/engineering industry in the country.
2.      The Committee was informed that during the year, the Central PSEs under the Department achieved a turnover of
more than Rs. l2,000 crore The BHEL contributed in the development of the power sector in the country. The company
recorded a turnover of Rs. 8, 653 crore (prov.) during 2003-04. PSEs are being encouraged to take up viable capital
investment programmes for their strengthening.
3.      The Department regularly interacts with various industry Associations and evolves plans for their growth through
policy initiatives, resolution of problems relating to tariff and trade, promotion of technological upgradation and
Research and Development.
4.      Since the beginning of liberalization and opening up of the economy, the Department has been continuously
restructuring Public Enterprises to improve their competitive viability in domestic and global market. Some of the
measures taken in this regard are necessary manpower rationalization, financial restructuring, upgradation of the
technology and improvement in the productivity. During the current year 2004-05, actions are being initiated for
revival/restructuring of PSEs, as per the Government’s policy.
5.      The Committee was informed that periodic review of the performance of PSEs was done at various levels within
the Ministry as well as in the Board. The system of signing MOUs  with PSEs has been effective in enhancing their
performance and ascertaining the accountability. The MOU system is also periodically reviewed and modified.
6.      The proposed plans of the Department include programmes  of renewals and replacement, additions, modifications
in PSEs. These initiatives are expected to improve their productivity.
7.      The Department of Heavy Industry had projected a demand of Rs. 223.24 crore to the Planning Commission for
the year 2004-05. The Planning Commission however finally agreed to an allocation of Rs. 131 crore. Some of the
schemes like Coal Gassification , Auto Testing and programmes  of ILK, Braithwaite etc. have been provided reduced
allocations.
8.      The Committee was informed that any shortfall, as a result, should be projected at RE stage and no project would
be allowed to suffer.
9.      The Committee impresses upon the Government to provide for the requisite funds at the RE stage as the proposed
plan of DHI have a direct bearing on the improvement of the productivity of its PSEs.

AUTOMOBILE SECTOR
39.    The Automobile Sector is highly capital intensive and technology oriented. Consequently, continuous research and
development expenditure is a key to the growth of the industry. The Committee was informed that in 2002-2003, the
total expenditure on R&D by the vehicle manufacturers had been Rs. 483.24 crores, which is almost 12% of gross profit
of the automobile manufacturers. The results are clearly seen in terms of  increasing  number of indigenously developed
light and heavy commercial vehicles.
40.    Moreover, the intensive R&D efforts in the industry has helped in upgradation  of  technology  for achieving
increasingly stringent emission and safety norms. Creation of new Testing Infrastructure for the automotive sector at the
R&D Institutes has enabled the Indian Automotive Industry to be globally more competitive and easy access to the
global market.
41.    The Committee was further informed that the upgradation and creation of Testing Infrastructure for the automotive
sector is a necessity in view of the imminent mandatory safety and emission standards. To realise  the objective .of
making India a hub of global automobile industry as envisaged in Auto Policy, a sound R&D base is essential.
42.    In fact, as recognition to the R&D capabilities developed domestically, the world’s major automotive
manufacturers, have been setting up R&D centres in India to cater to their overseas requirements.
43.    The Committee concurs that in view of emerging requirements of the automotive sector, there is an urgent need
for setting up of a World Class Testing and R&D Infrastructure in the country, which requires huge investment in the
next 3-4 years.
44.    The Committee takes note of the important project - National Automotive  Testing and R&D Infrastructure Project
(NATRIP) that has the potential to contribute towards GDP, exports and employment. The Committee recommends that
requisite budgetary support should be provided to such projects in view of the prospects for the country.
45.    The Committee also feels that the industry should come forward to share the expenditure so as to enable the
Government to set up world-class facilities. The Committee therefore impresses upon DHI to interact with concerned
federations and associations in this regard.
46.    The Committee was informed that the Government of India had extended the benefits of 150% weighted deduction
under Income Tax Act to automobile sector for R&D expenditure in the Union Budget 2004-05. While interacting with
various stakeholders in auto sector viz. SIAM, ACMA, ATMA, ARAI and HMT (Tractor division), the Committee
noted that the auto-industry has generally appreciated the provisions and direction of the budget. Further rationalization
of excise duty regime has been appreciated by the industry. Yet concerns were expressed by the industry pertaining to
rising prices of steel, natural rubber and other inputs. Industry has demanded further rationalization of excise duties.
47.    The Committee takes note of the need for excise duty rationalization in tractors to facilitate the producers to
transfer the benefits of reduced duty to the consumers. The Committee feels that the advantages of duty rationalisation
be such that benefits reaches the farmers.
48.    The Committee, therefore, agrees with this viewpoint and recommends that excise duties on the Tractor
components should be brought under CENVAT.

63.    Committee was informed about the constraints being faced by the PSEs. The PSEs suffer from paucity of orders,

INTERACTION WITH PSES
Heavy Engineering Corporation
69.    Established in 1952, HEC was the largest integrated, complex in the country that catered to the demands of
infrastructure sector, steel plants; railways, ship building; power plants, nuclear and. space research programs; ,defence
and mining industries. However in recent years the capacity and manpower of the Company has remained grossly
unutilized. Lack of assertive marketing, dependence of the protected market of Government and PSEs, inter-union
rivalry, leading to poor work culture, high cost of maintenance, of the equipments, consequent increase in interest
burden and shortage of working capital have collectively resulted in the Company being untenable and was referred to
BIFR in 1992. In July 2004 the BIFR recommended winding up of the Company. An appeal against the order in now
pending before AAIFR.
70.    In recent years however the Company has been able to reduce its operational losses and enhance the productivity.
The Company is now concentrating more on the areas of its core competence, while out sourcing low value addition

activities. It has also been rationalising its manpower. The Company hopes to benefit from the buoyant capital goods
market after a prolonged recession in steel industry.
71.    The Committee observes that the Company is yet to go a long way. The Committee notes with concern that HEC’s
order book position is far from satisfactory. The Committee is amazed to note that the Company does not have any full-
fledged marketing department. Due to lack of a proper marketing strategy, the Company is handicapped to harness the
growing market domestically, regionally or even globally. The Committee therefore recommends to the Government to
ensure that the Company has a proper marketing strategy and also has the full-fledged marketing department.
ANDREW YULE & CO.  LTD.
72.    The Company has been a Government of India enterprise since May 1979. It’s net worth is still negative at Rs.
34.93 crores. Tea is the major area of company’s business. However the recession in tea market has adversely affected
its financial performance. The recent price movement in tea has enhanced the prospects of Company’s tea-product. At
present the company is facing shortage of funds and owes mounting employee’s dues and other statutory dues. In 2003,
the Government approved a restructuring and revival package for the company that entailed Rs 49 crores of fresh equity,
Rs. 20 crores of Bond against Government’s guarantee and ploughing back Rs. 47 crore from the sale of investments in
group companies. The Government also agreed to convert Rs. 41.73 crores of loan into equity and waiver of interest on
its loan.
73.    The Committee was informed by DHI that with the improved tea prices the tea division of the company could be
in position to earn profit from 2006-07 onwards as per the restructuring plan.
74.    The Committee notes that due to NCMP, the group companies like Hoogly Printing Works and Tide Water Oil
could not be disinvested. The Company has submitted alternative proposal for assistance in place of its disinvested
units.
75.    The Committee therefore recommends that the proposal be considered by the Government so as to enable it to turn
around.
HINDUSTAN CABLES LTD.
76.    HCL was set up in 1952 to meet the increasing requirement of telecom cable by the telephone industry. Its main
products are jelly filled and fiber optic cables. However HCL is continuously making losses since 1995-96. Though a
package of assistance was approved by the Government in 1999, HCL was referred to BIFR in 2002: Reduction of
prices and burden of loans to pay VRS dues have reduced the working capital with the company.
77.    The Company requires non-plan assistance to clear salaries and wages and other statutory dues so as to enable it to
operate its bank accounts fully. It also requires assistance to settle its outstanding power-dues of its Rupnarainpur  unit
with Damodar Valley Corporation.
78.    The Committee was informed of lack of coordination between HCL and BSNL, which was the major buyer of its
cables. DHI suggested that ideally the BSNL’s requirement of jelly filled cable should be placed with HCL so that the
later covers 90% of their capacity. However due to fall in cable prices in last years, the price offered by BSNL is unable
to cover the cost of inputs. On the other hand the BSM., is getting cable at a much competitive price from smaller
companies. There is a need on part of HCL to reduce its cost of production. A study to this effect has been entrusted to
IIT Kharagpur. Meanwhile there are exports to obtain orders from BSNL and arrange for working capita.l  loan from
Allahabad Bank.
79.    The Committee observers that HCL was set up to meet the requirements of the predecessor of BSNL i.e. DOT and
presently suffers from lack of orders from them. The Committee recommends to the Government to resolve the issue
amicably at the earliest. The Committee further recommends that the HCL may be merged with BSNL and Government
may provide the Bank Guarantee for raising the working capital from Allahabad Bank.
HMT (BEARINGS) LTD.
80.    HMT (Bearing) Lid. is a Mini-Ratna company. It has been earning marginal though consistent profit till 2001-02.
It incurred loss in 2002-03, however the losses have come down in 2003-04 as rationalisation of manpower is underway.
81.    The Committee was informed that though there is huge domestic market of Rs. 2700 crores for bearings, HMT
(Bearing) Ltd. is only a marginal player with an annual production of Rs 2S-30 crores. Other major players in this field
in the country are SKF, NBC, FAG, Timken and NRB. Primary reason for company’s meager participation is absence
of technology upgradation and lack of funds for R&D. Also the slump in demand from HMT (Tractor), which was the
major buyer of its bearings, too adversely affected the finances of Company. The Company has not been able to find
fresh collaboration to validate its products. Though Company has the potential for a turnaround; it needs to upgrade its
technology.

82.    The Committee notes with concern that the Company is paying heavy interest on the market loans it has taken to
settle the dues of its VRS optees, which is further adding to the liabilities of the company. The Committee therefore
impresses upon the DHI to look into the issue and bring the company out of crisis.
83.    The Committee also recommends for expeditious decision on the revival proposals of HMT (Bearing) Ltd. of Rs.
77 crores that is under consideration with DHI. The revival plan includes infusion for Technology upgradation,
enhancing working capital and assistance for payment of dues of VRS optees.

84.    The Company has been serving the core and infrastructure sectors like power generation and transmission,
transportation, oil and gas, heavy industry, defence  etc. The Company has a vision to become an Indian multi-national
engineering enterprise providing total business solutions in field of energy, industry, transportation and infrastructure.
85.    The Committee noted that there has been an upward trend since 2001-02 in the profit earning of the Company,
with estimated profit of Rs. 1123 crores this year.
86.    However the Company sought assistance in terms of fiscal incentives to indigenous technologies exemption of
excise duty on indigenously developed R&D products, Iong term interest free loans. Availability of long term
competitive financing for the international projects by strengthening EXIM Bank. The company also sought level
playing field viz-a-viz foreign company that enjoy advantage in terms of low customs duty as compared to cost
disadvantage faced by domestic capital good manufacturers. The company also sought easier access to new technologies
by including a mandatory clause making obligatory to have local partner for foreign companies desirous to enter high
technology areas in the country.
87.    The Committee is in agreement with these demands and recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry
should take up the matter with concerned Ministries/ Departments and apprise the Committee of progress.
HINDUSTAN PAPER CORPORATION AND HINDUSTAN NEWSPRINT LTD.
88.    The Committee was informed about the financial, infrastructural, locational/geographic and other constraints faced
by the companies. These constrains mainly pertained to shortage of inputs and high cost of bamboo due to high royalty.
The companies are also facing competition from global giants in paper industry mainly from Nordic countries and
Canada due to low Customs duty. Further the HPC has sought permission from the Government of Assam for captive
afforestation on degraded land.
89.    The Committee was informed that company’s demand to increase the duty on the imported newsprint to the WTO
bound rate of 25% has not find favour in this year’s budget. The decision on allowing afforestation on the degraded land
is still pending with the Government of Assam and .being pursued by the Ministry of Heavy Industries. Similarly the
response of the State Government is still awaited on the issue of high royalty on bamboo.
90.    The Committee takes note of satisfactory financial situation of HPC and HNL.
91.    The Committee reiterates its recommendation contained in its 131
st Report for allowing the afforestation  on the
degraded land. It also recommends that the issue of high royalty on bamboo must be pursued with the State Government
in the interest of HPC. To provide HNL the level playing field, Government may also consider raising duty on imported
newsprint from existing 5% to the WTO bound rates at 25%.
92.    The Committee also reiterates its recommendation of 131
st report regarding Duty Exemptions to the units in NE
Region on the lines of petroleum refineries in this region.
93.    Regarding Nagaland Pulp & paper Company Ltd. the Committee was informed that the case has been referred to
AALFR. The draft report of M/s Development Consultants Pvt. Ltd., Kolkata  on revival NPPC was considered by DHI
in consultation with Economic Adviser and Internal Finance Wing. It was found that revival of NPPC did not make
much of economic  sense. However, Department of Heavy Industry is continuing to study the proposal in view of new
data and strategies.
MEASURES TO MEET THE SOCIAL OBLIGATIONS BY PSES
94.    The information furnished by the Department to the Committee reveals that most of the PSEs are committing less
and less percentage of their turnover for social overheads over the years. .
95.    The Committee observes that the PSEs were envisaged as the temples of modern India. Over the decades the
Public Sector has played a vital role in rapid industrial and technological development of the country. These PSEs have
played a key role in social development. The experience of recent years has shown that financial sickness of companies

151st Report of The Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/151streport.htm[04-07-2016 12:47:20]
has social ramifications too. The Committee therefore desires that social obligations be accorded due priority.
96.    As regards the constraints being faced by the PSEs, the Committee observes as under:
I.     Lack of orders mainly from the Government and other PSEs. In several cases the sickness of one PSE has had
corollary impact on other PSEs too.
II.    Another issue has been the fluctuating duty regime that have made PSEs non-competitive vis-a-vis other
global and domestic players.
III.   Obsolete technology and investment crunch due to reducing capital investment over the years in enhancing
the capacities of the PSEs has adversely affected the PSEs that have not been able to take the advantage of
economies of scale.
IV.   The PSEs at present are reeling under the burden of restructuring and rationalising their manpower. A larger
part of their resources goes into settling the dues often at a higher rate of interest.
V.    The Committee is of the view that in view of new economy and reducing Government support, PSEs shall
have to come to terms with new market realities. With expanding domestic, regional and global market, PSEs
shall have to take benefit of new opportunities.
VI.   In view of the NCMP that envisages a revitalized Public Sector, the Ministry of Heavy Industries should
evolve a Doctrine emphasizing that social obligations of the PSEs is a function of their financial health. The
two are not contradictory but complementary to each other. Therefore to meet its social obligations the Public
Sector must regain their financial health.
97.    Finally the Committee recommends that the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises may formulate its
responses to the observations and suggestions and apprise the Committee of the same periodically.

REPORT
          The Agro and Rural Industries Sector has been envisaged as an important avenue for creation of employment in
the rural non-farm sector for the balanced economic growth of the country. The importance of this sector lies in the fact
that it seeks to establish village industries at low cost based on the local raw materials, skills and technology for
providing employment opportunities to the local population and artisans who have been traditionally engaged in village
level economic activities. The main contribution of ARI sector to the National Economy has been in terms of production
and employment generation through setting up of village industries in the rural and semi-urban areas. Over the past five
decades, there has been a big growth in Village Industries (VI) Sector in terms of production and employment.
2.0     CHARTER OF FUNCTIONS OF MINISTRY OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
