2.1     The Ministry has a multi-pronged role to play in the quality implementation of policies, programmes and
schemes. In the role of a policy maker, the Ministry collects, collates and derives inferences, which act as critical input
to further policy formulation/amendments. In the role of an advocate, the Ministry advocates and puts up ‘felt needs’ of
the stakeholders involved in the sector as a whole. In the role of a facilitator, the Ministry facilitates, coordinates and
supports its field agencies in implementing the programmes and schemes both quantitatively and qualitatively. The
Ministry acts as a nodal agency for promotion and development of agro and rural industries in small towns and rural
areas, The Charter for the Ministry is as follows:----
          (i)    Coordination of the development of village and cottage industries, and Tiny/Micro Enterprises in both urban
and rural areas.
          (ii)    Coordination of matters relating to all Rural Industries.
          (iii)   Coir Industries including the Coir Board.
          (iv)   Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY).
          (v)   Khadi and Village Industries Commission.
2.2     The Ministry guides and coordinates with the implementing agencies to ensure development and achievement as
per the set mandate.
2.3     The Committee wanted to know the Monitoring mechanism working presently to oversee the functioning of
various organizations under the Ministry of Agro & Rural Industries The Ministry stated that the monthly performances
are reviewed in the case of KVIC and Coir Board whereas the Ministry makes a quarterly monitoring, As per the
Management Information System approved by the Cabinet Secretariat for Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries,
implementation of PMRY, coir exports, increase in utilization of raw material in coir sector and employment generation
under REGP and Khadi Package are reviewed. The activities of KVIC, PMRY and Coir Schemes are also reviewed by
Secretary on a monthly basis and a Brief Note is sent to the PMO and Cabinet Secretary. On the basis of monthly and
quarterly performances of progress in various sectors of development, appropriate instructions are issued to KVIC, Coir
Board and State Governments, This is being done on a regular basis.
2.4     The Committee hopes that the creation of independent Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would reinforce and
strengthen the functioning of the ARI sector as a whole, by highlighting its present status and ensuring timely policy
interventions when needed. The contribution of this sector can be further streamlined and strengthened by injecting
more professionalism in the areas of finance, marketing, HRD, technology and manpower upgradation in the KVI
sector, revival of sick khadi institutions, renovation and modernization of marketing outlets.
2.5     The Committee desires that the Government should conduct service auditing of the organizations working under
the Ministry of ARI with the purpose of improving their functioning in the better interest of the Agro and Rural
Industries.

to enhance its performance over the previous year. During 2003-04 production and sales were increased over the
previous years level. While the interest subsidy propelled the flow of working capital from banks, the rebate element
helped khadi institutions to boost sales and to get relief from the blockage of working capital to a certain extent.
11.3   For the financial year 2004-05, Rs. 86.35 crores has been allocated under khadi grant. This includes Rs.1.35
crores for Science & Technology. The funds will be spent for rebate on retail sales of khadi, Interest Subsidy on bank
finance for khadi working funds, Khadi design development and other miscellaneous expenditure. The Rebate and
Interest subsidy are two important components used for the furtherance of the Khadi programme. The rebate is a
promotional expenditure provided on khadi sales for neutralizing the cost due to higher wage component thereby to
boost its sales. Similarly the quantum of interest subsidy provided on funds availed from Commercial Banks against
ISEC issued by KVIC would help to enhance credit flow to khadi programme. KVIC has launched an Insurance Scheme
for the welfare of khadi workers which brings a sense of social security among the khadi workers. The portion of khadi
grant will be paid to Insurance Company as KVIC’s share of the premium under this scheme. Similarly KVIC has
launched a Product Development, Design Intervention and Packaging (PRODIP) for the betterment of khadi sector,
certain part of khadi grant will be utilized for this purpose also which in turn will help for the furtherance of khadi
sector.
11.4   As regards the details of appropriation of non-plan expenditure which has been earmarked to the tune of Rs. 55.40
crore in BE and RE 2003-04, the Non-Plan allocation of Rs. 55.40 crores during 
2003-04 was appropriated for the purposes Salary, Allowances, Pensions, T.A. During the financial year 2003-04, the
actual expenditure was Rs. 60.83 crores incurred under this head. Against this, apart from salary and allowances, a
major item was pension payment to its retired employees i.e. to the, tune of 
Rs. 18.03 crores. Being the committed items, KVIC has to meet all these expenditure from its non-plan allocation.
11.5   As regards the appropriation plan of non-plan expenditure projected to the tune of Rs. 55.40 crore in BE 2004-05
and the likely outcome thereof, the Ministry stated that during the financial year 
2004-05 KVIC will be spending an estimated amount of Rs. 68.00 crores under its non-plan head for meeting various
committed expenditure such as salaries, allowances, pension etc. This increased expenditure is mainly due to the recent
decision of DA instalment and also merging of 50 per cent of DA w.e.f. April 2004, besides the increased terminal
benefits like gratuity and commutation etc. in the case of retired employees.

11.6   The Committee notes with concern that almost all the plan outlay is meant for Khadi sales rebate and interest
subsidy. A meagre portion of it goes for R&D. This trend casts aspersion on the marketing style of KVIC which is
largely dependent on Khadi rebate, announced on 2nd October every year. Major sale of Khadi items takes place during
the period of rebate. The Committee feels that there is an urgent need for change in the marketing strategy which does
not depend on sales rebate borne by the Government. The Committee therefore, directs the Ministry of ARI and KVIC
to work upon a suitable marketing strategy and allocate more funds for R&D and raising working capital which would
benefit the KVIC in long run.
12.0   PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY KHADI & VILLAGE INDUSTRIES
12.1   In the market economy, quality is an important aspect. As such, to make khadi products competitive in the market
it is necessary to enhance the quality of the products as such to enhance the budget support for such schemes. Similarly,
shabby and dilapidated conditions of sales Outlets of khadi institutions is a weak area which require improvement for
attracting the customers. A scheme has been launched for this purpose by formulating a plan for modernization and
renovation of sales outlets. The proposal for renovation of other DSOs and Institutional Sales Outlets need adequate
budgetary support. Similarly, the efforts initiated by KVIC by launching the Product Design Innovation and Packaging
(PRODIP) for improving the Product Design and Packaging also taken up for vigorous follow up with adequate
financial support.
12.2   The Committee appreciates KVIC for launching Product Design Innovation and Packaging (PRODIP) and
directs KVIC to apprise the progress made in this regard.
12.3   Shortage of working capital is another major problem blocking the progress of khadi programme. Earlier, the
institutions were enjoying working capital assistance from KVIC’s budgetary support at zero rate of interest.
Subsequently, in view of budgetary crunch, the khadi institutions have been directed to avail of funds from banking
sector, against which KVIC issues Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC). However, the financial institutions are
not honouring the ISEC issued by KVIC to its full extent as such there is shortage of working capital in the Khadi
Sector. Further, large amount of pending rebate with various State Governments adds to the burden.
12.4   The Committee expresses its concern over the lack of support from the financial institutions to KVIC and
recommends that the Ministry of ARI should play pro-active role in enabling  KVIC to get sufficient credit, flow from
the banking sector and ensure that the financial institution honour the ISEC issued by KVIC. The Committee desires
that the Ministry of ARI should take up the issue of large amount of pending rebate with various State Governments so
that KVIC get some relief from the shortage of working capital.
12.5   Moreover, as on 31-3-2004, Rs. 238.02 crores was lying as outstanding balance with Khadi Implementing
Agencies under Consortium Bank Credit (CBC) for which they have to pay interest @ 4.5 per cent in addition to
refunding the same in instalments whereas under the working fund system adopted for Khadi programme the institutions
are permitted to keep the working capital in the form of working fund as long as they maintain certain level of
production.
12.5   The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure that Rs. 238.02 crore is lying as outstanding balance with
Khadi implementing agencies under Consortium Bank Credit(CBC) and recommends that the Government should take
initiative at the earliest to release the fund.
12.6   Another area which requires immediate assistance to Khadi institutions is tools and implements. The fact remains
that the charkhas and looms available with them are mostly outdated, which require replacement or renovation. A
separate fund may be made available for this purpose.
12.7   The Committee expresses its anguish and observe that tools and implements used for Khadi production have
become obsolete and outdated. The Committee therefore recommends that adequate funds should be earmarked for
modernization of the charkhas and looms for continuation and proliferation of Khadi.
12.8   Labour law is another important problems being faced by the khadi sector. A separate labour law exclusively for
khadi sector, considering its nature of operation, funding patterns etc, is very much essential.
12.9   The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI should come out with the specific details of labour reforms in the
interest of Agro and Rural Industries and take initiatives for the legislation.

15.1   KVIC has recently constituted a Confederation for Promotion of Khadi and Village Industries [CPKVI] in order
to bring a professional approach in its marketing activities. Besides, KVIC is also taking help of NIFTs, NID and
various others professional agencies like IITs for various service like R&D, Design Development etc.
15.2   The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI should ensure professionalisation in the working of KVIC
and hopes that the Constitution of Confederation for Promotion of Khadi & Village Industries [CPKVI] will
bring a professional approach in its marketing activities thereby promoting its sale and popularizing it among
the younger generation.
16.0   ACTION PLAN TO MAKE KVI AS A MEGA SOURCE OF EMPLOYMENT GENERATION AND
POVERTY ALLEVIATION PROGRAMMES
16.1   KVIC can cover larger size of employment in rural areas thereby help to alleviate poverty provided larger flow of
budgetary support in the form of margin money coupled with the willingness of banking sector to channelise required
level of loan funds. There is a good response from the field for REGP. As such, KVIC is in a position to generate about
10.00 lakhs employment per year. But for achieving this mega target it is necessary to enhance the REGP target by
providing required level of margin Money fund, including funds for forward and. backward linkages.
16.2   The Committee recommends that the Government should explore the potential of employment generation
in the Khadi sector keeping in view the abject reality of population growth rate and the scourge of poverty
largely due to unemployment in the rural areas.
17.0   "NATIONAL KHADI REVOLUTION"
17.1   The Committee wanted to know the steps undertaken for cost reduction of Khadi Products and for the
popularisation of Khadi and to make Khadi as product for the mass so as to usher “National Khadi Revolution.” the
Ministry replied that Khadi is a labour intensive handmade product. As it is produced by Khadi workers manually
without using any machine, it cannot be mass produced. Being a labour intensive handmade product, the cost of Khadi
is also comparatively higher than other varieties of cloth products. Because of these characteristics there is no much
scope for further reducing cost of Khadi products. However, KVIC makes various efforts to introduce improved tools
and equipment, which to a certain extent reduced wastage during the process of production. Various efforts are made in

18.2   The Khadi and Village Industries Commission functions in the rural and small towns to provide employment
opportunities at low cost to local artisans by utilising the local raw materials. To support such traditional industries,
Government has been giving loans for Khadi and Village Industries to be set up in rural areas through the KVIC.
18.3   The Committee was informed that during discussion at RE 2003-04 stage, due to financial constraint the provision
for interest subsidy on Khadi was reduced to the level of Rs. 3 crores only. Since, the amount of interest subsidy has
been accumulating every year, the budgetary provision for interest subsidy has been enhanced to the level of Rs. 22
crores to meet the requirements of annual book adjustment. The budgetary provision for interest subsidy is only the
book adjustment of interest on past loans. The provision of subsidy in lieu of interest may not be inconsistent with WTO
provisions.
18.3   The Committee wanted to know whether the provision made under interest subsidy under Major Head 2851 is as
per expectation of KVIC if not, the remedial measures therefor. The Ministry stated that the amount of interest accrued
to KVIC on loan has been subsidized by the Government through payment of subsidy in lieu  of interest over the years.
Thus, this subsidy in lieu of interest is not actually released to the KVIC but is provided for in the budgetary provision
both Plan” and Non-Plan for book adjustments, against the interest payable by KVIC to Government.
18.4   Pertaining to the Committee’s query whether the flow of institutional credit, to KVI sector is upto the expectation
of KVIC, the Committee was informed that the institutional credit flow to KVI Sector is just 50 per cent to 60 per cent
of the expectation. The RBI has issued separate guidelines after Kalia Committee Report in July, 1994. Wherein clear-
cut guidelines have been issued for calculation of the credit requirement of the Khadi institution, to remove the gap in
Interest Subsidy value vis-a-vis fund provided by bank all the banks has to follow the guidelines given by RBI in July,
1994 based on following points:
          (i)    KVIC will furnish the worksheet for assessment of Working Capital.
          (ii)    KVIC assessment may be accepted if it does not exceed the assessment made by the banks by more than 10
per cent.
          (iii)   In case KVIC assessment of Working Capital exceed the bank assessment more than 10 per cent. The
Working Capital may be arrived at by mutual dialogue between KVIC/institution and financing branch,
          (iv)   In case of sharp difference between the peak level and lean season credit requirements additional credit
limits may be sanctioned by the banks, KVIC will indicate such peak level credit requirements also in the
interest subsidy certificate.

20.1 The Village Industries being supported by KVIC have been categorized into seven broad groups viz. agro and food
processing industry, forest based industry, handmade paper and fibre industry, mineral based industry, polymer and
chemical based industry, rural engineering and bio-technology industry and service industry. The major problem for
setting up of such village industries have been the availability of credit at nominal interest rates, marketing of products
and technology upgradation. For dealing with interest rate problem, the KVIC has been making available finance to VI
institutions at the nominal rate of 4 per cent. Subsequently, they have introduced the REGP scheme, which provides a
capital subsidy but no interest subsidy. Further, the KVIC has built up a large network of rural Cottage Industrial Units
producing wide range of goods and articles catering the rural and partly urban markets Some of them have achieved
high standards for export as well but a vast majority lack support in maintaining standard quality and for want of
technical Back-up to upgrade the technology of their products. Keeping this in view, the KVIC had set up Technical
Back Up Units who will provide S&T inputs to the entrepreneurs engaged in KVI activities. The basic objectives of
these units would be to trigger and strengthen rural industrialization, through timely, continuous and appropriate S&T
inputs, R&D support, innovative ideas and technologies for value addition as well as for strengthening academic-
industrial linkages. These units have been set up in major Engineering Colleges, IITs, Technical Universities etc
20.2   Another difficulty being experienced by VI units relates to marketing of products. For this purpose, the KVIC has
taken number of proactive steps to give a fillip to the marketing of VI products. These include brand promotion,
exhibitions, marketing tie up with the Departmental Bhawans and sales outlets, etc.
20.3   As regards the lacunae in the interest subsidy scheme and the relative advantages of Margin Money scheme which
replaced the interest subsidy, the Committee was informed that the main implementing agencies of village industries are
individual entrepreneurs. However, the subsidy in lieu of interest was meant only for VI institutions and entrepreneurs
were not covered. By launching Margin Money scheme (REGP), this lacuna has been removed and Margin Money is
provided to both individuals as well as institutions. After the introduction of Margin Money, a considerable number of
individual entrepreneurs have been covered under the purview of KVIC and proved it as a successful instrument to set
up village industries projects in rural areas by channelising the institutional credit with corresponding of Margin Money
from. KVIC.
20.4   Regarding the Committee’s query whether the Margin Money components in the REGP is recoverable if the
project is not successfully implemented, the Ministry replied in the affirmative and explained that initially the Margin
Money component is kept with the Banks for a period of 2 years under fixed deposit in the name of the entrepreneurs If
the project fails, this margin money will not be released to the entrepreneurs. Further as the banks are providing loans to
the entrepreneurs under REGP they may initiate recovery measures as per terms and conditions stipulated in their loan
sanction.
20.5   The Committee observes that the experience gained so far is quite encouraging but there is much demand for
REGP in the field. As the Government has already decided to continue REGP till the end of Tenth Five Year Plan, the
Committee is of the view that with all probability the scheme may continue beyond Tenth Plan provided no other better
substitute is formulated.

23.1   The Finance Minister in his budget speech of the year 1999-2000 announced a National Programme on Rural
Industrialisation. The purpose is to set up 100 rural industrial clusters in the country every year so that it can boost up
the rural economy by creating more employment avenues for the rural youth in the non-farm sector, and slow down the
migration of the rural artisans to towns/cities. The office of the Development Commissioner (SmaIl Scale Industries)
was made the coordinating agency and the KVIC was envisaged to play an important role in setting up these clusters as
well as making good use of its extensive marketing outlets. No fund was provided separately for the programme and it
was felt that various Ministries/ Departments are having their own programmes in this area which could be coordinated
and their synergies exploited for greater impact. The programme is being implemented by KVIC, NABARD, SIDBI and
the States in 123 clusters.
23.2   In order to facilitate implementation of the programme, a scheme on NPRI has been formulated which has a
provision of extending financial assistance of Rs. 5.0 lakhs per cluster. The budget provision of Rs. 0.90 crore under the
scheme was reduced to Rs. 0.30 crore at RE stage for the year 2003-04 as adequate number of proposals were not
received for financial assistance under the Scheme from the implementing agencies. During the year 2003-04, 17
clusters have been taken up for diagnostic study /development under the Scheme and 50 per cent of the proposed cost of
the work to the extent of Rs. 17.69 lakhs have been released. The balance of Rs. 12.3 lakhs out of Rs. 30 lakhs of RE
2003-04 was expended under other schemes of the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries as the progress report of the
clusters taken up for diagnostic study/development and the proposals for financial assistance from the implementing
agencies were not received.
23.3   An amount to the extent of Rs. 17.7 lakhs shall be released to the States/ Agencies after receiving the progress
report of the clusters taken up for diagnostic study/development during the year 2003-04. Balance amount shall be
utilized for development of the other clusters under the Scheme after receiving the proposals. The States/Agencies have
already been requested to submit the proposals for financial assistance under the Scheme during the year 2004-05.
However, no proposal have been received from them so far. Considering the past experience of the expenditure under
the Scheme, the Budget Provision of Rs. 0.45 crore is kept under the Scheme.
23.4   The Committee is of the view that since the National Programme for Rural Industrialization has the potential for
real development and growth of rural economy, the Government should undertake concrete measures to combat the
problems in achieving the objectives, targets, credit-flow, implementation and monitoring mechanism and the “Key
Concern Areas” of NPRI.

26.0   REGISTRATION OF UNITS ENGAGED IN AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES AND STEPS TAKEN
FOR EFFECTIVE REGULARIZATION AND REGULATION OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
26.1   The Ministry supervises and coordinates the promotion of the Agro and Rural Industries through its field agencies
namely, the KVIC, Coir Board and the PMRY division (RBI, State Directorates of Industries). Each of these agencies
have their own specific schemes and programmes which are implemented by them and the Ministry monitors and
supervises the same at the Government level through various returns, reports and review meetings at the highest level.
Recently, an evaluation study was conducted by KVIC through the Vaikunthbhai Mehta Research Institute for
decentralized industries on the issue of evaluation of Rural Employment Generation Programme (REGP) of KVIC.
26.2   The agro and rural industries set up by the KVIC are either registered with KVIC or State KVIBs. The production
and employment of these units is regularized and regulated at the State KVIC Headquarters and by the State
Governments for the units registered with KVIBs. The performance of these units is also reviewed in separate meeting
with banks. This Ministry, however, keeps a close watch on these regulatory activities at the KVIC level. An overall
review is also undertaken in the meetings of Khadi and Village Industries Board under the Chairmanship of Minister
(ARI).
26.3   The Committee desires that government should initiates concrete steps for effective regularization and
regulation of Agro and Rural Industries.
27.0   IMPACT OF GLOBALISATION AND LIBERALIZATION ON THE GROWTH AND DEVELOPMENT
OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
27.1   The impact of liberalization has enhanced the competitive nature of the whole industrial
set up as such. Open market mechanisms have come in place of regulated and protected nature of
pre-liberalized economy. The challenge posed by globalized economy has enhanced and enabled
nurturing of the inherent competitive and resilient nature of the Agro and Rural Industries sector as such. The sector
mainly consists of Khadi, Village Industries, cottage industries (handicrafts), Coir, Tiny and Micro enterprises. The
products of this sector by their very nature are traditional, location specific and exclusively indigenous. This adds to the
specialized and exclusive nature of the sector as such and gives it a dynamic and resilient character. For example, herbal
products, organic manure, organic food, honey production, traditional crafts items, etc. are so exclusive by nature that it
offers immense export potential which is almost non-competitive in the world economy. This defines the future outlook
of the sector. The emphasis would be to highlight the exclusivity of ARI products and its suitability to specific local area
both for production as well as marketing as it addresses the felt local needs and to develop quality diversification and
aggressively enter the world market.
27.2   The Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI should carefully study the adverse impact of globalisation
and liberalization on the growth and development of Agro and Rural Industries and take suitable remedial measures for
protecting the domestic Agro and Rural Industries.
28.0   PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
28.1   The Major problems faced by the Agro and Rural Industries are primarily relating to lack of infrastructural
facilities, marketing linkages and modern technology. The same is being addressed by way of providing emphasis on the
development of market linkages, modernization of outlets, diversification of products, exposure to foreign markets and
infrastructural back up through cluster development, The impact of liberalization and WTO regime on the market
scenario are being responded by the Sector through policy initiatives which enhances the resilient nature of the sector as
a whole.
28.2   The Committee observes that there is need for a market-oriented approach to the overall sector and to inject
competitive edge which inter alia must include Market Development Assistance, aggressive marketing, brand building,
cluster development, technological upgradation, design and packaging facilities etc. Policy initiatives should be taken in
the ARI sector for envisaging massive product diversification and development based on collaborative research effects.
29.0   CREDIT FLOW TO AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES

152nd Report of Committee on Industry

29.1   Major credit flow to the Agro &Rural Industries is through banks. Credit flow to units in this sector is supported
by way of Margin Money/subsidy/loan/working capital. The loan part is accessed through the financial institutions and
the subsidy and margin money part of the project is borne out of the budgetary allocations to the concerned
implementing agency. Problems by way of unviable projects, cutting down financial size of the projects, lengthy
procedural formalities are faced in general by the beneficiaries or entrepreneurs in accessing credit for their units. This
may be, to a certain extent linked to unsatisfactory recovery of finances advanced. Hence the attempt is to constantly,
vigorously pursue recovery dues and at the same time ensure easy accessibility to new entrepreneurs.
29.2   The Committee recommends that constant attempts should be vigorously made for recovery of dues of finances
advanced for ensuring adequate circulation of credit to ARI units and at the same time making easy credit accessibility
to new entrepreneurs. The Committee further recommends that adequate steps should be taken for removing the
problems being faced by ARI entrepreneurs relating to unviable projects, cutting down financial size of the projects,
lengthy procedural formalities while accessing credit for their units.
30.0   REVIVAL OF THE RURAL INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT FUND (RIDF)
30.1   The Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) being operated by NABARD under
the Ministry of Rural Development is for the purpose of financing projects like irrigation, flood protection, watershed
management, construction of rural roads and bridges etc. in the rural areas, whereas the Ministry of ARI is concerned
with providing employment in the non-farm sector through setting up of agro and rural industries As such, the RIDF is
not directly concerned with this Ministry. However, because of better connectivity to be created in the rural areas by
way of roads and bridges under RIDF, the setting up agro and rural industries would definitely be helped in so far as
quicker availability of raw materials and marketing of the products are concerned. This will have spiraling effect on
further growth of agro and rural industries.
30.2   The Committee is of the view that even if the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) is not directly
concerned with the Ministry of ARI but for the better connectivity to be created in the rural areas by way of roads and
bridges under RIDF, the measure undertaken would be helpful in the setting up agro and rural industries.
31.0   “NEW DEAL” FOR RURAL INDIA
31.1   The Prime Minister in his address to the Nation has laid stress on overall growth of the national economy.
Employment generation has been identified as a tool to banish poverty, hunger and homelessness and improve the
standard of living of the mass of our people. The employment should be generated through environmentally sustainable
rural industries. The Prime Minister has also focused on expanding opportunities for gainful employment in agriculture
and in non-farm rural activities.
31.2   Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries through its various employment generation programme is already focusing
on setting up of industries in the rural areas in the non-farm sector. The Rural Employment Generation Programme
(REGP) being implemented by this Ministry through KVIC since 1995 has successfully generated employment
opportunities to 22.73 lakh persons. Similarly, under Prime Minister’s Rozgar Yojana (PMRY) since 1993, 29.05 lakhs
educated persons have been provided employment.
31.3   Since the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries is functioning in the rural sector, the interaction between farmer
and agro industries has greatly picked up. To improve interaction between farmers and agro industries, KVIC has taken
several measures to strengthen activities in the rural areas like bee- keeping, food processing industries, handmade paper
industries etc. These programmes along with other activities of the Ministry in the agro and rural sector will continue to
receive focus in the Ministry in line with the message enshrined in PM’s speech with a view to empower disadvantaged
sections of the society.
31.4   The Committee is pleased to note that the Government is extending adequate attention to the rural sector and
especially the Agro and Rural Industries. The Committee, however, desires that the Government should come out with
pragmatic planning for Agro and Rural Industries keeping in view the twin objectives of employment generation and
poverty alleviation. The Committee wishes to highlight that the Agro and Rural Industries has the potential of
employment generation and since large chunk of Indian population dwells in rural areas under the abject poverty
therefore, holistic and comprehensive planning for rural sector and its effective implementation is the need of the hour.

modernization of the Charkhas and looms for continuation and proliferation of Khadi.                                     (Para 12.7)
LABOUR LAW
          The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI should come out with the specific details of labour reforms in the
interest of Agro and Rural Industries and take initiatives for the legislation.                                                         
                                                                                                                                           (Para 12.9)
STOCK INVENTORIES
          The Committee, while expressing its deep concern over the stock inventories which has accumulated to the tune
of Rs. 612.30 crores worth stocks (Khadi Rs.551.19 crores Polyvastra 
Rs. 60.84 crores) desires that the Ministry of ARI should direct KVIC to chalk out an Action Plan for disposing of the
stock inventories in a time bound programme.                                                                               (Para 14.2)
PROFESSIONALISATION IN THE WORKING OF KVIC
          The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI should ensure professionalisation in the working of KVIC and
hopes that the Constitution of Confederation for Promotion of Khadi and Village Industries (CPKVI) will bring a
professional approach in its marketing activities thereby promoting its sale and popularizing it among the younger
generation.  (Para 15.2)
ACTION PLAN TO MAKE KVI AS A MEGA SOURCE OF EMPLOYMENT GENERATION AND
POVERTY ALLEVIATION PROGRAMMES
          The Committee recommends that the Government should explore the potential of employment generation in the
Khadi sector keeping in view the abject reality of population growth rate and the scourge of poverty largely due to
unemployment in the rural areas.                                                                                                                   (Para 16.2)
"NATIONAL KHADI REVOLUTION"
          The Committee observes that Khadi has been the National identity since the days of India’s struggle for
independence and therefore the Government should pay all attention for the continuation of Khadi as an identity in the
National life and culture.                                                                                                                                (Para 17.2)
OTHER VILLAGE INDUSTRIES
          The Committee observes that the experience gained so far is quite encouraging but there is much demand for
REGP in the field. As the Government has already decided to continue REGP till the end of Tenth Five Year Plan, the
Committee is of the view that with all probability the scheme may continue beyond Tenth Plan provided no other better
substitute is formulated.
                                                                                                                                           (Para 20.5)
COIR INDUSTRIES
          The Committee recommends that the following steps may be taken to promote the marketing and sales of
coir products in the domestic market:—
          (i)    Intensification of promotional measures like publicity through print and electronic media and increased
participation in trade fairs and exhibitions;

152nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/152ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:48:21]
          (ii)    Organisation of Buyer-Seller Meets in potential regions and organisation of special sales campaign and
festival discount offer to promote sales;
          (iii)   Organising collective participation of manufacturers in selected trade fairs and exhibitions; and
          (iv)   Popularisation of new products like coir geotextiles, garden articles, coir pith based products through
awareness creation programmes etc.
                                                                                                                                         (Para 21.11)
R&D ACTIVITIES FOR COIR INDUSTRIES
          The Committee recommendations that since the budgetary provisions for R&D for Coir Industries is sufficient all
efforts would be made for skimming out benefits of R&D for the proliferation and promotion of Coir Industries.           
(Para 21.14)
POTENTIAL OF COIR INDUSTRIES IN NON-TRADITIONAL STATES LIKE UTTAR PRADESH, ORISSA,
BIHAR AND JHARKHAND                                                                                                          
          The Committee desires that the Government should come out with the Action Plan for the promotion and
proliferation of Coir Industries in the non-traditional zone as has been sketched out in the case of West Bengal and
Andaman and Nicobar Islands.                                                                                                                             (Para
21.16)
ORGANIZATIONAL OVERHAULING RURAL EMPLOYMENT GENERATION PROGRAMME (REGP)
          The Committee is of the view that there is urgent need for organizational overhauling by providing additional
man-power, budgetary support and recruiting professionals. Further, the Boards have to be established in those States
where it is not established. The role of Ministry of ARI is of vital importance in implementation of the scheme in terms
of monitoring, coordinating, providing necessary guidance and liaisoning with other Ministry and organizations.(Para
22.6)
PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY KVIC AND KVIBS IN THE IMPLEMENTATION OF REGP
          The Committee observes that it is necessary to recruit professionals, familiar with project preparation, analysis,
consultancy etc. or avail their services from any other professional agencies. While enhancing employment target it is
imperative to proportionately increase the margin money component and corresponding funds for backward forward
linkages and place them with field officers of KVIC well in advance as per estimated requirements. The State KVI
Boards are major agencies involved in the implementation of REGP. Their weak infrastructure/organizational condition
often hinders the expeditious implementation of the scheme. KVIBs should be revitalized by the respective State
Governments.(Para 22.9)
BETTER WORKING OF REGP
          The Committee recommends that the Government should take the following steps for the better working of
REGP:—
          (i)    At present the lock in period of Margin Money is for 2 years. Government may extend it to 3 years so that
the sustainability and continuity of project as well as employment can be ensured.
          (ii)    Fiscal concessions in terms of tax exemption relating to establishment and running of the units, Octroi
exemption, Transport and Power subsidy may be provided at least for the period of 3 years.
          (iii)   In each backward block of the District, a Rural Industrial Estate may be established with all infrastructure
support, so that REGP units can grow without any hurdles.
                                                                                                                                         (Para 22.10)
NATIONAL PROGRAMME FOR RURAL INDUSTRIALISATION
          The Committee is of the view that since the National Programme for Rural Industrialization has the potential for
real development and growth of rural economy, the Government should undertake concrete measures to combat the
problems in achieving the objectives, targets, credit-flow, implementation and monitoring mechanism and the “Key
Concern Areas” of NPRI.                                                                                                                                 (Para 23.4)
FUND FOR MODERNISATION OF TRADITIONAL INDUSTRIES
          The Committee appreciates budgetary allocation made in 2004-05 to the tune of Rs. 100.00 crores for the
modernisation and regeneration of Traditional Industries. Since the artisans are facing various problems including non-
availability of timely credit and raw material, lack of market opportunities, the Committee hopes that the budgetary
provision so made would be able to solve the problems faced by the artisans. Since Traditional Industries are

152nd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/152ndreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:48:21]
functioning in the remote rural areas in a most decentralized manner, efforts should be made for organizing them under
appropriate organisational structure. Moreover, the rural traditional industries should be taken as a separate part of
priority sector and they should be provided necessary facilities accordingly.
                                                                            (Para 24.2)
LUMPSUM PROVISION FOR PROJECTS SCHEMES FOR THE BENEFIT OF NORTH EASTERN REGION
AND SIKKIM
          The Committee is of the view that the development of the NER region requires the special attention of the
Government. The special emphasis is required because of the fact that though the region has immense potential, the lack
of communication facilities, poor infrastructure, difficult terrain etc. have contributed to the region’s economic
backwardness. Since the region has lagged behind in progress as compared to other regions of the country, special
attention is required to strengthen and reinforce focused implementation of various schemes under the ARI sector.
Targets under REGP, PMRY coir industries should be accordingly set for the region.
                                                                                                                                           (Para 25.6)
REGISTRATION AND REGULARIZATION OF AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES UNITS
          The Committee desires that Government should initiates concrete steps for effective regularization and regulation
of Agro and Rural Industries.                                                                                                            (Para 26.3)
IMPACT OF GLOBALISATION AND LIBERALIZATION ON AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
          The Committee recommends that the Ministry of ARI should carefully study the adverse impact of globalisation
and liberalization on the growth and development of Agro and Rural Industries and take suitable remedial measures for
protecting the domestic Agro and Rural Industries.                                                                               (Para 27.2)
PROBLEMS BEING FACED BY AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
          The Committee observes that there is need for a market-oriented approach to the overall sector and to inject
competitive edge which inter alia must include Market Development Assistance, aggressive marketing, brand building,
cluster development, technological upgradation, design and packaging facilities etc. Policy initiatives should be taken in
the ARI sector for envisaging massive product diversification and development based on collaborative research effects.
(Para 28.2)
CREDIT FLOW TO AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES
          The Committee recommends that constant attempts should be vigorously made for recovery of dues of finances
advanced for ensuring adequate circulation of credit to ARI units and at the same time making easy credit accessibility
to new entrepreneurs. The Committee further recommends that adequate steps should be taken for removing the
problems being faced by ARI entrepreneurs relating to unviable projects, cutting down financial size of the projects,
lengthy procedural formalities while accessing credit for their units.                                                                    (Para
29.2)
REVIVAL OF THE RURAL INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT FUND (RIDF)
          The Committee is of the view that even if the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) is not directly
concerned with the Ministry of ARI but for the better connectivity to be created in the rural areas by way of roads and
bridges under RIDF, the measure undertaken would be helpful in the setting up agro and rural industries.    (Para 30.2)
“NEW DEAL” FOR RURAL INDIA
          The Committee is pleased to note that the Government is extending adequate attention to the rural sector and
especially the Agro and Rural Industries. The Committee, however, desires that the Government should come out with
pragmatic planning for Agro and Rural Industries keeping in view the twin objectives of employment generation and
poverty alleviation. The Committee wishes to highlight that the Agro and Rural Industries has the potential of
employment generation and since large chunk of Indian population dwells in rural areas under the abject poverty
therefore, holistic and comprehensive planning for rural sector and its effective implementation is the need of the
hour.                                                
                                                                                                                                           (Para 31.4)

INTRODUCTION
         I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Fifty-third Report on Demands for Grants (2004-05) pertaining to
the Ministry of Small Scale Industries.
2.      The Committee heard the oral evidence of the Secretary and other representatives of the Ministry of Small Scale
Industries on 12th August, 2004. The Committee also considered the pre-budget expectations and post budget reactions
of the Ministry of Small Scale Industries to have in-depth account of the impact of budget proposals (2004-05) on the
Small Scale Industries as a whole.
3.      The Committee examined the relevant documents and budget-papers furnished by the Ministry. The Committee is
thankful to the representatives of Ministry of Small Scale Industries who appeared before the Committee. The
Committee also wishes to thank the Ministry for furnishing the replies to the questionnaire and the points raised during
the course of oral evidence.
4.      The Committee at its meeting held on 25th August, 2004 considered and adopted the Report.

25th August, 2004
SANTOSH BAGRODIA
Chairman,

REPORT
          The Small Scale Industries (SSI) Sector is a vibrant segment of the Indian economy contributing over 39% of the
manufacturing sector output and 34 per cent of the nation’s exports and providing employment to over 270 lakh persons
through more than 115 lakh units, which are spread both in rural and urban areas across the country. The major
contribution of the SSI sector lies in creation of employment opportunities at lower capital cost. While one unit of
employment requires investment of  Rs. 0.72 lakh in SSI sector, the same is as high as Rs. 5 lakh in the large units.
During 2003-04, the SSI sector registered a growth rate of 7.6 per cent as against a growth rate of 6.9 per cent for the
overall industrial sector. The SSI sector contributed 6.81 per cent towards GDP in 2002-03, while the contribution of
manufacturing sector (including SSI) to GDP was around 25 per cent.
2.0     The Ministry of Small Scale Industries designs and implement the policies through its field organizations for the

153rd Report of Committee on Industry

promotion and growth of small scale industries. The implementation of policies and various programmes/schemes for
providing Infrastructural and support services to small enterprises is undertaken through its attached offices, namely
Small Industries Development Organisation (SIDO) and its field offices, and National Small Industries Corporation
Limited (NSIC), a public sector undertaking under the Ministry of SSI. The Ministry also promotes the
Entrepreneurship Development through three national level institutes under the control of the Ministry viz. National
Institute for Entrepreneurship and Small Business Development (NIESBUD), New Delhi, National Institute of Small
Industry Extension Training (NISIET), Hyderabad and Indian Institute of Entrepreneurship, Guwahati.
2.1     The Committee recommends that the Government should undertake steps for service auditing of organs under the
Ministry of Small Scale Industries so that their delivery system can be improved for the betterment of small scale
industries.

16.0   CREDIT LINKED CAPITAL SUBSIDY SCHEME
16.1   The purpose behind introduction of CLCSS is to motivate and facilitate SSI units to upgrade their technology
through infusion of institutional credit. The strategy adopted for this purpose is to provide 12 per cent upfront capital
subsidy on institutional finance availed to facilitate technology upgradation in small scale sector. The ceiling of loans
eligible under the scheme is presently Rs. 40 lakh. The corpus fund created under the scheme is Rs. 600 crore for years
of operation from Oct. 2000 to Sept. 30, 2005. So far an amount of Rs. 13.08 crore has been utilized under the scheme
which includes an advance of Rs. 5 crore to SIDBI and Rs. 3 crore to NABARD for operationalising the scheme. The
slow progress under the scheme is due to general inhibition on the part of SSI units to go for technology upgradation.
The announcement made under General Budget for the year 2004-05 for enhancement in the rate of subsidy and the
ceiling of loans eligible under the scheme will help to make the scheme popular among the SSI units. The scheme was
made operational in Oct. 2000 and will expire after Sept. 2005. However, after evaluating the utility of the scheme, it
may continue further.

16.3   At present, there are thirty sub-sectors and products eligible for availing subsidy under the scheme. These sub-
sectors/products have been included under the scheme on the basis of their contribution to the production in SSI sector
and need for their technology upgradation. The CLCSS is expected to promote Small Scale Industries by assisting them
to upgrade their technology by availing institutional credit and subsidy thereupon. Two committees have been
constituted for monitoring the scheme, namely, Governing and Technology Approval Board (GTAB) under the
Chairmanship of Secretary, SSI and ARI and Technical Sub-Committee under the Chairmanship of AS and DC (SSI).
These have representatives from Planning Commission, Ministry of Finance, DSIR, CSIR, ICAR, NSIC, NRDC,
SIDBI, Reserve Bank of India, State Bank of India, FASII, FISME, Laghu Udyog Bharti and CII.
16.4   Pertaining to the Committee’s query as to the impact of raising the ceiling for loans under the capital subsidy
scheme from Rs. 40.00 lakh to Rs. 1.00 crore (as announced by the Finance Minister in the General Budget for the year
2004-05) on promotion of Small Scale Industries, the Ministry replied that in the General Budget for the year 2004-05,
the scheme (CLCSS) has been made more attractive by raising the subsidy component from 12 per cent to 15 per cent.
With increase in ceiling, it is expected that a larger number of SSI units will be attracted to adopt better technology for
production. A budget provision of Rs. 6.0 crore has been made for subsidy under CLCSS for the year 2004-05. This is
likely to increase to Rs 10.0 crore at RE stage, considering the current trend of off take under CLCSS.
16.5   The Finance Minister has announced in the General Budget 2004-05 the raising of the rate of subsidy in the
capital subsidy scheme from 12 per cent to 15 per cent. The Committee raised the query regarding the exact strategy of
the Government and financial implication on the national exchequer. The Ministry replied that the strategy behind
enhancement of rate of capital subsidy from 12 per cent to 15 per cent under CLCSS is to provide a better package of
incentive for technology upgradation so that inertia for technology upgradation on the part of SSI units is broken. The
approved project cost of the scheme is Rs. 600 crore for five years starting from Oct. 2000 and it is enough to meet the

153rd Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/153rdreport.htm[04-07-2016 12:50:22]
expenditure due to enhanced rate of capital subsidy. Apart from the benefit to the units availing subsidy, there is likely
to be a demonstrative effect among SSIs and thus, the trend of technology upgradation in. SSI sector will grow
exponentially.
16.6   The Finance Minister in his Budget Speech (2004-05) has also announced that the capital subsidy scheme will be
enlarged by adding more sub-sectors and technologies eligible for assistance. At present, the subsidy under CLCSS are
available to the following thirty sub- sectors/products. Eight more sub-sectors are likely to be included under the scheme
after approval in the meeting of Governing and Technology Approval Board(GTAB) which is proposed to be convened
shortly. The sub-sectors likely to be added are Non-Ferrous Foundry, Sport Goods, Cosmetics, Readymade Garments,
Wooden Furniture, Mineral Water Bottle, Paints and beneficiation of Graphite and Phosphate.
16.7   The Tenth Plan Outlay for the scheme is sufficient to absorb additional expenditure due to announcement of
changes in the budget under the scheme. However, revised estimates for the year 2004-05 for the scheme may be
increased to Rs. 10.0 crore from Rs. 6.0 crore due to enhancement in the rate of subsidy and better response of the SSI
units for technology upgradatation due to additional benefit announcement in the budget. After the above mentioned
enlargement in the scope of the scheme, higher number of SSI units will be benefited in the following years.
16.8   Regarding the Committee’s query as to what extent the standard of technology employed in domestic Small Scale
Industries is comparable enough to technology employed in SSI sector in other developing/developed countries so as to
imbibe competitiveness in domestic SSI products vis-a-vis foreign products in view of its influx as the consequent of
removal of quantitative restrictions in the wake of WTO guidelines, the Ministry replied that the value of SSI exports
from India has been growing consistently and SSI contributes as much as 34 per cent to the nation’s exports. Thus the
Indian SSI products are competitive in the global market for quite a number of products.
16.9   The Committee observes that Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme is a very good scheme aimed at
technological up-gradation in SSI sector. The progress so far has been very tardy and in fact the scheme is yet to take
off. The Committee commend the announcements made in the budget speech (2004-05) and hopes that it would show
better results. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry of SSI to provide better package incentives to SSI units for
technology up-gradation and work out an effective strategy.
16.10The Committee recommends that government should undertake the following steps for improving the
functioning of credit linked capital subsidy:----
          (i)    Organising awareness programmes at various location all over the country to increase the awareness level of
industry association, banks, SIDBI and Industry Departments of respective States;
          (ii)    Review of progress of the scheme in meetings State Level Bankers Committees (SLBCs);
          (iii)   Incorporating inputs on the scheme into in service training courses of Bank Managers; and
          (iv)   Publicity measures to increase general awareness about the scheme.

19.1   The Scheme was announced on 30 th August 2000 and became operational in January 2001. Since inception, 46
banks and institutions (i.e., 26 Public Sector Banks, 14 Private Sector Banks, 6 Regional Rural Banks, NSIC, NEDFI
and SIDBI) have become Member-Lending Institutions under the Scheme, As on 30 th June, 2004, a total of 15,957

20.0   LOAN LIMIT UNDER THE CREDIT GUARANTEE SCHEME
20.1   The Credit Guarantee Scheme aims to alleviate the problem of collateral security among the SSI
units/entrepreneurs, particularly to tiny units. To cover the entire tiny sector, which is defined as units having
investment in plant and machinery upto Rs. 25 lakh, the Group of Ministers in its meeting held on 16 th August, 2004
decided to raise the loan limit under the scheme from Rs. 10 lakh to Rs.25 lakh.
20.2   The Committee observes that loan limit of Rs. 25 lakh for investment in plant and machinery under the
Credit Guarantee Scheme is not sufficient and needs to be enhanced at least to Rs. 1 crore. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that the Ministry of SSI to review the present limit with all concerned and raise the loan
limit to the desired level.
21.0   TARGETS AND ACHIEVEMENTS
21.1   Since the scheme is optional for the borrower and is implemented through the Member Lending Institutions
(MLIs), there are no year-wise targets set under the Scheme. The credit proposals involving both term loan and working

745 proposals. As on 30 th June, 2004 a total of 15,957 proposals were approved for guarantee cover for an aggregate
loan of Rs. 261.53 crore. While the progress under the scheme was slow to begin with, the same has picked-up well in
the last one year.
22.1   Working of the schemes in tackling the twin problem of unemployment and poverty
22.2   Replying to the Committee’s query as to what extent the credit guarantee fund scheme has been able to tackle the
twin problem of unemployment and poverty, the Ministry stated that one of the main objectives of the Scheme is to
generate more employment opportunities by facilitating collateral free loans to SSI/tiny units. It is estimated that the
loans guaranteed by the Trust were instrumental in creating around 61,000 new job opportunities as at June 30th, 2004.
The major beneficiaries under the Scheme are in the tiny sector comprising of rural artisans, self-employed
entrepreneurs etc.
22.3   The Committee is constrained to observe that despite the provision of the loans up to 25.00 lakh without
collateral/third party guarantee and the guidelines of the Reserve Bank of India thereto, Banks insists on the collateral
security and the third party guarantee and despite the Committee’s repeated recommendation to change the mind set of
the Branch Manager, nothing fruitful has come out. The Committee also notes that the Trust has been making concerted
efforts to create awareness about the Scheme among the Branch Managers of the banks by organizing regional/zonal
based Workshops-cum-Training Programmes where the information relating to the Scheme and the benefits available
are explained in detail. There is however, absence of mechanism assessing the impact of success of credit guarantee
scheme. The Committee impresses upon the Ministry to ensure the success of this scheme.
22.4   The Committee further observes that the credit guarantee fund scheme gets further rough whether due to high
upfront charges of banks like service charge, processing fee and that too differing from bank to bank. Under this scheme
also one time Guarantee Fee of 2.5 per cent of the sanctioned amount and 1 per cent Service Fee on the outstanding loan
is collected as on 31 st March each year. These fees are however, fixed and do not vary from bank to bank. The
Committee feels that this fee should further be reduced and recommends that the Ministry of SSI should take up
necessary action in this regard.
22.5   The Committee wanted to know as to what extent the working of income tax exemption under the credit
guarantee fund trust proved helpful in making the Small Scale Industries self sustainable. The Ministry answered that
the total funds added to the surplus of the Trust owing to tax exemption are to the tune of about Rs.20 crore which has
enabled the Trust to leverage additional credit of about
Rs. 100 crore.
22.6   As regards the criteria for appropriating the fund among various states/UTs of the country and the related working
mechanism for appropriation of amount of Rs. 172.80 crore among states/UTs, the Ministry informed the Committee
that the funds allocated in the Budget is provided for enhancing of the Corpus Fund created under the Scheme and no
States/UT wise allocation is made. All the eligible proposals received from the States/UTs are extended guarantee cover
under the Scheme.
22.7   Stating the reasons for increase in Plan Outlay which has been projected at Rs. 186.44 crore at RE stage during
the 2003-04 in comparison to the provision of Rs. 172.80 crore at the BE stage and the actual expenditure during the
year and how many cases were covered, the Ministry informed that the Government is committed to contribute Rs. 2000
crore to the Corpus Fund under the Scheme for enhancing the total corpus to Rs. 2500 crore by the end of Tenth Five
Year Plan. The Corpus Fund was Rs.427.02 crore by the end of FY 2002-03. With the higher plan outlay of Rs. 186.44
crore during 2003-04, the Corpus Fund was enhanced to Rs. 686.19 crore by the end of FY 2003-04. The Credit
Guarantee Scheme is not a normal Plan Scheme of expenditure but the provision is for contribution to Corpus Fund
created under the Scheme. As the number of units covered under the scheme increases, the liability of the Trust also
increases on account of borrowers. As regards the incurring of expenditure, it may be pointed out that the scheme was
operationalised on January 1, 2001 and only three and a half years have elapsed since it became operational. As there is
a provision of two years lock-in period for claim settlement, so far only 33 claims have been received from MLIs for
settlement involving an amount of Rs. 22.06 lakh. Of this, 11 claims have been settled with an outflow of Rs. 4.77 lakh.
During the year 2003-04, a total number of 6369 proposals were approved for guarantee cover under the Scheme.
22.8   The Plan Outlay has been decreased to the tune of Rs. 176.29 crore in BE 2004-05 in comparison to Rs. 186.44
crore in RE 2003-04. The Committee wanted to know the target set for year 2004-05 and whether the amount so
earmarked would prove sufficient for the intended purpose, if not, the actual requirement and the bases for the same.
The Ministry explained that the provision made under the Scheme is for contribution to the Corpus Fund and the
Government is committed to build a corpus of Rs. 2500 crore by the end of Tenth Five Year Plan. But with a Plan

24.0   TINY AND MICRO ENTERPRISES
24.1   A provision of Rs. 414.40 crore has been made for the Ministry of Small Scale Industries in the Budget 2004-
2005. There is no separate allocation for the Tiny Enterprises in the Budget. However, for Micro Finance Programme a
provision of Rs. 2.00 crore (including provision for NER & Sikkim) has been made in the Budget 2004-2005.
24.2   Tiny Enterprises are such units which have investment in plant and machinery upto Rs. 25.00 Lakhs. As such all
such industrial activities which are eligible for registration as SSI are also eligible for registration in the tiny sector as
long as its investment in plant and machinery is upto the prescribed limit of Rs. 25.00 lakhs The majority activities in
Khadi and Coir Industry which are predominantly in rural areas and have investment below Rs. 25 lakhs are covered
under Tiny/Micro enterprises in Agro and Rural Industries.
25.0   STEPS TO STRENGTHEN AND STREAMLINE THE TINY SECTOR TO GIVE TINY SECTOR AN
ORGANIZED OUTLOOK
25.1   The Policy Measures for Promoting and Strengthening Small, Tiny and Village Enterprises, placed on the table of
the House on 6th August, 2000 and Comprehensive Policy Package announced on 
31st August, 2000, while envisaging a separate package of facilities and incentives for promotion of tiny industries
included earmarking of credit (60 per cent of the total lending earmarked for SSI Sector under Priority Sector lending),
raising of composite loan upto Rs. 25 lakhs, provision of 20 per cent or projected annual turnover as working capital
loan, concession in rate of interest from NSIC on composite loan of Rs. 25 lakhs, concessional rate of refinance to the
tiny sector by SIDBI, raising of project cost limit from Rs. 23 lakhs to Rs. 50 lakhs under the National Equity Fund
(NEF) Scheme, enhancement of family income eligibility limit from Rs. 24,000 per annum to Rs. 40,000 per annum
under PMRY Scheme, earmarking of 50 per cent plots for tiny sector under the Integrated Infrastructure Development
(IID) Scheme, cluster development programme under the National Programme for Rural Industrialization, preference in
Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation, etc.
25.2   Government has announced under the National Common Minimum Programme that a major promotional package
for SSI sector will be brought out soon to support credit, technological and marketing support, freeing the SSI Sector
from inspector raj, modernization of coir, garments, food processing, leather, pottery and other cottage industries etc.
This package will further strengthen and streamline the Tiny Sector.
25.3   The Committee recommends that effective measures must be taken for (i) better importing of
entrepreneurs skills and training, (ii) acquiring marketing techniques, (iii) Access to appropriate technology, (iv)
strengthening capital base and institutional credit and (v) providing infrastructural facilities.
26.0   CREDIT RATING
26.1   The Finance Minister in his Budget speech (2004-05) declared that “SSI units will be encouraged to obtain credit
rating”. The Committee desired to know as to the steps which are being taken to develop the credit rating system for SSI
unit or group of SSI units along with the criteria for assigning weightage in the credit rating. The Ministry elaborated
that NSIC in consultation with the various stake holders i.e. Small Industries Associations, Indian Banks Association,
and various Rating Agencies namely CRISIL, ICRA, Dun & Bradstreet (D& B) and ONICRA, has formulated a Rating
Scheme for Small Scale Industries in the country. The rating methodology shall cover a combination of credit and
performance factors including parameters measuring operational, financial, business and management risks.
Accordingly, the Scheme will be titled “ PERFORMANCE & CREDIT RATING SCHEME FOR SMALL
INDUSTRIES”. The Indian Banks Association has accorded its consent to support the Scheme. The Scheme is under
examination of the Ministry and on approval, this Scheme shall be implemented and Rating Agencies shall be
empanelled.
26.2   The Committee strongly recommends for a Credit Rating Mechanism covering both the credit and
performance factors. The Committee accordingly recommends the Ministry to expedite the process of initiating
and popularizing the Credit Rating System for SSI units.
27.0   TECHNOLOGY UPGRADATION IN SSI SECTOR
27.1   The Finance Minister in the Budget speech (2004-05) highlighted that technology upgradation of SSI units is the
most urgent requirement to do business in a competitiveness environment. The Committee desired to know the steps
which are being envisaged during 2004-05 to achieve the intention of Finance Minister for accelerating and strengthen
the partnership approach to develop linkages between large and small enterprises, revitalization and regeneration of

Private partnership for technology up-gradation in SSI sector. The Committee is of the considered view that
Public-Private partnership would give the requisite boost to the technology up-gradation in the SSI sector.
28.0   POLICY OF DE-RESERVATION IN SSI SECTOR
28.1   During the course of interaction with the Committee the representatives of CII stated that the Policy of
Reservation discourages investment competition and Technology up-gradation in the small sector. The representatives
of CII further added that a gradual and phased de- reservation from the list of reserved items, enable this sector to
become globally competitive.
28.2   The Committee desired to know as to what extent the de-reservation of items, as identified by the Ministry in
regard to 85 items as declared by the Finance Minister in the General Budget (2004-05) is in the interest of SSI sector.
The Ministry of Small Scale Industries replied that Small-scale sector manufactures more than 7500 items out of which
only 675 items are reserved for exclusive manufacture in small-scale sector. These items mainly are labour-oriented
with very less investment and low technological requirements. Most of these items are produced in self-employment
ventures and do not attract big players in the field. However, the Ministry of Small Scale Industries clarified that some
hi-tech export oriented items like hosiery, hand tools, drugs & pharmaceutical and stationery, have been provided with a
higher investment limit in plant and machinery, i.e. up to Rupees five crores to enable them to meet the requirements of
technology upgradation and face the global and domestic competition.
28.3   The Ministry of Small Scale Industries further added that as such, the reservation policy does not discourage
investment. On the contrary the policy is instrumental in employment generation and meeting the concern of regional
imbalances. Where ever it is felt that the reservation of any particular item needs to be dispensed with in the interest of
growth and development of the small scale sector, the issue is discussed with the stake holders and the respective
administrative Ministries, and depending upon the general opinion, the item is de- reserved with the recommendation of
the Advisory Committee constituted under ID&R Act, 1951. Accordingly, the list of reserved items has come down
from 873 in 1984 to 675 as on date. There is a proposal to de-reserve 85 more items during this year as announced in the
Budget Speech of 2004-05, which will further shorten the list of reserved items. De-reservation of 85 items, as
announced in the Budget (2004-2005) will help the small scale sector to meet the demand for technological up-
gradation, encourage research and development and make the sector competitive to face the domestic and global
competition.
28.4   The Committee is of the view that reservation of items to SSI sector should not become a restriction to the
growth of this sector as far as investment and technology upgradation is concerned. The Committee, however,
strongly, feels that Government should take precaution while taking out an item from the reserved list so that
labour oriented units remain protected.
29.0   ADOPTION OF “BEST PRACTICES CODE”
29.1   Adoption of “Best Practices Code” for large corporate dealing with the SME Sector on the line of the code for
payments for large industries/corporate would greatly help the sector regarding timely payment to SMEs. The
Committee pointed out that despite RBI’s Guidelines on Fair Practices code for Lenders, nothing has practically been
achieved. The Committee desired to know the required modification in the Delayed Payment Act ( as amended in 1998)
and mechanism reinforcing their use and application. The Ministry elaborated that the Interest on Delayed Payments to
Small Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertaking Act, 1993 was enacted in 1993 and amended in 1998 to ensure prompt
payment of money to SSIs. The Act has, therefore, been in operation for more than 10 years. During this period, there

153rd Report of Committee on Industry

have been substantial discussions and debates on the effectiveness of the Act among Government Departments, Industry
Groups and Small Scale Industry Associations. It was felt that certain amendments should be carried out in the Act so as
to make it more effective. Therefore, the Ministry after detailed discussions with various Government Departments,
Industry Groups and Small Scale Industry Associations is contemplating certain amendments to enable SSI
units/suppliers to get payments as agreed upon. The proposed amendments address the issue of bringing down the time
limit of payment to SSI Units, changing the penal interest rate and better disclosure norms in the Annual Statement of
accounts.
29.2   The Committee is of the view that there is a need for amendment in the provision of the Delayed Payment
Small Scale and Ancillary Industrial Undertaking Act 1993 as amended in 1998 and the relevant provisions of
the Companies Act i.e. mandatory provision requiring the large enterprises to show in the entries of their
Balance sheets the amount due for payment to the SSI units to enable SSI units/suppliers to get payments as
agreed upon. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should come out with the requisite
amendment in the said Act without further delay.
30.0   PROGRESS IN REGARD TO ENACTMENT OF LIMITED PARTNERSHIP ACT
30.1   The Ministry of SSI has discussed the matter with various Small Scale Industries Associations, RBI, SIDBI,
Department of Company Affairs and Ministry of Law. During the discussions, it was felt that the appropriate Ministry
to bring in the legislation on Limited Partnership is the Department of Company Affairs. Accordingly, Department of
Company Affairs was requested to enact the above Act. The Department of Company Affairs constituted a High Level
Committee under the Chairmanship of Shri Naresh Chandra on this issue. They have informed that the
recommendations of the Naresh Chandra Committee have not been processed further, as the Department would be
withdrawing the Companies (Amendment) Bill, 2003 and in its place a comprehensive set of amendments are proposed
to be placed before the Parliament. Provisions to enable limited liability partnership are likely to be part of this set of
amendments. No time frame has been indicated, as it involves wide consultation and approval of Cabinet, etc. The
Naresh Chandra Committee’s Report and the stand by Department of Company Affairs was examined in Ministry of
SSI. However the Committee’s contention that such Act is not required for the SSI Sector at present has not been agreed
to by the Ministry. Therefore, the Ministry has taken up the matter with the Department of Company Affairs and
recommended that a separate Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) Act for the SSI Sector should be introduced.
Department of Company Affairs has informed that they are examining the recommendations of Naresh Chandra
Committee, and a final decision on recommendations for introducing a Limited Liability Partnership (LLP) Act is yet to
be taken.
30.2   The Committee is in agreement with the view of the Ministry of SSI that the SSI sector needs the Limited
Liability Partnership (LLP) Act, therefore, recommends that the Ministry of SSI should continue to pursue for
legislation of the Limited Liability Partnership Act in the interest of Small Scale Sector.
31.0   SUNRISE INDUSTRIES IN THE SSI SECTOR
31.1   The Office of DC(SSI) has conducted various information/training programmes in respect of sunrise industries in
the SSI sector. These programmes have been conducted in areas like IPRs, IT & Bio-Technology. Various
Entrepreneurial Development Programmes on Bio Technology are being conducted in SIDO’s field offices. Technical
officers of SIDO have recently been deputed for training Programme organized by SIDO in collaboration with Bio
Technology Consortium of India so as to engage them in Bio Technology Training programme. Nano technology being
a new and relatively capital intensive as well as R&D intensive activity, is yet to be focused in the SSI sector.
31.2   The promotion of IT will go a long way in encouraging sunrise industries as most of the sunrise industries have a
strong IT component built into them. Training for IT and IT enabled services has been taken up in a big way in the
SISIs, IPR protection and management of rapid up-scaling through infusion of technology is important for development
of SSI sector in these areas. The Office of DCSSI has been conducting Intellectual Property Rights (IPR) training
programmes all over the country for the last few years. This year also, 28 IPR training programmes have been planned
to be conducted under the aegis of the various SISIs. Enablement of the entrepreneurs to take up the issue of IPR
protection and management of rapid up-scaling of operation on priority basis is expected through these programmes.
The small scale entrepreneurs are being sensitized towards the need for protection and methodology to be adopted for
IPR management through not only diffusion and upgradation of technology but also employing existing IPR resources
for the purpose.
31.3   The Committee desires that adequate steps should be taken to identify the sunrise industries in the SSI
sector e.g. Information Technology (IT), Biotechnology (BT) Pharmaceuticals and Nan technologies along with

32.0   STREAMLINING AND STRENGTHENING THE ANTI-DUMPING MECHANISM
32.1   The Anti-Dumping mechanism comes under the purview of the Directorate General of Anti-Dumping and Allied
Duties under the Ministry of Commerce and Industry and, the Ministry of Commerce and Industry is monitoring the
progress of anti-dumping cases. However, this Ministry has formulated a Market Development Assistance (MDA- SSI)
Scheme to enhance the exports by the SSIs. Under the Scheme, financial assistance for participation in international
exhibitions, overseas study, tours, assistance towards the production of publicity material, market studies etc. is given.
Under this Scheme, financial assistance upto Rs. l lakh can also be given to SSI Associations who have initiated anti-
dumping investigations. The above Scheme was approved during August 2001.
32.2   The Department of Commerce has revised the Indo-Nepal Treaty of Trade and the revised protocol with effect
from 6.3.2002 for a period of 5 years. To protect the industry the following steps have been taken:
          (i)    Rules for granting Certificate of Origin have been changed. Only following articles can now be imported
preferentially:
                 (a)    Those which are manufactured in Nepal wholly from Nepalese and/or Indian materials.
                 (b)    The articles involve a manufacturing process in Nepal that brings about a change in classification in 4
digit level.
                 (c)    There is value addition of at least 43 per cent from 6th March 2003.
          (ii)   In addition to certain special provisions with respect to import of vegetable fats (vanaspati), acrylic yarn,
copper products and zinc oxide will be allowed in India subject to a fixed quota per year as prescribed and no
preferential facility will be available for import of items like alcoholic liquors, beverages and their
conservatives except industrial spirits, perfumes and cosmetics with non-Nepalese/non-Indian brand name
and cigarettes and tobacco.
32.3   Anti-dumping actions initiated by the Director General of Anti-dumping have been imposed on certain products
of SSI concern like Dry-Cell Batteries with effect from 2.8.2001 and on imports of sports shoes on 25.9.2001. The anti-
dumping Authority in the Ministry of Commerce and Industry is responsible for the anti-dumping actions when
