Industries in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.
3.     The Sub-Committee-IV for the Action Taken Reports at its meeting held on 8th December, 2004 considered and
adopted the Report.
4.     The Committee at its meeting held on 9th December, 2004 considered and adopted the Report.
NEW DELHI ;
9th December, 2004
SANTOSH BAGRODIA
 Chairman,
Department-relatedparliamentary  Standing
Committee on Industry.
 
REPORT
         The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Agro and Rural
Industries on the Recommendations contained in the 141st Report (of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry) on the Potential and Promotion of Coir Industries in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar
Islands pertaining to the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries . The Report was presented / laid on the Table of Rajya
Sabha and Lok Sabha on the 23rd December, 2003.
2. Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries in respect of the
recommendations contained in the Report. These have been categorized as follows:
Chapter - I- The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry. The Committee is pleased
to observe that the Ministry has accepted its recommendation as mentioned in Chapter -I of the Report.
Chapter - II- The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the
Government’s replies. In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic and explanation
advocated by the Ministry and therefore does not want to pursue further.
Chapter - III- The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the
Ministry. The Committee expresses its concern over the non­-implementations of recommendations contained in
Chapter-III and desires that the Ministry should furnish logical explanation in respect of these recommendations.
Chapter - IV- The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not been
received. In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry has either furnished the interim replies or
couched its language in vague terms like noted for compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desires that the
Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to
the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
3. The Details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH  HAVE  BEEN  ACCEPTED
BY  THE  GOVERNMENT
Recommendation
1.0    ROLE OF COIR BOARD
l.l      The Committee in its 91 st Report on ‘Coir Board-A Performance Review’ has made a detailed study of
performance of Coir Board. However, the Committee appreciates the role of Coir Board and the West Bengal
Government in chalking out action plan for the promotion and proliferation of coir industries in West Bengal and
Andaman & Nicobar Islands on the suggestion and guidelines of the Sub-Committee of Department-related
Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry for the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries during its study visits to
Kolkata and Port Blair. The Committee desires that the Coir Board should emphasize on the participation of the Private
Sector and NGOs in the development of the Coir Industry for optimum utilization of resources, exploitation of untapped
export market, national level project for creation of awareness about Coir Products, up-gradation of technology, brand
endowment, institutionalization and co-operativisation of Coir Sector, development of Coir Industry, adequate stress on
R&D activities, sketching of appropriate marketing strategy for development of Coir Industry as a whole.

157thReport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/157threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:25]
Action Taken
1.1.1Efforts would be made to attract more and more Private parties and NGOs to Coir industry so that optimum
utilisation of resources can be made. Introduction of the Reform Policies of the Government, adoption of liberal
Promotional Regime and abolition of the controls have encouraged more private participation in the development of coir
industry. Assistance is being provided to the private sector for market delegations/ participation in various international
exhibitions etc. for exploitation of untapped export market under the Ministry of Commerce’s Scheme of “Marketing
Development Assistance” and Coir Board’s scheme of “External Market Development Assistance”. For domestic
market development, showroom and sales depots have been established in important cities all over India and publicity
for Coir products is being given through electronics and print media. The R & D activities have resulted in notable
achievements in manufacturing technology and development of new products. The Coir Board developed a new
technology for reducing the retting period of husk in the manufacturing process of white fibre from 12 months to 3
weeks. Another notable achievement in R & D was the development of a technique to convert the waste material Coir
pith, generated in the process of manufacturing Coir fibre into an organic manure. It was also possible to develop some
new coir processing machinery. Anugraha, a low cost handloom made of mild steel which could even be operated by
women workers is the latest addition. Joint collaborative projects with academic institutions and private sector
participation resulted in product diversification for new applications such as packaging materials, wood substitute etc.
New technologies developed by the Coir Board are being disseminated to the industry through extension services.
Under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Co-operativisation, assistance is being given to Coir producing States
including West Bengal for developing co-operative societies and to undertake Coir related activities.
Recommendation
1.2    ENHANCEMENT OF THE PERFORMANCE AND OPERATIONAL EFFICIENCY OF COIR SECTOR
1.2.1The Committee recommends that the following measures may be undertaken for the enhancement of the
performance and operational efficiency of coir sector in West Bengal and Andaman and Nicobar Islands:­
i.      Restructuring of the Coir Industry, Creation of Utility Demand, modernisation for increased productivity to
face price competition, encouraging Brand based Publicity, Quality improvement;
ii.     Market Survey to understand the market demand, market trend, market potential etc; Encouraging SSI Coir
Exporters to obtain ISO certification;
iii.    Creation of a Guidance Cell to collect, compile and disseminate information on quality standards;
Participation in Exhibitions/ Fairs abroad; Product Promotion Programmes; Catalogue Shows;
iv.    External Market Development Assistance; Assistance for Sales Promotion Tour and for Participation in Fairs
and Exhibitions abroad;
v.     Organisation of specialized exhibitions in India like IITF, Carpet Expo, Heimtextil etc.;
vi.    Production of Brochures/Folders/Catalogues/Directory of Exporters/ Interactive CD-Rom etc.;
vii.   Awards to be instituted by the State/UT Government/ Coir Board for outstanding performance in different
fields would have positive impact on the performance and operational efficiency of Coir Sector.
Action Taken
1.2.2Some of the steps identified by the Committee and recommended for implementation for enhancing the
performance and operational efficiency of coir sector in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands are the measures
already undertaken for the development of the industry and its domestic and export market on the whole. For example,
quality improvement, increased productivity through modernisation to face price competition, participation in trade fairs
and exhibitions in India and abroad, participation in Product Promotion Programmes, Catalogue Shows etc., extending
External Market Development Assistance to the exporters for participation in trade fairs and undertaking sales
promotion tours, organisation of specialized exhibitions in India like India International Trade Fair, Carpet Expo. Etc.
production of publicity literatures, brochures, folders, catalogues, directory of exporters, presentation of coir industry
awards in recognition of excellent performance in various fields of the industry etc. are promotional measures
undertaken on continuous basis under the annual plan programmes of the Coir Board. Such measures will be made
applicable in the case of coir sector in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands also.
1.2.3As suggested by the Committee, market surveys will be undertaken to assess market demand, market trend,
potential etc. It may be noted that there is already a scheme included in the annual plan proposals for 2004-2005
providing for encouraging coir exporters to obtain ISO certification.
Recommendation

157thReport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/157threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:25]
1.3    EXPORT PROMOTION
1.3.1The Committee recommends that the Coir Board should explore the potential of growth in export of coir and coir
products both in terms of quantity and value as produced in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands. The
Committee recommends that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries should take promotional steps to enhance the
export potential of Coir Products. The Committee recommends that necessary infrastructure in the form of offices of the
Coir Board may be set up in Kolkata for arranging awareness programmes and training programmes for the benefit of
private entrepreneurs and labourers.
1.3.2The Committee recommends that a thrust may be given to boost export of coir products and assistance of Export
Credit Guarantee Corporation (ECGC) may be sought in the matter. The Committee also recommends that possibility of
mutual cooperation in possible area between India and other neighboring countries like Sri Lanka, Vietnam, Thailand
and Philipines may be explored. The Committee understands that the promotion of export market for coir and coir
products is of vital importance for the growth of Indian coir industry, therefore, there should also be an attempt to
develop the brand image for the Indian coir, which should instantly evoke a sense of unique craftsmanship and assured
quality.
Action Taken
1.3.3There is potential for developing West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands as export centres of Coir and Coir
products like Kerala and Tamil Nadu. In the post yarn sector, coir industry in those areas is in the nascent stage. The
industry needs to be developed to make itself capable of producing exportable products of international standards. This
requires concerted efforts towards skill development through intensive training and infrastructure development. Besides
active co-operation of the concerned State Governments, Coir Board should have sufficient budgetary support in the
annual plan allocation for achieving this mission. The Committee recommended setting up of Office of the Coir Board
in Kolkata for arranging awareness programmes and training programmes for the benefit of private entrepreneurs and
labourers.
1.3.4Coir Board has established a Regional Office at Bhubaneswar in Orissa in February, 2004. Development of Coir
Industry covering West Bengal, Orissa, North Eastern and Northern States comes under the jurisdiction of this Regional
Office.
1.3.5There have been some attempts in the past to explore areas of co-operation between India and other Coir producing
countries. In fact, the R & D and market development projects being implemented under the auspices of Inter
Governmental Group on Hard Fibres of FAO, taken into consideration these aspects of mutual co­operation between
different coir producing countries.
1.3.6As recommended for by the Committee, creation of a brand image for Indian Coir in the overseas market and
thereby instantly evoking a sense of unique craftsmanship and assured quality will go a long way in promoting our
export to the overseas market. Keeping this objective, a study on the possibility of introducing brand image for Indian
Coir through M/s. A.F Fergusan & Co., Chennai has already been undertaken. A proposal in this regard is being framed
.
Recommendation
1.4    Collection of Coconut Husk
1.4.1The Committee observes that the Coir Industry gravely suffers from shortage of fibre both white and brown which
sometime has to be imported. The shortage is mainly because of absence of adequate machinery for collection of
coconut husk from consumers of coconuts in the States in general and West Bengal and Andaman and Nicobar in
particular. In the State of West Bengal only the coconut traders or Goldars collect the husk from the primary coconut
agriculturist market. The Committee feels that existing arrangements are able to collect only 180 tonnes brown fibre
annually. With the available husks there is scope of at least 10 modern markets brown fiber manufacturing units to
enhance the production to the level 200 mt. per annum. The Committee, therefore, impress upon the Coir Board and the
Government of West Bengal to make serious efforts for the intensive collection of husk and the system needs to be
institutionalized.
1.4.2The Committee further impresses upon the Government to take a holistic view of the problems being faced in the
Car Nicobar area. A serious planning is the need of the hour to provide logistic support to the Car Nicobar Islands. In
order to solve the problem of the husk collection, the Committee suggests if it is not possible at the local level the
outside agencies may be brought in to do the job even on commercial line.
1.4.3The Committee further recommends that the Government also facilitate the Governments of West Bengal and

157thReport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/157threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:25]
Andaman and Nicobar Islands the logistic support for import of brown fibre from the neighbouring country like Sri
Lanka and Philipines in order to meet the shortage of brown fibre.
Action Taken
1.4.4 Concerted efforts are being made to alleviate the problem of fibre shortage in coir producing States through
various measures. The efforts have yielded positive results and the availability of Coir fibre has improved resulting in
stabilisatioin of prices. It is expected that the position would improve in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands
when the Action Plan, already drafted, gets implemented. When the industry in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar
Islands develops in the post fibre/yarn sector with the development of infrastructure and skilled manpower, the problem
of fibre shortage could be suitable addressed; if necessary through outsourcing.
Recommendation
1.5    COIR INDUSTRIAL INFRASTRUCTURE
1.5.1The Committee recommends that in all major coconut growing areas in the state of West Bengal and the Union
Territory of Andaman & Nicobar, more clusters may be identified where coir industrial activities may be established. In
these clusters coir industrial infrastructure should be set up preferably in the private sector. Basic techno-economic
feasibility/consultancy can be given by the Coir Board for setting up such production infrastructure. The Committee
further recommends that suitable state level project may be evolved for creation of awareness about coir products,
development of market, production of new and diversified goods of mass consumption and quality assurance. A
Regional Coir Trade Information Centre may be opened for collection analysis its dissemination of information in the
state of West Bengal, Andaman & Nicobar, Orissa, Jharkhand and Bihar. It should become one of the principal
activities of the Coir Board in the region. Coir sector can be developed in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar
through flow of information especially marketing and technology, which is possible through IT assisted programmes.
Action Taken
1.5.2In order to develop Coir industrial infrastructure in non-traditional areas, certain programmes have already been
chalked out one of the programmes is “Suvarnajayanthi Coir Cluster Vikas Yojana”. The scheme also aims at overall
development of Coir industry including welfare of workers and artisians, enhancement of export, generation of
additional employment in non-traditional areas etc. All over India, 50 Coir industrial clusters will be identified for
appropriate interventions under the Scheme. To begin with, 11 clusters have been identified in different States for this
purpose. 24 South Parganas in West Bengal is one of the Coir producing centres identified for provision of
infrastructural facilities in this scheme. Some other programmes identified for implementation in these clusters are
organisation of Entrepreneurship Development Programmes, Extension of R & D results, Exposure Tours, Workshops,
Orientation Training Programmes, Skill Development Programmes etc.
Recommendation
1.6    TECHNOLOGY  UP-GRADATION
1.6.1 The Committee reiterates its observation as made in its 91st Report that Technological upgradation is a sina qua
non for the development of the coir industry. Eco-friendly process and production technologies, development of cost-
effective and efficient machinery with higher productivity, which reduces drudgery will have to be developed. Progress
in the development of coir machinery has been very tardy. The Committee understands that once the potential of the
coir industries in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar are being assessed the next step should be to strengthen the R &
D projects. In this regard, the Committee recommends that special efforts have to be made to identify the potential coir
machinery manufacturers who can be supported with appropriate technology transfer from any available areas. This
activity may be taken up as joint venture programmes with greater emphasis on private sector participation ensuring
faster commercialization.
1.6.2The Committee feels that the State Government of West Bengal and UT Government of Andaman & Nicobar in
consultation with the Coir Board should aim at rapid modernization for the overall sustainable development of the coir
industry, focusing on research and development, quality improvement, human resource development, better marketing
of products and welfare support to the needy, particularly the less-privileged group like women coir workers who
constitute more than 80 per cent of the work-force. The Committee stresses the need for greater emphasis on the
involvement of the private sector as well as the concerned state government. The Committee recommends that the Coir
Board, in coordination with State Governments should make an endeavour to undertake more sponsored R & D projects
in association with reputed agencies in both the public and private sectors.

Action Taken
1.6.3The R & D activities of the Coir Board are mainly carried out at the Central Coir Research Institute, Alleppey
(Kerala) and Central Institute of Coir Technology, Bangalore (Karnataka). Results of the R & D activities are promptly
passed on to the trade through its extension service activities. In fact, one of the important assignments of the Regional
Offices of the Coir Board in various Coir producing States is extension of the results of its R & D activities. The Coir
Board has been awarded the prestigious National Research and Development Corporation (NRDC) Technology Awards
twice for its research investigations and development of new technologies. Development of COIRRET, to reduce the
retting period, development of PITHPLUS to convert Coir pith into organic manure, development of POLYCOIR, a
wood substitute, and development of a number of cost effective and efficient machinery with higher productivity like
“Anugraha”, a compact metallic handloom for weaving Coir geo-textiles even by women workers were some of its
achievements. Some of the R & D works of the Board have been done in collaboration with reputed outside agencies.
Most of the technologies developed in its R& D institutes have been transferred by the Board to reputed
agencies/private entrepreneurs for commercialization. No efforts would be spared in developing new technologies in the
processing and production technology and dissemination of the same to the trade in traditional as well as non traditional
Coir products manufacturing States.
CHAPTER - II
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT
DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
Recommendation
2.0    MODEL COIR VILLAGE SCHEME
2.1.1The Committee is of the view that the model coir village scheme would go a long way in the industrialization
process in the coir sector in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar . The Committee agrees with the views of Institute of
Rural Management, Anand, Gujarat for continuance of Model Coir Village Yojana for effective proliferation and wide
promotion of coir industries in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar.
Action Taken
2.1.2A new Scheme named “Production Oriented Welfare Scheme for Coir Workers” has been formulated. The scheme
has two components. The first component aims at development of necessary infrastructural facilities needed for
development of Coir industry and the aim of the second component is improvement of productivity of the workers. An
insurance scheme against hospitalisation of Coir workers has also been incorporated in the scheme. It is believed that
the scheme will go a long way in the development of Coir industry in all Coir producing States. Most of the salient
features of the erstwhile Model Coir Village Scheme have been retained in the new scheme. Through the scheme it is
proposed to provide production oriented infrastructural facilities in all Coir producing States/UTs.
CHAPTER - III
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE

Recommendation
3.0    RESILIENT MONITORING-MECHANISM
3.1.1 The Committee hopes that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries must guide the Coir Board in the execution
of action plan meant for West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar. A resilient monitoring mechanism is required for timely
implementation of developmental programmes and for achieving the cherished objectives and mission underlining each
and every scheme. The Committee recommends that the Coir Board should be guided by the principle of management
by objectives (MBO) and not merely management by activities. The Committee is of the view that Khadi and Village
Industries as well as the coir industries can facilitate agro and rural base of economic development of West Bengal.
Therefore, the State Department of Industries has to play the pivotal role in guiding the developmental pattern within a
determined economic policy. By having statistical information at the grass root level, that is at the block and the district
level, the District Magistrate or the Development Commissioner of the region should come out with a strategy for the
economic development of the State preferably chalking out district wise action plan. At the same time, officials at the
helm of affairs at the State and the Central level should encourage and facilitate the officials at the grass root level for

157thReport of Committee on Industry

effective implementation of policies and action plan at the grass root level. Therefore, better coordination and
collaboration between the Central and the State Government and effective implementation machinery at the grass root
level is desirable.
Action Taken
3.1.2The recommendations of the Committee are noted for compliance.
Further Recommendation
3.1.3The Committee would like to know from the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries the following informations:- ­
(i)    whether the Ministry of ARI has chalked out any guidelines for the Coir Board for the timely execution of
Action Plan meant for West Bengal and Andaman and Nicobar, if yes, the details thereof and if not the
reasons therefor.
(ii)    the details of monitoring mechanism for implementation of  developmental programmes and achievement of
objectives and missions of each and every scheme.
(iii)   steps taken and outcome thereof identifying various facets and dimension of Khadi and Village Industries
and Coir Industries in West Bengal; so and to widen the ARI’s base and enhancing its contribution to State’s
economy.
(iv)   steps taken and the details thereof regarding collection of data and information at the grass root level
pertaining to status, problems and prospects of Coir Industries.
(v)   district- wise details of development strategies and Action Plan thereon.
(vi)   the details of linkage machinery for co-coordinating and collaboration between the central and state
Governments to work as effective implementation machinery.
3.1.4The Committee understands that the Action Plan meant for proliferation of Coir Industries contains noble ideas but
need is to streamline the implementation machinery.
Recommendation
3.2    POTENTIAL  OF  EMPLOYMENT  GENERATION  BY  COIR  MANUFACTURING  UNITS
3.2.1 The Committee knows that since Coir Industry is an employment intensive industry, efforts should be made for
searching avenues for generating sustainable and regular employment in the Coir Sector. Employment of large number
of women in the Coir Sector would fulfill the dreams of empowerment of women and due share to the economically and
socially backward classes (SCs/STs/OBCs) would enhance the standard of living of people of weaker section of society.
Action Taken
3.2.2 There is a potential for development of Coir industry in West Bengal and it can serve as a source of employment
generation for economically and socially backward rural people. At present, only 20% of coconut husk is made
available for Coir industry and only about 3140 workers are engaged by the industry in West Bengal. Mahila Coir
Yojana, a self -employment scheme of the Board for women is given adequate thrust in the plan of actions being
implemented in various States for generation of more employment to women.
Further Recommendation
3.2.3The Committee is of the opinion that national economy must be capable of generating employment which is
concomitant to poverty alleviation, general improvement in standard of living, savings, credit formation, investment and
further opening of avenues for employment generation potential. Since the Coir Industry is employment intensive
industry, the Committee thought it pertinent to recommend for searching avenues for generating sustainable and regular
employment in the Coir Sector. At the same time the employment generation potential of Coir Industries can be utilised
for empowerment of women and weaker section of society of general improvement in standard of living.
3.2.4 The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of ARI is in agreement with the employment generation
potential of Coir Industries. However, the Committee is constrained to express its displeasure that in response to
Committee’s recommendation for generating employment in Coir Industries in West Bengal, the Ministry of ARI in its
Action Taken Note merely enumerated the existing fact that only 3140 workers are engaged by the Coir Industry in
West Bengal as there is only 20% collection of coconut husk in West Bengal. What the Committee desired in the Action
Taken Note is in fact the plan envisaged and action taken in regard to harness the potential of employment generation
which remains to be utilized at least by the five fold as accepted by the Ministry of ARI itself. The Committee desires
that the Mahila Coir Yojana needs to be strengthened so as to be result oriented, on similar line Sarvodaya Coir Yojana

157thReport of Committee on Industry

may be launched for employment of weaker sections of the society in Coir Industries. What the Committee desires is in
fact the objective increment in employment generation in actual number through Coir Industries in West Bengal for
general improvement in living standard in the State. The Committee therefore, impresses upon the Ministry of ARI and
Coir Board to work out a time bound programme for employment generation by utilizing the potential available in the
State of West Bengal.
Recommendation
3.3    A  SEPARATE  CELL  FOR  THE  COIR  INDUSTRY  IN  THE  RESPECTIVE  DEPARTMENTS OF 
INDUSTRY.
3.3.1 The Committee recommends that both the State and UT Governments may be advised to set up a separate cell for
the coir industry in their respective Departments of Industry, preferably under the SSI sector. The District Industries
Centre or the District Rural Development Agencies of the concerned districts may be made the nodal agency for the
development of coir where there is coconut cultivation, and entrusted with the responsibility of imparting training,
entrepreneurship development, assistance in getting micro credits, and organizing the workers into Self Help Groups for
production and marketing. The technical inputs may be provided by the Coir Board in extending training, especially in
the production of value-added goods and in getting trade information. Kolkata and Port Blair as well as Car Nicobar
should have at least one outlet of the Coir Board and exhibitions may be held periodically in all cities and small towns
of the State/UT for awareness as well as marketing.
Action Taken
3.3.2The Government is prepared to provide all technical support for the development of this industry in the State
especially in the production of value added goods and in getting trade information. There is already a showroom cum
sales depot of the Coir Board in Calcutta (established in 1959) for popularization of Coir products. Coir Board can also
be allowed to participate in leading exhibitions in the State/Union Territory for awareness as well as marketing..
Further Recommendation
3.3.3 The Committee made recommendation for advising the respective State and UT Government for setting up a
separate cell for the Coir Industries in their Department of Small Scale Industries and endowing district industries center
or the district rural development agencies of the concerned districts to act as nodal agency for accelerated proliferation
of Coir Industries in West Bengal and Andaman and Nicobar. The Committee would like to know whether the Ministry
of ARI has communicated to the Government of West Bengal and Andaman and Nicobar in line-with recommendation
of the Committee, if yes, the response of those Government and if not, the reasons therefor. The Committee would also
like to know whether the Coir Board had approached the State and UT Government for providing technical support for
development and production of Coir Industries. The Committee would like to know further as to what actions have been
taken for renovating and modernization of showroom - come sales depot at Kolkata and setting up of a outlet of the Coir
Board at Port Blair and Car Nicobar.
Recommendation
3.4    STEPS TO PROMOTE FAIR COMPETITION AMONG PRODUCERS AND EXPORTERS OF                 
COIR AND COIR PRODUCTS
3.4.1The Committee desires that the Coir Board should promote fair competition from among the exporters and
manufacturers. The suggestion for formation of Manufacturers Consortia and Setting up of Common Facility Centres
(CFC) to reduce unfair competition may be acceded to, as the same would encourage the coir manufacturers and
exporters in new found land like West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar.
Action Taken
3.4.2All assistance to producers and exporters is being extended for fair competition through improvements in quality
standards. Formation of Manufacturers Consortia and setting up of Common Facility Centres (CFC) are two activities
for which the Coir Board gives maximum priority.

3.4.3 The Committee is pleased to note the readiness of Coir Board for extending all assistance to producers and
exporters regulating fair competition through improvement in quality standards, at the same time the Committee would
like to know as to what action have been taken on the part of the Coir Board for formation of manufacturers consortia
and setting up Common Facility Centre (CFC) for which the coir board is giving maximum priority. An early decision
in this regard on the part of the coir board would be helpful in promoting and in fact ensuring fair competition among
producers and exporters in exporting coir and coir products.
Recommendation

ISLANDS
3.8.1The Committee feels that the financial assistance for technology upgradation, revitalization and augmentation of
training centers in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands is required . Such assistance should also be given for
cluster development programmes and marketing both for internal consumption and export. Since there is total absence
of credit plan for the coir industries in most of the States including Kerala and West Bengal as coir industries is not
being identified as the Key Industry, the Committee recommends that all the bankers and the district collectors in the
State of West Bengal and UT of Andaman & Nicobar Islands should ensure that credit plan for coir industries is shown

all the banks at the apex level must be given direction to the state level unions to provide credit to coir industries. Once

markets the products which is essential for the survival of the industry.

industry in the Banks’ Credit Plan has also been taken up with the Reserve Bank of India. The credit flow to this sector
in West Bengal and Andaman & Nicobar Islands can be improved if the State/UT Governments concerned initiate
necessary action in association with Coir Board.

3.8.3The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries are making serious efforts for
ensuring adequate credit flow to Coir Industry for technology up-gradation, opening new avenues for fresh
entrepreneurs, revitalization and augmentation of training centers, promotion of cluster development programmes etc.
The Committee desires that the Ministry of ARI should take-up follow-up action with the Reserve Bank of India for
segregated allocation for coir industry in the Bank’s credit plan. Once the segregated allocation for Coir Industries in the
Bank’s Credit Plan is made the district level credit plan may be chalked out by the Banks. The Ministry of ARI in
tandem with the Coir Board should chalk out the requirement of credit for the coir industry for expansion and
proliferation of coir units in various States including the West Bengal and Andaman and Nicobar Islands. The Ministry
of ARI should communicate to State and Union Territory Governments to initiate necessary action in association with
Coir Board for optimum utilisation of credit earmarked for coir industries. A co­operative and communicative centre-
state relation is essential for the furtherance and proliferation of Coir industries. It is the Coir Board and the Ministry of
ARI which must undertake the lead role in associating and motivating the State Government for chalking out district
level credit plan and involving the NGOs for expansion and promotion of Coir Industries in various states including the

non­-traditional coir States.
Recommendation
3.9.   TRANSPORT SUBSIDY TO THE COIR INDUSTRIES IN ANDAMAN AND NICOBAR ISLANDS
3.9.1The Committee is of the considered view that for the promotion and proliferation of coir industries in Andaman
and Nicobar Islands transport subsidy and freight subsidy should be given to the areas which are at some locational
disadvantages. The Ministry of ARI may take up this issue with the Ministry of Finance. There is a need to formulate
graded level of transport subsidy i. e. somebody who is at the Car Nicobar should be given higher level of subsidy than
the one at Port Blair. That is because there are some inherited challenges in the Island with the population of 3,57,000
out of that the so called urban population at Port Blair is 2,56,000 having a different population composition than the
population composition of the main land. The island has a very small market. Any industry which needs to be sustained
has to look at the main land for the market. There is very high freight cost handling cost and labour cost. The price index
is very high when the products come to main land market, they become uncompetitive. Therefore, the Island needs to be
treated at a separated footing as comparing to the other main land State because of connectivity problem, labour cost etc.
Action Taken
3.9.2The recommendations of the Committee are noted for compliance.
Further Recommendation
3.9.2The Committee reiterates that Andaman and Nicobar Islands being at locational disadvantages must be granted
transport subsidy and freight subsidy for the promotion and proliferation of Coir Industries in the union territory. The
Committee reiterates that the Ministry of ARI should take-up this issue with the Ministry of Finance without further
delay.

RESILIENT MONITORING-MECHANISM
         The Committee would like to know from the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries the following informations:- ­
(i)    whether the Ministry of ARI has chalked out any guidelines for the Coir Board for the timely enecution of
Action Plan meant for West Bengal and Andaman and Nicobar, if yes, the details thereof and if not the
reasons therefor.

objectives and missions of each and every scheme.
(iii)   steps taken and outcome thereof identifying various facets and dimension of Khadi and Village Industries
and Coir Industries in West Bengal; so and to widen the ARI’s base and enhancing its contribution to State’s
economy.

pertaining to status, problems and prospects of Coir Industries.
(v)   district-wise details of development strategies and Action Plan thereon.

Governments to work as effective implementation machinery.                                             (Para 3.1.3)

but need is to streamline the implementation machinery.                                             (Para 3.1.4)

         The Committee is of the opinion that national economy must be capable of generating employment which is
concomitant to poverty alleviation, general improvement in standard of living, savings, credit formation, investment and
further opening of avenues for employment generation potential. Since the Coir Industry is employment intensive
industry, the Committee thought it pertinent to recommend for searching avenues for generating sustainable and regular
employment in the Coir Sector. At the same time the employment generation potential of Coir Industries can be utilised
for empowerment of women and weaker section of society of general improvement in standard of
living.                                       (Para 3.2.3)
         The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of ARI is in agreement with the employment generation
potential of Coir Industries. However, the Committee is constrained to express its displeasure that in response to
Committee’s recommendation for generating employment in Coir Industries in West Bengal, the Ministry of ARI in its
Action Taken Note merely enumerated the existing fact that only 3140 workers are engaged by the Coir Industry in
West Bengal as there is only 20% collection of coconut husk in West Bengal. What the Committee desired in the Action

turnover can be quantified and measured in realistic and observable terms. The Committee desires that the Coir Board

REPORT
         The Present report is the Action Taken Report on the Action Taken Note received from the Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises on the recommendations contained in the Committee’s 143rd Report on “Level
Playing Field for the Indian Capital Goods Industry”. The said report was presented to the Rajya Sabha and laid on the
table of Lok Sabha on 23rd December, 2003.
2.      The Committee’s 143rd Report outlines the Government’s Exim  Policy in the context of the liberalization and
globalization process and the consequent impact on the domestic capital goods industries. In the early eighties, when
India’s economy was on an uptrend, there was need for investment in the infrastructure sector. Investment from within
India was not forthcoming mainly because of higher rate of interest and private sector risk aversions. Investment during
those years was mainly from multilateral/bilateral funding agencies. For judicious usage of these funds, the projects
were established under International Competitive Bidding procedures. Indian companies were also eligible to participate
in the bidding procedure. Overseas suppliers could enjoy soft export financing from their exim banking and other export
benefits prevailing in those countries. The Indian companies were also extended the duty free raw material imports and
refund of excise duty on their finished goods to have a level playing field. Supplies to such projects were termed as
Deemed Exports.
3.      The Industrial Policy of 1991 started the process of de-licensing. The process of de-regulation was aimed at
enlarging competition and allowing new firms to enter the markets. The market was opened up to domestic
entrepreneurs/industrialists, which was reserved for public sector undertakings, and foreign capital was provided free
entry up to 51% equity in high technology areas. With the advent of globalization, when World Bank-aided projects
started coming in the country, the lifting of import control and drastic reduction of import duties, competition from
overseas posed a problem to the domestic capital goods industry. It became difficult to stay in the race for this industry
in the face of stiff competition from the multinational giants.
4.      As a part of the commitment given to WTO, the peak rate of customs duty was to be brought down to a level
agreed with WTO in a time-bound manner and accordingly the rate of customs duty for the projects was also reduced
gradually. Project import duty for the power projects was settled at 20% and Nil CVD since 1992-93.  Since the import
tariffs were coming down, the domestic industry was facing tough competition from the foreign suppliers. Till the time
the customs duty was 20% with Nil CVD, the domestic industry was getting the refund of Terminal Excise Duty as most
of the projects were multilateral/bilateral funded projects. Later, as the economic conditions improved, the investment
started coming from within the country as well. Recognizing the importance of infrastructure projects in the area of
power and refinery sector, DGFT announced that the supplies to such projects will be treated as deemed exports, even if
these were not funded by multilateral/bilateral agencies. Therefore all the supplies to power projects were treated as
deemed exports w.e.f. 3lst March, 1997. In the absence of CVD on the direct import under Project Imports, there was no
level playing field for the, domestic industry, as these supplies were subjected to Excise Duty. Therefore, domestic
industry represented to the Government for refund of TED, which was permitted by DGFT form 18th October, 1996.
5       After l8th October, 1996, there were equal opportunities for the foreign suppliers and the domestic suppliers as the
imports were subjected to customs duty @ 22% with Nil CVD and domestic supplier was getting the refund of TED.

This position remained unchanged till 28th February, 1999. During the period 1996-99, power projects attracted basic
customs duty of 20% with Nil CVD. The terminal excise duty paid by Indian manufacturers was refunded by the office
of DGFT. This provided protection of 20% to indigenous industry against the disadvantages suffered on account of sales
tax and other local levies on inputs/final product, higher cost of finance, infrastructure inadequacies etc.
6.      During the budget of 1999-2000, the customs duty was reduced to 5.5% from 22% but CVD was imposed @16%.
The overall impact on the imported goods was 22.38%: Therefore, this change in the duty structure had not impacted
much on the imports. Domestic suppliers continued to get the refund of TED in spite of imposition of CVD @ 16%. But
DGFT while announcing the Exim Policy effective from the year 2000, discontinued the refund of TED to the domestic
suppliers. Although the domestic suppliers were permitted duty free imports, the earlier gap between the foreign
supplier and domestic supplier, which was 22.38% reduced to 8.03% [22.38% - 16% + 1.65% (5.5% of the import
content of 30%)]. This gap has been further reduced to 7.45%, since the surcharge of customs duty is withdrawn [21.8%
- 16% + 1.65% (5% of import content of 30%)]. This has put the domestic suppliers in a disadvantageous position.
7.      It is pertinent to note that prior to 31st March, 2000 i.e. the date when refund of terminal excise duty was
withdrawn, domestic manufacturers have secured orders under international competitive bidding by passing on to the
customer the benefit of refund of TED as applicable in the Exim Policy. In case of power and fertilizer projects, where
the cycle time for competition is normally 3-4 years, the schedule for supply of capital goods is invariably 3 years. In
this category of projects, the domestic industry has been requesting the Central Government for refund of TED, which
was withdrawn on the supplies made from 1st April, 2000. It was mentioned that the domestic industry is suffering from
cost disadvantages like inadequate and high cost of infrastructure, higher cost of financing, sales tax, Octroi and other
taxes etc., which are of the tune of 14% to 23% depending upon the location of the project and the supplier.
8.      The Committee had been deliberating on the issue of refund of TED for a long time and it had given its
recommendations on the issue in its 36th, 45th and 59th reports. The Department of Heavy Industries in their Action
Taken Notes informed the Committee that the matter did not find favour of the DGFT on one or the other ground. The
Committee considered the Export-Import Policy announced on 31st March, 2000 which had withdrawn the refund of
Terminal Excise duty in case of fertilizer and power projects. This has created a situation where indigenous
manufacturers have been put to cost disadvantage compared to foreign suppliers. Domestic manufacturers suffer
inherent cost disadvantages to the extent of 18% to 28% of the equipment price on account of sales tax and other local
levies on inputs/final product, higher cost of finance, infrastructure inadequacies etc. indigenous manufacturer is
allowed to import its inputs at zero duty under deemed export scheme instead of 5% applicable for direct imports by the
project authorities. Assuming an import content of 40%, this gives an advantage of only 2%. After taking into account
4% (effective 4.64%) Central Sales Tax applicable on indigenous supplies and exemption of Special Additional Duty
(SAD) on direct imports, there is negative protection of 2.64% on account of customs duties alone.
9.      The Committee in its 143rd Report underlined the fact that one of the objectives of Exim  Policy was to provide
consumers with good quality goods and services at internationally competitive prices while at the same time a level
playing field for the domestic players. The Government provided a level playing field for the domestic producers and
therefore, wherever, the domestic producers secure orders even from within India, such suppliers were treated as
Deemed Exports, provided such orders were secured through International Competitive Bidding procedure. Deemed
Exports were eligible for all benefits in respect of manufacture and supply of goods.
10.    All power projects are entitled to get (i) advance license and Deemed Exports, (ii) Deemed Exports drawback and
(iii) Refund of Terminal Excise Duty (TED). But, domestic suppliers in power projects with domestic funding are
getting only first two benefits. Prior to 1st April, 2000, such suppliers were getting many more benefits. With the
announcement of Exim Policy on lst April, 2000 the refund of Terminal Excise Duty (TED) was discontinued with the
reduction of Basic Custom Duty (BCD) and imposition of CVD. Such mid term policy changes resulted in either the
manufacturer/supplier absorbing substantial loss or project cost substantially going up. When the matter was taken up
with DGFT, they maintained that changes effected in the Exim  Policy came into affect immediately and all supplies
effected from 1st April, 2000 were not entitled for  Terminal Excise Duty (TED).
11.    The Committee in the 143rd report observed that the basic concept of Exim  Policy was to provide a level playing
field between domestic supplier and foreign supplier. It started from those projects which were funded by multilateral
agencies where items were allowed under zero duty to give the domestic suppliers a level playing field so that they can
compete with the foreign companies. But in the light of Chaturvedi  Report, BCD was brought down from, 20% to 5%
and CVD was introduced 16% and TED was withdrawn. CVD was the protection given to domestic industry over and

above 5% BCD. The industries are supposed to have a built in cushion of 5% and they are getting the deemed export
benefit. But there are certain inefficiencies and bottlenecks in our systems. The domestic industries have to pay various
taxes to the State Governments and they have some legacies of the past in the form of townships, which are social
obligations, and the cost of this in our country is very high. These disadvantages are not neutralized. The Committee felt
that some sort of balance is to be stuck to neutralize the disadvantage faced by the domestic industries. The Committee
observed in that Report that Government should see how domestic industry would survive in the present globalised
world. The Government had to see the interest of domestic industries as compared to the foreign companies.
Government should also look into the matter relating to the local taxes domestic industry has to pay.

requested to furnish the Action Taken Replies on the Committee’s recommendations contained in that Report. The
Ministry of Heavy Industry and Public Enterprises have not furnished the Action Taken Notes para-wise as under along
with Committee’s further observations/recommendations thereon.
Recommendation
Refund of Terminal Excise Duty
12.1  If a contract has been awarded earlier and if the Government make any changes in policy, the whole contract
remains in dispute. This makes the projects very difficult. The Committee, therefore, recommends that whenever change
is made in the EXIM Policy, it should be for the prospective contracts.
(Para 6.15)
12.2  Since disadvantage forced by the domestic industries due to mid-term policy change, the Committee recommends
that where orders/letters of intent has been placed before 31st March, 2000 for power and fertilizer projects, the
provision of EXIM Policy of 1999-2000 may be made applicable to allow refund of Terminal Excise Duty.
(Para 6.16)
Action Taken
12.3  As directed by the Sub-committee-III of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, a
Committee of Secretaries was constituted to look into the issue of Refund of Terminal Excise Duty (TED), which
considered the matter and referred it to Department of Revenue.
12.4  The recommendations of the Committee in the above paras were referred to the DGFT and Department of
Revenue. DGFT have commented that no further action is due on their part and it is for the Department of Revenue to
reconsider the matter. The comments of Department of Revenue are awaited.
Further recommendation
12.5  The Committee reiterates its stand that the change in the EXIM policy should have the prospective effect. Giving
effect the change in the EXIM policy the retrospective implementation had amounted to change the rule of the game in
the mid -course. It was the retrospective implementation of the changes ‘in the EXIM policy which adversely affected
the PSUs like BHEL in the completion of its projects. That is why the Committee recommended in its 143rd Report that
if a contract has been awarded earlier and if the Government make any change in the EXIM policy at later stage it
should be for the prospective contracts.
12.6  The Committee is of the view that Government should review its policy of giving duty concessions to the foreign
companies in as much as it leads to disadvantages to the domestic companies especially the PSUs. It is the considered
view of the Committee that foreign companies should not be shown favour at the expense of domestic companies.
DGFT should consider, as special case, to issue notification for refund of terminal excise duty for projects ordered/bids
under International Competitive Bidding prior to 1st April, 2000.
12.7  The Committee reiterates its recommendation as made in 59th Report that DGFT should also issue notification for
refund of terminal excise duty for projects ordered/bid under International Competitive Bidding (ICB) prior to lst April,
2000 when such a refund was allowed under the extant EXIM Policy but withdrawn subsequently. In such a situation,
where customers are neither agreeable to re­negotiate the prices to compensate the manufacturers, nor are they ready to
pay the applicable excise duty, the refund of terminal excise duty for at least these projects which were ordered/Letters
of Intent (LOI) placed before 1st April, 2000 under ICB must be allowed under a special notification.
12.8  The Committee therefore, recommends that the Department of Revenue should reconsider the matter and

13.5  The above modifications announced by the Ministry of Finance indicate that our suggestion regarding duty

13.6  The Committee understands that the basic concept of EXIM policy is to provide a level playing field between
domestic supplier and foreign supplier. The Committee is of the view that Government should see how domestic
industry would survive in the present globalised  world. The Government has to see the interest of domestic industries
compared to the foreign companies. The Government should also look into the matter relating to the local taxes
domestic industry has to pay. Because the domestic industries have to pay various taxes to the State Governments and
they have some legacies of the past in the form of townships, which are social obligations,  and the cost of this in our
country is very high. These disadvantages are not neutralized. The Committee feels that some sort of balance is to be
struck to neutralize the disadvantage faced by the domestic industries.
13.7  The Committee is constrained to note that the suggestion of the Committee for rationalization of duty structure i.e.
20% Custom duty, nil CVD and corresponding refund of TED to the domestic suppliers in order to provide a level
playing field for the Indian capital goods industry could not receive the attention of the Ministry of Finance. The
Committee notes the announcement of changes in the indirect tax modification in the basic custom duty and SAD w.e.f.
9th January, 2004 and its adverse impact on the domestic industries in the heavy electrical sectors including BHEL. The
Committee notes the observation of the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises that the reduction of peak
basic custom duty rate from 25% to 20% would adversely affect the domestic capital goods industry’s competitiveness
vis-a-vis foreign suppliers. The basic customs duty on project imports has been reduced from 25% to 10% in case of all
projects (including ongoing projects) with an investment of at least Rs. 5 crores in plant and machinery (excluding land
and buildings) e.g. for CPP. The basic customs duty on captive power plants (CPP) of 5 MW or more reduced from 25
% to 20%. In fact, customs duty @ 20% becomes redundant as an importer can very well import @ 10%, i.e. at a lower
duty rate, under this scheme. BHEL has most of its projects in this category and their competitiveness shall be highly
affected as effective duty rate has now been made 10% compared to 30.8% as applicable earlier.
13.8  The Committee reiterates its observation as made in its 36th Report as under:­
“BHEL has successfully withstood the changes brought about by the liberalization of Indian economy. The impressive
track record of it calls for a special mention of its achievements. As a matter of fact, BHEL is a role model for other
PSUs of Ministry of Heavy Industry. For it has managed to stay in the race despite the odds faced by it as a result of
stiff competition unleashed by the multinational giants operating in its field of specialization namely, manufacture of
power plants. Though BHEL has managed to sustain its viability yet it is facing some unfair challenges. The absence of
a level playing field vis-a-vis its multinational competitors has been posing stiff challenges to the company. This is
leading to an ever-increasing pressure on its profitability. Despite this, the company has been constantly upgrading its
technology and has also been successful in acquiring state of the art technology used in HVDC power projects. This
reflects the commitments of the company as a whole to serve the nation even when the odds are stacked against it.
Therefore, what this company requires is a little help from the Government in the form of suitable policy measures. In
this regard, the sub-committee draws the attention of the Government to the issues of price and purchase preference to
BHEL, and import duty concessions to the foreign companies. Though in some cases price and purchase preference is
granted to the PSUs , the positive results of this measure are negated by the import duty concessions extended to the
foreign companies by the Government. These concessions and exemptions are precisely the reasons for the playing field
not being level for domestic companies or for that matter PSUs as the bids offered by foreign players are much lower in
comparison to the ones offered by PSUs . In other words, the competition is killed well before it begins. The committee
believes that the need of the hour is not to go back to the days of protectionism rather to provide a level playing field to
all the players for the sake of healthy competition.”

INTRODUCTION
        I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred fifty ninth  Report on the Action Taken by the Government on the
recommendations contained in the Committee’s 145th Report on Problems being faced by Small Scale Industries in the
procurement of Steel.
2.     The Committee examined and considered the Action Taken Notes supplied by the Government (Ministry of Small
Scale Industries) on the recommendations contained in its 145 th Report on Problems being faced by Small Scale

Industries in the procurement of Steel.

adopted the Report.

NEW DELHI ;
9th December, 2004
SANTOSH BAGRODIA
Chairman,

Committee on Industry.
 
REPORT
         The Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries on the
Recommendations contained in the 145th Report (of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on
Industry) on the Problems being faced by Small Scale Industries in the procurement of Steel pertaining to the Ministry
of Small Scale Industries . The Report was presented /laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha on the 4 th
February, 2004.
2.      Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Small Scale Industries in respect of the
recommendations contained in the Report. These have been categorized as follows:
Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries---- (Chapter
- I).
Recommendations:- 3.4 (i), 3.4 (iii), 3.4 (iv), 3.4 (vi), 3.4 (viii) c, 3.4 (viii) e.
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government’s
replies : (Chapter - II)
Recommendations:- 3.4 (vii) a, 3.4 (viii) d, 3.4 (viii) f, 3.4 (viii) g, 3.4 (viii) h.
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the Ministry of
Small Scale Industries : (Chapter - III).
Recommendations:- 3.4 (ii), 3.4 (viii) b.
Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry of Small Scale Industries have
not been received: (Chapter - IV).
Recommendations:- 3.4 (v).
3.      The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry of Small Scale Industries has accepted its recommendation
as mentioned in Chapter -I of the Report.
4.      In respect of the recommendations made in Chapter-II the Committee is convinced with the logic and explanation
advocated by the Ministry and therefore does not want to pursue further .
5.      The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementation of the recommendations contained in Chapter-
III and desires that the Ministry should furnish logical explanation in respect of these recommendations.
6.      In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry has either furnished the interim replies or
couched its language in vague terms like noted for compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee directs that the
Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to
the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
7.      The Details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
