Recommendation
l.l       ASSURED SUPPLY OF STEEL AS A RAW MATERIAL TO THE UNITS OF SMALL SCALE
INDUSTRIES
1.1.1Assured supply of steel as a raw material to the units of small scale industries:­--- keeping in view the importance
of Small Scale Industries steel producers should ensure that SSI mills are not forced to close down because of non
availability of raw materials. The Ministry of SSI must assess the requirement of raw material for the SSI units
throughout the country and forward the same in advance to the Ministry of Steel for ensuring that the supply of these
items to the small units is not arbitrarily reduced.
1.1.2The Government should consider introducing alternative institutional measures to ensure smooth supply of raw
materials----pig iron, coke, scrap iron, aluminium, copper, plastic raw materials, etc., at stable prices to the Foundry
units and SSI units working in the engineering and allied sectors. Even though the Government has dispensed with the
price control it should take note of the severe crisis situation that prevails in the SSI Sector because of the non-
availability of steel items and should step in with adequate alternative measures to ensure availability of raw materials
with the small scale manufacturers.
1.1.3The Committee is of the considered view that the Government must ensure the supply of raw materials at stable
prices for a period of 6 months to begin with. .All the buyer vendor agreements for private as well as the Government
purchases should have escalation clauses. Penalty clauses for the belated supplies should be introduced to protect the
interest of the Small Scale Sector.
1.1.4The Committee recommends that the consumer associations and the small scale industries associations could enter
into MoUs with the SAIL and other steel producers and get benefit of the incentives available to the long-term contracts
of the large scale industries.                                                                                             [Para 3.4. (i)]
Action Taken
1.1.5For assessing the requirement of iron and steel for the SSI units throughout the country, the Ministry of SSI had
requested all the States/UT Governments to furnish the projected demand for 2004-05, type/grade-wise. The Ministry of
SSI also held meetings with the State/U.T. Governments for expediting the requisite information. Based on the
information received from the States / U.Ts, the Ministry of SSI forwarded a consolidated statement in respect of 29
States /UTs to the Ministry of Steel for ensuring adequate supply of raw material to the SSI units in these States / UTs.
The Ministry of Steel convened a meeting on 7th April, 2004 with the representatives of State Corporations, major steel
producers and National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) to decide on the allocations of iron and steel for the year
2004-05. The first meeting of the Coordination          Committee was also held on 26th April, 2004, which was inter-alia
attended by the representatives of producers and consumer Associations. In the meetings, the Ministry of Steel informed
that allocations for the year 2004-05 in all those States where SSICs exist        would be made as per the demand
furnished by the States / U.Ts. Further, it was decided that supply of iron and steel would also be made through NSIC,
especially in those States where the SSICs do not exist and through other private steel producers like Jindal, Ispat, Essar,
JVSL etc. (without JPC rebate). The major steel producers agreed to enter into MoU with the consumer SSI
Associations and provide them maximum rebate / discount as given to any other agency lifting the same quantity.
1.1.6Furthermore, in order to ensure smooth supply of raw materials to the SSI units at reasonable prices, the
Government has issued Notification on 24.2.2004, lowering the customs duty on non-alloy steel items, pig iron, sponge
iron and met coke by 5 per cent In addition, vide Notification dated the 28th February 2004, the Government has
reduced the customs duty on coking coal (with ash content below 12 per cent) to 0 per cent and on non-coking coal and
pig iron to 5 per cent.
Recommendation
1.2    ESTABLISHMENT OF CO-ORDINATION COMMITTEE
1.2.1The Committee is of the view that there is a need to set up a Co-ordination Committee consisting of the
representatives of Ministry of Steel, Ministry of SSI and representatives of producers and consumers. This Co-
ordination Committee may look at the prices although not with the intention to regulate the prices but keep an eye on the
prices. This Committee may also assess the requirement of steel by the SSI sector and ensure timely
supply.                                           [Para 3.4. (iii)]

159thReport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/159threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:26]
Action Taken
1.2.2 A Co-ordination Committee has been set up under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Steel), consisting of Members
from the Ministry of Steel, Ministry of SSI, Department of Revenue, State Governments, Small Scale Industries
Development Corporations, producers and SSI Associations to assess the requirement of steel materials by the SSI
sector and the supply of such materials by the producers. The Committee shall also identify the problem areas and the
various bottlenecks and suggest measures, both short term and long term, for the assured supply of steel materials to the
SSI sector. The Committee shall meet at least once every quarter. The first meeting of the Coordination Committee was
held on 26th April, 2004 under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Steel).
Recommendation
1.3    STRENGTHENING  OF  STATE  SMALL  SCALE  INDUSTRIES  CORPORATIONS
1.3.1The Committee expresses its concern over the failure of several State Small Scale Industries Corporations in lifting
the steel for distribution to the units of the Small Scale Industries. It noted with concern the following statement made
by the representatives of Ministry of Steel before the Committee:­----
         “The Ministry of Steel gets demand chart from all the Small Scale Industries Corporations and they in turn give us
the aggregate demand of the SSI units. Based on the demand pattern, the Ministry of Steel ask the main producers
namely, the SAIL, IISCO, TISCO and others to tell us how much they need. More or less, the Ministry of Steel makes
efforts to match the demand with the supply. For example the Ministry of Steel allocated 5.4 lakh tonnes of steel based
on demand from the SSI Corporations. However, the State Small Scale Industries Corporation lifted only 40-50 per cent
of it on the stand that the price was high. They also change the requirement of the grades of steel”.
1.3.2The Committee gathers that the Small Scale Industries Corporations are given allocations every year based on their
demand. At the beginning of every year, material is allocated amongst the main producers, and an element of subsidy is
also provided to the Small Scale Industries Corporations. The Committee is of the view that the strengthening of State
Small Scale Industries Corporations would really help the small producers. The Committee also recommends that the
Small Scale Industries Corporations in the States should be made accountable for non-lifting of steel. The Ministry of
SSI should activate the Small Scale Industries Corporations in various States and chalk out the strategy to protect the
Small Scale Industries. The Committee noted with concern that the Ministry of SSI was not even aware of the non-
lifting of steel by the SSI corporations till the Ministry of Steel brought this information to the notice of the
Committee.                  [Para 3.4. (iv)]
Action Taken
1.3.3All the State/UT Governments have been apprised of the concerns of the Parliamentary Standing Committee
regarding non-lifting of iron and steel by the Small Scale Industries Development Corporations (SSIDCs) and the
recommendation of the Committee that the SSIDCs in the States should be made accountable for non-lifting of steel.
Furthermore, the State/UT Governments were requested to suggest measures, both short term and long term, needed to
revitalize the SSI Corporations/State Industrial Development Corporation (SIDCs) for their effective functioning. The
Ministry of Steel had also written to all the State Governments seeking co-operation in ensuring effective working of the
SSICs.
1.3.4The State / U.T. Governments have informed that poor lifting of raw material by the SSICs / SIDCs is mainly due
to the operational problems being faced by the Corporations vis-a-vis the steel producers. Some of the suggestions given
by the State / U.T. Governments for strengthening the functioning of SSICs/ SIDCs are: (i) the raw material should be
offered to the State Corporations at the same prices as to the private traders and same discount/ rebate should be
extended to them; (ii) the SSICs should be accorded priority by the producers for facilitating smooth supply to the SSI
units; (iii) the major steel producers should enter into MoUs with the State Corporations; (iv) required quantities of type
/ grade-wise iron and steel should be made available to the Corporations etc. These issues were discussed in detail in the
meetings convened by the Ministry of Steel. It was decided that main producers should route their supplies to SSI units
through SSICs and the SSICs should work in close coordination with the producers. The producers were advised to
schedule their rolling plan in accordance with the demand registered by the SSICs to the maximum extent possible. The
steel producers also assured to extend full cooperation to the Corporations in the supply of material.
Recommendation
1.4    NEED FOR SETTING UP OF COMPETITION COMMISSION
1.4.1During the course of interaction with SSI associations the representatives of Indian Micro Small and Medium
Enterprises and the Automotive Component Manufacturers Association of India (ACMA) complained about the
phenomenon of cartelisation by steel majors resulting in massive jump in steel prices and shortage of steel as a raw
material to the units of small scale industries. SSI units which are under contractual obligation to supply goods to
various States/Central agencies and other parties are incurring losses as the price increases in steel items are not

159thReport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/159threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:26]
included in the contract. Moreover, SSI units at present are not in a position to sign any long-term contract for exports
because of uncertainties over the price hike in steel. The Committee feels that if the prevailing situation is allowed to
continue for a longer period it may break the backbone of small scale industries and thus adversely affecting the national
economy. Therefore, the Committee strongly feels that there is an urgent need to set up the Competition Commission to
pre-empt such cartelisation. The Committee further recommends that the Government must also take up the question of
international cartelisation of steel with the WTO at the earliest.[Para 3.4. (vi)]
Action Taken
1.4.2 The recommendations of the Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry have been
brought to the notice of the Department of Company Affairs, which is the Administrative Department for the
Competition Commission and to the Ministry of Commerce regarding international cartelisation of steel. The
Department of Company Affairs has informed that a Competition Commission has already been set up.
Recommendation
1.5    HIGH PRICES OF NICKEL
1.5.1 Nickel is an 100 per cent imported raw material which bears a Custom Duty of 15 per cent ad volram, 16 per cent
CVD. The London Metal Exchange Rate with reference to Nickel has gone up to US$ 12800/- which is unprecedented.
This has almost crushed the tiny / SSI units who use nickel as their basic raw material. The rates have gone up to Rs.
850/- per kg. from Rs. 400/- per kg. The Committee observes that duty on Nickel should be drastically brought down
and MMTC should canalize the import to ensure the supply at reasonable rates.[Para 3.4. (viii) (c)]
Action Taken
1.5.2 The Government has already reduced the customs duty on nickel from 10 per cent to 5 per cent The Special
Additional Duty (SAD) of customs of 4 per cent has also been abolished with effect from 9th January, 2004.
Recommendation
1.6    CUSTOMS DUTY ON PRIME CRGO STEEL
1.6.1The Committee was apprised that the Prime CRGO steel is classified under Chapter 72 of the Customs Act, it is
bundled with other steels like mild steels, alloy steels, stainless steels etc., with a custom duty of 25 per cent which is
meant to protect the Indian Steel Industry against dumping of imported steel products. The high incidence of basic
customs duty @ 25 per cent on an important raw material (like CRGO steel) for transformer manufacturers is not
warranted as there is very limited indigenous availability. Therefore, the Committee is of the view that a reasonable
import duty on prime CRGO steel (electrical steel) will encourage usage of prime material in the manufacture of power
and distribution transformers in the Small Scale Sector. The Committee was assured by the Ministry of Small Scale
Industries that by using the proper CRGO steel, the quality of the transformers will be improved resulting in reduction
of transmission and distribution losses thereby effecting considerable savings.                                         
                                                              [Para 3.4. (viii) (e)]
Action Taken
1.6.2The Department of Revenue has informed that the general policy of the Government has been to prescribe, as far as
possible, the same rate of duty for the same class of products so as to avoid mis-declaration and disputes. Any reduction
in customs duty in respect of only a specific grade of electrical steel would mean that all steel consignments will need to
be examined/tested by customs in order to avoid misuse which may result in disputes and delay in customs clearances.
The Ministry of Steel has informed that M/s EBG India is the only producer of CRGO in the country and the firm is able
to meet the domestic requirement only partially. The customs duty on prime CRGO has been brought down to 15 per
cent w.e.f. 24.2.2004.
CHAPTER - II
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES
NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES
Recommendation
2.0    RATIONALISATION OF TAX STRUCTURE
2.1.1During the course of interaction with the representatives of SSI Associations the Committee considered the
following proposals and feels that the Government should seriously give its thought for accepting and implementing

159thReport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/159threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:26]
them.
         (a)  Custom Duty on Prime Steel
         The Committee feels that the custom duty on prime steel may be reduced from 20 per crnt to 10% as per the
recommendations of Dr. Kelkar Committee, so as to provide level playing field. Even otherwise, the custom duty on
import of Iron and Steel material is to be reduced to 10 per cent by 2005 under the W.T.O. obligations. The removal of
non-tariff barriers and minimum floor rate would be ineffective if the custom duty is not brought down to 10 per cent.
[Para 3.4. (viii)]
Action Taken
2.1.2The Ministry of Finance has informed that the WTO binding for prime steel for 2005 is 40 per cent. As against this
binding, Government has already reduced the customs duty on prime steel from 25 per cent to 15 per cent. The Special
Additional Duty (SAD) of Customs of 4 per cent has also been abolished. Thus, the Government has reduced the overall
import duties on steel by about 17 per cent points. There is a strong domestic angle involved in respect of iron and steel,
and any further reduction in customs duty on steel may affect the domestic manufacturers of steel. Hence any further
reduction in customs duty on steel can be considered only in consultation with the Ministry of Steel.
Recommendation
2.2    CUSTOM DUTY ON SCRAP
2.2.1The Committee was apprised by the SSI Associations that at present the Customs Duty on scrap is 5 per cent plus
16 per cent CVD. In case, the scrap is imported by traders, the duty rules at 20 per cent. Thus, the cost of imported scrap
has increased to more than double. Moreover, the scrap is not available in India as China and Bangladesh have started
importing scrap from India. This trend has adversely affected the secondary producers for whom it is the basic raw
material. Keeping in view the interests of the domestic industries, the Committee feels that the customs duty structure
on scrap may be suitably rationalized enabling the tiny and SSI units to compete internationally as well as prohibiting
the dumping of scraps in Indian steel domestic market. A judicious decision on the part of the Government is required as
the steps taken for rationalization of custom duty on import of scrap must strike a balance in protecting the SSI units as
well as strengthening the anti dumping mechanism for the steel industry.                                                      [Para 3.4.
(viii) (f)]
Action Taken
2.2.2 The Department of Revenue has informed that the general rate of customs duty for iron and non-alloy steel is 15
per cent and iron and steel scrap imported for melting has been prescribed a concessional rate of 5 per cent. Melting
scrap is used in the induction/electric arc furnaces for melting (and manufacture of semi finished steel products) whereas
other forms of scrap such as re-rolling scrap can be directly re-rolled into finished steel products. It is not possible either
through testing or visual inspection to distinguish between melting scrap and other ferrous/non-ferrous scrap metal.
Hence an end use condition has been prescribed for availing the customs duty concession for melting scrap, so as to
avoid misuse of the concession. Customs duty on melting scrap has been continued at 5 per cent since 1994, whereas the
duty on re-rolling scrap has been gradually reduced by the Government and the customs duty on re-rolling scrap was
reduced from 25 per cent to 15 per cent. The Special Additional Duty (SAD) of Customs of 4 per cent has also been
abolished. The Department of Revenue is of the view that rationalisation of customs duty rates is a continuous process.
Recommendation
2.3    LEVYING OF CENTRAL EXCISE DUTY ON SHIP BREAKING
2.3.1The SSI Associations advocated the abolition of the 16 per cent central excise duty recently levied on ship breaking
which is according to them absolutely uncalled for as central excise duty can only be levied on the process of
manufacture as per the Act and ship breaking is not a process of manufacture by any standard. In their view such a step
would provide scrap for the secondary producers of Iron and Steel at cheaper rates. However, the Committee was
apprised by the representatives of the Ministry of Steel that the ship breaking industry has been recognized as the
manufacturing industry. In fact, the ship breakers have been fighting for being recognized as manufacturing industry.
Till 1994, they were not recognized, and after fighting for it, they got the status of manufacturing industry. Now, they
have gone to the Supreme Court because one of the High Courts has given a ruling that the ship breaking industry is not
a manufacturing industry and therefore, excise is not leviable. The excise duty paid by the ship breaking manufacturers
are modvatable as they collect it from the customer and pass forward. The Ministry of Steel has taken up their demand
that the duty should be reduced to 10 per cent. The Committee is of the view that pending decision of the Supreme

159thReport of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/159threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:26]
Court in the matter, the Central Excise Duty may be reduced to the level as low as
possible.                                                                      [Para 3.4. (viii) (g)]
Action Taken
2.3.2The Department of Revenue has informed that the Supreme Court, in the case Ashish Steel Pvt. Ltd. vs. Collector-
1999 (108)E.L.T.A.180(S.C.) had rejected an appeal against the Tribunal Order holding that ship breaking is to be
considered as manufacturing activity under Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985. The process of obtaining goods specified in
Section XV of the First Schedule to the Central Excise Tariff Act, 1985, by breaking up of ships is deemed to be a
process amounting to manufacture for the purpose of levy of excise duty in view of Note 9 of the said Section. Excise
Duty paid on scrap, by ship breakers, is eligible for being taken as CENVAT credit by the downstream manufacturers.
Hence, it should not have any adverse effect on the prices of scrap.
Recommendation
2.4    ADEQUATE SUPPLY OF PIG-IRON TO THE FOUNDRY UNITS IN SMALL SCALE SECTOR
2.4.1The Committee is pleased to note that the Ministry of Steel has directed PSUs especially RINL not to export pig-
iron and the RINL has released about 10,000 metric tonnes of pig iron in the market and tenders have been floated.
However, the Committee hopes that the steel PSUs wiIl continue to supply adequate quantity of the pig iron to the units
of the small and the medium enterprises.                                                                              [Para 3.4. (viii) (h)]
Action Taken
2.4.2The Ministry of Steel has set up the Co-ordination Committee to ensure adequate supply of raw material to the SSI
units. The steel producing PSUs have assured to extend full cooperation to the SSICs in the supply of iron and steel.
CHAPTER - III
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE COMMITTEE HAS NOT
ACCEPTED REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY OF SMALL SCALE INDUSTRIES
Recommendation
3.0    SUPPLY  OF  STEEL  TO  THE  SSI  UNITS  AT  REASONABLE  PRICE
3.1.1Although the Committee appreciates that in an open economy the prices are determined by the market forces the
need for introducing appropriate mechanism for keeping the prices stable for a given period should receive the
immediate attention of the Government. A “Triggered Price Mechanism” should be considered by the Government as a
short-term measure to overcome the present crisis situation faced by the SSI Sector. There is 5 per cent reduction in
basic duty and 4 per cent in SAD and in effective implementation the duty reduction comes to 10.5 per cent which has
been announced some time ago. Further reduction in duty, should be considered as an intermediate measure of relief to
the SSI Sector, at least for a period of six months to begin with. It should be linked with the Triggered Price Mechanism
for example if the international price of HR coil goes beyond 400 dollars per tonne, duty can be reduced. If it comes
below 400 dollars per tonne, duty should remain the same. Under such a mechanism the duty automatically becomes
plus or minus depending on the price.            Para 3.4. (ii)
Action Taken
3.1.2The Department of Revenue has informed that customs duties cannot be a ‘correcting mechanism for market forces
as the prices of commodities vary on account of several factors including increase in input costs, demand-supply
situation etc. In case of steel, the prices of the inputs like coking coal, met coke etc., have increased steeply. It is thus
not possible to link the customs duty rates to the international prices of commodities.
         The Ministry of Steel has, however, informed that they would make appropriate recommendations to the Ministry
of Finance on “Triggered Price Mechanism” as proposed by the Committee.
Further Recommendation
3.1.3The Committee is in agreement with the opinion of Department of Revenue that the custom duty is not the only
correcting mechanism for the determination of price of the commodities as the price of the commodities are determined
by the market forces and other prices determinants including input costs, demand supply situation etc. but the market
situation is sometimes manipulated / where scenario of short supply of an item is reflected. In the present context, steel
products, which are also required by domestic small scale units as a raw materials have been supplied to China and other

countries at discriminatory price tag in comparison to the domestic industries and the result was that the small scale
industries had run short of its basic raw materials.
3.1.4It is known to the Committee that the price of the steel is determined by inputs cost like coking coal, met coke and
rise and fall in inputs cost which leads to rise and fall in the steel prices. But the question arises has the rise in the steel
prices been in proportion to in the rise in inputs cost of the steel ? However, the basic concern of the Committee is the
supply of the steel to SSI units at reasonable price.
3.1.5The Committee is of the considered view that the Ministry of SSI and Steel should pursue the “Triggered Price
Mechanism” as a short term measure to ensure the supply of steel raw material to SSI units at reasonable price.

in steel industry for monitoring price stabilization of steel products and related issues in line with Telephone Regulatory
Authority of India (TRAI) which would ensure discplined price fluctuation by steel players both in Public and Private
sectors.
Recommendation
3.2    INTER-SECTORAL CO-OPERATION AND COLLABORATIVE ATTITUDE AND APTITUDE
3.2.1Inter-sectoral Co-operation and Collaborative Attitude and Aptitude:- The Committee strongly feels that in order to
achieve the cherished national goal of Gross Domestic Product (GDP) above 10% it is essential that concerted and
considered impetus must be given to the equitable and proportionate growth and development of various sectors of
economy with the aid and advice of good governance and regulations under the liberalized and globalised regime. Such
holistic and integrated model of industrial growth and economic development is possible only when the element of
inter-sectoral cooperative and collaborative attitude and atmosphere prevails in all the rungs of the governance. There is
a great need for closer coordination among the Ministries of Small Scale Industries, Steel, Commerce and Finance for
sorting out the problems being faced by the SSI units under the prevailing circumstances.                                          
       Para 3.4. (vii)
Action Taken
3.2.2All the concerned Ministries/Departments have been apprised of the recommendations of the Committee. The
Department of Revenue has informed that tariff changes in customs and excise duties on various commodities are
carried out, inter alia, after consultation with the Administrative Ministries and taking into account the revenue needs of
the Government.
Further Recommendation
3.2.3The Committee is of the considered view that the equitable and proportionate growth and development of various
sectors of economy is the sina­qu-non for overall rapid and balanced growth and development of national economy.
That is possible only through integrated economic planning and inter ­sectoral co-operation and collaborative aptitudes.
Development of a particular segment of economy at the expense of other segment would only lead to segment ­-
specific-regional growth but such growth would retard the rapid national economic growth. In this context, the
Committee would like to highlight that small scale industries has the great potential of employment generation
particularly in the rural or semi urban areas where the pace of economic development needs to be accelerated. In order
to promote SSI sectors to its optimum potential and to encourage SSI to enhance its contribution to the growth and
development of national economy to the maximum extent, a rational tax regime needs to be applied. An objective
assessment of the other problems being faced by SSI units, other than taxation provisions, needs to be identified for their
immediate redressal. The Ministry of SSI should identify those problems and communicate the same to the concerned
Departments/Ministries and the concrete solution must be explored without delay for providing timely solution to the
SSI units. That is why, the Committee recommended for adoption of co-operative and collaborative attitude and aptitude
by the various Ministries towards SSI sectors. Such inter-sectoral co-operation should have objective base / contribution
and not merely on philosophical plane. SSI needs concrete assurance from the concerned Ministries including the
Department of Revenue.
Recommendation

CHAPTER -I
Balancing the Industry-Friendly Tax Regime and Consolidation of Fiscal
Measure for Revenue-Generation
l.1     It is a well known fact that industrial sector play the pivotal role in the development and growth of the economy. It
also plays the paramount role in balanced regional economic development of the nation. In order to downplay the
pressure; occupational structure on the land/agricultural sector, industrial sector has to be promoted and proliferated.
Investment has to be made in the industrial sector as new avenues for employment- generation and liberation from the
curse of poverty. The industrial sector, at present, needs the guided direction and assistance of the Government.
1.2    The Committee on Industry in its meeting held on l2th April, 2005 was apprised by the Department of Revenue
that the Fiscal Responsibility and Budgetary Management (FRBM) Act, 2003 (as amended) requires the revenue deficit
to be eliminated by 2007-08. A road map of reduction in revenue deficit has already been notified under the FRBM
Rules, 2004.
1.3    The Secretary, Department of Revenue informal that the indirect taxes have already been moderated through a
calibrated reduction in customs and excise duties. As regards customs duty, the peak rate on non-agricultural goods has
already been lowered, in this year’s budget 2005-06 to only 15 per cent. In fact, the Government is already committed to
a gradual reducing customs duties to ASEAN levels. In case of excise duty, the stated policy is that most manufactured
goods should attract the Cenvat rate of 16 per cent.
1.4    Under the circumstances, while it would be essential to keep the tax rates stable so as to be conducive to growth,
compliance and investment, it is also necessary for the Government to consider measures to raise tax revenues and the
tax-GDP ratio so as to meet the ever-growing Government expenditure and to meet the FRBM targets.
1.5    The Committee was further informed that the Government is making efforts to augment the tax resources through
various measures which have not resulted in substantially increasing the revenue, which paints a pessimistic picture on
the Tax-GDP ratio. Therefore, the Government is making earnest efforts in order to achieve higher Tax-­GDP Ratio.
Thus the Department of Revenue faces a severe limitation while considering any recommendation for reduction or
exemption from customs or excise duties or Service Tax.
1.6    During the course of interaction the Secretary, Department of Revenue apprised the Committee of the budgeting
procedure indicating the wide consultation with the representatives of various segment of industries. He indicated that
the Department interacted with the 78 industrial associations and after mutual consultation the provisions of the budget
have been drafted.
1.7    The Secretary, Department of Revenue also apprised the Committee that Parliament has instructed very tight fiscal
revenue deficit limits. The Parliament has passed the Fiscal Responsibility and the Budget Management Act under
which the revenue deficit has to be eliminated by 2007-08, and it must come down by 0.5 per cent of GDP every year.
Likewise, the fiscal deficit under section 4.1 of the Fiscal Responsibility and the Budget Management Act has come
down by 0.3 per cent of GDP every year.
1.8    The Secretary, Department of Revenue quoted a portion of Finance Minister Budget speech as under :­
         “Mr. Speaker, Sir, in the Budget Estimates from 2005-06, the total expenditure is estimated at Rs.514,344 crore
revenue receipts of the Central Government at Rs.351,200 crore and the revenue expenditure at Rs.446,512 crore.
Consequently, the revenue deficit is estimated at Rs.95,312 crore which is equal to 2.7 per cent of the estimated GDP.
The fiscal deficit is estimated at Rs.l5l,144 crore, which is 4.3 per cent of the estimated GDP.
         Consequent to accepting the recommendations of the Twelfth Finance Commission and the drastically changed
pattern of devolution and funding, there has been a considerable strain in making the Budget for 2005-06. I was left with
no option but to press the pause button vis-a-vis the FRBM Act. I am relieved that we have not been forced to go in the
opposite direction. I may add that we are perilously close to the limits of fiscal prudence and there is no more room for
spending beyond our limits.”
1.9    The Secretary, Department of Revenue further stated as under :­
         “There are very high priority objectives in the National Common Minimum Programme on which the expenditure
has to be incurred, and simultaneously, devolution to the States has also got to go up because of the Twelfth Finance
Commission almost by Rs.25,000 crores this year. There is a substantial increase in the demands on the revenue

160th Report of Committee on Industry

Department. The Revenue receipts which were in the Revised Estimates at Rs.3,06,000 crores, for this year, we have to
earn more than Rs.3,50,000 crores in 2005-06, a huge increase.”
1.10  The Committee understands that the Small Scale Industries is today on the move world wide, therefore, Small
Scale Industries in India should be given top -priority by the Planning Commission and the Ministry of Finance not only
in plan -allocation, so that small scale units may get adequate space for maturing into medium enterprises, but also tax
exemption and concession for catching up the global trend . The Department of Revenue should provide the logistic
support to the SSI sector so far the tax concession is concerned. The Small Scale Industries needs to be strengthened to
remain competitive in market-led global economy and also for the reason for generating the additional employment
opportunities. The Government should assist the SSI sector in accessing (or provide) proper and timely inputs like
adequate credit from financial institutions/banks; funds for technology upgradation and modernization; adequate
infrastructural facilities; modern testing facilities and quality certification laboratories; modern management practices
and skill upgradation through suitable training facilities; marketing assistance; and level playing field at par with the
large industries sector.
l.11   The Committee understands the daunting task of revenue - collection. The Committee also understands that
revenue-collection is indispensable in order to shoulder the responsibility endowed with the Government but at the same
time the Committee wishes to point out that the Department of Revenue should follow the principle of equity in the
matter of distribution of tax burden in line with horizontal and vertical equity i.e. tax payer with equal ability, in like
circumstances should contribute equally and tax payer with unequal capacity, i.e. unlike circumstances should
contribute correspondingly differently. In this context the Committee is of the view that the Department of Revenue
should examine the issues of tax proposals keeping in view the taxable capacity of the various segments of industry in
ordinary and extra ordinary circumstances i.e. the stages of the Industrial Development in general and their needs for
protection in the domestic field and promotion in the international market arena. Imposition of the taxes or their
exemptions / concessions should be guided by the principle of efficiency of the producers keeping in view all   
domestic and international factors. It is desirable that the Department of Revenue should not bank on the principle and
practice of “plucking the goose despite squealing all around”, paying little attention to the logistics of “sparing the goose
in order to bask the golden eggs.”
l.12   The Economic Reforms in India encompassing structural reforms with components of liberlisation, privatization
and globalization has exposed the domestic industries to global industrial giants/MNCs, without having been given an
opportunity for consolidation of domestic industries. The PSEs of Nehru-Mahalois Era has thrived and grown under
protective regime where inter-sectoral co-operation reigned to a large extent and purchase preference policy were the
protective pillars of PSUs.
1.13  Even under the prevailing WTO regime countries like USA, China, Japan, Germany determine the economic
policy keeping in view the strength of the local industries and there competitive resileince to face the challanges of the
global competition, and these developed countries never forget to protect their domestic industries in the sector/field
where their products cannot compete with the products of other countries including India for example iron and steel
products. These countries impose anti-dumping measure and adopt/adhere to the other fiscal measures to discourage
Indian products with the motive to encourage/protect/promote there domestic industries. Such selective measure
adopted by developed nations goes against the interest of industries in the developing countries like India where on
practical plane there is enhanced need for protecting the domestic industries more than that of the developed nations as
the responsibility for developmental activities lies more with the Government of developing nations than the developed
one. That is so because the Governments in the developing nations has to overcome the mammoth problem of poverty,
population explosion and unemployment. Under the circumstances, a developing nation like India, the Government has
the added responsibility to protect, promote and consolidate the domestic industries from the onslaught of MNCs
unleashed due to on going liberalisation and globalisation process in the post WTO - regime. Indian domestic industries
must be strengthened and consolidated before their global exposure. Need is to imbibe competitive resilience into the
Indian industries of various segments.
1.14  The Committee understands that the tempest of globalisation would also gallop the Temple of Modern India unless
and until level playing field is provided to the domestic industry. Therefore, the Committee is of the strong view that the
architect of Modern India should not forget to have the protected layer of extending certain tax concessions/exemptions
to protect against the onslaught of Faustian MNCs.
CHAPTER -II
TAX  PROPSALS  AFFECTING  SSI  SECTOR

160th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/160threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:27]
2.1    The Committee was apprised that the prevailing pattern of tax structure, including the announcements made by the
Finance Minister in the Budget Speech has bearing on the promotion of Small Enterprises Sector: ­
(i)     General SSI excise exemption upto Rs. 1 crore on the first clearances of specified goods during the year, for
SSI units. Units availing of this exemption are not entitled to take CENVAT credit on the inputs or utilize the
CENVAT credit on capital goods.
(ii)     Excise exemption on branded goods manufactured by SSI units located in rural areas.
(iii)    Tax holiday under the Income Tax Act for new and existing enterprises including SSI enterprises in the
States of Himachal Pradesh, Sikkim, Uttaranchal and North Eastern States and also the enterprises which go
for substantial expansion, i.e., increase in investment in plant and machinery by at least 50 per cent of their
book value.
(iv)    Small service providers having gross annual turnover less than Rs. 4 lakh have been exempted from the
purview of Service Tax.
(v)    Service Tax on business auxiliary service has been exempted for persons producing/ processing goods, from
the inputs received from a manufacturer and sending the resultant product to the same manufacturer for
further manufacture of final products, which are cleared on payment of excise duty.

2.24  Issue: Imposition of Service Tax on production of goods on behalf of the client vide notification No. 14/2004
dated 10.9.2004 affecting Tiny/ SSI sector. However, Government has exempted agriculture, printing, textile processing

2.25  The Department of Revenue informed the Committee that in budget 2004, Service Tax has been imposed on the
service provided by a job worker, namely, the activity of ‘production of goods on behalf of the client’. But if such
activity amounts to ‘manufacturer’, it is not leviable to Service Tax since such cases are covered under levy of excise
duty. For instance, process of galvanization of articles of iron and steel which amounts to manufacture under Central
Excise Law is not liable to Service Tax.
2.26  However, activities provided by a job worker in relation to agriculture, printing, textile processing or education are
exempted from levy of Service Tax. The activity of electroplating/ zinc plating is generally performed on metals to
impart certain characteristics to the finished product. Thus, electroplating/ zinc plating undertaken on behalf of a client
being process which does not amount to manufacture is leviable to Service Tax. Electroplating/ zinc plating metal do
not fall under the category of agriculture, printing, textile processing or education and hence exemption is not available.
2.27  The Committee was further apprised that in this year’s budget, exemption from Service Tax has been extended to
persons providing taxable service of ‘production of goods on behalf of the client’ provided that the service provider
produces goods from the raw materials or semi-finished goods received from a manufacturer and the goods so produced
are sent back to the manufacturer for further manufacture of final products, which are cleared on payment of excise
duty. Thus, job worker performing the activity of electroplating/ zinc plating for a manufacturer of final products who
clears such final products after payment of excise duty would be exempted from payment of Service Tax.
2.28  Further, in this year’s budget, exemption from Service Tax has also been extended to provide relief to all small
service providers (with aggregate value of taxable service upto Rs. 4 lakhs in the preceding financial year), including
job workers, upto an aggregate value of taxable service upto Rs. 4 lakhs in a financial year. Genuinely small units
undertaking electroplating/ zinc plating on behalf of their client would thus be exempt from Service Tax. In view of the
above, it is not felt desirable to extend exemption from Service Tax on the activity of electroplating/ zinc plating.
2.29  Issue: Central Excise on Iron and Steel ----- The Government had earlier provided protection to the main
producers under non-tariff barriers, etc. and had brought down the excise duty from 16 per cent to 8 per cent. However,
the Government has now raised central excise from 8 per cent to 12 per cent in the interim budget 2004-05 which has

further been raised from 12 per cent to 16 per cent and thus affecting adversely the light engineering industry in the
Tiny/SSI sector.
2.30  The Department of Revenue informed the Committee that iron and steel have generally attracted the mean rate of
excise duty at par with other metals. Excise duty on iron and steel was 15 per cent upto 1998-99, and was rationalised to
16 per cent w.e.f. 1999-2000. There has been a steady and steep increase in international prices of both steel as well as
certain critical inputs for the steel making industry, namely, metallurgical coke/coking coal, during the past over one
year. The domestic steel manufacturers have been taking advantage of the high international prices of steel and steadily
increasing the domestic prices of steel. The steel user industry has been seriously affected by this steady increase in steel
prices. In order to bring about a reduction in domestic steel prices, excise duty on iron and steel (of chapter 72) was
reduced from 16 per cent to 8 per cent w.e.f. 28.2.2004, involving a substantial loss of revenue. However, it was
observed that the steel manufacturers had not passed on the benefit of these duty reductions to the consumers and
instead had adjusted their assessable value whereby the cum-excise duty price of steel did not come down. Moreover,
the general policy is that most manufactured goods should attract the CENVAT rate of 16 per cent. Steel is a leading
metal and other leading metals such as aluminium, copper, zinc, lead, etc. attract 16 per cent excise duty. Thus, in order
to partially recoup the revenue loss and as a step towards moving towards the mean CENVAT rate, excise duty on steel
was raised from 8 per cent to 12 per cent in budget 2004. The excise duty on iron and steel has been restored to the
CENVAT rate of 16 per cent in budget 2005-06.The total production of steel in India is about 36 million tonnes per
year. Flat products (HR/CR coils/sheets, etc.) are manufactured primarily by the integrated manufacturers and the total
production of flat steel is about 16-17 million tonnes. The flat products are mainly used for further manufacture of pipes
and tubes, automobiles, capital goods, etc. The duty paid on iron and steel would be eligible to be taken as input credit
by the further manufacturing units in most cases.
2.31  The Committee was further informed that the long products (rods, bars, channels, structures, etc. mainly used in
construction) are manufactured both by integrated as well as secondary (induction furnaces/ re-rollers) manufacturers
and the production of long products is about 17-18 million tonnes. About 55 per cent of the long products (i.e., 9-10
million tonnes) are produced by the secondary sector. The long products are mainly used in the construction industry.
2.32  The Department of Revednue clarified that it may be recalled that credit of duty has already been allowed across
goods and services and thus the excise duty on iron and steel even if used in construction is eligible to taken as input
credit for payment of Service Tax on taxable services. Commercial and industrial constructions have already covered
been brought under the Service Tax net in budget 2004-05. In this year’s budget construction of planned residential
complexes, with more than 12 dwelling units, developed by builders, are proposed to be brought under Service Tax. In
view of the above, the increase in excise duty on iron and steel should have little effect on prices because the entire duty
is convertible by most categories of consumers.

Issue: Service Tax on transportation of SSI products is paid by the manufacturers and not by the transporters
2.39  The Department of Revenue informed the Committee that the Services provided by a goods transport agency in
relation to transport of goods by road in a goods carriage are leviable to Service Tax. Service Tax is generally leviable
on the service provider, however, the liability for payment of Service Tax may be cast on any other person [as per
provisions of section 68(2) of Finance Act, 1994]. In case of transportation of goods by road, where the consignor or
consignee of goods are a factory, company, corporation etc. the liability for payment of Service Tax is on the person
paying freight instead of the goods transport agency (service provider). This provision has been made keeping in view
that in such cases the person liable to pay Service Tax is already engaged in commercial activity and also the fact that
the Service Tax being an indirect tax the tax burden is ultimately borne by the person paying the freight. Moreover, if
such persons are the manufacturers of excisable goods or providers of taxable services, the Service Tax paid is available
as credit which can be utilised to discharge his duty liability. Shifting of tax liability is, thus, only for a procedural
convenience and would not cast any additional burden on the person paying the tax. An abatement of 75 per cent from
gross freight has been provided in respect of taxable service of transportation of goods by road. Thus, effectively only
2.5 per cent of the gross amount is payable as Service Tax.
Issue: Penal interest of 24 per cent on delayed payment of excise duty
2.40  The Department of Revenue informed the Committee that prior to budget 2003-04, in case of default in payment
of excise duty by the due date, the manufacturer was denied the benefit of utilisation of CENVAT credit for certain
period and in certain cases, even the facility of paying excise duty in instalments was liable to be withdrawn. In budget
2003-04, the provisions relating to penalties, etc. in such cases were made simpler so as to provide that in case of
default, the facility of paying duty in instalments would not be withdrawn nor would be the assesses be denied the use of
his CENVAT credit for payment of duty. Instead, the assesses was made liable only for a penal interest of 2 per cent per
month or Rs. 10,000 per day, whichever is higher, subject to the amount not exceeding the duty amount. Thus the penal
interest of 24 per cent has been prescribed for such delayed payment in order to check misuse of the facility of paying
excise duty on monthly instalments. Any further relaxation of this provision would not be desirable at this stage.

CHAPTER- III
TAX PROPOSALS AFFECTING THE INDUSTRIES IN GENERAL
3.1    The Committee has been apprised of the implications on some of the PSEs of the tax proposals contained in the
Union Budget 2005-06. Peak custom duty has been reduced from 20 per cent to 15 per cent, having negative impact on
the PSEs under DHI where they face competition from imported products. Moreover, custom duty of capital goods
sector has been reduced from 15 per cent to 10 per cent and to 5 per cent in some cases, having a negative impact on
PSEs like BHEL, HMT.
3.2    Excise duty on tyres had been reduced to 16 per cent. This would benefit the tyre manufacturing industry
including, Tyre Corporation of India. Infrastructure projects are likely to spur growth in cement sector. Cement
Corporation of India (CCI) is likely to benefit. Moreover, thrust to rural electrification will provide benefit to PSEs in
the Electrical Industry like AYCL.
3.3    The Committee views that current regime of lowering the customs and increasing the excise duty on items like
steel will have serious implications for the PSEs in capital goods sector. The Committee cautions the Government that
such a Duty regime would result in an uneven competition with PSEs facing serious handicap against cheaper imports
and MNCs. If the Government is serious about reviving the PSEs, it must help them regain their standing in domestic
market instead of imposing a duty regime that perpetuates the disadvantage against cheap imports. It is the
responsibility of the Government to seek redressal, if necessary, against such an uneven competition under the WTO
provisions.
3.4    The Committee took note that the benefit of 150 per cent weighted deduction u/s 35 (2AB) of Income Tax for Act
in-house R&D expenditure to the automotive industry has now been extended upto 31 March 2007. A number of OEMs
would be utilizing this benefit for continuously upgrading their R&D set up in India to meet the new emission and
safety norms over the next few years as also for new product and process developments in India which otherwise
requires considerable R&D effort.
3.5    In its interaction with auto associations, the Committee noted that the auto Sector has generally supported the
application of VAT but has sought further streamlining. The auto associations further apprised the Committee that
reduction in depreciation rates would adversely effect the new investments; customs duty on auto-components have
been reduced to below ASEAN levels, which will be a disincentive for value addition; custom duty on raw materials is
higher compared to ASEAN levels; Imposition of Cess on Petrol and Diesel would adversely affect the growth of Auto
Sector.

INTRODUCTION
        I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorized
by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Sixty first 
 Report on the Action Taken by the Government on the
recommendations contained in the Committee’s 132 nd Report on MoU Performance in respect of select Public Sector
Undertakings pertaining to the Department of Public Enterprises.
2.     The Committee examined and considered the Action Taken Notes supplied by the Government (Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises) on the recommendations contained in its 132 nd Report on MoU performance in
respect of PSUs of Power Sector (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises)
3.     The Committee in its meeting held on 3rd May, 2005 considered and adopted the Report.
 
SANTOSH BAGRODIA
NEW DELHI ;                                                                                                                                                  Chairman,
3rd May, 2005                                                                                                             Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry.
REPORT
         The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Department of Public Enterprises
(Ministry of Heavy Industries & Public Enterprises) on the Recommendations contained in the 132
nd Report (of the
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry) on MoU Performance in respect of PSUs of Power
Sector. The Report was presented /laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha on the 22nd December, 2003.
2.      Action Taken Notes have been received from the Department of Public Enterprises (Ministry of Heavy Industries
& Public Enterprises) in respect of the recommendations contained in the Report. These have been categorized as
follows:
Chapter - I- The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry :
Para : 2.32; 3.6 ; 3.13 ; 3.22 ; 4.25 ; 4.26
The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry has accepted its recommendation as mentioned in Chapter -I of
the Report.

161st Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/161streport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:27]
Chapter - II- The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the
Government’s replies:
Para 2.31; 2.34; 3.1 l; 3.17 ; 3.21; 4.24;
In respect of these recommendations the Committee is convinced with the logic and explanation advocated by the
Ministry and therefore does not want to pursue further. Chapter - III- The recommendations/observations in respect of
which the Committee has not accepted replies of the Ministry:
Para 2.36; 2.37; 3.16; 3.19; 3.23; 4.28
The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementations of recommendations contained in Chapter-III and
desires that the Ministry should furnish logical explanation in respect of these recommendations.
Chapter - IV- The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not been
received: Para 4.30
         In respect of recommendation Para 4.30 in Chapter-IV, the Ministry has either furnished the interim reply or
couched its language in vague terms like noted for compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desires that the
Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respects of recommendation categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to
the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendation of the Committee.
3.      The Details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
Recommendation
1.0    Measures to attain optimum growth
1.1    The Committee observes that although NTPC have taken measures to attain optimum growth of the company by
taking several measures like reducing the number of Government Directors on the Board, and inducting professional
from finance and technology side to improve its efficiency but there is still scope for improvement although the
Company has a happy experience of working along the MoU instrument. In view of the increasing global
competitiveness MoU parameters for NTPC should be modified to raise it to the status of the global Company that
NTPC needs to attain in the present scenario of liberalisation of economy.                                                     (Para 2.32)
Action Taken
1.1.1Ministry of Power and NTPC have informed that the company has already included parameter indicating
globalization efforts of the Corporation in the MoU.
1.1.2During the current year also, parameter indicating global nature of the Corporation has been incorporated.
Recommendation
1.2    Weightages Assigned to the Financial Parameters
1.2.1Having heard the explanation given by the representatives of the Corporation regarding any change to be
incorporated in the weightages assigned to MoU parameters the Committee observes that the weightages assigned to the
Financial Parameters under MoU may be revised to 60% from present level of 40%.                        (Para 3.6)
Action Taken
1.2.2Ministry of Coal and Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC) have informed that Department of Public Enterprises in
its revised guidelines for drafting MoU for 2004-05, has fixed the weightage for the financial parameters as 50%.
However, NLC is in agreement with the views of the Committee.
Recommendation
1.3    Sustained R&D developed by NLC
1.3.1The Committee observes that the sustained R&D developed by NLC in the area of Lignite Mining and Power
Generation should be utilised effectively. The Committee is however of the view that the feasibilities from Lignite
Projects in other parts of the country should be explored.                                   (Para 3.13)

161st Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/161streport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:27]
Action Taken
1.3.2Ministry of Coal and Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC) have informed that NLC has planned to put up a lignite
mine-cum-power project at Bikaner, Rajasthan State. The project is in the advanced stage of approval by the
Government.
Recommendation
1.4    Deeper lignite and adverse geological conditions
1.4.1The Committee also expresses its concern over the progressively deeper lignite, adverse geological conditions and
the constraints in land acquisition for mining. The Committee therefore urges upon the Government to come out with
necessary action plan to meet the constraints facing the NLC to make it more viable.                  (Para 3.22)
Action Taken
1.4.2Ministry of Coal and Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC) have informed that NLC is exploring the various
alternative technologies including Underground Coal Gasification (UCG) and extraction of Coal Bed Methane (CBM).
NLC has proposed to study the UCG process in a geologically suitable Lignite block in Rajasthan, on pilot scale. If the
technology becomes proven, the same will be utilised in NLC’s future projects.
Recommendation
1.5    Growth potential in the core area of EHV transmission
1.5.1The Committee also observes that the further growth potential in the core area of EHV transmission should be fully
utilised by the Government and thereby the target of National Grid would be achieved by the year 2012.  (Para 4.25)
Action Taken
1.5.2Ministry of Power and Powergrid Corporation of India Limited have informed POWERGRID completed first
phase of National Grid in September, 2002, establishing an inter-regional power exchange capacity of 5,000 MW.
Commissioning of projects associated with second phase of National Grid has already commenced and inter-regional
transfer capacity has been enhanced to 89500 MW. POWERGRID was able to facilitate transfer of 22,500 MU of
energy across the regions during the year 2003-04, an increase of 70% from previous year. Such transfer has taken place
mostly from power surplus Eastern Region to other regions. Thus, inter-regional transfer of power worth Rs. 4,500 crore
was facilitated most of which would have remained bottled up without the facilities created by POWERGRID.
1.5.3To implement various inter-regional transmission systems, Feasibility Report cum Detailed Project Report of
various projects have been/ are being prepared progressively. Expeditious investment approval of these and availability
of Non-Budgetary Support as equity would go a long way in achieving targets of National Grid by 2012.
Recommendation
1.6    Long distance communication
The Committee further observes that the potentials in the area of long distance communication and use of optic fibre and
state of the art technology should be fully exploited.                                      (Para 4.26)
Action Taken
1.6.1Ministry of Power and Powergrid Corporation of India Limited have informed POWERGRID had diversified into
Telecom to utilise spare telecommunication capacity of its Unified Load Dispatch Centre (ULDC) scheme and rolling
out over-head optical fibre cable on its transmission network with additional investment of about Rs.1,000 Crore.
POWERGRID’s over 20,000 Kms. of Telecom Network, to be commissioned shortly will provide a robust highway of
tele-communication at affordable cost with ultra modern and eco-friendly implementation techniques. Moreover, the
surplus created from this diversified business shall be utilised in funding the core business area. In fact, POWERGRID
has already operationalised 13,000 Kms. of telecom network and commercial operation already commenced on some of
the links, namely Delhi-Chandigarh, Delhi-Simla, Delhi-Jaipur-Lucknow-Mumbai-Ahmedabad.
CHAPTER - II
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO
PURSUE IN VIEW OF THE GOVERNMENT’S REPLIES.

161st Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/161streport.htm[04-07-2016 12:51:27]
Recommendation
2.0    Rating needs to be modified
2.1    The Committee observes that the MoU rating in respect of NTPC over the last 16 years have been graded as
excellent this kind of rating needs to be modified in view of the power scenario in the country i.e. Gross generation of
Power and requirement. It is a fact that NTPC is the bulk power generator in the country. However, power supply of
country still fall short of the requirement. In view of this, excellent rating seems to be a misnomer. The Committee
therefore recommends that MoU ratio in respect of NTPC should be integrated with the actual need of the power of the
Country and production. Targets should be fixed in the national perspective.                                    (Para 2.31)
Action Taken
2.1.1The Ministry of Power and NTPC have informed that NTPC has been signing the MoU with Government of India
since the inception of the MoU system. The installed capacity of NTPC is only about 19% of country’s total installed
capacity and its generation is 27% of country’s generation. The targets with respect to generation and other parameters
for yearly MoU are fixed after detailed discussions/deliberations within the company, with Ministry of Power and
finally with Task Force in MoU keeping the company’s and national perspective in view.
2.1.2MoU ratings are declared by the Department of Public Enterprises based on the actual performance of the company
against pre-defined MoU targets at the end of the year.
Recommendation
2.2    Growth criteria for power generation
2.2.1The Committee observed that the growth criteria for power generation under MOU should be measured year after
year and not from what it was since its inception i.e. 1998-99 if the growth percentage is based from year to year, the
growth trend of this Company is not very encouraging. It is reflected in the gross generation and the total requirement of
the power in the country. MoU system should be framed in such a way so as to exhibit growth trend year after year and
encourage and invite it. Project should be completed with in a fixed time frame.                         (Para 2.34)
Action Taken
2.2.2Ministry of Power and NTPC have informed that the target for generation for the company are fixed based upon
actual installed capacity and new capacity addition during the proposal period. The targets are fixed and measured on
yearly basis i.e. year after year. The targets are discussed/deliberated within the company with Ministry of Power and
with Task Force on MoU in DPE and in the process, the targets are stretched one.
2.2.3NTPC has a good record of completing the projects within scheduled time-frame. All efforts are made to cut short
the project execution time.
Recommendation
2.3    Power generation and the skill
2.3.1The Committee observes that the expertise of NLC in view of its overall performance achieved in terms of power
generation and the skill should be properly utilised and further Company should avail the opportunities in this regard to
achieve self sufficiency in the power sector. The Committee feels that NLC has a long way to go to achieve self
sufficiency in the power sector and should not get complacent.                                      (Para 3.11)
Action Taken
2.3.2Ministry of Coal and Neyveli Lignite Corporation (NLC) have informed that NLC was incorporated in the year
1956. The first lignite mine faced problem right from the commissioning. The imported Specialised Mining Equipment
could not operate to their rated capacity because of the presence of hard sand stone in the soil. The lignite output was
much below the rated capacity and consequently the capacity utilisation of the downstream units was also low. With the
addition of higher capacity mining equipment, NLC wiped out its accumulated losses in the year 1981-82. NLC put up a
second mine of 10.5 MTPA with the linked power station of capacity 1470 MW in the 1980’s, taking the total lignite
mining capacity to 17 MTPA and the power generating capacity to 2070 MW. The company further expanded by
putting up Mine-I Expansion project (4.0 MTPA) with a linked Thermal Power station of 420 MW and Mine-IA project
(3MTPA) to supply to an independent power producer (IPP) at a total cost of about Rs.3800 crores. The company has
also proposed other projects in Neyveli region as described below:
(i)    Mine-II Expansion-4.5 MTPA.

(ii)    Thermal Power Station-II Expansion-2X250 MW
(iii)   Mine-III-8MTPA
(iv)   Thermal Power Station-III-1000 MW
(v)   TPS-I Second Expansion-125 MW.
2.3.3NLC in its endeavour to become a leading mining and power company has also embarked on the following
projects:
(i)    Rajasthan Mine and Power project.
(a)   Lignite Mine project at Rajasthan-2.1 MTPA
(b)  Linked Power project-250 MW
(ii)    Coal based power project at Tuticorin-1000 MW
(iii)   Coal based power project in Orissa -2000 MW
(iv)   Coal based power project at Madhya Pradesh-1000 MW
(v)   Refinery residue based power project at Chennai-492 MW
2.3.4After completion of these projects, NLC shall have power generating utilities with installed capacity of 8857 MW
and a total mining capacity of 38.60 million tone of lignite per annum.
Recommendation
2.4    Safety related activities viz. risk assessment and safety audit
2.4.1 The Committee was informed that the safety related activities viz. risk assessment and safety audit for NLC
Mines, Thermal Power Station are regularly done and 2% weightage has been given in MoU 2003-04. The Committee
expressed its satisfaction with the performance.                     (Para 3.17)
Action Taken
2.4.2Ministry of Coal and Neyveli Lignite Corporation have informed that the observation of the Committee has been
noted.
Recommendation
2.5    Inordinate time taken in the appointment of non-official, part time Directors
2.5.1The Committee is constrained to note the inordinate time taken in the appointment of non-official, part time
directors and observes that the Government should not only avoid such delay but also expedite the process of
decentralization of power among the PSUs and thereby relieving them from the clutches of the archaic administrative
set up to give impetus to their development and further expansion in the wake of the competitive environment in the
light of liberalisation and globalisation.

Recommendation
2.6    Import duty exemption PGCIL on the lines of BHEL
2.6.1The Committee, therefore recommends that the case of PGCIL should be sympathetically considered by the
Government for import duty exemption on the lines of BHEL which is given in terms of mega project.             (Para
4.24)
Action Taken
2.6.2Ministry of Power and Powergrid Corporation of India Limited have informed that as per the mega power policy,
power generation projects with capacity of 1000 MW and more for thermal and 500 MW and more for hydro and
supplying power to more than one State are considered as a mega project. Accordingly, such projects are exempted from
Custom Duty, avail Deemed Export benefit as per EXIM policy and enjoy tax holidays for any block of 10 years within
the first 15 years. Thus, Mega Power Project status reduces the cost of projects. However, it is presently not available to
associated transmissions schemes.
2.6.3It has been suggested that the fiscal concessions available for mega projects be extended to all those transmission
projects, which are associated with Mega Generation Projects. The matter is presently under inter-Ministerial
consultation.
2.6.4This matter was taken up with Ministry of Finance also and they have informed that no specific proposals for
import duty concessions for projects undertaken by PGCIL appear to have been received either from the Ministry of
Power or from PGCIL. Details such as the nature of the goods sought to be imported, the revenue involved, etc. are not
available and it would not be possible to offer any specific comments on the recommendation at this stage. However it is
observed in the context of the said recommendation of the committee :­ -----
(a)   Eleven specified mega power projects were originally exempted from import duties on the basis of a Cabinet
decision approving the mega power policy. The exemption was subsequently extended to eight more mega
power projects (also on the basis of Cabinet/CCEA approval) and as a policy, extended to all mega power
projects which satisfy the specified criteria, i.e. inter-state thermal plants of 1000 MW and above or inter-state
hydel power plant of 500 MW and above, in budget 2003-04. There is no such Cabinet approval in this case.
Hence, the request of PGCIL made to the Committee, in respect of transmission projects, cannot be treated at
par with the Mega Power Projects for the purpose of import duty exemption.
(b)   There is a strong domestic angle to transmission and distribution equipment, and hence any import duty
concession to such equipment is likely to affect the domestic industry. In fact, the Ministry of Heavy
Industries and Public Enterprises, in its comments on the Cabinet note on ‘Large sized Power Project Policy’,
prepared by the Ministry of Power, had opposed extending of duty exemption for goods imported for
transmission systems associated with large power projects.
(c)   There is already a concessional customs duty of 10% on transmission and distribution projects. Further,
specified goods required for high voltage power transmission project are also at a concessional customs duty
of 5%.

REPORT
         The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Small Scale Industries
on the recommendations contained in the 146 th Report (of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee
on Industry) on Credit Flow to SSI Sector in Maharashtra pertaining to the Ministry of Small Scale Industries. The
Report was presented/laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha on the 26th August, 2003.
2.      Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Small Scale Industries in respect of the
recommendations contained in the Report. These have been categorized as follows:----
Chapter-I - The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry :- 51 and 52.
         The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry has accepted its recommendations as mentioned in Chapter-
I of the Report.
Chapter-II - The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the

Government’s replies:- 56.

Chapter-III - The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the

Chapter-IV - The recommendations/observations in respect of which final replies of the Ministry have not been

         In respect of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry has either furnished the interim replies or

Ministry should furnish Action Taken Notes in respect of recommendations categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to

3.      The details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
Recommendation
1.0    Technology up gradation and modernization
1.1    The Committee is of the view that to face the challenges emanating from the WTO agreement, SSI units
irrespective of their size need technology up gradation and modernisation. An awareness about the implications of WTO
agreement has to be created and SSI entrepreneurs needs to be educated in this regard. Technology is the key element
contributing to productivity quality, competitiveness and market acceptability of products. The preparation for
competitiveness needs to be done by the Government as well as entrepreneurs and the corporate sector.(Para 51)
Action Taken
1.1.2The Ministry of Small Scale Industries (SSI) has conducted various programmes to create awareness among SSI
entrepreneurs about the WTO agreements and their impact on small scale industries. These include 29 WTO Awareness
Programmes/Seminars, 5 product specific WTO Seminars and 29 Workshops on Intellectual Property Rights (IPRs),
besides a one-day sensitization workshop on Geographical Indications and 17 Information Dissemination Seminars on
Anti-Dumping Investigations. Some of these awareness programmes are being continued during 2004-05.
1.1.3In order to enable the SSI units to upgrade their technology so as to improve the productivity, quality,
competitiveness and market acceptability of their products, the Office of Development Commissioner (DC) (SSI) has
launched the following schemes/programmes:-
(i)    Small Industry Cluster Development Programme (SICDP): This takes a holistic approach to development of
clusters in respect of technology upgradation, marketing, exports, skill upgradation, etc. So far, 59 clusters
have been taken up for development, which include 5 National Programmes, in collaboration with the United
Nations Industrial Development Organisation (UNIDO) for development of Toy, Machine Tools, Locks,
Stone and Hand Tools Industry in the country.
(ii)    Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme for Technology Upgradation of the SSIs (CLCSS): This provides
12% capital subsidy for induction of well ­established and improved technology in the specified
products/sub-sectors (39 products/sub-sectors covered currently). As announced in the Union Budget for

1.2    Compatibility with WTO Provisions
1.2.1The Committee recommends that to achieve compatibility with WTO provisions, there is need for the sector to
develop and cement sub-contracting/outsourcing arrangements. The Sector-specific association can play an active role
in creating          mechanisms for studying the impact of WTO developments and to keep pace with the challenges of
change. Collaborative efforts on the part of different partners of the SSI sector are expected to yield better results than
isolated endeavors. A product-wise market research on the implications of WTO and other related aspects should be
done. The outcome of such studies could be made available to Industry Associations/Entrepreneurs for wider market
understanding and use by the members and SSIs at large.(Para 52)
Action Taken
1.2.2 The process of economic liberalization and globalization and adherence to WTO norms have led to intensifying
competition for the Indian industry, particularly the Small Scale Industries (SSI) sector.
1.2.3As the principal financial institution for the SSI sector, SIDBI undertook detailed policy supportive research
studies on select sub-sectors of importance to the SSI sector, which were aimed at assessing the impact of WTO, support
requirements of the SSI sector and the necessary policy interventions. In the first phase, WTO-related studies in respect
of 6 industrial sectors were undertaken and the salient findings and major observations and recommendations circulated
to the various agencies concerned, major industry associations, etc. Seminars to disseminate the findings and the
emerging issues among the SSIs and the Industry Associations were also organized. Second phase of the WTO Impact
Assessment studies, covering 3 more industrial sectors, have also been completed and similar action is proposed with
regard to these studies as well.
1.2.4The Ministry of SSI is supporting the Industry Associations financially to develop monitoring mechanisms on the
performance of four selected product clusters in terms of growth, implications of removal of Quantitative Restrictions
(QRs), surge in imports, etc. These Associations/clusters are Confederation of Indian Industry-Food Processing and
Machine Tools, Federation of Indian Micro and Small and Medium Enterprises-Shaneel and Kishangarh Marble
Association-­Marble cluster located at Pune, Bangalore, Panipat and Kishangarh respectively. The study reports on
Shaneel cluster at Panipat and Marble cluster at Kishangarh have been finalized. Other reports are in various stages of
finalization.
1.2.5The Ministry of SSI has got five sectoral studies conducted in areas which have a strong SSI presence, so as to
formulate a pro-active strategy and fine tune the existing policies and programmes. These studies have been undertaken
with the assistance of the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP). The sectors selected for the studies are
Hand Tools, Medicinal Biotechnology, Glass and Ceramics, Bicycle Parts and Flavour and Fragrance. Five product-
specific workshops on the impact of WTO Agreements on these sectors have already been organized. The industry and
their Associations have participated in these workshops and the study reports have been discussed with them during the
Seminars. The views/suggestions of the industry and their Associations have also been obtained and duly considered in
finalizing the reports. The report on Glass and Ceramics has been finalized. Other reports are in various stages of
finalization.
