 3.20  Constraints being faced by the PSEs
3.20 .1 As regards the constraints being faced by the PSEs, the Committee observes as under:
(i)
                  Lack of orders mainly from the Government and other PSEs.  In several cases the sickness of one PSE
has had corollary impact on other PSEs too.
(ii)                Another issue has been the fluctuating duty regime that have made PSEs non-competitive vis-a-vis other
global and domestic players.
(iii)               Obsolete technology and investment crunch due to reducing capital investment over the years in
enhancing the capacities of the PSEs has adversely affected the PSEs that have not been able to take the
advantage of economies of scale.
(iv)
              The PSEs at present are reeling under the burden of restructuring and rationalising their manpower.  A
larger part of their resources goes into settling the dues often at a higher rate of interest.
(v)                The Committee is of the view that in view of new economy and reducing government support, PSEs
shall have to come to terms with new market realities.  With expanding domestic, regional and global
market, PSEs shall have to take benefit of new opportunities.
(vi)             In view of the NCMP that envisages a revitalized Public Sector, the Ministry of Heavy Industries and
Public Sector Enterprises should evolve a Doctrine emphasizing that social obligations of the PSEs is a
function of their financial health, both are not contradictory but complementary to each other.  Therefore,
to meet its social obligations the Public Sector must regain their financial health.(Para 96)
 
ACTION TAKEN
  3.20.2 Government have taken a number of steps for improving the performance of PSEs.  These include manpower
rationalization, temporary financial assistance to sick units, purchase preference, restructuring/asset sale, MOU system
for close monitoring and disinvestment etc.  As per the Public Sector Policy contained in National Common Minimum
Programme, (NCMP), profit making PSEs (9 PSEs)will not be privatized and are to be strengthened by providing
greater autonomy. 27-loss making PSEs will be considered for revival/closure.  This Department is engaged in an
exercise on carefully appraising the fundamentals and capabilities of each of the PSEs and formulating restructuring
plans for each of them with the assistance of professional consulting agencies. As distinct from previous efforts,
restructuring strategies now being undertaken would incorporate comprehensive financial, managerial, technological,
organizational and marketing restructuring to lead to an enterprise whose working would be meaningful and profitability
sustainable.   Such proposals shall be placed before the Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises
(BRPSE). 
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
3.20.3  The Committee is of the view that PSE which has been envisaged   once as the 'Temple of Modern India' during
the heyday of welfare state when these PSEs met the social obligation and thus plaged pivotal role in economic and
social building of the nation.  These PSEs are now reeling under deep trouble due to lack of orders, fluctuating duty
refine, obsolete  technology and investment crunch and are under the burden of restructuring and retionalising there man
power.  The PSEs are not  competitive and resilient enough to face the stark-realities of fast emerging now market
economy.  All previous steps for improving the financial  health of PSEs fumbled one after another.  Under the
circumstances, the Government has to take careful and cautious efforts to rescuers the PSEs out of red.  The constitution
of Board for Reconstitution of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE) under National Common Minimum Programmes is a
new spectrum of rays of hopes which can inject 'Sanjivini booti' (new lease of life)  there PSEs.

REPORT
The Action Taken Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Ministry of Agro and Rural
Industries  on the Recommendations contained in the  152 nd     Report (of the Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry) on  Demands for Grants (2004-05) pertaining to the Ministry of Agro and Rural
Industries .  The Report was presented /laid on the Table of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha on  the 26th  August, 2004.
2.         Action Taken Notes have been received from the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries    in respect of the  
recommendations contained in the Report.   These have been categorized as follows:
Chapter - I- The recommendations/observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry :- Paras : 2.4 ; 12.2;  12.5; 17.2;
20.5;  21.11; 21.14; 22.9;  25.6;  26.3 and  29.2
 The Committee is pleased to observe that  the   Ministry  has accepted its  recommendation as  mentioned in Chapter –I of the 
Report. 
Chapter - II- The recommendations/observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the
Government's replies: - Paras :- 4.9  and 11.6
 In respect of these recommendations the Committee is  convinced  with the logic and explanation  advocated by the
Ministry  and therefore   does not want to  pursue  further. 
Chapter - III- The recommendations/observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the Ministry: -
Paras: 12.4; 12.9; 14.2; 16.2; 21.16;  23.4;  24.2; 27.2; 28.2; 30.2 and 31.4
 The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementations  of recommendations contained in  Chapter-III  and desires
that the Ministry should furnish  logical  explanation  in respect of these recommendations.  
Chapter - IV- The recommendations/observations in respect of which  final replies of the  Ministry have not been received :- 2.5
;  9.2; 10.7; 12.7; 15.2; 22.6 and 22.10
In respect  of recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry has  either   furnished the interim replies or couched its
language in  vague terms like  noted for compliance/guidance, therefore, the Committee desires  that the Ministry should furnish
Action Taken Notes in  respects of recommendations categorized   in Chapter-IV  in detail and to the point, as per the intention
and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
3.         The Details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.
CHAPTER - I
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN ACCEPTED BY THE GOVERNMENT
Recommendation
1.0       Professionalism in finance, marketing, HRD, technology and manpower upgradation in the KVI sector
1.1       The Committee hopes that the creation of independent Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would reinforce
and strengthen the functioning of the ARI sector as a whole, by highlighting its present status and ensuring timely policy
interventions when needed. The contribution of this sector can be further streamlined and strengthened by injecting
more professionalism in the areas of finance, marketing, HRD, technology and manpower upgradation in the KVI
sector, revival of sick khadi institutions, renovation and modernization of marketing outlets.
ACTION TAKEN
1.1.1    Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries appreciates the recommendations of the Committee.    Government has
taken the following fresh initiatives in this direction:
1.2       Revamping of KVIC
1.2.1    In the National Common Minimum Programme, the Government has declared to revamp the Khadi and Village

Industries Commission (KVIC).  Towards this objective, the Government has dissolved the KVIC with effect from 14
October 2004 and  by an order dated 01 December 2004, the Government has also set up  a ten-Member Expert
Committee under the chairpersonship of Shri D.M. Sukthankar, former Secretary to the Government of  India, with the
following terms of reference:
(i)
                  to review the existing structure, functioning and performance of the KVIC since its inception;
(ii)                to review the Khadi and Village Industries Commission Act, 1956 (61 of 1956), KVIC Rules, 1957 and the
Regulations made thereunder and to recommend restructuring, along with modifications, if any, in these
statutes, to achieve the objectives of  (a)  development of  Khadi  and Village  Industries (KVI)  and (b)
making KVIC a more professional and effective body for implementation of the existing KVI programmes/
 
schemes and/or launching new programmes/schemes with a view to enhancing employment and income generation
in the rural areas and expanding the markets for (including export of) Khadi and Village Industry products; and
(iii)
               to recommend any other measure(s) considered necessary by the committee to revamp the KVIC and to
launch new, appropriate programmes/schemes.
 1.2.2   The Expert Committee is expected to give its recommendation in March, 2005, based on which the Government
will initiate necessary action on various issues relating to the Khadi and Village Industries Commission, in  particular
and the sector, in general.
1.3       Other initiatives   
 1.3.1   The  newly formed  Confederation for Promotion of Khadi & Village Industries Products (CPKVI)  is expected
to involve more professionals in the area of marketing.  As far as human resource development (HRD) is concerned,
training centers of KVIC and State KVI Boards are providing training of Entrepreneurship Development Programme
(EDP)  training required under REGP, Rural Engineering and Bio-Technology with the help of   in-house faculty  
available with  these centers. Further, services of   experts are also outsourced in trades like, computer software and
hardware, servicing of Electrical articles, motor winding,  repairing/servicing of T.V. & Radio,  servicing of
Telephones,  tailoring and embroidery,  manufacture of Fibre Reinforced Plastics (FRP), Jewellery Article making,
Manufacture & Servicing of Voltage stabilizer, Servicing & Repairing of Mobile phones and  Servicing of Electronics
Goods etc.  In addition to above, for certain specialized topics like management, marketing, brand building, export &
packaging, etc., guest faculties are also invited.  Again, for up gradation of  technology, KVIC has  developed  13
technical interfaces with premier technological institutes ( IITs and NITs) under Area Specific R&D for providing S&T
inputs, R&D support, innovative ideas, technical backup etc. to the KVI units within their jurisdiction.  So far MOU  has
been signed with 17 such institutes  and it is expected that expertise of premier institutions will be availed by the grass
root level artisans for   upgradation  of technology and production of quality goods.  
1.3.2    It has also been decided to set up in house testing laboratories  at the cost of Rs.2.00 lakhs each, which will
undertake quality awareness campaigns, accreditation for ISO-9000, standardization of product & process, preparation
of quality control manual for documentation of standards, use of Hologram of branding items – ‘Khadi India’
1.3.3    Further, KVIC has tied up with-
·
        IGNOU for certification courses for traditional artisans, field workers, etc. In the 1st phase   certification
courses for potters     have been devised.
·        Institutions of repute to promote bio-fertilizers, bio-pesticides, panchagavya etc.
·        IIT, IISE for promotion of herbal produdcts in a big way for which quality testing has been arranged
during the year.
·        Textile Committee for testing of Khadi through Textile Committee labs in the country.  Stamping of
Khadi being made mandatory.
·        IIT Delhi for development of soft and stiff finish for khadi.   Implementation done in Barabanki, UP &
Dausa in Rajasthan. Other zones being covered in a phased manner.

1.4.1    PRODIP
The Committee appreciates KVIC for launching Product Design Innovation and Packaging  (PRODIP) and directs
KVIC to apprise the progress made in this regard.

1.5       Consortium Bank Credit 
The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure that Rs. 238.02 crore is lying as outstanding balance with Khadi
implementing agencies  under Consortium Bank Credit (CBC) and recommends that the Government should take initiative at

1.5.2     Government has now  agreed to convert the outstanding balance under  the CBC Scheme into working capital loans. All
necessary documentation in this regard has been executed and forwarded to the lead bank, Sate Bank of India (SBI) by KVIC.  
RECOMMENDATION
1.6"National Khadi Revolution."
1.6.1    The Committee observes that Khadi has been the National identity since the days of India's struggle for
independence and therefore the Government should pay all attention for the continuation of Khadi as an identity in the
National life and culture.
ACTION TAKEN
1.6.2    The Ministry  has been providing all help and assistance in  the development and promotion of khadi. Ministry is
also implementing the following programmes:-  
 1. Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme.
 2. Product Development, Design Intervention and Packaging      (PRODIP)
 
New Initiatives
(a)      Brand Building
1.6.3    For the development of Village Industries, KVIC has launched  the "Sarvodaya" brand for its products. Toilet
soaps, honey, agarbattis and pickles would be covered under this brand. It is expected that this step would create a brand
name for these products, through a marketing network.

(b) Marketing Promotion
1.6.4    KVIC has also taken steps to launch a new marketing confederation for marketing of VI products in the name of
Confederation for Promotion of Khadi and Village Industries (CPKVI). For organic food products, the new brand name
of "Desi Aahar" has been introduced by the KVIC.
(c) Research & Development
1.6.5    R&D projects have been taken up to develop a new range of products in the areas of herbal products, essential
oils, muslin Khadi, etc.   As a part of quality assurance for Khadi goods, KVIC has signed an M.O.U. with the Textile
Committee, Mumbai where Khadi institutions spread throughout the country, have been linked to 14 Laboratories of
Textile Committee  to conduct testing of khadi produced by them.  In collaboration with IIT, New Delhi, standards for
khadi has been developed and communicated to all. KVIC has also sanctioned a project on ‘ Ready-to-Use Mission’ ion
Khadi where large-scale production of readymade will be done in a standardized manner under close supervision of
local outfit of NIFT.
(d) India International Trade Fair Exhibitions
1.6.6    KVIC participated in Indian International Trade Fair (IITF) New Delhi from 14 to 27 November 2004.   For the
first time, a theme pavilion “ Khadi as a Way of Life ” was introduced,  KVIC was awarded the Gold medal for best
designed stall by the ITPO.
(e)  North Eastern (NE) Exhibitions
1.6.7    For popularizing products of North Eastern Region, Uttar Purwa Khadi Gramodyog Darshan/Mela was also been
organized.  These exhibitions were held in the following places :-
1.    Mumbai –     11 to 15 June, 2004 at World Trade Centre.                       
2.    New Delhi -  17 December,2004 to 5 January, 2005 at Griha
       Kalyan Kendra, Sarojini, Nagar, New Delhi.
3.    Bangalore -  3 February to 3 March, 2005
RECOMMENDATION
1.7       Coir Industries
1.7.1    The Committee recommends that the following Steps may be taken  to promote the marketing and sales of coir
products in the domestic market:-
 
(i)
                  Intensification of promotional measures like publicity through print and  electronic media and increased
participation in trade fairs and exhibitions
(ii)                Organisation of Buyer –Seller Meets in potential regions and  organisation of special sales campaign
and festival discount offer to promote sales.
(iii)               Organising collective participation of manufacturers in selected trade fairs and exhibitions and
(iv)              Popularisation of new products like coir geotextiles, garden articles, coir pith based products through
awareness creation programmes etc.
Action Taken
1.7.2    Various measures have been adopted to popularize coir and coir products in India. These include advertisement
through electronic and print media, erection of hoardings, distribution of pamphlets, distribution of calendars and
diaries, etc.    Product promotion advertisements have been given in leading magazines and journals, highlighting the
unique features of coir and coir products as an eco-friendly live-in- style product. The Coir Board participated in 54
exhibitions in the country during the year.  The participation in these exhibitions has contributed to popularizing coir  
products, particularly in areas where the use of coir products were less known.
Advertisements were also released  through the print media in local languages.  Display of banners at vantage points is
another publicity measure. The recommendations of the Committee are noted and the promotional measures will be
intensified.
1.7.3    The Coir Board participates in important exhibitions and also in specialized exhibitions for floor coverings,
handicraft items, gift items, etc., held in metropolitan cities.
Under the Market Development Assistance Scheme, assistance is provided to Apex Co-operative Societies, Central Co-
operative Societies, Public Sector Enterprises, etc. for innovative marketing strategies, including an element of
discounts.
1.7.4    The recommendation of the Committee to organize Buyer-Seller Meets is noted.
1.7.5    Assistance is provided to coir product manufacturers to participate in  exhibitions and fairs. In most cases,
participation in selected exhibitions is facilitated by  the Coir Board bearing the space rent fully/partially. The

166th Report of Committee on Industry

observation of the Committee with regard to organizing collective participation in domestic trade fairs and exhibitions is
noted and  will be implemented.
1.7.6    The fruit of research and development activities are demonstrated and popularized.  In addition,
Entrepreneurship Development Programmes are organized at various places in  the country and latest developments in
the coir industry are disseminated in order to persuade more entrepreneurs to enter the industry.  The development of
this industry at a fast pace in non-traditional States of the country ( e.g., Orissa, Jharkhand, Uttar Pradesh & Bihar) is
due partially to these activities. 
1.7.7    During 2003-2004, two geo-textile projects at Silchar in Assam and Kohima in Nagaland were implemented in
association with the Border Roads Organization. 
1.7.8    All new products developed are displayed with prominence in the exhibitions participated. Wide publicity is also
given to items through “Coir News”, the monthly journal of the Coir Board.  As a result, the coir garden articles and coir
pith based products like Coir Pith Organic Manure (CPOM) have earned  acceptability  in India  and also, to some
extent, elsewhere in the world.
RECOMMENDATION
1.8       R&D activities for Coir Industries
1.8.1    The Committee recommends that since the budgetary provisions for R&D for Coir Industries is sufficient all
efforts would be made for skimming out of benefits of R&D for the proliferation and promotion of Coir Industries.
ACTION TAKEN
1.8.2    Concerted efforts are being made for promotion of coir industry by propagating the new technologies developed
and the machinery fabricated for modernization of the industry. Technologies like application of Coirret has been
successfully transferred to enable  faster retting  and  to eliminate drudgery in retting operation, use of coir pith for
manufacture of coir Pith Organic Manure (C-POM) so as to avoid pollution being created by the coir pith hillocks in the
coir production centres, skill upgradation training in the spinning of coir yarn on motorised traditional ratt and
motorised ratts in the traditional sector, etc.
1.8.3    A new compact metallic handloom called "Anugraha" has also been developed for weaving of coir mattings,
even by women workers without  drudgery. The scientists who were instrumental for development of the loom were 
given technology awards by the National Research Development Corporation, New Delhi. Efforts have also been made
to transfer the technology for production of the looms and the design of the looms to the  six coir machinery
manufacturers registered with the Coir Board.     One of the major exporters from the coir sector has put up 36 compact
metallic looms for weaving coir geotextiles in a newly established coir unit in the Thirunelveli district of Tamil Nadu.
Assistance has also been extended to the exporter in fabrication of the loom as well as training the women workers in
weaving of coir geotextiles.  It is proposed to popularize the technology of the new loom in the non-traditional sectors
and include the loom inthe list of equipment eligible for payment of subsidy under the Mahila Coir Yojana.
1.8.4    Efforts are also being made to popularize diversified products in coir sector like coir ply boards, which is
considered to be a wood substitute, for its use in the Railways and other sectors. A collaborative project with the
Konkan Railway Corporation has already been taken up by the Coir Board for construction of foot- over bridge using
coir composites. The project may open up  a large market for coir composites.
1.8.5    Concerted efforts are being made for  popularization of coir pith    products. The export of coir pith from India
has made a quantum jump in the recent past.  During 2003-04, a total quantity of 29179   MTs of coir pith valued at
Rs.1975.92 lakh was exported from the country as against 21064  MTs valued at Rs. 1493.01 lakh during  2002-03. 
Apart from  its export, possibilities of using coir pith in  areas like extraction of valuable organic compounds and  as an
absorbents of toxic materials, for which a collaborate project has already been taken up by the Coir Board with the
Bhabha Atomic Research Centre, Mumbai, are being explored. Regarding manufacture of C-POM using pithplus, a
technology for composting the pith in situ using perforated pipes in the hillocks of coir pith for increasing aeration has
been developed.  Using this method, the composting period of coir pith could be reduced to 21 days from 30 days.
RECOMMENDATION
1.9       Problems being faced by KVIC and KVIBs in the implementation of REGP
1.9.1     The Committee observes that it is necessary to recruit professionals, familiar with project preparation, analysis,
consultancy etc. or avail their services from any other professional agencies. While enhancing employment target it is
imperative to proportionately increase the margin money component and corresponding funds for backward forward linkages
and place them with field officers of KVIC well in advance as per estimated requirements.  The State KVI Boards are major
agencies involved in the implementation of REGP.  Their weak infrastructure/organizational condition often hinders the
expeditious implementation of the scheme.  KVIBs should be revitalized by the respective State Governments.

ACTION TAKEN BY THE GOVERNMENT
1.9.2    At present, REGP projects are being appraised by  professionals from banks who conduct a financial appraisal of
the  project before sanctioning loan. KVIC has launched the scheme of  Rural Industries Consultancy Service  (RICS)
and 49 such centres have already been set up under this Service to provide consultancy service for  preparation of
bankable projects under the REGP.     In order to revitalize the functioning of State/U.T. KVI Boards a communication
was issued on 17.5.2004 to Secreary (Industries) of all State Government/U.T. Administration requesting them to
develop monthly monitoring system, to clear pending Ucs / Audit Para  expeditiously, recovery of loan and also to
popularize & take advantage of new schemes launched by KVIC.
1.9.3    As regards enhancing the margin money to meet the enhanced targets, it may be stated that during 2003-04, an
amount of Rs. 281.75 crore has been disbursed for implementation of the programme.  Out of this, Rs. 265.74 crore  has
been utilized in terms of margin money by the programme implementing agencies, i.e., State KVIC agencies/State
KVIBs etc.  In addition, Rs. 4.78 crore was allocated  to meet the expenditure on backward and forward linkages in this
field.  During the year 2003-04, financial institutions extended credit of Rs. 664.35 crore to the entrepreneurs.  During
2003-04, REGP generated 4.71 lakh additional employment.  For the year 2004-05 and 2005-06, the additional
employment targets are 5.25 lakh and 5.51 lakh, respectively.  An amount of Rs. 326 crore has been earmarked at the
RE stage for the year 2004-05 for implementing the REGP  and  Rs. 412 crore has been earmarked for 2005-06.
RECOMMENDATION
1.10     Lumpsum Provision For Projects Schemes For The Benefit Of North Eastern Region And Sikkim
1.10.1   The Committee is of the view that the development of the NER region requires the special attention of the Government. 
The special emphasis is required because of the fact that though the region has immense potential, the lack of communication
facilities, poor infrastructure, difficult terrain etc. have contributed to the region's economic backwardness.  Since the region has
lagged behind in progress as compared to other regions of the country, special attention is required to strengthen and reinforce
focused implementation of various schemes under the ARI sector.  Targets under REGP, PMRY coir industries should be
accordingly set for the region. 
Action Taken
1.10.2  For the financial year 2004-05, Government of India has made a budget allocation of Rs.34 crore, for  the North
Eastern Region (NER).  Allocation for REGP has been  further increased  to Rs. 47.50 crore for the year  2005-06.
During 2004-05, it is proposed to set up 2626 REGP projects for generating 52000 additional employment in the NER. 
During  2005-06, it is proposed to generate 55000 additional employment opportunities in the North Eastern States.
1.10.3  In respect of  PMRY, the Ministry shares the views of the Committee on  economic status of  the States in the
NE Region.  Therefore, the Ministry agreed to allocate  targets, as requested by the State Governments  concerned in the

1.11     Registration  and regularization  of Agro & Rural Industries  units
1.11.1  The Committee desires that government should initiate concrete steps for effective regularization and regulation
of Agro & Rural Industries.
Action Taken
1.11.2  In the initial phase of implementation of REGP, registration with Khadi and Village Industries Commission
(KVIC)/ State KVI Boards was not a pre-requisite.  However, with effect from 1 January 2003, registration of REGP
units with KVIC/KVIB has been made mandatory for grant of margin money.  As the projects are being financed with  
bank loans, the flow of funds and adjustment of margin money against the repayment scheme, etc., are regulated by
banks  as per  KVIC guidelines.  Further, regular meetings are also  held to review the progress of implementation of the
programme and  take corrective/remedial measures, wherever necessary. 
Recommendation
1.12     Credit flow to Agro & Rural Industries
112.1   The Committee recommends that constant attempts should be vigorously made for recovery of dues of finances
advanced for ensuring adequate circulation of credit to ARI units   and at the same time making easy credit accessibility
to new entrepreneurs. The Committee further recommends that adequate steps should be taken for removing the
problems being faced by ARI entrepreneurs relating to unviable projects, cutting down financial size of the projects,
lengthy procedural formalities while accessing credit for their units.
Action Taken
1.12.2  With a view to  ensuring  recovery of loan dues, review  meetings   are  held with banks and  followed up with
the entrepreneurs under REGP who  have accessed Bank credit.  As per recent report on Evaluation Study of  REGP
conducted by a research institute viz., Vaikunthbhai Mehta Research Centre for Decentralised Industries, Mumbai,
shows that none of the beneficiaries  under REGP was considered as total defaulter by the financial agencies.  It can,
therefore, be said that under REGP, the recovery rate is 100 per cent.  It was further observed in survey that REGP
scheme, in majority of the cases,  resulted in good relations between the financial institutions and the entrepreneurs.  
KVIC has also launched the  scheme for Rural Industries Consultancy Services (RICS) Centres in order to help the
entrepreneurs in preparation of viable projects, thereby reducing the rejection rate. 
1.12.3  Several measures have been taken  for improving the recovery of loan over dues under the PMRY Scheme. 
These include  linking  additional targets with recovery performance, joint recovery drives by banks with DIC officials,
constitution of Recovery Cells in the Zonal offices of the banks, requesting State Governments to notify the recovery of
loan over dues under the PMRY Scheme at par with land revenue arrears and notify it under the respective land revenue
recovery laws.  During meetings with the banks and the State Governments emphasis has been laid on the recovery of
loan overdues.   It has been decided to restructure curriculum and methodology of training under the PMRY.  Under the
restructured curriculum and methodology, emphasis has been laid on making the entrepreneurs aware about the need for
timely repayment of loan taken under the PMRY and on selection of viable projects.  The need for selection of ‘viable
projects’ was also stressed in the meetings with the implementing banks and the States.  The RBI has advised the
implementing banks to fix area wise minimum unit cost of activity to tackle the under-financing of projects by banks. 
Several measures have been taken to cut down the time required for completing procedural formalities, e.g., issue of 
‘no-dues’ certificate within one month of the date of issue of verification request by the banks, time limit of fortnight for
disposing applications involving credit limit of Rs.25,000/- and those for over Rs.25,000/- within 8 to 9 weeks,
convening DIC Task Force Committee Meeting at least once in a month or more depending upon the applications
received in the district etc.

3.6       National Programme For Rural Industrialisation
3.6.1    The Committee is of the view that since the National Programme for Rural Industrialization has the potential for
real development and growth of rural economy,  the Government should undertake concrete  measures to combat the
problems in achieving the objectives, targets, credit-flow, implementation and monitoring mechanism and  "Key
Concern Areas" of NPRI.
Action Taken
3.6.2    It is true that the NPRI Scheme has the potential for real development and development and growth of rural
economy, but the performance under the NPRI Scheme has not been very satisfactory. Some of the reasons to this could
be the meager financial assistance of Rs 5.0 lakh per cluster for cluster-wide interventions, fill-in-gaps arrangements,
non-availability of credit-linked subsidy component, inadequate synergy with the Ministries/departments with their own
schemes in this area etc. The budget provision of Rs. 0.45 crore under the scheme was reduced to Rs. 0.05 crore at RE
stage for the year 2004-05 as adequate number of proposals were not received for financial assistance under the Scheme
from the implementing agencies.  During the year 2001-02 and 02-03, no funds could be expanded. During 2003-04,
funds amounting to Rs.17.7 lakhs expanded for development of the clusters under NPRI.  During the year 2004-05,
funds amounting to Rs 2.25 lakh expended towards diagnostic study  for the clusters already approved during 2003-04.
In total, an amount of Rs. 19.9 lakhs have been sanctioned under NPRI scheme from 2001-02 till 2004-05 for
development of 19 clusters. Besides, SIDBI, NABARD and KVIC are also developing the clusters under NPRI out of
their own budgetary resources.
3.6.3    Therefore, the Ministry proposes to subsume the NPRI Scheme into the new proposed Scheme namely, Scheme
of Funds for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI). The liability of the NPRI may be met out of the
subsequent provisions of budget under NPRI/ other schemes of the Ministry.
3.6.4    The revised scheme, titled the Scheme of Funds for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) has been
drafted. This scheme is based on cluster development approach and also addresses the concerns raised by the Ministry
of Finance (MoF). The EFC note along with the revised draft scheme has been circulated to the Ministries/Departments
concerned for their comments on 15 February 2005.  ‘SFURTI’  will be implemented in 2005-06 for which a provision
of Rs. 30 crore has been kept.
Further Recommendation
3.6.5    The Committee is of the considered view that by changing the name of the programme / scheme, from National
Programme for Rural Industrialization to Scheme Of Funds For Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) is not
going to provide any remarkable achievement in regard to the stated objectives of the scheme originally conceived.  The
Ministry of ARI should have extracted the benefits of SWOT analysis of NPRI and accordingly the Ministry should
have taken adequate and suitable steps for combating the problems of NPRI i.e. meager financial assistance of Rs 5.0
lakh per cluster for cluster-wide interventions, fill-in-gaps arrangements, non-availability of credit-linked subsidy
component, inadequate synergy with the Ministries/departments with their own schemes in this area etc. with all
seriousness.  The Committee is of the considered view that NPRI should remain in force as it contains the cherished
objectives having potential for employment generation and consolidation of rural economy and growth.  At best,
SFRUTI can be made one of the component of NPRI or it can launched as a separate scheme.  That is so because re-
generation of traditional industries may cover only the confined component of the earlier conceived  National
Programme for Rural Industrialization.
Recommendation

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
Lack of support from the financial institutions
           
            The Committee is perturbed to note that despite efforts made by the Ministry of SSI to enable KVIC to get
sufficient credit flow from the banking sector could not yielded into satisfactory result.   Moreover, financial institution
does not honour the Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) issued by KVIC in favour of khadi institution on the
basis of approved pattern of assistance resulting into insufficient flow of  working capital to khadi institutions. During 
2002-03, Rs. 378.07 crore worth of ISEC certificates were issued for providing working capial assistance to khadi
institutions.  Against this, the institutions could avail of Rs. 253.72 crore only , i.e., 67 per cent of the  amount in the
ISEC issued.  For 2003-04, the  amount of ISEC issued and  credit availed  of in the khadi sector was Rs. 387.09 crore
and Rs. 298.78 crore respectively, i.e., 77 per cent of the ISEC issued- although showing an improvement of 10 per cent
in availing  of the total ISEC  amount.
            The Committee also takes not of the fact that part of the working capital of the khadi institutions is also blocked
with various is also blocked with various State Governments in the form of arrears  of admissible rebates, therefore, the
Committee recommends that Ministry of ARI should apprise the Committee, state-wise the details of arrears on account
of admissible rates and take up follow up actions with the respective States Government and accordingly apprise the
Committee the outcome of its efforts so made.
The Committee is constrained to express its displeasure that the recommendation of the Committee has not been taken
in right spirit.  As the Committee has presented the 152
nd Report in August, 2004 with the recommendation that the
Ministry of ARI should come out with specific details of labour reforms for improving Agro and Rural Industries and
after the lapse of seven months in March, 2005 the Ministry of ARI come out with the idea that observation of the
Committee are noted for future guidance.   The Committee's recommendation in this regard intails a particular course of
action on the part of the Ministry of ARI i.e. brain storming session for chalking out the areas /  issues for reform in
existing labour laws affecting the ARI sector.  Here at the Committee has not issued any behavioral modification which
could have been noted for future guidance which performing a task.  Therefore, the Committee desires that the Ministry
of ARI should have taken its recommendation in right earnest and avoid replying in a very casual manner.
Stock Inventories 
The Committee observes that the reduction of stock inventories from Rs. 612.30 crore ( khadi – Rs. 551.19 crore and
Polyvastra –Rs. 60.84) as on 31
st March, 2003 to Rs. 611.11 crore ( Khadi – Rs. 549.45 crore and Polyvastra Rs. 61.66
crore) as on 31 st March, 2004 is a very minute achievement in regard to Action Plan for disposing of the stock
inventories in a time bound programme.  The Committee is of the considered view that unless and until stock
inventories is not cleared, the shortage of working capital would continue to be felt on the part of the KVIC.
The Committee expresses its pleasure  over the increasing trend of employment generation in the khadi sector.  During
2002-03 and 2003-04, the employment in the khadi sector has increased slightly to 8.59 lakh persona and 8.61 lakh
persons respectively.  However, for further widening the employment generation avenues in the khadi sector, the KVIC
and the Ministry of ARI should  pay adequate attention to production and sales planning, particularly product quality
and marketability, provide working capital to KVIC institutions, undertake suitable steps for disposing of inventories
stocks and undertake effective steps for  payment of arrear rebates by the State Governments.
Potential of coir industries in non-traditional states like Uttar Pradesh,  Orissa ,Bihar and Jharkhand.
The Committee appreciates the efforts undertaken by the Coir Board in proliferation of Coir Industry in the
major coconut producing States like Kerala, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh & Tamilnadu .  The Committee is also
appreciative of the initiative taken by the Coir Board in promoting coir industries in Orissa where a Rubberized Coir
Manufacturing unit at the cost of Rs. 417.00 lakh is being established under the Centrally Sponsored Scheme of Co-
operativisation.  The Committee hopes that the Coir Board would implement its strategy to set up coir units in the non-
traditional states like U.P., Bihar and Jharkhand by sourcing coir fibre from the nearest available place and imparting
training to the local artisans in spinning and weaving products.  The Committee desires that concerted efforts must be
made to establish coir units in the non-traditional areas by sourcing fibre from the nearest coir producing States.
National Programme For Rural Industrialisation
The Committee is of the considered view that by changing the name of the programme / scheme, from National
Programme for Rural Industrialization to Scheme Of Funds For Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) is not
going to provide any remarkable achievement in regard to the stated objectives of the scheme originally conceived.  The

Ministry of ARI should have extracted the benefits of SWOT analysis of NPRI and accordingly the Ministry should
have taken adequate and suitable steps for combating the problems of NPRI i.e. meager financial assistance of Rs 5.0
lakh per cluster for cluster-wide interventions, fill-in-gaps arrangements, non-availability of credit-linked subsidy
component, inadequate synergy with the Ministries/departments with their own schemes in this area etc. with all
seriousness.  The Committee is of the considered view that NPRI should remain in force as it contains the cherished
objectives having potential for employment generation and consolidation of rural economy and growth.  At best,
SFRUTI can be made one of the component of NPRI or it can launched as a separate scheme.  That is so because re-
generation of traditional industries may cover only the confined component of the earlier conceived  National
Programme for Rural Industrialization.
Fund for Modernization of Traditional Industries
            The Committee observes that the Government has been the witness to the withering away of the cherished
objectives and mission of consolidation of rural economy and arresting the rural migration to the urban areas under
National Programme for Rural Industrialization and thereafter, when the Government has drafted a substitute scheme
i.e. SFRUTI, although it does not cover all aspects of NPRI, Government is taking to much time in clearing the
SFRUTI.  Therefore, the Committee desires that SFRUTI may be launched without delay.
Impact of globalisation and liberalization on Agro & Rural Industries
            The Committee feels that the Ministry of ARI should take up the issue of exemption the of KVI products from
state level Value Added Tax (VAT) to the concern authorities advocating that the KVI products are not in a position to
face stiff competition from the organized sector.
Problems being faced by Agro & Rural Industries
The Committee, while appreciating the components of Product Development Design Intervention and Packaging
(PRODIP), recommends that the scheme should be implemented in letter and spirit.  The Committee would like to know
the details about the functions of Rural Industries Service Centre (RISC) and its distribution in various states.  The
Committee would further like to know the details of "transfer of technology and technological intervention from
Technology Information Forecasting and Assessment Council (TIFAC) and outcome thereof.
Revival of the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF)
The Committee knows and understands that Revival of the Rural Infrastructure Development Fund (RIDF) falls within
the jurisdiction of Ministry of Rural Development, however, sine the Agro and Rural Industries may be one of the major
beneficiaries of RIDF, therefore, it should be the Ministry of ARI which should come out and make efforts in tandem
with the Ministry of Rural Development chalk out action plan to boost the development of the clusters in economically
backward states like Bihar, M.P., Chhatisgarh, Orissa and Jharkhand.
"New Deal" for rural India
The Committee is of the view that the Government, beside REGP, should come out with comprehensive scheme for
rural employment with the purpose of alleviating rural poverty and integrating rural economy with the national
economy.

1.8Streamlining  and strengthening the Anti-dumping mechanism
1.8.1    The Committee desires that the Ministry of SSI should make efforts for ensuring the following things:-
Working of renewed provision in Indo-Nepal Treaty in Trade Transit w.e.f. 6th March, 2002, in checking influx of Chinese goods
en-route Nepal;
Conversion of quantitative restriction (QRs) into rationalised tariff regime for providing protection to the domestic SSIs;
Rationalisation of countervailing duties and safeguard duties to protect domestic producers in consonance with WTO provision; and
Expeditious disposal dumping cases and anti-dumping actions thereto, in view of almost all SSI products under open general licence
(OGL) list.
(Para 32.4)
Action Taken
1.8.2    The Government  (Department of Commerce) has revised the Indo-Nepal Treaty on Trade and Transit and the revised
protocol is valid for a period of five years with effect from 6.3.2002. To protect the Indian industry, the following steps have been
taken:
(a)        Rules for granting Certificate of Origin have been changed. Only the following articles can now be imported preferentially:
*          Articles, which are manufactured in Nepal wholly from Nepalese and/or Indian materials.
*          Articles that involve a manufacturing process in Nepal, which brings about a change in classification at the 4-digit level.
*          Articles in which there is value addition of at least 43% from 6
th March 2003.
(b)        Representations received from SSI Associations regarding the problems   being faced by the industry due to revised Indo-Nepal
Treaty on Trade and Transit are taken up with the Department of Commerce, the nodal agency, dealing with the Indo-Nepal Treaty of Trade
and other concerned Departments/Agencies, viz., Directorate General of Foreign Trade (DGFT), Central Board of Excise and Customs
(CBEC) so as to protect the interests of domestic industry.
1.8.3     Under the WTO regime, all Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) have been abolished except 430 QRs maintained on account of public
morality, safety, etc.  The current average applied customs tariff on import of products related to the SSI sector (whether reserved for
manufacture in SSI sector or otherwise) is 20%. These tariffs are among the higher tariffs applied by various member states of WTO.  The
Ministry of Commerce while monitoring trade of various products, including the products related to the SSI sector, keeps a watch on the
applied tariff rates on these products so as to provide needed tariff protection by taking suitable action for increasing the tariff.
1.8.4    Even after removal of the QRs, there are ways to protect our domestic industry, such as, Article 6 of the General Agreement
on Trade & Tariffs (GATT), which permits the Government to levy anti-dumping duty. The GATT, 1994 also permits the
Government to reimpose Quantitative Restrictions (QRs) because any WTO member is free to suspend any obligation incurred by
it if imports of products into its territory cause or threaten to cause a serious injury to the domestic producers. Therefore, in an
emergency situation, the Government can reimpose suitable quantitative restrictions. Accordingly, the Government is in the process
of amending the provisions of Foreign Trade (Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 so that safeguard action in the form of QRs
could be applied, if there are sudden and massive imports.
1.8.5    The small scale industries can be given protection by increasing the applied (customs) tariff rates up to the bound levels,
wherever permissible and required. India’s tariffs have been bound at fairly high levels, enabling the Government to intervene
effectively wherever any unusual increase in imports is noticed.
1.8.6    The Director General of Safeguards has taken up action in respect of 15 products for investigation.  So far, safeguard duties
in respect of 8 cases have been imposed.  The Government is in the process of amending the provisions of Foreign Trade
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1992 so that safeguard action in the form of QRs could be applied if there are sudden and
massive imports. There is also the provision for imposition of   countervailing duty, if required.
 1.8.7   Anti-dumping action has been taken by the Director General of Anti-dumping on certain products of SSI concern, like dry-
cell batteries, with effect from 2.8.2001 and on imports of sports shoes on 25.9.2001.  The time taken by the Indian authority to
dispose of anti-dumping cases compares favourably with other major users of anti-dumping measures in the world, as is evident
from the table given below:

3.2       Necessary Funds at RE Stage
3.2.1    The Committee observes that SSI sector is a major manufacturing sector contributing substantially to the export and
employment generation.  This sector needs a boost which can largely come from the Government.  A reduction of allocation to the
extent of 57% of the Ministry's requirement will adverse affect the growth of SSI sector.  The Committee therefore impresses upon
the Government to provide necessary funds at RE stage.Para 3.1)
Action Taken
3.2.2    The major reduction during the year 2004-05 has been under the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme, the Annual Plan allocation
for which was proposed at Rs.495.00 crore but was restricted to Rs.196.29 crore in BE 2004-05. The other schemes that are affected
due to reduced allocation are Tool Rooms, Integrated Infrastructural Development Scheme, Small Industry Cluster Development
Programme and Credit Linked Capital Subsidy Scheme. The Ministry of SSI requested the Planning Commission to provide
additional Plan provision of Rs.415.12 crore at the stage of RE, 2004-05 but this request was not considered.
Further Recommendation
3.2.3    The Committee is perturbed to know that the Planning Commission has not yielded the RE stage the genuine requirement of
the Ministry of SSI in regard to providing additional plan allocation (Rs.415.12 crore) for Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme and
against this requirement only Rs.196.29 crore was provided in BE 2004-05.  Not only this, the other SSI promotional scheme viz
Tool Rooms, Intergraded Infrastructural development Scheme got scuttled as a result of reduced allocation.  The Committee
expresses its deepest concern.  On the one hand the Government is proposing for giving adequate space to SSI units to grow and
thrive, which is  appropriate move keeping in view the global trend for strengthening of Small Enterprises but the planning and
budgetary process  in India is not adequately pushing the SSI sector ahead.  SSI sector has the tremendous potential for employment
generation and its contribution to the national exchequer is also commendable.  So why not the SSI sector is being treated as the
priority sector?  The Committee is of the considered view that SSI sector needs the sympathetic consideration from all quarters for
its accelerated promotion and proliferation and to remain competitive in the liberalized and globalized economy.  Therefore, the
Planning Commission and the government approach towards SSI sector must be focused on the same wavelength with congruence
and consensus-aid-idem which is, in the Committee's view, is lacking at present.

Recommendation
3.11     Friendly tax regime for SSI
3.11.1  The Committee desires that the Ministry of SSI should take initiatives/ measures for SSI friendly tax regime and other fiscal
measure required to promote SSI at an accelerated pace keeping in view the on going liberalization and globalization process and
the need to protect the domestic SSI Sector. In order to promote the SSI sector, certain fiscal measures need to be taken to establish
a SSI-friendly tax regime. 
Extension of General SSI Excise Exemption to SSI units manufacturing branded goods in urban areas, as available in rural areas.
Increase in the excise exemption from Rs.1 crore to Rs.2 crore to new as well as existing SSI units in rural as well as urban areas.
To increase the turnover eligibility limit for availing the General SSI Excise Exemption from Rs.3 crore to Rs.5 crore.
Lower rates of excise duties on items having large presence of SSI units in their manufacturing.
Rationalisation of custom duties in cases involving raw material and finished products for the same product category.
Lower custom duties on import of raw material (basic raw material and intermediate goods) and higher duties on finished products.
Incentives to facilitate exports by the SSI units.
In order to induce SSI Sector to undertake technology upgradation, excise and customs duty relief / concession be provided to SSIs
on purchase of new plant and machinery for technology upgradation.
Incentives for ancillarisation so as to establish better linkages between the large and small industries.
once concession / new fiscal provision is announced, it should be maintained for at least three years in order to maintain continuity
and growth.(Para 37.5)
Action Taken
The matter was taken up with the Ministry of Finance in September 2004, which has informed that to check misuse of SSI
exemption by multinationals, it was provided that the SSI exemption would not be available to units manufacturing branded goods.
However, an exception was made later, so as to promote industrialisation in rural areas. However, that Ministry has conveyed its
inability to extend the exemption to the urban areas. 
Ministry of Finance has mentioned that the number of SSI units paying central excise duty is about 37,000, which contribute only
about 2.57% of the total revenue from central excise duties.  SSI exemption, thus, adversely affects the tax-GDP ratio. Excise duty
being a tax at the manufacturing stage (the first stage), exemption from it also leads to non-accounting of production, which in turn
leads to non-payment of other taxes, such as income tax, sales tax, etc. and generation of black money. Such exemption also leads to
misuse of CENVAT credit by large duty-paying units against duty-paid documents for materials supplied to the exempted SSI
sector. It also results in breaking of the CENVAT chain. Central Government has proposed to implement State-level Value Added
Tax (VAT) from 1
st April 2005.  Grant of more exemptions would adversely affect the implementation of VAT. In view of the
above-mentioned facts, Ministry of Finance has informed that it would not be possible to accede to the suggestion.
The turnover eligibility limit for availing the General SSI Excise Exemption has been increased from Rs.3 crore to Rs.4 crore in the
Union Budget 2005-06.
Over the last few years, excise duty structure has been rationalized.  At present, 16% is the mean rate of excise duty. SSI units
already get a lower rate. Units having a turnover up to Rs. 1 crore are either fully exempt or pay a concessional duty of 60% of the
normal duty. Ministry of Finance is of the view that it would not be possible to have a separate rate for SSI units, as it would
completely distort the duty structure.
Ministry of Finance is of the view that lower rates of customs duty on raw materials for the SSI sector would necessarily involve
end-use conditions and is prone to misuse. Monitoring of such end-use conditions would result in avoidable increased interface
between the units and the tax collecting Department.

It would also require that such units are registered with the Excise Department and follow elaborate procedure, which would be
difficult for units having turnover less than Rs. 1 crore and availing of full exemption from excise duty. It would thus not be
desirable to lower the rates of customs duty on raw materials for SSI sector.
The customs duty rate, in general, is being reduced gradually taking in account the interests of both users and producers. It is also
difficult to define finished product, as finished product of one industry may be raw material of another industry. Ministry of Finance
has informed that Government will take care to ensure that for final consumption goods, duty rate are charged taking in account the
domestic angle.
3.11.8  The Income Tax Act provides a variety of fiscal incentives for promoting the industrial sector and facilitating exports, which
are also available to the small scale industries. The Act provides for a 100% deduction of export profits of 100% Export Oriented
Units (EOUs) engaged in the manufacture or production of any article, thing or computer software under section 10B and of units
engaged in the export of wood-based handicrafts under Section 10BA, upto assessment year 2009-10. In addition, a 10-year tax
benefit is provided under Section 10A of the Act to units in Special Economic Zones (SEZs).   
3.11.9  Lower rates of customs and excise duty on capital goods for SSI sector would necessarily involve end-use conditions and be
prone to misuse. Monitoring of such end-use conditions would result in avoidable increased interface between the units and the
Department. It would also require that such units are registered with the Excise Department and follow elaborate procedure, which
would be very difficult, particularly for units having turnover less than Rs. 1 crore and availing of full exemption from excise duty.
Thus, Ministry of Finance is of the view that it would not be desirable to extend such relief / concession to the SSI sector.
            Further, except for those SSI units which operate under full exemption, there is no need to prescribe a lower rate of excise
duty paid on such capital goods, as CENVAT credit of excise duty paid on such capital goods is in any case available under the
Cenvat Credit Rules 2004.
3.11.10 In order to establish better linkages between the large and small industries and provide incentive to large enterprises to sub-
contract and out-source their branded goods to the SSI units, the Ministry of SSI has again recommended to Ministry of Finance that
the SSI excise exemption should be restored to all SSI units manufacturing branded goods irrespective of their location.
3.11.11            Central Board of Excise and Customs (CBEC), Ministry of Finance has informed that no major changes have been
made in the present SSI Excise Duty Exemption Scheme since 2000, i.e., for the last four years. However, it may sometimes be
necessary to change the duty rate on various considerations, like raising revenue. Further, the Central Board of Direct Taxes
(CBDT) has informed that the fiscal incentives provided for promoting the industrial sector are aimed at encouraging continuity and
stability of the tax regime so as to facilitate growth in the economy.
Further Recommendation
3.11.12    The Committee reiterates the need for undertaking initiatives/measures for SSI freindly tax regime and other fiscal
measure required to promote SSI at an accelerated rate keeping in view to not only to  protect the domestic SSI sector from the
onslaught of  on going liberalization and globalization process but also to give sufficient space to Small Scale Industries to grow
and thrive into the medium enterprises.

OBSERVATIONS/CONCLUSIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE
Service auditing of Organs under the Ministry of Small Scale Industries
The Committee is of the view that Government should undertake service auditing of the organs under the Ministry of Small Scale
Industries by the outside agencies and not by the DC (SSI) so that their delivery system can be improved for the betterment of the
Small Scale Industries in the real terms.  By the service auditing the Committee does not intend just the financial auditing, although
the same is indispensable, but the purpose is to improve the delivery system.( 3.1.3)
Necessary Funds at RE Stage
The Committee is perturbed to know that the Planning Commission has not yielded the RE stage the genuine requirement of the
Ministry of SSI in regard to providing additional plan allocation (Rs.415.12 crore) for Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme and against
this requirement only Rs.196.29 crore was provided in BE 2004-05.  Not only this, the other SSI promotional scheme viz Tool
Rooms, Intergraded Infrastructural development Scheme got scuttled as a result of reduced allocation.  The Committee expresses its
deepest concern.  On the one hand the Government is proposing for giving adequate space to SSI units to grow and thrive, which is 
appropriate move keeping in view the global trend for strengthening of Small Enterprises but the planning and budgetary process  in
India is not adequately pushing the SSI sector ahead.  SSI sector has the tremendous potential for employment generation and its
contribution to the national exchequer is also commendable.  So why not the SSI sector is being treated as the priority sector?  The
Committee is of the considered view that SSI sector needs the sympathetic consideration from all quarters for its accelerated
promotion and proliferation and to remain competitive in the liberalized and globalized economy.  Therefore, the Planning
Commission and the government approach towards SSI sector must be focused on the same wavelength with congruence and
consensus-aid-idem which is, in the Committee's view, is lacking at present.

Undertakings.

                   •  Matters relating to Counselling, Retaining and Redeployment of rationalized employees of  CPSEs.
1.2        DPE have constituted the Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE) to strengthen and restructure CPSEs.
1.3        The Department of Public Enterprises acts as the nodal Department for all Central Public Sector Enterprises, assists in the
formation of policies pertaining to performance evaluation, autonomy, delegation, personnel management and related areas.
2.         ROLE OF DPE IN THE NEW LIBERALIZED ECONOMY
2.1        With the onset of liberalization, Government has taken various steps for CPSEs to cope up with the new challenges. Managerial
and Financial autonomy have been given to CPSEs. DPE has already deleted more than 762 guidelines in a bid to provide more
autonomy to CPSEs. Voluntary Retirement Scheme has been formulated for the workers of CPSEs to protect their interest. In order to
improve the order book position to sustain in the competitive market, guidelines have been issued by DPE on Purchase Preference Policy.
As a safety net, Counselling, Retaining and Redeployment Scheme has been introduced to rehabilitate the rationalized employees of
CPSEs.
2.2        The NCMP provides for making the public sector strong and effective. Government is considering to give enhanced financial and
operational autonomy so as to enable CPSEs to take quick and timely decisions. Further, the cases of sick and loss making CPSEs are to
be considered by the BRPSE and recommendations made for their revival/rehabilitation/closure/sale as the case may be to the
Government. The revival packages may include financial and business restructuring, formation of joint ventures, modernization of plant
and machinery, technology upgradation, need based cash infusion, rationalization of manpower, improved marketing strategy etc.
2.3        The financial restructuring of sick companies will increase the credibility of the enterprises in the market resulting in increase in
bankability of their product. Further, formation of joint venture may bring both finance and technology to the Company. Funds may also
be mobilized by sale of surplus land and other assets. Need based funds may also be provided by the Government.
2.4        The Committee was informed that after the abolition of some of the Divisions of DPE, viz., production, construction etc., DPE
has withdrawn its role for monitoring of the schemes/programmes of CPSEs. It is the primary responsibility of Administrative
Ministries/Departments to monitor the schemes/activities of CPSEs working under their administrative control.
2.5        The Committee feels that abolition of some of the divisions is unacceptable. It observes that without constant monitoring and
consultations, the policy formulation will be reduced to a mere academic exercise. The Committee considers that such a situation will
limit the full-potential and utility of a Department and thereby affecting the efficiency of the policy. Governance requires an objective
and periodic assessment of the policies by the agencies that formulate such policies. As envisaged in its mandate, to evolve DPE as the
key policy-coordinating department for the CPSEs, it must undertake constant monitoring, consultations and modifications of its
guidelines. It must also compile the data pertaining to the PSEs under all the Ministries/Departments and make appraisal. These
information should be posted as its Website for public access.

13.        BRPSE
13.1      The Committee was informed of the mandate of Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE). The Board will
advise the Government on ways and means for strengthening Public Sector Enterprises in general and making them more autonomous
and professional; consider restructuring – financial, organizational and business (including diversification, joint ventures, seeking
strategic partner, merger and acquisition) of CPSEs and suggest ways and means for funding such schemes; examine the proposals of the
Administrative Ministries for revival/restructuring of sick/loss making CPSEs for their turn around and to make suitable
recommendations related thereto; advise the Government on disinvestments/closure/sale, in full or part, in respect of chronically sick/loss
making companies which cannot be revived, in respect of such unviable companies the Board will also advise the Government about
sources of fund including sale of surplus assets of the enterprise for the payment of all legitimate dues and compensation to workers and
other costs of closure; to monitor incipient sickness, i.e., PSEs incurring loss for two consecutive years; and make recommendations and
advise the Government on such other matters as may be assigned to it from time to time.
13.2      The Board consists of Chairman, three Non-official Members and Secretary, Expenditure; Secretary, Disinvestment as Official
Members and Secretary, DPE as Member Secretary. The Department of Public Enterprises provides secretariat assistance to the Board.
Chairman, Public Enterprises Selection Board is a permanent invitee and the Secretary of the concerned Administrative
Ministry/Department is a special invitee to the meetings concerning his Ministry.

Expenditure has, however, advised this Department to manage the fund within the budget ceiling for 2004-05. For the year 2005-06,
Ministry of Finance have also advised to accommodate the expenditure within the approved BE 2005-06 and if necessary, additional fund

advise on techno-financial issues pertaining to revival of PSEs. The Committee, accordingly, recommends the Government to provide

13.6      The Committee was informed that as per the resolution of the Government constituting BRPSE, the Board would be expected to
make recommendations within two months from the date of receipt of the complete proposal from the Administrative
Ministry/Department and will also fix reasonable time limit for implementation of the recommended package. Since BRPSE has

13.7      The Committee, however, expresses concern over delay in finalizing the revival of PSEs that has incurred heavy cost of such

14.        LINKAGE BETWEEN BRPSE AND BIFR
14.1      BRPSE is an advisory body, BIFR is a statutory one to sanction suitable revival/rehabilitation packages in case of viable sick
industrial Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and recommend winding up in case of unviable units. The scope for BRPSE is
larger as it may consider cases of non-industrial enterprises as well as incipient sick enterprises also. The mechanism of BRPSE is
expected to expedite the process of revival/rehabilitation of sick and loss making CPSEs. The Board may also take the advice of experts
in the relevant field, if considered necessary. The recommendations of the Board shall be advisory in nature. The implementation of the
recommendations of the Board will essentially be the responsibility of the concerned administrative Ministry/Department, which shall, in
consultation with DPE, monitor their timely implementation. The administrative Ministries/Departments have been advised to identify
the sick CPSEs under their administrative control and submit comprehensive proposal for taking holistic view by the BRPSE. Since the
definition of sick industries for BRPSE has been broadened, the cases of enterprises which are continuously loss making but the networth
is still positive may also be considered by the BRPSE to avoid further erosion of the networth.
14.2      BIFR being a statutory body all industrial CPSEs whose accumulated losses are equal to or more than the networth are
mandatorily to be referred to BIFR. Hence, in case of such enterprises registered with the BIFR decision is taken by this body only.
However, the Government while forming its point of view on the proposals relating to revival/rehabilitation of CPSEs may consult
BRPSE.
14.3      The Repeal of Sick Industries Companies Act Bill, 2001 has already been passed by both the Houses of Parliament in December,
2003. It has also got assent of the President of India in January, 2004. As soon as the notification of Repeal of SICA is issued the BIFR
will be dismantled and all pending cases with it will be abated. However, in case of revival schemes already sanctioned the new body
namely National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT) will continue to monitor such schemes. The setting up of NCLT is held up due to the
matter being sub-judice in the Supreme Court.
14.4      The Committee observes that pending the notification to repeal SICA, the linkage between the two bodies BIFR and BRPSE
remains undefined.
14.5      The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should decide on linkage between BIFR and BRPSE at least, till
such time a final decision on BIFR is taken by the competent Court.

16.1      India is a founder member of International Centre for Promotion of Enterprises (ICPE), Ljubljana, Solvenia. Secretary, DPE is
currently, the President of the ICPE Council. India makes an annual membership contribution of US$ 75000 to ICPE from DPE budget.
DPE has been associating itself closely in the ICPE activities by way of taking part in its Assembly and Council Sessions and finalization
of ICPE – Work Programme for management development of enterprises in the developing countries both in private and public sector,
which inter-alia includes management development programmes (Long-term/Short-term), development projects, studies on topics of
interest in the public sector enterprises in the scenario of globalization/economic liberalization. ICPE has introduced some new short-term
management development programmes in the field of Total Quality Management, Advanced Management, Sustainable Development
Management, Public Policy and Management and Project Management. The programmes are instrumental in providing international
exposure and upgradation of skills to the middle/senior level executives of PSEs in India to the best management practices, which can be
emulated for further growth and the development of their PSEs.

17.        DOMESTIC SKILL ENHANCEMENT PROGRAMMES
17.1      The Committee was informed that DPE is supplementing the efforts of the Public Enterprises towards Human Resource
Development by organizing Executive Development Programme (EDP's) for senior and middle level executives in collaboration with
premier management/training institutes in the country. EDPs programme covers wide range of activities viz. management techniques,
technologies, financial management, production management etc. Human Resource Development is the thrust area of Public Sector
performance. These programmes are organized in collaboration with Indian Institute of Management, Institute of Public Enterprises,
Hyderabad, National Institute of Financial Management. During the last three years 112 executives of CPSEs have been benefited under
these programmes.
17.2      The Committee recommends that DPE must make efforts with concerned Departments and Institutions, to conduct similar EDPs
in India, with Indian Professional Institutions, for other ICPE members. Indian institutions must enter into huge global market of
professional training and consultancy. Such programmes for other countries will enhance the academic and professional profile of our
premier professional institutions.
17.3      The Committee notes with reservation that there was no specific programme for enhancing the skills of shop-floor level
technique. The Committee views it to be a stunted approach towards overall human development in PSEs.
17.4      The Committee, therefore, recommends that DPE must organize orientation and skill development programme for floor-shop
level technical functionaries as they are the end users of new material management and production techniques. The efficiency at shop-
floor level ultimately reflects in the corporate performance of the Company. The Committee recommends that CPSEs must adhere to the
principles of Total Quality Management.
17.5      As regards, training in industrial health and safety measures the Committee was informed that "As far as impart training for
industrial health is concerned, the management of PSEs also provide training to their executives regarding capital market negotiation
strategies and skills, health and stress management, industrial relation and labour issues etc. EDP programmes are devised in such a way
that they cover almost all the aspects of the industries. In addition, the management of CPSEs also imparting training to their personnel
about the safety measures. In order to maintain the industrial health, management also remains in constant touch with workers
representative to avoid hartal, lockout, strike tc."
17.6      The Committee finds the reply hardly convincing, and impresses upon the DPE to give a more serious effort to impart more
structured and elaborate orientation to the management and technical staff in this regard.

18.        MoU SYSTEM
18.1      On its query on the Government's obligations as one of the contracting party in the MoU, the Committee was informed that the
Government/Administrative Ministry's obligations were to support the PSEs to achieve the pre-defined targets in the MoU. The specific
issues which are incorporated in the MoUs pertain to approval of various projects, delegation of powers, financial assistance,
coordination with various Government agencies etc.
18.2      The Committee would like to know the nature of such support to PSEs in achieving the targets in MoU. The Committee observes
that the number of PSEs earning favourable ratings is increasing while those getting 'Poor' rating have decreased. Keeping this in view,
the Committee has also observed that the number of PSEs entering the MoU has been falling from 108 in 1999-2000 to 96 in 2003-04.
The Committee wonders, if the PSEs having poor ratings are being excluded from the MoU system. If that is true, is it safe to construe
that the Government's support under MoU system is practically not available to the loss making PSEs. The Committee would like to
know if there is a policy to exclude such PSEs from signing the MoU. If so, the Committee would like to know the rationale behind such
policy.
18.3      The Committee desires that the Government should extend its support to the PSEs signing MoU without compromising the MoU
parameters. The policy should be such so as to include more PSEs to sign MoU. It desires the PDE to examine the issue.
19.        DETAILS OF MOU PARAMETERS
19.1      There are four categories of the parameters against which achievements of any PSE is rated :
                   •  Static Parameters,
                   •  Dynamic Parameters,
                   •  Enterprise-specific Parameters, and
                   •  Sector-specific Parameters.
19.2      Static parameters reflect cost and benefits associated with the operation of the enterprise in a given period of time, while the
dynamic parameters result in benefits in the future. Static variables referred to financial performance indicators (profit related), financial
indicators (size related) and financial returns indicators (total factor productivity/labour productivity). Variables that depict the health of
the company such as product quality of the future, products share with high value realisations, customer satisfaction, extent of
globalisation, market share, R&D outlay etc., are referred to as dynamic factors. Enterprise specific parameters relate to parameters like
safety, environment, ecological considerations viz., Parameters that do not get reflected in increased profits either during the year of
investment or later but considered important from the view point of the society. Sector specific parameters reflect how the macro
environment affects the PSE.
20.        RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE NCAER ON MOU SYSTEM
20.1      The Committee was informed of the efficacy of the MoU system that has been appreciated by the CEOs in the study conducted
by the NCAER on the issue.
20.2      All recommendations in respect of guidelines made in the NCAER Report were accepted and incorporated in the MoU
Guidelines. The Committee is informed that in the Guidelines, the total weight in MoU assessment format was divided into points against
groups of parameters viz. common parameters, sector-specific parameters and enterprise-specific parameters. The common parameters
carry 80% weight which includes 'static financial parameters (50%) and dynamic parameters (30%)' applicable for all PSEs other than
social, financial trading and consultancy PSEs. Sector-specific parameters, which reflect sectoral thrusts and priorities, carry 10% weight
and enterprise-specific parameters, which reflect performance improvement measures at the enterprise/unit level carry 10% weight.
20.3      Added value concept has been incorporated in the MoU system to capture productivity improvement in real terms. Added value
is to be computed as gross margin less returns to capital, which in turn may be computed as capital recovery factor @ 4% the capital
employed for social sector PSEs and @ 10% of the capital employed for all other PSEs.
20.4      The Committee feels that the financial parameters in the MoU system still do not reflect the fact that the PSEs are still largely
