20.5      The Committee takes note with reservation that DPE has not conducted any specific Survey conducted in relation to
technological obsolence of PSEs.
20.6      In view of the fact that the PSEs were established as the pioneers in industrial technology, the Committee recommends that the
Government must undertake a survey to ascertain the technology status of PSEs that has definite bearing over profitability and efficiency
of the Public Sector. The DPE being the nodal coordinating Department on non-financial policies, must prepare a comprehensive
approach paper on Sector-wise technological status of PSEs in consultation with respective PSEs, Administrative Departments and expert
agencies like DSIR.
20.7      The Committee was informed that Research and Development has been given 4% weightage in the MoU guidelines for the year
2005-06. As regards technology status in the MoU parameters, no such weightage has been given, but a provision has been made to
incorporate any dynamic parameters if the Task Force comes to the conclusion that new parameters are relevant to that particular PSE.
20.8      Considering that the PSEs were envisaged as the pioneers in industrial technology, the Committee observed that Technology and
R&D have not been suitably factored in MoU ratings of the PSEs that are essentially Techno-commercial entities. As such Technological
upgradation and R&D should be an integral part of revival strategy of the PSEs. It is observed by the PSEs that most of the PSEs do not
have an elaborate R&D set up. The Committee wonders if PSEs have owned any patent in recent years, which itself is a distinct
commercial activity.
20.9      The Committee recommends that technology upgradation and R&D must be given due weightage in MoU parameters in
consultation with expert bodies like DSIR.
20.10    The Committee also recommends that as a part of re-aligning with market, the PSEs should involve in technology trade and
consultancy services that may be enhance their profitability at a lesser additional investment.
21.        POLICY OF PROFESSIONALISATION OF BOARDS
21.1      The Committee notes that while routine functions of the PSE are performed by the Functional Directors and Policy decision is
vested with the Board of Directors consisting of Functional Directors, Official Directors and Independent Directors. The
professionalisation of Board of Directors was considered by various Committees and on the recommendations of these Committees,
detailed guidelines were issued in September, 1984 which was subsequently modified in 1992 with a view to professionalise the Board of
PSEs.
21.2      The Committee has been informed by the DPE that emphasis is laid on inclusion of such persons from outside in to the Boards
who have experience in the industry or academics or research in the relevant fields. The policy advocates that measures must be taken to
make these enterprises more growth oriented and technically dynamic which would not have been possible without inducting
professionals on the Board of Directors. The non-official Directors to be inducted on the Board are to be drawn from the public men,
technocrats, management experts and consultants and professional managers in industry and trade with a high degree of proven ability.
21.3      Department of Public Enterprises accordingly issued guidelines in 1991, which stipulates that outside professionals should be
inducted on the Board of PSEs and also the number of such Directors should be at least 1/3rd of the actual strength of the Board. The
guidelines also provide that the number of Government Directors on the Boards should not be more than one-sixth of the actual strength
of the Board subject to a maximum of two. Apart from this there should be some functional Directors on each Board whose number
should not exceed 50% of the actual strength of the Board. In the case of listed PSEs headed by executive Chairman, the number of non-
official Directors (Independent Directors) should be at least half of the strength of the Board.
21.4      The Committee has studied the implementation of the policy of including Independent Directors in the Boards and its impact on
Professionalisation of Boards, during its interaction with the representatives of the PSEs across the sectors viz., Coal India Ltd., NALCO,
Hindustan Copper Ltd., MSTC Ltd., KIOCL, BPCL and Chennai Refineries, Goa Shipyard, HAL and BEML.

21.5      Despite elaborate policy intentions to include persons of proven expertise in the Boards of PSEs, the Committee has observed
that former bureaucrats, serving representatives of autonomous organisations under Government, representatives of subsidiary
companies, have been included in the Boards as Independent Directors in addition to Functional and Official Part-time Directors. In

seriously imperiled the viability of such PSEs.

appointments in the PSEs under the Ministry of Defence, on the plea that Armed Forces were the premier customers of these PSEs. The

being involved in the defence sector, why cannot the defence related PSEs harness potential in civilian and export market with their dual-
use products and technology.
22.        APPOINTMENT OF DIRECTORS
22.1      The Committee was informed of the institutional mechanism for the appointment of Directors. Appointment of Functional
Directors are done on the recommendations of the Public Enterprises Selection Board. The recommendations of the Board are processed
by the concerned Administrative Ministry/Department and with the approval of concerned Minister/ACC. In case of PSEs other than
Miniratna and Navratna, the appointment of non-official Directors is done by the concerned Administrative Ministry on the
recommendation of PESB and with the approval of ACC. In case of Navratna and Miniratna PSEs, the Government has set up a Search
Committee for selection of Non-Official Directors. The recommendation of Search Committee is processed by the Administrative
Ministry for obtaining approval of ACC.
23.        COMPOSITION OF PESB
23.1      The PESB consists of one Chairperson and three Members. The Chairperson and Members shall be persons who have had a long
and distinguished career in management of public or private corporations or public administration and have a proven record of
achievements, preferably, in the field of personnel, finance, production or marketing. The three Members of the PESB shall be :
                   •  A distinguished former Chief Executive of a PSE;
                   •  A distinguished behavioral scientist with experience in selection of top management personnel;
                   •  A distinguished former civil servant with experience in management of PSEs or in areas of finance, industry or economic
affairs.
24.        CATEGORIES OF DIRECTORS ON THE BOARD
24.1      There are three categories of Directors in a Board of Directors of the CPSEs consists of the 
followings :
                   •  Functional Directors including CMD/MD
                   •  Part-time Official Directors/Government Directors
                   •  Part-time Independent Directors/Non-official Directors
24.2      The Functional Directors are appointed by the Government with reference to the job descriptions of each post and following the

27.        PURCHASE PREFERENCE POLICY
27.1      As per the Purchase Preference Policy (PPP) where the quoted price is within 10% of the lowest price, other things being equal,
purchase preference should be granted to the public enterprise concerned, at the lowest valid price bid (L 1). The main objective of this
policy was to enable the CPSEs to adjust themselves to the new environment of competition and efficiency in the wake of
liberalisation/globalization. The policy aimed at to make the CPSEs viable through utilization of the created/installed capacities to the
fullest extent by improving order booking. It was however, provided that the quality requirements and delivery schedules should of
course be enforced.
27.2      As per available information, during 2002-03 and 2003-04 CPSEs obtained orders of Rs. 2745 crore under the policy. The details
are as under :–
Year No. of CPSEs Amount of order
2002-03 36 Rs. 1167 crore
2003-04 35 Rs. 1578 crore
27.3      As compared to turnover of the 36 CPSEs during 2002-03 the percentage of orders received by these enterprises due to purchase
preference was only 0.40%.
27.4      In response to a querry on over dependence of PSEs on Government orders, the Committee was informed that the Government is
not the only major buyer in many sectors such as Oil, Steel, Chemicals, Consumer Goods, Fertilizers. In these sectors, the PSEs are
supplying their products to their customers both in the Government and Non-Government sector. The quantum of orders received due to
PPP is merely 0.40% of the turnover.
27.5      Many PSEs particularly in Heavy Industry Sector, have complained lack of orders from Government and PSEs as major cause of
their financial constraints. The Committee would like DPE to identify the Sectors that still rely heavily on Government orders.
27.6      The Committee feels that Purchase Preference Policy could be treated only as an interim arrangement. Such as arrangement
contributes practically nothing to the Consolidated Fund by way of earning from market. The PSEs must be increasingly encouraged to
diversify in the open market and realign themselves with the emerging market through Joint Ventures and global marketing alliances
instead of relying solely on Government/PSEs for orders. Though the Policy provides a cushion for PSEs, they must take benefit of
current buoyancy in the market.

The Committee wonders, if the PSEs having poor ratings are being excluded from the MoU system. If that is true, is it safe to construe
that the Government's support under MoU system is practically not available to the loss making PSEs. The Committee would like to
know if there is a policy to exclude such PSEs from signing the MoU. If so, the Committee would like to know the rationale behind such
policy.                                                                                  (Para 18.2)
            The Committee desires that the Government should extend its support to the PSEs signing MoU without compromising the MoU
parameters. The policy should be such so as to include more PSEs to sign MoU. It desires the DPE to examine the issue.            (Para
18.3)
            The Committee feels that the financial parameters in the MoU system still do not reflect the fact that the PSEs are still largely
dependent on bulk Government orders. Most of the PSEs still do not have any significant presence in global export market despite being
in the business for long. Most of the Excellent-rated PSEs function in monopoly market environment. The PSEs have not been able to
secure the 'Brand loyalty' of customers, wherever the sector has been opened up for private sector and this is reflected in the receding
market share of such PSEs. The Committee would like to have DPE's comment on its observations.            (Para 20.4)
            The Committee takes note with reservation that DPE has not conducted any specific Survey conducted in relation to technological
obsolence of PSEs.                                                                                         (Para 20.5)
            In view of the fact that the PSEs were established as the pioneers in industrial technology, the Committee recommends that the
Government must undertake a survey to ascertain the technology status of PSEs that has definite bearing over profitability and efficiency
of the Public Sector. The DPE being the nodal coordinating Department on non-financial policies, must prepare a comprehensive
approach paper on Sector-wise technological status of PSEs in consultation with respective PSEs, Administrative Departments and expert
agencies like DSIR.                                                                          (Para 20.6)
            Considering that the PSEs were envisaged as the pioneers in industrial technology, the Committee observed that Technology and
R&D have not been suitably factored in MoU ratings of the PSEs that are essentially Techno-commercial entities. As such Technological
upgradation and R&D should be an integral part of revival strategy of the PSEs. It is observed by the PSEs that most of the PSEs do not
have an elaborate R&D set up. The Committee wonders if PSEs have owned any patent in recent years, which itself is a distinct
commercial activity.                                                               (Para 20.8)
            The Committee recommends that technology upgradation and R&D must be given due weightage in MoU parameters in
consultation with expert bodies like DSIR.                                                                            (Para 20.9)
            The Committee also recommends that as a part of re-aligning with market, the PSEs should involve in technology trade and
consultancy services that may enhance their profitability at a lesser additional investment.        (Para 20.11)
            Despite elaborate policy intentions to include persons of proven expertise in the Boards of PSEs, the Committee has observed that
former bureaucrats, serving representatives of autonomous organisations under Government, representatives of subsidiary companies,
have been included in the Boards as Independent Directors in addition to Functional and Official Part-time Directors. In several cases the
retired bureaucrats are reappointed as Independent Directors. The Committee feels that such an arrangement does not fall in the spirit of
the policy of appointing Independent Directors on the Boards of Directors of the PSEs. The Committee also expresses reservation on the
practice of renewing the tenures of existing Directors in some cases. The Committee urges the department to ascertain that the
implementation of policy is in consonance with its true objectives and bring to the notice of this Committee any dilution in the
'Professionalisation' of Boards.                                                                      (Para 21.5)
            While interacting with the PSEs, the Committee has observed a clear disjoint in the Central and State Governments that has

168th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/168threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:52:31]
seriously imperiled the viability of such PSEs.                                                                        (Para 21.6)
            The Committee is of the view that greater involvement of the stakes of the respective State Government is essential to clear such
disjoints. Also a senior representative of the concerned State Government should be included in the Boards of PSEs as one of the two
Government Directors.                                                                                                                                        (Para 21.7)
            The Committee observed that distinct preference was given to serving officers from Armed Forces in the Board level
appointments in the PSEs under the Ministry of Defence, on the plea that Armed Forces were the premier customers of these PSEs. The
Committee wonders, if such an arrangement reduces PSEs as a captive Company instead of an autonomous commercial entity. The
Committee is of the view that the products of these PSEs have a large civilian market too. The Committee feels that if the private sector is
being involved in the defence sector, why cannot the defence related PSEs harness potential in civilian and export market with their dual-
use products and technology.                                                              (Para 21.8)
            The Committee is of the opinion that there should be uniformity in the qualification, selection and mandate of Non-Functional
Part-Time Directors, as too many categories within one Board may affect its efficiency and autonomy. The Board must be defined in
terms of its mandate and the interest of the Company and not by the categories of its Directors. The Committee would like to have
Government's comments on the need for uniformity in Part-time Directors.             (Para 24.3)
            The Committee recommends that the Government must impress upon the concerned 
Ministries to adhere to the time-frame for the selection of Directors and expedite the appointments of Directors.          (Para 25.4)
            The Committee is constrained to observe that the information provided by the DPE was not only evasive but also insufficient and
incomplete. The Committee observes that DPE has not reacted to the criteria of "Independent Directors" as elaborated by the Naresh
Chandra Committee. Similarly the DPE has not responded to the Narayan Murthy Committee's recommendation on "Nominee
Directors".                                                                             (Para 25.6)
            The Committee observes that these Expert Committees were set up by the Government or the agencies under its control. The
Reports of these Expert Committees are extremely relevant to the issue of Professionalisation of Boards as they deal extensively the
mandate, functional 
autonomy, obligations and the constitution of Boards of Directors. Their findings can be applied to enhance the autonomy and efficiency
and draw greater degree of professional excellence to the Boards of Directors.          (Para 25.7)
            The Committee recommends that the DPE should assess these reports more fruitfully instead of dismissing them for
administrative nuances and inform the Committee of its view and rationale thereof.                   (Para 25.8)
            The Committee feels that the minimum educational qualification should be raised to a Post-Graduate Degree/Diploma from a
premier institution in a professional course, management, engineering, financial management of HR management. Also the size of
corporate body should be specified for the CMD/MD being appointed as the Independent Directors. (Para 26.2)
            The Committee feels that a Joint Secretary belongs to a generalized service, he may not have requisite and relevant expertise to
become an Independent Director in a PSE unless he has the experience of those many years in the field relevant to the functioning and
corporate objectives of the PSE. The Committee recommends that this aspect should be specified in the eligibility criteria for Independent
Directors.                                                                                        (Para 26.3)
            The Committee feels that the maximum age for Independent Directors too should be appropriately reduced to maintain uniformity
in the Board of Directors.                                                                                    (Para 26.4)
            Many PSEs particularly in Heavy Industry Sector, have complained lack of orders from Government and PSEs as major cause of
their financial constraints. The Committee would like DPE to identify the sectors that still rely heavily on Government Orders. (Para
27.5)
            The Committee feels that Purchase Preference Policy could be treated only as an interim arrangement. Such an arrangement
contributes practically nothing to the Consolidated Fund by way of earning from market. The PSEs must be increasingly encouraged to

current buoyancy in the market.                                             (Para 27.6)
            The Committee seeks information on the action taken by the DPE and the Government on the outcome of these meetings.

INTRODUCTION
 
            I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been
authorised by the Committee, hereby present this One Hundred Sixty-nineth Report on Demands for Grants (2005-06)
pertaining to the Department of Heavy Industry (Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises).
2.         The Committee during its detailed discussion held on the 29th and 30th March, 2005 with the representatives of
the Ministry of Heavy Industries, Six Public Enterprises and Auto Associations assessed the performance of the PSEs
under the Department, the industry in general as well as the prospects and constraints before Auto Sector.
3.         The Committee's queries, recommendations and observations are reflected at appropriate places in this Report.
4.         The Committee acknowledges the cooperation of the Ministry of Heavy Industries and Public Enterprises in
providing useful inputs.
6. The Committee at its meeting held on 3rd May, 2005, considered and adopted the Report.
 
New Delhi;
3rd May, 2005
SANTOSH  BAGRODIA
Chairman, Department-related Parliamentary
Standing Committee on Industry.
 
REPORT
 
1.         THE MANDATE OF DEPARTMENT OF HEAVY INDUSTRY (DHI)
1.1       The Department focuses on promoting the development and growth of capital goods and engineering industry in
the country and administratively dealing with 48 PSEs. The Department of Heavy Industry is also concerned with the
development of the heavy engineering industry, machine tool industry, heavy electrical industry, industrial machinery
and auto-industry and administers 48 Central PSEs.
1.2       The industries covered by this Department meet the requirement of equipments for basic industries such as steel,
non-ferrous metals, fertilizers, refineries, petrochemicals, shipping, paper, cement, sugar etc. The Department is
responsible for development of a wide range of intermediate engineering products like castings, forgings, diesel engine,
industrial gears and gear boxes.They cater to the need of goods and services for almost all sectors of the economy,
including power, rail and road transport etc.
1.3       The Committee takes note that the current structural readjustment and liberalization programme launched in
early 1990s ought to effect public sector reform. At present the public sector enterprises appear to have constraints in
withstanding the global and domestic competition due to financial, structural and technological factors.
1.4       The Committee observes that many of the PSEs, however, have not been able to retain their original position in
the market and withstand the global competition in the new liberalized economy.
DEMANDS FOR GRANTS
2.0       Status of PSEs under DHI
2.1       The Committee in the process of assessing the Demands for Grants for 2005-06 in respect of Department of

169th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/169threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:53:32]
Heavy Industry took an overview of the PSEs under the Department. The Committee was informed by the DHI that
there were 48 PSEs under the Department out of which 9 were closed and another 5 were not in operation, thus leaving
the Department with 34 PSEs. As per the financial results of 
(2003-04), only 9 out of 34 PSEs made profit and remaining 25 incurred loss. Out of the 25 loss making PSEs, 17 are
registered with BIFR after they became sick. Even of the nine profit-making PSEs only four have got favourable MoU
ratings in 2003-04.
2.2       The Committee was informed that by 31st March, 2004, Government and the holding PSEs had made an
investment of Rs. 3861.44 crores in the PSEs under the Department. The aggregate net worth of the 34 operational PSEs
is negative to the tune of Rs. 3930.92 crores (negative).
2.3       The Committee notes that most of the companies under major conglomerates like BBUNL, BYNL, HMT,
AYCL, with diversified business in heavy engineering, are making losses. These companies rely on major Government
projects for orders to generate working capital. The Committee feels that these engineering conglomerates have critical
potential for the capital goods sector in the country and need to be re-aligned to the larger market. The Committee
would like to know of the measures that are being considered in this respect for these companies.
2.4       The Committee was informed that the losses in the PSEs is mainly attributed to the shortfall in production in
some enterprises owing to poor order book, shortage of working capital, surplus manpower, obsolete plant and
machinery, increase in the cost of inputs etc. PSEs are carrying the conventional baggage of disadvantages like excess
manpower and low level of functional autonomy in addition to disadvantages of location etc. Not only inadequacy of
investment but lack of timely investment have caused significant damage to public sector capabilities. Government
investments and loans including loans for VRS are flowing to PSEs at exorbitant rate of interest further crippling their
financial performance. VRS funds flow to the companies at 17.5% rate of interest largely eclipsing the advantages in
wage bill arising out of manpower rationalization.
2.5       Productivity of PSEs has been generally very low. The Committee has been informed that the ratio of wages and
salaries as a percentage of turnover is very high. In most cases, salary and wages component is unsustainable and eats
up most other advantages that PSEs enjoys.
2.6       With the onset of globalisation, tariff levels are gradually coming down thereby putting pressure on domestic
industries and on PSUs in particular to perform in this environment. While the profit-making PSE are making funds
available from their own internal resources for keeping pace with the technological development, whereas the loss
making PSEs rely heavily on budgetary support. It was informed that some structural measures for improving the
performance of the PSEs should be taken as an alternative to privatization, e.g. :–
            •           Providing greater functional autonomy
            •           Professionalisation of Boards of PSEs
            •           Signing of MoU between PSEs and Government
2.7       However, the Committee observes that most of the PSEs are too heavily dependent on Government for finances
and business orders to exercise the autonomy.
2.8       The Committee observes that the Government has to take necessary steps to reduce the dependence of PSEs on
Government for finances and orders; Professionalise the Boards of the PSEs, in the spirit of Government's policy
leading to more and more autonomy and enter into MoU agreements with more companies, setting out elaborate
objectives for better results.
3.0       FIVE-YEAR TREND OF AGGREGATE LOSS/PROFIT INCURRED BY THE PSES UNDER DHI
3.1       The Committee was informed that the PSEs under DHI have incurred huge net losses before tax during recent
years is as under :–
(Rs. in crores)
 1999-2000 2000-01 2001-02 2002-03 2003-04
Profit of profit making PSEs 545 384 750 851 1123
Loss of loss making PSEs –923 –1254 –1550 –1877 –1936
Net profit (+)/Loss (–) –378 –870 –800 –1026 –813
3.2       The Committee observes with grave concern that the PSEs under DHI have been incurring huge aggregate losses
that not only eatup the aggregate profits earned by few companies but also burden the exchequer with huge net losses.
The Committee is more worried as the losses are increasing year after year. The Committee impresses upon the
Government to not only arrest the decline but also reverse the trend so that loss making companies can also earn profits.
The Committee also desires that it may be apprised of the specific steps taken in this regard.
4.0       PSES RELIANCE ON GOVERNMENT ORDERS
4.1       The Committee was told that the PSEs were set up to achieve accelerated growth of the core sectors of the

169th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/169threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:53:32]
economy, to cater to the equipment needs of strategically important sectors like Railways, Power, Telecommunications,
Defence etc., with a view to achieve self-sufficiency in these sectors. Since many of these sectors are still dominated by
Government/PSEs etc. Therefore, dependence on orders from these sectors is likely to continue at least for some more
time.
4.2       The Committee recommends that the public sector enterprises should be encouraged and advised to gradually
and increasingly compete in private sector projects as more and more sectors have been opened up for private sector.
PSEs may be given preference for Government orders but it does not preclude them from exploring larger market
domestically or globally. PSEs must not be allowed to suffer due to drying up of Government orders. In any case, by
supplying the Government orders practically does not add anything to the Consolidated Fund of India. It is only
'Deemed Earning'.
4.3       The Committee recommends that with the opening up of the economy and WTO regulations coming into force.
PSEs must make use of new opportunities by entering into JVs and marketing tie-ups to enter into larger global market.
The Department should issue specific guidelines to its PSEs to explore export markets.
4.4       The Committee further recommends that diversification of market should be incorporated as one of the
significant factor in MoU rating of the PSEs so as to encourage them to explore new market.
5.0       EXPORT PERFORMANCE OF PSEs
5.1       Aggregate export performance of PSEs under DHI during the last 3 years has been as under :–
(Rs. in crores)
Exports 2001-02 2002-03 2003-04
Physical Exports 1062 692 632
Deemed Exports 1560 1562 1473
Total Exports : 2622 2254 2105
5.2       The Committee observes that except BHEL and HMT, not many PSEs have any significant export earnings. Out
of the total exports, more than 95% of the exports is contributed by BHEL as the company is trying to become more and
more competitive.
5.3       The Committee also wonders if Deemed exports create a benchmark in international market.
5.4       The Committee recommends that the Department of Heavy Industry must evolve a strategy, as an integral part of
revival scheme for PSEs to promote exports given the country has a well-laid capital goods sector.
5.5       The Committee notes that the growth in exports is hindered due to non-availability of adequate supplier's credit
to buyers, higher rates of interest and lower duration for which the credit is available. The Committee recommends that
the Government must take a favourable view of the proposals made by the Department of Heavy Industry with regard to
availability of adequate supplier's credit to buyers, low rate of interest and longer duration of credit to facilitate growth
in export performance of the PSEs.
6.0       SCENARIO OF HEAVY CAPITAL GOODS INDUSTRY
6.1       The Committee was informed that the capital goods sector, has posted a robust growth of 13.6 per cent in 2003-
04 and has maintained its growth momentum during the current year as well. Prospects are encouraging for sustaining
domestic growth in view of the beginnings of an investment cycle.
6.2       Majority of the PSEs under DHI are in the capital goods sector catering to the requirement of sectors like Power,
Petroleum, Railways, Fertilizer, Chemicals etc. The capital goods sector in the country registered a growth of 13.3% in
April-December 2004, compared to which the PSEs under DHI registered a matching growth rate of 13.1%.
6.3       The Committee observes that while the aggregate growth in PSEs under DHI compares well with the capital
goods growth, but this level of growth is mainly contributed by one PSE namely Bharat Heavy Electricals Ltd. (BHEL)
which showed a growth of 15% during this period. Most of the PSEs have shown a negative growth mainly due to
financial, marketing and technological constraints.
6.4       The Committee apprehends that despite robust growth in capital goods sector, the PSEs find difficult to secure
orders and in several cases to execute the orders due to lack of working capital and other constraints. The Committee,
accordingly, recommends that efforts should be made by the PSEs to utilize current opportunities in the market. As the
capital goods market is essentially technology-intensive, PSEs must undertake the technology upgradation to secure
high-end market.
7.0       PSES UNDER DHI REFERRED TO BIFR
7.1       The Committee took note of the role of Board for Industrial Financing Reconstruction in deciding the revival of
PSEs. It determines the preventive, ameliorative, remedial measures which need to be taken with respect to such
companies and the enforcement of the measures. The measures are mainly legal, financial restructuring and managerial.
The BIFR through the services of the Operating Agencies consider the required technological upgradation while

finalizing the revival package in a comprehensive manner. In most of the cases, the Techno-Financial studies are
prepared by another expert agency on behalf of Operating Agency (OA). The views of PSE and the concerned
Ministry/Department are invariably incorporated in the Draft Rehabilitation Scheme (DRS) proposed under the aegis of
BIFR. Requirement of technological upgradation are addressed in the DRS.

8.0       THE MANDATE OF NEW BRPSE
8.1       The mandate of Board for Reconstruction of Public Sector Enterprises (BRPSE) is to undertake strengthening,
modernizing, reviving and restructuring of public sector enterprises. The BRPSE was constituted by Government on
6.12.2004 consisting of a Chairman and three non-official members and three official members.
8.2       The Board will advise the Government on ways and means for strengthening Public Sector Enterprises in
general and making them more autonomous and professional; consider restructuring - financial, organizational and
business (including diversification, joint ventures, seeking strategic partner, merger and acquisition) of CPSEs and
suggest ways and means for funding such schemes; examine the proposals of the Administrative Ministries for
revival/restructuring of sick/loss making of CPSEs for their turnaround and to make suitable recommendations related
thereto; advise the Government on disinvestments/closure/sale, in full or part, in respect of chronically sick/loss making
companies which cannot be revived, in respect of such unviable companies the Board will also advise the Government
about sources of fund including sale of surplus assets of the enterprise for the payment of all legitimate dues and
compensation to workers and other costs of closure; to monitor incipient sickness i.e. PSEs incurring loss for two
consecutive years; and make recommendations and advise the Government on such other matters as may be assigned to
it from time to time.
9.0       LINKAGE BETWEEN BRPSE AND BIFR

9.1       The Committee was informed that there was no direct linkage between BRPSE and BIFR. Further, though the
Government proposes to repeal Sick Industries Companies Act (SICA), which would mean disbanding of BIFR and
replace it by National Company Law Tribunal (NCLT). As the matter is sub judice, no further action could be taken by
the Government.
9.2       The Committee observes that there is no major qualitative difference in the mandates of BRPSE and BIFR. It
seems a replacement of BIFR, a quasi-judicial body by the BRPSE that is a recommendatory body. The Committee is
yet to understand whose decision will have precedence in case of contradiction?
9.3       The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government should decide the on linkage between BIFR and
BRPSE at least, till such time a final decision on BIFR is taken by the competent Court.
9.4       The Committee also observes with concern that multiplicity of agencies even in deciding the revival may and
has resulted in differences in opinion, successive appeals and costly delays. Even after deciding, the revival packages
have failed in several cases. The Committee apprehends that in the process of analyzing the cases of BIFR has assessed
the Techno-Financial feasibilities of individual PSEs prepared by expert agencies. Yet the appeals are filed in AAIFR
and High Courts/Supreme Court and now these may further will be referred to new BRPSE for appraisal before a final
decision is taken by the Cabinet. The entire process is time consuming and costly. The cost of delay has been immense
in terms of rising liabilities that have eaten up the net worth of the PSEs. It may be an effort in duplication.
9.5       The Committee recommends that the Department must take steps to expedite the decision and implementation
for the PSEs' sustainable revival. Accountability must be fixed for the successful and sustained revival once case is
decided by the competent authority.
9.6       The Committee further recommends that the Government should inform the Committee of the revival packages
approved by the Cabinet before approaching the Parliament for Supplementary Demands. The Department must also
give a post-revival SWOT analysis of the PSEs and that must reflect its Technological strengths and market viability.
9.7       The Committee was informed that a total requirement of Rs. 1475 crore as budgetary support for the year 2005-
06 was projected to the Planning Commission. However, Planning Commission recommended a drastically reduced
amount of Rs. 406 crore as budgetary support to Ministry of Finance. The Committee observes that out of the total
budgetary support of Rs. 406 crores under plan expenditure in 2005-06, a meager amount of Rs. 149.70 crores has been
provided for 34 functioning PSEs under Department of Heavy Industry.

24.0     IMPLICATIONS OF TAX PROPOSALS ON PSEs
24.1     The Committee was informed of the implications on some of the PSEs of the tax proposals contained in the
Union Budget 2005-06 :–
            (i)         Peak custom duty has been reduced from 20% to 15%. This will have negative impact on the PSEs under
DHI where they face competition from imported products.
            (ii)        Custom duty of capital goods sector has been reduced from 15% to 10% and to 5% in some cases. This
will have a negative impact on PSEs like BHEL, HMT.
            (iii)       Excise duty on tyres had been reduced to 16%. This would benefit the tyre manufacturing industry
including, Tyre Corporation of India.
            (iv)       Infrastructure projects are likely to spur growth in cement sector. Cement Corporation of India (CCI) is
likely to benefit.
            (v)        Thrust to rural electrification will provide benefit to PSEs in the electrical industry like AYCL.
24.2     The Committee views that current regime of lowering the customs and increasing the excise duty on items like
steel will have serious implications for the PSEs in capital goods sector.
24.3     The Committee cautions the Government that such a duty regime would result in an uneven competition with
PSEs facing serious handicap against cheaper imports and MNCs. If the Government is serious about reviving the PSEs,
it must help them regain their standing in domestic market instead of imposing a duty regime that perpetuates the
disadvantage against cheap imports. It is the responsibility of the Government to seek redressal, if necessary, against
such an uneven competition under the WTO provisions.
25.0     IMPACT OF INFRASTRUCTURE INITIATIVES ON PSEs
25.1     Proposed infrastructural initiatives in the budget are likely to generate demand in these sectors.
25.2     However, the Committee only wonders whether the PSEs have the capacity to take advantage of the new
opportunities or they will cede the advantage to foreign competitors in an open market.
26.0     IMPACT OF BUDGET PROPOSALS ON AUTO INDUSTRY
26.1     The Committee was informed that the budget for the current year to a large extent provides for a growth
environment for the automotive industry. The reduction of corporate tax, the continuation of the benefit for in-house
R&D, the reduction of taxes on inputs and raw materials, the reduction in duty for electric vehicles parts are some of the
positives of the budget. Introduction of VAT has been welcomed by the auto industry. Increased allocation for
automotive R&D from Rs. 72 crore to Rs. 206 crore will also help in setting up of world-class testing and R&D
facilities under NATRIP.
26.2     The Committee took note of the benefit of 150% weighted deduction u/s 35 (2AB) of Income Tax Act for in-
house R&D expenditure to the automotive industry has now been extended upto 31 March, 2007. A number of OEMs
would be utilizing this benefit for continuously upgrading their R&D set up in India to meet the new emission and
safety norms over the next few years as also for new product and process developments in India which otherwise
requires considerable R&D effort.
26.3     In its interaction with auto associations, the Committee noted that the Auto Sector has generally supported the
application of VAT but has sought further streamlining.
26.4     The auto associations further apprised the Committee that reduction in depreciation rates would adversely effect
the new investments; customs duty on auto-components have been reduced to below ASEAN levels, which will be a
disincentive for value addition whereas customs duty on raw materials is higher compared to ASEAN levels. Imposition
of cess on petrol and diesel would adversely affect the growth of auto sector.
26.5     Fringe Benefit Tax to increase cost of operations and erode competitiveness of industry, specially export
oriented industry.
26.6     The ARAI informed the Committee of the adverse impact of the Notification No. 50/96 of Department of
Revenue, Ministry of Finance, pertaining to exemption of customs duty to the Companies engaged in R&D. ARAI,
despite being the premier R&D institution in auto sector is left out of the ambit of this exemption as it is registered as a
'Society' and not as a Company.
26.7     The Committee was further told that the Notification No. 51/96 of Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance
extended certain import facilities to the 'public funded research institution' registered with DSIR. The Notification
practically excludes ARAI as it is a self-sufficient R&D institution. However, the Committee recognizes that extension
of such facility to ARAI, would enhance the R&D capability in the auto sector.
26.8     The Committee recommends that the benefits of the Notification Nos. 50/96 and 51/96 should not discriminate
against the premier R&D institutions like ARAI for nuances. The Committee directs the DHI to pursue the matter with
Ministry of Finance.

            (i)         Indian coals, which have a high ash content, can be utilized to generate power in more environment-
friendly manner.
            (ii)        Emission of oxides of nitrogen (NOx) and oxides of sulphur (SOx) will be reduced, resulting in
preventing "acid rain".
            (iii)       Emission of particulate matter (ash) will be reduced, resulting in cleaner, dust free atmosphere.
            (iv)       Efficiency of generating power from coal will be increased, resulting in less coal being burnt to generate
same amount of power. This will help in reducing the production of carbon dioxide (CO
2) which is the cause of the
"Green house effect" resulting in global warming.
28.0     FLUID CONTROL RESEARCH INSTITUTE
28.1     The Committee appreciated that the flow measurement technique developed at FCRI has been applied by BHEL
for its large hydro generation sets supplied to Karnataka State and elsewhere. In Hydrocarbon product handling for oil
and gas/water distribution network, FCRI is being approached as 'Referral Agency' for measurement and certification of
relevant products. Import substitution for specific requirements has been carried out by FCRI for BARC, Southern
Pressure Casting Ltd. etc. and the developmental outcome has been shared and is used by these industries for
commercial/industrial process plant operation.
28.2     New R&D works being carried out by American companies like General Motors, General Electric Co. etc., in
their R&D Cells at Bangalore are being offloaded to FCRI for advanced engineering data generation/modelling
simulation for automotive sector. Several agencies have authorized FCRI as a certifying agency for flow control devices
also for pertinent R&D programmes. Many of these activities were earlier being referred to laboratories abroad.
28.3     The Committee recommends that both the R&D projects namely Coal Gassification Project and FCRI
must be supported till they achieve commercial viability.
29.0     TECHNOLOGICAL CONSTRAINTS BEFORE PSEs
29.1     The Committee appreciates that PSEs face difficulties due to low technological profile, obsolete plants, and swift
changes in product/processes ushered in by a fast globalizing economy. The Committee has held detailed consultations
with major players, resources, agencies, Government Departments and stakeholders in technology upgradation in capital
goods sector.
29.2     The Committee recognizes that with the technology progressing at an unprecedented pace, the technology life
cycle has become shorter and industries around the world are under pressure to develop newer technology to stay ahead
of the competition. The local market in developing countries have become easier to access by foreign competitors while
their competitiveness may not be strong enough to enter the international market. Consequently, development and
commercialization of new technologies has become an activity of focal attention and a force to reckon with.
29.3     With the globalization of the Indian economy the MNCs/Proprietary Technology holders now have direct access
to the Indian market. In many cases, they are unwilling to transfer the high and critical technology to Indian partners, as
they do not perceive a commercial advantage or incentive to do so. Even the existing manufacturers having foreign
collaboration or equity participation in the capital goods sector like machine tools, textile machinery, industrial
machinery, power plant equipment, etc. are finding it extremely difficult to get the contemporary technology in these
fields.
29.4     The Committee observed that the fast pace of technology developments and obsolescence has left very little
choice on technology front for developing countries like India. The Committee, therefore, desires that the Government
should ensure the development and commercialisation of new technologies. The Government should come out with a
policy providing for technology upgradation in general and the PSEs in particular.
30.0     STATE OF TECHNOLOGY IN THE PSEs
30.1     The Committee recognizes that in the past India has been predominantly a technology follower and limited
focused attention has been given for development of a strong R&D base in the country. The poor expenditure on R&D
by the domestic industry is often due to lack of resources. The R&D expenditure as percentage of turnover in 2002-03
was only 0.1% for all PSEs, 1% for the PSEs in the Department of Heavy Industry as compared to the global average of
3-5%.

169th Report of Committee on Industry

30.2     Most of the existing manufacturers in the capital goods sector like machine tools, textile machinery, industrial
machinery do not have a viable basic R&D set up to develop a product from design board to commercialization, mainly
due to their smaller sizes and limited budget. Most of the R&D units in these companies operate only as an adjunct to
the manufacturing facilities and merely act as a product testing/improvement department. Majority of them do not have
separate R&D budget and they are wholly dependent on the transfer of technology from their collaborator, where they
have collaboration agreement or import of drawing/design.
30.3     The Committee acknowledges that until and unless the economic size of the manufacturing company is
increased and their production crosses the specific threshold in terms of global volume, there may not be any possibility
of having viable research and development or influence on foreign technology suppliers to jointly develop technology
for such products as may be required in India or for export. This is particularly applicable to PSEs after liberalization.
31.0     TECHNOLOGICAL UPGRADATION OF PSEs
31.1     The Committee was informed that a new budget head with a token provision of Rs. 1 crore has been created for
overall restructuring/revival of PSEs under DHI. Funds would be separately sought for by individual PSEs whenever a
revival plan is approved by the competent authority. So far as present allocations are concerned, the budgetary support
is provided for minor renewals/replacements, de-bottlenecking and new machinery where the requirements are of
emergent nature.
31.2     The Committee takes serious note of the fact that the budgetary allocations do not sufficiently reflect the concern
for technological upgradation of PSEs and R&D which has direct bearing over the efficacy of the companies keeping in
view that PSEs were established as pioneers in industrial technology. The Committee feels that the Government should
actively involve in the technological upgradation of PSEs and if necessary extend the financial support.
31.3     The Committee is of the view that the Department has still not prepared a detailed strategy for the reconstruction
of PSEs including their technological upgradation. Allocations for revival are still ad-hoc in nature for immediate
purposes.
31.4     The Committee recommends that regular technology audit must be conducted by agencies like DSIR or other
resource agencies to assess the technology update of the PSEs.
32.0     JOINT VENTURES OR TECHNOLOGICAL ALLIANCE TO BRING ABOUT A TECHNOLOGICAL
REVIVAL OF THE PSES
32.1     The Committee was informed that with liberalization of the FDIs, there is no compulsory requirement for the
foreign partner to have a domestic partner. As such the global technology leaders have direct access to the Indian market
and do not need technical collaboration agreements with Indian companies. In recent years, the foreign companies have
been securing large contracts in India.
32.2     The Committee notes that the Chinese model, where the technology transfer to a domestic manufacturer is
mandatory for an MNC to get an order in that country, could be an effective policy in facilitating technology transfer.
China is successfully leveraging its market access to foreign manufacturers, to acquire technology and ensure that a
significant share of the equipment of strategic economic importance is manufactured locally in China. Similarly, the
Bhoomiputra policy of Malaysia has been evolved within the WTO framework to ensure technology transfer in
manufacturing industry and a similar approach would improve the access for the latest technology for the Indian
industry.
32.3     The Committee would like to have the view from Government that in order to bring about the technological
revival of the PSEs one of the important issues is, if the foreign companies securing large contracts in India, could be
obliged to associate competent local companies for technology transfer, as is the policy in some other developing
countries such as China and Malaysia.
32.4     The Committee further suggests that in order to ensure that the PSEs gain from technology alliances, it is
necessary that strong learning capabilities are built up to facilitate skill acquisition, internal training. The receptivity in
the PSEs also would have to be built up to accumulate, retain and transfer of knowledge to take the full advantage of the
Joint Ventures or any other technological alliance.
33.0     MAKING INDIA THE HUB FOR MANUFACTURING OUTSOURCING
33.1     The Committee notes that many fast-growing economies have recorded a much higher growth in manufacturing
than the other sectors. It gives India an opportunity to emerge as the hub for manufacturing outsourcing.
33.2     The Committee recommends that the PSEs could be effectively used for the creation of infrastructure and
promotion of skills to capitalize on our competitive advantage.
34.0     POLICY INITIATIVES TO FACILITATE TECHNOLOGY TRANSFER TO CAPITAL GOODS
SECTOR
34.1     The Committee recommends that the Government should consider the following policy initiatives to facilitate

technology transfer to capital goods sector :
            (i)         Issue suitable technology transfer policy guidelines so that for all capital goods and services any foreign
vendor desirous of supplying the same in the domestic Indian market must necessarily source at least 30% of the
proposed bid from local companies within India. Moreover, the foreign vendor must also give an option for transferring
technology to the desirous and capable local company for critical equipment and service involved in the project/product.
            (ii)        Enhance bilateral/multilateral co-operation with developed countries for state-of-art technology transfer
and exchange of technical experts in the areas of emerging technologies.
            (iii)       While granting FDI approval for trading/sale service, wherever there is a provision for setting up a
manufacturing facility in due course with adequate investment, a clause should be incorporated and implementation
monitored meticulously for materialization of such investment on a time bound basis.
35.       MAIN ELEMENTS OF RESTRUCTURING PLANS OF THE PSEs
35.1     The Committee observes that so far the restructuring is confined to manpower rationalisation and book clearing.
Committee feels that such a limited restructuring is not sustainable.
35.2     The Committee was informed that in the policy regime of disinvestment of the non-strategic public sector
undertakings pursued in the past, only partial capital restructuring was undertaken to a point of viability so as to make
them attractive for the private entrepreneur. While the new policy environment exhorts to comprehensively modernize
and restructure sick PSEs on a sustainable basis, which necessarily involves being competitive in the globalized
economy.
35.3     The Committee observes that the restructuring exercise should now involve a major strategic repositioning of the
company's competitive focus so as to enhance its value and to strengthen it adequately to compete effectively by
improving its resilience and the earning potential. The Committee recommends that the companies must re-align with
the market, identify and create niche in the market. This will require comprehensive marketing strategy, techno-value
addition of products-profile and diversification of market.
35.4     The Committee observes that the revival effort should aim to optimally allocate resources to ensure the
increasing returns over the long run by improvement in the innovation and implementation capacity and increasing its
reserve capacity to meet the challenges of the market driven globalized economy.
36.0     SUGGESTED STEPS FOR REVIVAL
36.1     The Committee recommends that the objective of the restructuring effort should be :
            (i)         Improvement in the innovation ability of the PSEs by : strengthening the R&D and technology
management and absorption.
            (ii)        Improvement in implementation capacity by : improving the management knowledge and skills,
marketing skills, product quality, and technology familiarity.
            (iii)       Reduction in the vulnerability by improving liquidity and cash flow coverage.
36.2     Furthermore, the restructuring exercise should include :
            (i)         Operational restructuring by modifying production process by bringing economies of scale, improving
the level of the quality and improvement in the process technology. Technological upgradation to target the high-end
market.
            (ii)        Marketing restructuring by repositioning and diversifying the marketing and the distribution channels.
            (iii)       Financial and capital restructuring to increase earning power of the company that may entail increased
reserve capacity, bankability and ability to generate extra-budgetary resources.
            (iv)       Organizational restructuring to motivate performance and formulate a long-term objectives in
accordance with the projected trends of market.
36.3     The Committee would like to know the comments and the concrete, tangible action taken or to be taken by the
Department on these steps.
37.0     INTERACTIONS WITH PSEs
37.1     In the course of discussing the Demands for Grants for 2005-06, the Committee interacted with six PSEs under
Department of Heavy Industry.
38.0     HEAVY ENGINEERING CORPORATION LTD.
38.1     The Committee was informed that the company's production and productivity indices have shown rise in recent
times. Company has been able to liquidate the statutory dues towards its employees with the funds provided by the
Government and the working capital situation has also eased with the additional cash credit from bank. The Committee
was informed of the steps taken to reduce the overhead expenditures.
38.2     Despite decision by the BIFR, a prolonged uncertainty on revival has resulted in immense cost in terms of
finances and investments in the company. The Committee, however, notes that despite uncertainties pending final

decision on the revival, the company expects major orders from Steel, Railways, Defence, Coal and Mining Sectors.
38.3     The Committee notes that the Jharkhand Government has refused the proposal to convert the assets into
resources. The Committee takes serious note of the clear disjoint in the policies of Central and State Governments that
has seriously affected the prospects of the company.
38.4     The Committee directs the DHI to take up the issue to removing bottlenecks with the Government of Jharkhand
and inform the Committee of the outcome.
39.0     BHARAT YANTRA NIGAM LTD.
39.1     BYNL is the holding Company with six subsidiaries namely : Bharat Heavy Plate & Vessels (BHPV), Vizag;
Bharat Pump & Compressors Ltd. (BPCL), Naini; Bridge & Roof Co. (I) (B&R), Kolkata; Richardson & Cuddas
(R&C), Mumbai; Triveni Structures Ltd. (TSL), Naini and Tungabhadra Steel Products Ltd. (TSPL).
39.2     The Committee notes the diverse range of business in which Subsidiaries of the BYNL are involved. The
Committee also notes despite repeated recommendations by this Committee and other expert studies to merge the
subsidiary Companies into single entity; no initiative has been taken in this respect. The Committee would like to know
the view of the Government in this respect.
39.3     The Committee also notes that of the seven Companies, five have been referred to BIFR. Of the seven
companies only Bridge & Roof is earning profit. Appeals against BIFR's decision in respect of R&C and TSL are
pending before AAIFR. The Committee also notes that the Companies under the BYNL group are being placed before
BRPSE in phases. The Committee hopes that BRPSE would expedite the matter.
39.4     The Committee notes that accumulated loss of BYNL during 2003-04 was Rs. 1001.50 crores. The Company
with a paid-up capital of Rs. 186 crores has had a negative net worth to the tune of Rs. 838.36 crores in 2003-04. The
Committee directs the DHI to apprise the Committee of its course of action.
39.5     The Committee notes with grave concern that the financial parameters of the holding Company and five of its
subsidiaries are dismal. The Companies that have been referred to BIFR are still waiting for revival or otherwise.
40.0     PRAGA TOOLS LTD.
40.1     The Committee was informed of the improvement in the turnover and order book position of the Company.
However, the net worth of the Company still remained negative. The Company still has huge liabilities. Company is
facing stiff competition from private players with better technology and low overhead costs. Company's market share
has also been effected by the delays in deliveries due to capital shortage and structural and technological constraints.
The Company still faces heavy interest burden and shortage of working capital.
40.2     The Committee notes that BIFR had sought finalisation of the revival plan of the Company by April, 2004.
However, the revival plan was reviewed by the BRPSE only in March, 2005, after a delay of good one year. After
approval of BRPSE, the revival plan is now under the consideration of Cabinet. The revival entails an expenditure of
Rs. 253.37 crores on the part of the Government including waiver of previous liabilities and infusion of fresh funds.
40.3     The Committee notes that the Company's productivity and profitability suffers from old machinery
causing frequent breakdowns and high rate of rejections. The Committee, accordingly, recommends for urgent
upgradation of technology and machines and hopes that the revival plan would take care of this aspect.
41.0     TYRE CORPORATION OF INDIA LTD.
41.1     The Committee takes note of the proposed revival scheme of the Company. Already the Tangra unit of the
Company has been sold and a one-time settlement with the consortium of banks been finalised. The Company has also
implemented its manpower rationalisation plan.
41.2     The Committee also notes that in view of growing auto market in the country, the Company with the
implementation of revival scheme can regain its profitability on a sustained basis. However, the Company faces stiff
competition from the tyre majors and growing trend towards radial tyres.
41.3     The Committee notes that the Company lacks marketing infrastructure in a competitive market and has been
dependent largely on job-works from major Companies. The Company has been trying for Joint Venture, that is crucial
for its long term profitability.
41.4     The Committee recommends to the DHI to assess the profitability prospects of TCIL and if satisfied, assist
the Company in regaining its financial viability.
42.0     RAJASTHAN ELECTRONICS AND INSTRUMENTS LTD.
42.1     The Committee notes that Company was of vital importance for the growth of non-conventional energy in the
country. The Committee appreciated the financial performance of the Company. However, considering the massive
energy needs of the country, the non-conventional energy sector has not been able to achieve the economies of scales,
thereby its per-unit cost is comparatively higher.
42.2     The Company is likely to face competition with major players entering the high end market with better

technology. The Company is dependent on its competitors for Solar Cells.
42.3     The Committee was informed that the Company proposes to undertake major diversification projects in respect
of Wind Turbine Generator and SPV Cell manufacturing, for which it needs sufficient funds.
42.4     The Committee recommends that Government must support the Company's resource and technology
requirements to harness the potential of non-conventional energy in the country. The Committee is of the view that the
Government must help this sector in attaining the economies of scales. The non-conventional energy will be
economically feasible for the community-based consumption in obscure villages and remote areas where the cost of

43.0     BHARAT HEAVY ELECTRICALS LTD.
43.1     The Committee appreciates the financial performance of the BHEL which is a Nav Ratna Company. The
Committee also appreciates the Company's efforts to become a prominent global player.
43.2     However, the Company has been facing constraints in acquiring technology and uneven competition in the
domestic as well as global market due to certain structural constraints.
43.3     The Committee notes that though initially the Government acquired technologies from Companies in the UK,
USSR and Czechoslovakia for BHEL. Over the years, BHEL has successfully absorbed these technologies and
continually upgraded its technology to contemporary levels through a judicious mix of in-house development and
technology acquisition. A high level of self-reliance with respect to power equipment has thus been achieved in India,
with full support from the Government.
43.4     BHEL is most competitive in its product line within the country and in several export markets. Indian Utilities
have significantly gained in this process by setting up power plants most cost effectively. BHEL has also fully supported
the utilities with spares and services over the entire lifetime of the plants. However, some of the collaborators of BHEL
have now become competitors in an open domestic market. In the last few years, leading power plant equipment
manufacturers in the world have been consolidating through mergers and acquisitions, thereby enabling them to increase
their product offerings and earmarking higher R&D funds to develop technologically advanced products. Indian
manufacturers are not in a position to deploy the enormous resources required to keep abreast to the latest
advancements.
43.5     Further, potential customers are also generally risk-averse and are hesitant to try new products. Technology
transfers from foreign companies will, therefore, continue to play an important role.
43.6     Indian customers are now planning to introduce advanced power plants and transmission systems. While inviting
tenders, customers usually specify qualification requirements such as two years' operating experience and at least two
units of similar advanced systems at two different locations. Indian manufacturers do not qualify due to lack of
operating experience, even when they have already developed, or are in a position to develop the new products and/or
have technology support from OEMs through an ongoing collaboration agreement.
43.7     At present, foreign companies that are technically qualified can participate in tenders and secure orders, on their
own, without any obligation to transfer technology to an Indian Company. Indian manu-facturers are, therefore, finding
it difficult to source technology from foreign Original Equipment Manufacturers (OEMs).
43.8     This is leading to a situation where certain foreign licensees of OEMs, having their own qualifying references,
may secure orders from Indian customers; whereas, an Indian manufacturer, though having technology support from
OEM and own capability to design and manufacture the equipment, is prevented from even competing in the tender.
43.9     In this scenario, our self-reliance, painstakingly developed over the last few decades, could get eroded.
Therefore, a conscious attempt, at the policy level, needs to be considered to ensure that in selected areas of strategic
economic interest, having a multiplier effect on the Indian economy, a policy of self-reliance is pursued vigorously, so
that foreign OEMs are obliged to share technology with Indian manufacturers especially where the large Indian market
is leveraged for this purpose.
43.10   The Committee recommends that constraints faced by BHEL, need to be addressed by the Government
with a favourable view to support this flag-ship company that is financially self-reliant but facing uneven
competition due to the policy structure.
44.0     MULTIPLICITY AND DUPLICATION IN BUDGETARY SCHEME
44.1     The Committee observes that the Budgetary scheme and explanatory notes on expenditures do not give sufficient
explanation/details of the allocations. There is always a possibility of duplication of expenditures through multiple
Head. The test criterion of the budget is clarity and transparency instead of ambiguity. The objective of the
parliamentary scrutiny of budget is to know efficacy of the objective and efficiency of expenditure to achieve the
objective. Expenditures are split into classes and sub-classes, thereby preventing a clearer picture of expenditure for a

169th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/169threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:53:32]
particular objective. The Committee would also like to know the rational necessity and objective criteria of the
classification of diverse expenditures under one category and Budget Head instead of the details of allocations. The
Committee feels that the DHI should take up these issues for consultation with the Ministry of Finance.
45.0     NO TANGIBLE LONG TERM OBJECTIVES SET BY DHI FOR ITS PSEs
45.1     The Committee notes that DHI was unable to commit on firm and tangible long-term objectives in quantitative
terms that could be a benchmark against which the performance is assessed. On most of the long-term issues
Department's reply has been elusive. The Committee observed that despite huge financial liabilities all the major
decisions are still left to BRPSE. Pending its recommendations being approved by the competent authority, the
Department is taking measures that are ad-hoc window-dressing of depleted worth of PSEs. The Committee is of the
opinion that scarce resources cannot be lost endlessly amidst huge liabilities of PSEs. A lasting solution has to be found
urgently and accountability must be accordingly fixed for which it is necessary to determine the benchmarks of
performance.
45.2     The Committee recommends that the Department should formulate a road map for the consideration of
Government on the major challenges faced by PSEs like obsolete technology and lack of marketing strategy. The
Committee also suggests to take into account the cumulative cost of delay, previously due to pendency of cases under
BIFR regime and now under BRPSE in finalizing a decision on PSEs.
45.3     The Committee observes that the multiplicity of agencies involved had led to inefficient delays in finalizing
revival. The Committee is of the view that steps must be taken to reduce multiplicity of agencies in preparing, assessing
and revival proposals.
45.4     DHI has the mandate to promote the development and growth of capital goods and engineering industry in the
country, which in turn has critical bearing over the infrastructure development in the country. However, plight of the
PSEs urgently requires an expeditious and consistent action by the DHI instead to postponing the decision on
successive series of multiple bodies.
45.5     The Committee notes that while the PSEs in the heavy engineering and capital goods category are facing the
constraints due to lack of orders mainly from Government and competition from foreign companies due to opening up
of domestic market. Heavy wage bill, inability to generate internal resources or extra budgetary resources due to huge
liabilities and previous NPAs, over reliance on the budgetary support even for working capital and also for the orders,
inability to upgrade the product line according to market needs, technological drawbacks, lack of corporate dynamism,
inability to create new niche in the market or locate new market are the major constraints for any sustainable revival of
the PSEs.
45.6     The Committee, therefore, recommends that technological upgradation, upgrading the product line according to
new niche market and identifying new domestic and export markets have to be the cardinal elements for a sustained
viability of the PSEs.
45.7     The Committee observes that there are some cases where a clear disjoint between Central and State Government,
has seriously imperiled the viability of the PSEs. In order to clear the administrative bottlenecks, the Committee
recommends the Government to consider making respective State Governments a significant shareholder in the PSE.
The representative of the State Government can be a member of the Board of Directors as one of the two Government
Directors at present.
45.8     The Committee recommends that certain Companies in capital goods sector are critical for development of
heavy engineering and infrastructure sectors irrespective of their financial condition. These Companies in any case rely
heavily on the Government's investment in huge infrastructure projects. While they can be encouraged to generate their
internal resources through innovative corporate strategies like global tie-ups and JVs. Government must at the same
time support such facilities.
45.9     The Committee would like to suggest to the Government to consider the critical utility of any Company before
deciding on its sustainable and comprehensive revival/restructuring instead of going only by their precarious financial
condition. The criticality will depend on long-term prospects of the Company in terms of technology spin-offs and self-
reliance in mega-machinery in strategic areas.
45.10   The Committee recommends that DHI should apprise it of the Revised Estimates and the Supplementary
Demands.

approved by the Cabinet before approaching the Parliament for Supplementary Demands. The Department must also

(Para 9.6)
            The Committee notes that the expenditures are classified into two parallel categories Capital/Revenue
expenditures and Plan/Non-Plan expenditures. These two parallel categories are curiously hybridized into four
supposedly distinct categories of expenditure. The Committee would like to know the rational principles for such
classifications and sub-classifications, instead of description of expenditure under these categories.      (Para 10.6)
            The Committee is of the view that existing classification heads needs further rationalisation and desires that the
Government should review the same.     (Para 10.7)
            The Commission desires to know that on what ground the Planning Commission's approval was sought for
certain Revenue and Capital expenditures leaving remaining sizable Revenue and Capital expenditures unapproved. If
any guideline is followed in this respect. The Committee would also like to be appraised on such a categorization in the
Budget. The Committee also desires to know if such segregation is scientific and does not affect the efficiency of
expenditure. Further, the Committee would like to have a comment from the Department, if there is need to improve the
Budget scheme.  (Para 10.11)
            The Committee observes that the character and nature of the expenditure is too diverse to be kept under same
sub-category. The Committee is not convinced of the classification of such varied expenditures like R&D projects and
modification of offices being kept under the same category of expenditure as Plan-Revenue Expenditure. Such
classification appears to be unscientific. The Committee would like to have Department's comments on the need for a
more rational classification.                             (Para 11.3)
            The Committee observes enhanced allocations for almost all the PSEs for the renewals/replacements, additions,
modifications etc. However, the Committee notes several allocations are of Rs. 1 lakh. The Committee observes with
concern if any sustainable purpose could be served with such meager Plan Capital allocations, particularly keeping in
view that similar allocations were made the previous year too.     (Para 12.3)
            The Committee recommends the allocations for the renewals/replacements, additions, modifications etc. should
be judicious and should be justified by the objectives it is likely to achieve. Allocations should not be for mere token
symbolism as it may amount to blocking scarce resources, which the country can only ill-afford. The Committee was
informed that such allocations were necessary for the technical requirements of budgetary process. The Committee feels
that such small amount obscures the entire scope and scenario of prospective expenditure. The Department may avoid
blocking such amount in future.            (Para 12.4)
            The Committee observes that there is a multiplicity of allocations for similar purposes. Apart from allocation for
Plan Capital expenditure to individual PSEs, there are allocations for crucial balancing, for
addition/modification/replacement and for restructuring the PSEs. Also Rs. 150 crores is allocated as lump-sum Non-
Plan Capital expenditure for the revival of the PSE.            (Para 12.7)
            The Committee would like to know if there is any significant qualitative difference between these categories of
expenditures for which distinct allocations are made. If not, Government should find out the way how this multiplicity
could be avoided, even if by clubbing such allocations together.                           (Para 12.8)
            The Committee further observes that there are too many lump-sum allocations for Plan-Capital expenditure that
have not been sufficiently elaborated. The Committee has been further informed that these allocations are liable to be
raised at the subsequent stages. The Committee shall be apprised if such unexplained expenditure that cannot be
estimated, could at all be Planned-Capital expenditure.    (Para 12.9)
            The Committee recommends that the lump-sum expenditures should be sufficiently elaborated for Parliamentary
approval in future.         (Para 12.10)
            The Committee is in agreement with the allocation made in respect of specific project with BEML. The
Committee would however, like to know the terms of agreement, if any.      (Para 13.3)
            The Department has closely associated with the promotion of Automobile R&D facility in the country. However,
a significant Grant-in-Aid of Rs. 25 crores to R&D institution is still treated as a Non-Plan Revenue expenditure along
with Secretariat expenditure and Interest subsidy. 
The Committee observes that the character of expenditure is too diverse to be kept under similar category.        (Para
14.2)
            The Committee notes with grave concern that out of the total allocations of Rs. 861.32 crores, more than Rs. 400
crores are lump-sum allocations. Last year too similar allocation of Rs. 400 crores was made. Such a practice
undermines the principle of Parliamentary scrutiny of Budget.                                         (Para 15.4)
            The Committee takes serious note that against the total investment of Rs. 8590 crores and projected outturn of
